# Chapter Three

## Fear Becomes Judgment

By sunrise, the roads surrounding House Darkheart were no longer empty.

Scouts returned mud-soaked and sleepless, carrying reports from every direction. Columns of soldiers had been sighted beyond the eastern ridge. Siege wagons moved through the southern valleys. Northern banners had crossed the river before dawn, and riders from the west had begun seizing villages to establish supply lines.

Twelve kingdoms had not yet formed a true alliance.

They did not trust one another enough for that.

But fear had given them something almost as dangerous.

A shared destination.

Castle Darkheart.

The fortress woke beneath the sound of preparation.

Blacksmiths worked without rest. Arrowheads piled beside the walls. Witches renewed ancient defenses carved into stone generations earlier. Soldiers dragged barrels of oil toward murder holes and reinforced gates already thick enough to survive rams. Messengers rode through the inner city calling every reserve banner back to the capital.

House Darkheart had survived wars before.

This felt different.

No one could say whether the armies came for conquest, survival, religious terror, or simple panic.

Most did not care.

They were coming.

That was enough.

King Victor Darkheart stood over the war table in silence.

Wooden markers surrounded the carved representation of his kingdom.

Too many.

Captain Vale remained across from him while generals argued over roads, troop strength, and which kingdom would likely strike first.

Victor barely heard them.

The prophecy remained inside his head.

Not all of it.

One line.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

He had repeated it so many times through the night that the words no longer sounded like language.

They had become fear.

“Your Majesty?”

Victor looked up.

The High Marshal was waiting.

“Say it again.”

“The southern coalition is moving fastest. If they continue at their current pace, their advance force reaches our border settlements by tomorrow night.”

“And the east?”

“Two days.”

“The north?”

“Difficult terrain. Perhaps three.”

Victor nodded.

“Evacuate the villages closest to the border.”

The marshal hesitated. “Into the capital?”

“Into the fortified interior. Leave nothing useful behind.”

“Food stores?”

“Take what we can. Burn what we cannot.”

Several generals exchanged looks.

Victor saw them.

“Do you have a better way to feed an invading army?”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“Then carry out the order.”

The marshal bowed.

Victor placed both hands upon the table.

“Every gate closes by sundown. No foreign traveler enters after that. No merchant leaves with military information. Double the watch around the western tunnels and place witches at every old passage beneath the castle.”

Captain Vale glanced toward him.

“The nursery as well?”

The room went quiet.

Victor’s eyes moved to him.

“Especially the nursery.”

One of the generals shifted uneasily.

“Protection for the prince?”

Victor answered too slowly.

“Yes.”

The word came without warmth.

Captain Vale heard it.

No one else challenged the king.

The orders continued.

But the nursery remained in Victor’s thoughts.

Not because he feared someone would reach Zee before House Darkheart could protect him.

Because he had begun to fear what would happen if no one ever could.

—

Queen Aurelia refused to remain in bed.

The physicians protested.

She ignored them.

By midday, she sat in the royal nursery wrapped in a heavy black robe, Zee cradled against her chest while the crimson hatchling slept near her feet.

The newborn dragon had eaten poorly.

No one knew what to feed him.

The kitchens tried raw meat, cooked meat, milk, blood, fish, and even crushed gemstone offered by a terrified servant who claimed dragons ate treasure.

The hatchling rejected nearly everything until Zee began crying from hunger.

The sound changed him.

His little head lifted.

A simple feeling moved across the strange connection between them.

Hunger.

Not his.

Zee’s.

The hatchling climbed clumsily toward the queen and nudged her arm.

Aurelia stared.

“You know.”

The hatchling chirped.

She did not understand the bond.

She only understood what she saw.

He knew Zee needed something.

Aurelia fed her son.

The hatchling settled again.

When Zee relaxed, so did he.

Aurelia smiled faintly.

“There is more sense between the two of you than in half the royal court.”

The door opened.

Victor entered.

He had not changed clothes since the previous night.

Aurelia’s smile faded.

“You look terrible.”

“I have twelve kingdoms marching toward my walls.”

“You had twelve kingdoms marching toward your walls yesterday.”

“Yesterday they were threatening.”

“And now?”

“They are moving siege equipment.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child slept peacefully.

“Because of him.”

Victor said nothing.

Aurelia studied his face.

Something had changed.

Not suddenly.

But undeniably.

“You have not touched him since last night.”

Victor looked toward the cradle.

The hatchling opened its eyes.

A low warning sound rolled from its tiny chest.

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“That creature does that every time I enter.”

“It does it when armed men enter.”

“I am always armed.”

“Perhaps that is the problem.”

Victor nearly smiled.

He did not.

Aurelia noticed.

“What did you find beneath the castle?”

He remained silent.

“Victor.”

“The burial keeper found something that should not have been there.”

“What?”

“A prophecy.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“No.”

“You have not heard it.”

“I do not need to hear it.”

Victor stepped closer.

“It spoke of the Blood Rain.”

Aurelia’s fingers tightened around Zee.

“It spoke of wolves losing themselves.”

“Stop.”

“It spoke of three lives within one body.”

“Stop.”

Victor did.

The room fell silent.

Aurelia looked at him with anger now.

“Do not bring old bones into my child’s cradle and call them truth.”

“You think I want this?”

“I think you are frightened.”

“I am.”

“Then say that.”

Victor looked at Zee.

The child stirred.

“Every army outside these walls is frightened too.”

“They do not know him.”

“Neither do we.”

“He is our son.”

“That does not answer what he is.”

Aurelia stood too quickly and winced.

Victor instinctively reached toward her.

She stepped back.

“Do not.”

His hand lowered.

“You held him yesterday,” she said. “You looked at him and saw your child.”

“I still see my child.”

“No. You are trying not to.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“The prophecy says—”

“The prophecy does not feed him.”

“Aurelia.”

“It does not know how he sleeps. It does not know the sound he makes when he is hungry. It does not know that he reaches for you.”

Victor looked away.

That hurt more than she intended.

She continued anyway.

“You want something ancient to tell you who your son is because you are afraid to learn for yourself.”

Victor’s voice lowered.

“You did not hear the final line.”

“I do not care.”

“I do.”

Aurelia’s eyes flashed.

“That is what frightens me.”

The hatchling rose between them.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered along his crimson scales.

He did not understand the argument.

He understood fear.

Zee felt it through him.

The newborn’s Crimson Mana stirred.

The lamps flickered.

Victor stepped back.

Not because the mana threatened him.

Because the movement confirmed something inside him.

Even as an infant, Zee responded.

Adapted.

Reacted.

The prophecy whispered again.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

Victor looked at the crimson glow around his son.

For the first time, he wondered whether love itself might be another blade.

And whether mercy could become the cruelty that doomed them all.

—

That evening, the first foreign campfires became visible from Castle Darkheart.

Hundreds at first.

Then thousands.

They burned along the distant plains like a second constellation beneath the horizon.

Citizens gathered along the inner walls to watch.

No one celebrated.

No one panicked openly either.

House Darkheart had survived too much for that.

But fear moved through the capital in quiet ways.

Shops closed early.

Parents kept children indoors.

Shrines filled with offerings.

Old swords were pulled from family chests.

Witches prepared healing rooms in temples and military halls.

Rumors multiplied faster than soldiers.

Some said the prince had been born drinking blood.

Others claimed he had transformed into a wolf before his first breath.

One story insisted the dragon hatchling had bowed to him.

Another said every vampire in the east now carried Zee’s heartbeat.

None were true.

That did not matter.

Fear rarely waited for truth.

Within the war chamber, Victor listened as Captain Vale read the newest demands.

“Three kingdoms still request surrender.”

“Request?”

“Demand.”

“Then call it what it is.”

Captain Vale continued.

“Four demand execution witnessed by neutral envoys.”

Victor’s face did not change.

“Neutral.”

“Yes.”

“There are no neutral crowns left.”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“And the others?”

“Two demand the queen and child be removed from the royal line.”

Victor’s hand tightened.

“On what authority?”

“None that House Darkheart recognizes.”

“The remaining three?”

Captain Vale paused.

“They have stopped sending demands.”

Victor looked up.

“Why?”

“They are preparing to attack.”

The council went silent.

Victor walked toward the window.

From there he could see faint fires beyond the hills.

“Twelve kingdoms,” he said.

Captain Vale nodded.

“Against one newborn.”

“No.”

Victor turned.

“Against House Darkheart.”

Several nobles exchanged relieved looks.

It sounded like pride.

Sovereignty.

Defiance.

The king they understood.

Then Victor added, “And they will not decide his fate.”

The room changed.

Captain Vale heard the difference immediately.

Victor no longer said they would not kill Zee.

He said they would not decide.

That distinction was becoming larger every hour.

—

Later that night, Victor returned alone to the burial chamber.

The broken bone remained where it had split.

He had ordered no one to touch it.

The chamber smelled colder now.

He knelt and gathered the pieces.

No voice spoke.

No new words appeared.

The prophecy had given what it intended to give.

Nothing more.

Victor stared at the fragments.

“What are you?”

Silence.

“What does he become?”

Nothing answered.

Victor laughed once.

There was no humor in it.

“You tell me enough to fear him and not enough to know why.”

He looked toward the ceiling as though he could see through stone into the nursery above.

“My son.”

The words nearly broke him.

He closed his eyes.

He remembered Zee’s hand around his finger.

The small weight against his chest.

Aurelia’s smile.

Then he imagined the armies outside the walls multiplied a hundred times.

A thousand.

He imagined every kingdom someday falling.

Not because the prophecy promised it.

Because Victor’s fear supplied the rest.

That was how the prophecy began winning.

Not by revealing the future.

By forcing a frightened man to imagine one.

Victor opened his eyes.

“If they attack him...”

The line returned.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

His breathing slowed.

The problem was no longer only that Zee might survive an attempt on his life.

The problem was what survival might do to him.

Victor began to think like a king confronting an enemy.

Quietly.

Methodically.

Terribly.

He could not allow foreign rulers to test the prophecy.

He could not allow witches, vampires, wolves, or armies to discover whether hurting Zee truly made him harder to destroy.

He could not allow anyone else to control the experiment.

The thought arrived so naturally that Victor did not recognize how far he had fallen until it was already complete.

*If the prophecy must be tested...*

His stomach turned.

He stood abruptly.

“No.”

The word echoed through the chamber.

For several breaths, he fought himself.

Then he whispered,

“Not yet.”

That was worse.

—

In the nursery above, Zee woke.

No sound had reached him.

No spell touched the room.

Yet discomfort spread through his small body.

The crimson hatchling opened his eyes at the same moment.

Danger.

Not a place.

Not a face.

Only the instinctive feeling of something wrong.

The hatchling crawled closer.

Zee’s tiny hand found his scales.

Safe.

The feeling passed between them.

Small.

Simple.

Desperate.

Outside the nursery, two additional guards arrived under direct royal order.

Then two more.

By midnight, no one could enter the corridor without Victor’s permission.

Aurelia believed the king had increased protection because foreign armies were approaching.

She slept beside her son without knowing the truth.

Victor was not only keeping the world away from Zee.

He was beginning to keep Zee where he could control him.

By the end of the night, the child in Victor’s mind had become two things at once.

His son.

And the prophecy wearing his son’s face.

# Chapter Four

## The First Decision

The first arrow landed before dawn.

It struck the outer wall of Castle Darkheart and shattered against stone.

No soldier died.

No gate broke.

But the message tied beneath the arrow survived.

Captain Vale carried it personally to the throne room.

King Victor read it once.

Then again.

Queen Aurelia stood several paces away, Zee in her arms.

The crimson hatchling rested against her side beneath the folds of a heavy cloak, hidden from the growing number of foreign eyes beyond the walls.

Victor handed the message to no one.

Aurelia watched his face.

“What does it say?”

He folded the parchment.

“Nothing new.”

“Then read it.”

Victor looked at her.

Aurelia did not move.

Finally he spoke.

“They demand Zee be brought beyond the eastern gate before midday.”

“And if we refuse?”

“They begin the siege.”

The queen’s expression turned cold.

“Then let them begin.”

Several ministers shifted uneasily.

Victor said nothing.

Aurelia looked toward the assembled council.

“You heard me.”

The High Marshal lowered his head.

“My Queen.”

“We do not surrender children to armies.”

“No,” Victor said.

Every eye turned toward him.

He stepped down from the throne.

“We do not.”

Aurelia studied him carefully.

For one moment, she heard the man from before the prophecy.

Then Victor continued.

“Not because they are wrong to fear him.”

The room chilled.

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“Victor.”

“But because no foreign crown decides what happens inside House Darkheart.”

The distinction was unmistakable now.

The council heard it.

Captain Vale heard it.

Aurelia heard it most of all.

“You speak of our son as though he were property.”

“I speak as a king.”

“You used to speak as his father.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“This is not the place.”

“No. The place was our nursery, and you stopped speaking there too.”

The hatchling stirred beneath her cloak.

Zee’s Crimson Mana brightened faintly.

Victor noticed.

Of course he noticed.

Now he noticed everything.

Every flicker.

Every change in Zee’s breathing.

Every strange movement of the dragon beside him.

He collected details as if building a case against his own child.

Aurelia saw that too.

Fear turned slowly into anger.

“You will not touch him.”

The council went completely silent.

Victor’s eyes met hers.

“I have not said I would.”

“You no longer need to.”

Before he could answer, the fortress shook.

A deep impact thundered against the eastern wall.

Then another.

Siege stones.

The war had begun.

—

The first assault lasted three hours.

House Darkheart’s witches stood upon the battlements and cast through carved defensive channels built into the ancient walls. Violet force struck ladders from stone. Blue-white frost from enchanted siege wards froze ropes and shattered wooden towers. Green fire spilled across an advancing ram.

None of it carried Crimson Mana.

That belonged to Zee alone.

Darkheart soldiers filled the air with arrows.

Boiling oil rained from murder holes.

Foreign troops screamed beneath the walls while their kings remained safely beyond range.

The castle held.

But House Darkheart paid for it.

By midday, bodies filled the eastern courtyard.

Some belonged to invaders.

Many did not.

A healer died with both hands inside a soldier’s open abdomen.

A tower collapsed after repeated strikes and buried seventeen archers.

A captain Victor had known since boyhood bled out against the inner gate.

War did what fear always promised.

It made everything simpler by making everything worse.

Victor walked among the dead.

Blood covered his boots.

A young soldier grabbed his cloak.

“My King.”

Victor crouched.

The soldier could not have been older than eighteen.

“Did we hold?”

“Yes.”

The boy smiled.

Then died.

Victor remained there for several seconds.

Behind him, another siege stone struck the wall.

The prophecy whispered.

*The world shall break before it teaches him how to die.*

Victor looked toward the castle tower where Zee slept.

For the first time, resentment entered his fear.

Not hatred of the child.

Hatred of what followed him.

That distinction would not survive forever.

—

In the nursery, Aurelia heard the war through stone.

Every impact made dust fall from the ceiling.

Every horn sent the crimson hatchling into alert stillness.

Zee had begun crying.

Not loudly.

But enough to make Aurelia’s heart ache.

She held him close.

“I know.”

Another strike shook the room.

“I know.”

The hatchling crawled into her lap and pressed his head against Zee.

Fear moved between them.

Then comfort.

Their strange link did not give either child knowledge.

Only presence.

Neither was alone.

The eldest royal witch entered with blood across her sleeve.

Aurelia looked up.

“Are the walls holding?”

“For now.”

“How many dead?”

The witch hesitated.

“Too many.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

The woman approached Zee.

Crimson Mana drifted around him more strongly than before.

“His power responds when the castle is struck.”

Aurelia’s eyes opened.

“Do not call it power as if he commands it.”

“I know he does not.”

“Then say what you mean.”

The witch nodded.

“His mana becomes more active when he is distressed.”

Aurelia looked down at him.

“Like any child.”

“Perhaps.”

The uncertainty mattered.

The witch did not pretend to understand.

She had learned better.

Aurelia asked, “What happened to your magic during his birth?”

The woman considered carefully.

“It remained inside me.”

“But?”

“I could not reach it.”

“Because of Zee?”

“I do not know.”

“You felt his mana.”

“Yes.”

“Was it stronger?”

The witch looked toward the infant.

“Overwhelming.”

“That is not the same answer.”

“No.”

Aurelia appreciated the honesty.

The witch continued.

“I have spent my life learning the shape of my own magic. That night, I knew it was still there. I simply could not hear myself beneath him.”

“Beneath my newborn son.”

“Yes.”

Aurelia looked toward the window.

Outside, men were killing one another because everyone believed observation had already become understanding.

It had not.

No one knew what Zee was capable of.

No one knew what he would become.

No one knew whether the Blood Rain had been caused by him, announced him, reacted to him, or merely occurred beside him.

Yet armies had come anyway.

Fear had filled every unanswered question with the worst possible answer.

Aurelia whispered, “Victor is doing the same thing.”

The witch did not respond.

She did not need to.

—

That evening, a second message came beneath a white flag.

The foreign coalition requested a single representative.

Victor allowed one envoy inside the outer gate.

The man entered without armor.

He was elderly, gray-bearded, and exhausted.

Victor met him in the lower audience hall rather than the throne room.

“You have lost thousands today,” the envoy said.

“So have you.”

“We can lose more.”

“So can we.”

The man looked at Victor for a long moment.

“Is that what you want?”

“No.”

“Then end it.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“You know our terms.”

“You have no terms. You have a demand.”

“We have terror.”

“That is not law.”

“No. It is stronger.”

Victor almost drew his sword.

The envoy raised both hands.

“I am not your enemy, Victor.”

“You arrived with an army.”

“I arrived because my king watched blood fall from the sky.”

“So did mine.”

“Wolves slaughtered villages.”

“I know.”

“Witches became helpless.”

“They recovered.”

“Vampires screamed about a heartbeat that was not theirs.”

Victor said nothing.

The envoy stepped closer.

“And every report leads here.”

“To a child.”

“To something no one understands.”

Victor’s eyes sharpened.

“Then perhaps none of you should pretend you know enough to kill him.”

The envoy nodded slowly.

“Perhaps.”

Victor had not expected agreement.

“But perhaps you do not know enough to let him live.”

That landed.

The man saw it.

“You are his father.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“You think I cannot see it?”

The envoy lowered his voice.

“I think you are more frightened than any king outside these walls.”

Victor stared at him.

“Leave.”

“Victor—”

“Leave before your white flag becomes your burial cloth.”

The envoy bowed.

At the door, he stopped.

“If you refuse us, the assault resumes at dawn.”

Victor did not turn.

The door closed.

He remained alone.

More frightened than any king outside these walls.

The insult should have angered him.

Instead, it felt true.

—

That night, Victor summoned Captain Vale.

No council.

No ministers.

No Aurelia.

Only the two of them inside the king’s private chamber.

Victor poured wine but did not drink it.

“How many guards outside the nursery?”

“Eight.”

“Double them.”

Captain Vale hesitated.

“Against what?”

Victor looked at him.

“Everyone.”

“Foreign assassins?”

“Yes.”

“Court factions?”

“Yes.”

Vale waited.

“And the queen?”

Victor said nothing.

The captain’s expression changed.

“My King.”

“No one removes Zee from that wing without my command.”

“Not even Queen Aurelia?”

Victor’s eyes hardened.

“I said no one.”

Vale breathed slowly.

“You understand what that order means.”

“Yes.”

“Do you?”

Victor stepped toward him.

“I will not have twelve kings tear apart my kingdom deciding what should happen to my son.”

“Then what will happen?”

“I decide.”

Vale stared at him.

For years, he had followed Victor through wars without hesitation.

This frightened him more than battle.

“You intend to kill the prince?”

Victor’s face tightened.

“No.”

The answer came immediately.

Too immediately.

Then he looked away.

“Not tonight.”

Captain Vale went still.

Victor heard his own words.

There was no taking them back.

The king walked toward the window.

Far beyond the walls, enemy fires covered the plain.

“If the prophecy is true, attacking him may make him worse.”

“May.”

“Yes.”

“And if it is false?”

Victor looked toward him.

“Then a child dies.”

The words nearly broke whatever remained of the father inside him.

Vale spoke carefully.

“That should matter.”

“It does.”

“Then stop.”

Victor closed his eyes.

He wanted to.

Aurelia’s voice echoed through his memory.

*You held him yesterday.*

He remembered Zee sleeping against him.

His son.

His heir.

Then another siege stone struck the outer wall.

The room trembled.

Victor opened his eyes.

“And if I stop and every kingdom burns because I was too weak to act?”

“You do not know that will happen.”

“I do not know that it will not.”

Vale shook his head.

“That is fear speaking.”

“Yes.”

Victor turned toward him.

“And kings who ignore fear bury kingdoms.”

He walked to a locked cabinet and removed a small iron key.

Captain Vale stared at it.

“What does that open?”

“The old execution chamber beneath the western tower.”

Vale’s face went pale.

Victor placed the key on the table between them.

“I am not ordering his death.”

“Then why prepare the chamber?”

Victor looked at the key.

“Because if I decide the prophecy leaves me no choice... I will not make that decision with twelve foreign armies watching.”

The captain said nothing.

Victor’s voice became colder.

“No foreign king will claim they killed a Darkheart prince.”

“No priest will parade his body.”

“No vampire will take his blood.”

“No witch will dissect what remains.”

“If Zee dies, it will happen inside these walls.”

Vale whispered, “By your hand.”

Victor did not answer.

That was answer enough.

—

Near midnight, Aurelia woke and found Victor standing beside the cradle.

She sat upright.

“What are you doing?”

Victor looked toward her.

“Watching him.”

The crimson hatchling was awake.

His body pressed against Zee.

Teal-and-gold mana trembled faintly across his scales.

Danger.

Zee shifted in his sleep.

Victor reached toward him.

The hatchling hissed.

Aurelia stood.

“Do not.”

Victor stopped.

The distance between his hand and his son was less than an inch.

For several heartbeats, no one moved.

Then Zee opened his crimson eyes.

He saw Victor.

His tiny hand lifted.

The same gesture as before.

An invitation without understanding.

Victor stared at it.

Every part of him that remained a father wanted to take that hand.

He almost did.

Then the prophecy returned.

The dead soldier in the courtyard.

The armies outside.

The Blood Rain.

The wolves.

The impossible heartbeat.

Victor lowered his hand.

Aurelia’s face changed.

She understood.

Not everything.

Enough.

“You decided.”

Victor looked at her.

“I decided nothing.”

“You prepared something.”

His silence betrayed him.

Aurelia moved between him and the cradle.

“If you ever come near him with death in your heart, you will have to go through me.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“You are threatening your king.”

“I am warning my husband.”

The hatchling curled tighter around Zee.

Victor stared at his family.

His wife.

His son.

The impossible dragon who had appeared beside him.

For one brief moment, grief almost conquered fear.

Almost.

Then another war horn sounded beyond the walls.

Victor stepped backward.

“No foreign ruler determines what happens to Zee.”

Aurelia’s voice was quiet.

“And neither does a frightened father.”

Victor left without answering.

He walked through the sleeping castle until he reached the western tower.

Below it, servants had already begun clearing dust from the old execution chamber.

Iron chains were removed from the walls.

A stone table was washed.

Torches were lit.

Victor stood at the top of the stairs and watched.

He had not yet ordered Zee brought there.

He had not yet raised a weapon against him.

He had not yet crossed the final distance between fear and murder.

But he had prepared the place where he might.

Outside, twelve kingdoms waited for Castle Darkheart to surrender the First Tribrid.

Inside, Queen Aurelia held her son and understood that the walls protecting Zee had become another kind of danger.

And before any foreign king could reach the newborn prince, the first man to decide Zee might have to die had already been crowned long before Zee was born.

His father.

# Chapter Five

## The First Attempt

The siege began again before sunrise.

This time, the kingdoms did not test the walls.

They tried to break them.

Three siege engines released at once, hurling stones large enough to crush houses. They struck the eastern battlements with enough force to split ancient masonry and throw soldiers from the walls. Horns answered from every direction. Arrows darkened the pale morning sky. Witches on both sides raised barriers, curses, and counterspells while infantry advanced beneath layered shields.

Castle Darkheart answered with violence of its own.

The Witch Kingdom had been built for war.

Runes buried deep within the fortress stone awakened under the hands of Darkheart battle-witches. Entire sections of wall shimmered beneath defensive magic. Enemy ladders caught fire before touching stone. The ground beneath one advancing battalion cracked open and swallowed horses, soldiers, and siege shields alike.

None of it stopped the next wave.

There were too many kingdoms.

Too many soldiers.

Too much fear.

King Victor stood upon the eastern battlement as arrows struck the barrier before him and burst into splinters.

“Left tower!”

A commander shouted the warning.

Victor turned just as an enemy stone smashed through the upper section of the tower.

Black stone exploded outward.

Men screamed.

A witch vanished beneath falling masonry.

Victor raised one hand and unleashed a violent burst of dark violet force. The largest pieces stopped in midair long enough for several soldiers to escape before crashing into the courtyard below.

“Get the wounded inside!” he ordered.

The High Marshal rushed toward him.

“We cannot hold every wall at this rate.”

“We do not need every wall.”

“My King?”

Victor pointed toward the eastern approach.

“They are attacking where they believe we are strongest.”

The marshal followed his gaze.

Understanding came quickly.

“A distraction.”

“Exactly.”

Victor looked south.

“Send riders to the lower tunnels. If even one foreign soldier enters beneath this castle, collapse the passage with them inside.”

“Yes, Your Majesty.”

The marshal hurried away.

Victor remained on the wall.

Below him, thousands of men were dying.

For Zee.

Because of Zee.

The thought came before Victor could stop it.

He hated himself for thinking it.

Then another soldier beside him screamed as an arrow pierced his throat.

Victor caught the man before he fell.

Blood poured over the king’s hands.

The soldier looked at him desperately.

“My King…”

Victor pressed one hand against the wound and tried to slow the bleeding.

The man died before the nearest healer reached them.

Victor stared at the blood covering his palms.

The prophecy returned.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

Victor looked toward the tower where his son slept.

Something inside him hardened.

Not completely.

Not yet.

But enough.

—

Queen Aurelia had not slept.

She sat beside the nursery window with Zee wrapped tightly against her chest.

The crimson hatchling remained pressed against them both.

Each impact against the walls made the tiny dragon flinch.

Each time he flinched, Zee stirred.

Their link carried only the simplest things between them.

Fear.

Unease.

Warmth.

Near.

Safe.

The hatchling pushed his snout against Zee’s shoulder.

Zee’s fingers closed weakly around one of his small horns.

The dragon calmed.

Aurelia watched them in silence.

“They are trying to kill you,” she whispered.

Zee did not understand the words.

His crimson eyes opened briefly.

Aurelia stroked his cheek.

“And your father is deciding whether to help them.”

The admission hurt more once spoken aloud.

The eldest royal witch stood near the door.

She had volunteered to remain with Aurelia.

Not under Victor’s command.

Under her own.

“My Queen…”

Aurelia looked at her.

“If he orders you to take Zee from me, what will you do?”

The witch did not answer immediately.

That frightened Aurelia.

Finally, the woman said, “I serve House Darkheart.”

“So do I.”

“Yes.”

“And?”

The witch looked toward the child.

“I do not believe fear is enough reason to murder a newborn.”

Aurelia’s shoulders loosened slightly.

“Then you will help me.”

“If it comes to that.”

“It already has.”

The witch lowered her eyes.

Outside, another impact shook the castle.

Dust drifted from the ceiling.

The dragon hatchling growled.

Then every flame in the nursery bent toward Zee.

The witch looked up sharply.

Crimson Mana thickened around the child.

Not violently.

Not consciously.

It simply gathered.

Zee’s breathing changed.

His heartbeat deepened.

The witch took one step backward.

Aurelia noticed.

“What?”

“I do not know.”

“Do not begin guessing.”

“I wasn’t.”

The woman studied Zee carefully.

“Something about him is reacting.”

“To the siege?”

“Perhaps.”

“To fear?”

“Perhaps.”

“To the dragon?”

“Perhaps.”

Aurelia’s jaw tightened.

“You truly know nothing.”

The witch looked at her.

“No.”

Then, after a moment:

“And I am beginning to think that is the only honest answer anyone in this kingdom has.”

—

By midday, the first outer village burned.

Victor watched smoke rise from beyond the walls.

It belonged to farmers who had refused evacuation.

The enemy had taken the settlement without resistance.

Then burned it anyway.

The High Marshal approached.

“They are sending another envoy.”

Victor did not turn.

“Kill him.”

The marshal froze.

Victor closed his eyes.

“No.”

He exhaled.

“Bring him inside.”

The correction came quickly.

But the marshal had heard the first answer.

So had Victor.

The envoy entered the lower audience chamber less than an hour later.

This one was younger.

He wore no crown colors.

Only plain gray cloth and a silver chain marking him as a neutral herald.

Victor laughed when he saw it.

“There are no neutrals left.”

The envoy bowed.

“Then consider me useful instead.”

Victor remained standing.

“What do they want now?”

“The same thing.”

“My son.”

“Yes.”

“Alive?”

The envoy hesitated.

Victor’s expression darkened.

“Answer.”

“Not necessarily.”

Silence filled the chamber.

The envoy continued carefully.

“Some rulers would accept proof of death.”

“And the others?”

“Some want the body.”

Victor’s face changed.

The envoy saw the danger too late.

“Leave.”

“My King—”

“Leave.”

“I was sent to explain—”

Victor crossed the distance between them in three strides and seized the man by the throat.

The guards moved instinctively.

No one interfered.

Victor lifted the envoy from the floor.

“If one foreign hand touches my son’s corpse…”

The words caught in his throat.

His son’s corpse.

He nearly released the man.

Then fear returned.

“If anyone attempts to claim his body as a trophy, relic, weapon, specimen, sacrifice, or prize…”

Victor tightened his grip.

“I will tear apart every kingdom represented outside my walls.”

The envoy clawed weakly at Victor’s hand.

Victor dropped him.

The man collapsed, coughing.

“Tell them no.”

The envoy looked up.

Victor’s voice lowered.

“And tell them something else.”

The room seemed colder.

“Zee Darkheart belongs to House Darkheart.”

The envoy stared at him.

Victor heard the words after saying them.

Belongs.

Not lives.

Not is protected by.

Belongs.

The envoy slowly stood.

“Then you intend to decide his fate yourself.”

Victor did not answer.

The man bowed.

“I think that is what they feared.”

He left.

Victor remained alone.

For a long time.

—

That evening, the castle changed around Zee.

The guards outside the nursery doubled again.

No one entered without being searched.

Windows were sealed.

Servants were replaced by soldiers personally selected by Victor.

Aurelia noticed every change.

So did the royal witch beside her.

“This is no longer protection,” Aurelia said.

The witch remained silent.

Aurelia stood.

“Pack what Zee needs.”

“My Queen?”

“Clothes. Blankets. Food.”

“For where?”

Aurelia looked toward the sealed window.

“Anywhere my husband cannot reach him.”

The witch’s face tightened.

“You are speaking of fleeing Castle Darkheart during a siege.”

“I am speaking of keeping my son alive.”

“The roads are surrounded.”

“Then we do not use roads.”

The witch looked toward the nursery door.

“There are old passages.”

Aurelia nodded.

“Exactly.”

The crimson hatchling lifted his head.

A simple feeling passed through the Link.

Move.

Zee stirred.

Aurelia looked down.

“Even he knows.”

The witch began gathering supplies.

Neither woman heard the footsteps approaching.

The door opened.

Victor entered.

Alone.

Aurelia stopped.

The witch did not.

She continued folding linen into a travel satchel.

Victor noticed.

“Where are you going?”

Aurelia answered without hesitation.

“With my son.”

“Where?”

“Away from you.”

Victor’s expression tightened.

“Aurelia.”

“You prepared an execution chamber.”

He went still.

The witch stopped packing.

Silence swallowed the room.

Victor looked at her.

“How do you know?”

“Do you think stone servants do not speak?”

“I gave no order to execute him.”

“You prepared for it.”

“That is not the same.”

“It is when the child is two days old.”

Victor stepped closer.

Aurelia moved between him and Zee.

The hatchling rose.

Teal-and-gold mana flickered around his crimson scales.

Victor saw it.

“Move.”

Aurelia did not.

“You are frightening him.”

“He is a newborn.”

“He knows fear.”

Victor looked toward Zee.

The infant stared back with crimson eyes.

No accusation.

No understanding.

Just recognition.

Father.

That simple truth almost undid everything.

Victor’s face softened.

For one moment.

Aurelia saw it.

“Victor…”

His eyes remained on Zee.

“He held my finger.”

Aurelia said nothing.

“He trusted me.”

“He still does.”

Victor swallowed.

“That is the problem.”

“No.”

Aurelia’s voice hardened.

“That is the only thing left worth saving.”

Victor looked at her.

“You heard what the prophecy says.”

“I heard what you told me it says.”

“Every attack may make him harder to kill.”

“You do not know that.”

“He was born under Blood Rain.”

“That is not an answer.”

“Wolves lost control.”

“Not an answer.”

“Vampires felt him in their blood.”

“Still not an answer.”

“The witches—”

“Still.”

“Not.”

“An answer.”

Each word struck harder than the last.

Victor’s voice rose.

“What would satisfy you?”

“Knowing who our son becomes by allowing him to become someone.”

The room fell silent.

Even the hatchling stopped growling.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“You are condemning him for surviving a future that has not happened.”

Victor’s breathing slowed.

“And if I am right?”

“And if you are wrong?”

He had no answer.

Another siege stone struck the castle.

The entire nursery shook.

A crack appeared across one wall.

The hatchling cried out.

Zee startled.

Crimson Mana erupted from him.

Not as an attack.

As instinct.

A wave of red force passed through the nursery.

The falling stones stopped before reaching the cradle.

For one impossible moment, fragments of ceiling hung in the air.

Victor stared.

Aurelia stared.

The witch stared.

Then the stones dropped harmlessly around the room.

Zee began crying.

A true newborn cry.

Small.

Frightened.

Human enough to make Aurelia’s heart break.

She gathered him into her arms immediately.

The hatchling pressed close.

Victor did not move.

His eyes remained on the fallen stone.

The prophecy returned.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

The castle had been struck.

Zee had responded.

Victor saw confirmation.

Aurelia saw a terrified child.

That difference destroyed the last fragile bridge between them.

Victor whispered, “It has started.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“No.”

He backed away.

“You saw it.”

“I saw my son survive falling stone.”

“He stopped it.”

“He was afraid.”

“Exactly.”

Victor’s fear crystallized.

Every danger would teach Zee.

Every attack would reveal more.

Every survival would become something else.

He no longer saw possibility.

He saw escalation.

Aurelia saw the change happen in his face.

“Victor.”

He turned toward the door.

“Lock the nursery.”

The guards outside stiffened.

Aurelia’s expression went cold.

“You will not imprison me.”

“This is not about you.”

“It is now.”

Victor looked toward the royal witch.

“You remain.”

The witch hesitated.

A dangerous mistake.

Victor noticed.

“Is there a problem?”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“Good.”

He stepped into the corridor.

Aurelia called after him.

“What are you going to do?”

Victor stopped.

For several breaths, he faced away from her.

Then he answered.

“What a king must.”

The doors closed.

Locks turned from the outside.

Aurelia rushed forward.

“Victor!”

No answer came.

Only retreating footsteps.

The crimson hatchling pressed against Zee.

Danger.

The feeling crossed the Link more strongly than ever before.

Zee cried harder.

—

Victor descended beneath the western tower.

Alone.

No guards.

No council.

No witnesses.

The execution chamber had been restored.

The stone table stood clean beneath iron chains.

A brazier burned in each corner.

Weapons once used against traitors and enemy kings rested along the wall.

Axes.

Blades.

Hooks.

Iron spikes.

Victor ignored them.

He walked toward the center of the chamber.

There, on a smaller table, sat something newly brought from the royal armory.

A dagger.

Nothing mystical.

Nothing ancient.

Nothing tied to prophecy.

Simple steel.

Victor had chosen it for exactly that reason.

No magic.

No ritual.

No spectacle.

If Zee was only a strange child born beneath terrible omens...

The blade would prove it.

If the prophecy was true...

Victor did not allow himself to finish the thought.

He picked up the dagger.

His hand trembled.

“No foreign king.”

His voice echoed through the chamber.

“No frightened mob.”

“No vampire.”

“No witch.”

“No wolf.”

He stared at the blade.

“If this must be done…”

His breathing became uneven.

“I decide.”

For a moment, he almost dropped it.

Then he remembered the soldier dying in his arms.

The villages burning.

The twelve armies.

The falling stone freezing above the cradle.

Fear won.

Not completely.

Enough.

Victor slipped the dagger beneath his cloak.

Above him, Aurelia pounded against the locked nursery doors.

The royal witch whispered hurriedly over an old hidden passage beneath the floor.

The crimson hatchling stood over Zee, tiny wings spread as wide as his newborn body allowed.

And beneath Castle Darkheart, King Victor Darkheart began walking toward the first murder attempt of Zee’s life.

Not as a foreign invader.

Not as a monster.

As his father.

# Chapter Six

## The First Death

The hidden passage beneath the nursery had not been opened in eighty-three years.

Dust filled the narrow stairwell. Ancient roots had pushed between the stones, twisting through the walls like petrified veins. The royal witch knelt beside the concealed entrance with both hands pressed against a faded seal while Queen Aurelia held Zee against her chest.

The crimson hatchling refused to leave him.

He clung to Aurelia’s shoulder with tiny claws, his tail wrapped around the cloth covering Zee. Teal-and-gold mana trembled across his scales whenever footsteps passed beyond the locked nursery doors.

Danger.

The feeling moved through the Dragon Link without words.

Zee felt it.

His crying had stopped.

That frightened Aurelia more.

He simply stared toward the door with wide crimson eyes.

“Can you open it?” she whispered.

The witch gritted her teeth.

“This passage was sealed by one of your husband’s ancestors.”

“Then break it.”

“I am trying.”

Purple mana spread through cracks in the floor. The old seal resisted, not because it possessed greater power, but because it had been woven into the foundations of Castle Darkheart.

Another impact from the siege shook the tower.

Dust fell.

The hatchling hissed.

Aurelia looked toward the nursery door.

“How long?”

“Minutes.”

“We do not have minutes.”

A sound came from the corridor.

Metal sliding against metal.

The locks.

Someone was opening them.

The witch looked over her shoulder.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia knew.

“Keep working.”

The first lock turned.

Then the second.

Then the third.

The witch increased the pressure of her spell.

The floor seal cracked.

Aurelia stepped backward until the cradle pressed against her legs.

The nursery doors opened.

King Victor stood beyond them.

Alone.

His cloak hung over one shoulder.

His face was pale.

His right hand remained hidden beneath the folds of fabric.

Aurelia’s eyes went immediately to it.

“No.”

Victor entered.

The guards outside remained motionless.

“Leave us.”

No one obeyed.

Captain Vale had arrived behind Victor.

He looked from the king to the queen and understood enough.

“My King…”

Victor did not turn.

“I said leave us.”

Vale’s hand rested on his sword.

“Your Majesty, perhaps—”

“Leave.”

The command struck the corridor.

Vale’s jaw tightened.

He bowed.

The guards withdrew with him.

Victor closed the doors himself.

Aurelia stared at him.

“You brought no witnesses.”

“I did not want witnesses.”

The hatchling climbed down from Aurelia’s shoulder and placed himself between Victor and Zee.

He was absurdly small.

His wings barely reached the width of Aurelia’s forearm.

His growl sounded more like a broken purr than a threat.

Victor looked at him anyway.

The Dragon Link flooded with simple instinct.

Protect.

Zee’s Crimson Mana stirred.

Aurelia saw it.

So did Victor.

“Do not,” she whispered.

“I have not done anything.”

“You came here with a weapon.”

Victor froze.

Aurelia’s voice broke.

“I know you.”

His hand emerged from beneath the cloak.

The dagger caught the firelight.

The witch stopped working on the passage.

For several seconds, no one breathed.

Then Aurelia laughed.

Not because anything was funny.

Because grief had become too large for silence.

“You actually brought it.”

Victor looked down at the weapon as though seeing it for the first time.

“Aurelia.”

“You held him.”

“I know.”

“He trusted you.”

“I know.”

“You called him your son.”

“He is my son.”

“Then put the dagger down.”

Victor’s fingers tightened around the hilt.

“I cannot.”

The queen’s face changed.

Whatever remained between husband and wife began dying in that moment.

“You mean you will not.”

Victor swallowed.

“There is a difference between fear and cowardice.”

“You are about to murder a newborn because a piece of bone frightened you.”

“I am about to prevent something none of us may survive.”

“You do not know that.”

“The prophecy—”

“Does not know him.”

“It knew enough.”

“Enough for you to finish the rest yourself.”

Victor stared at her.

She stepped closer.

“You imagined kingdoms burning.”

His face hardened.

“You imagined Zee destroying everything.”

“Aurelia—”

“You imagined him becoming a monster.”

“Stop.”

“And then you decided your imagination was evidence.”

“Stop.”

“You became afraid of what our son might become, so now you are trying to become worse first.”

Victor’s expression broke.

For one heartbeat, the king disappeared.

The father returned.

He looked at Zee.

The infant watched him.

No hatred.

No understanding.

Only recognition.

Victor’s hand began to lower.

Then another siege stone hit the castle.

The wall behind Aurelia split.

The hatchling cried out.

Zee startled.

Crimson Mana erupted.

This time, the force was stronger.

The cracked wall stopped moving.

Falling stone hung motionless for a breath.

Then every fragment shifted away from Aurelia and Zee, striking the opposite side of the room.

The witch stared.

Victor stared.

Zee began crying.

And Victor’s fear returned greater than before.

“You see?”

Aurelia looked at him in disbelief.

“He protected himself.”

“He is two days old.”

“He is terrified.”

“He is two days old!”

Victor shouted it now.

The chamber went still.

“No witch child does that.”

“No vampire child does that.”

“No wolf child does that.”

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“He is not any one of them.”

Victor flinched.

The words confirmed what everyone already feared.

Three natures.

One child.

The First Tribrid.

Victor looked at the dagger.

Then at Zee.

The prophecy whispered inside his mind.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

He had spent the night fearing that line.

Now he made the cruelest possible decision.

He decided to test it.

Victor stepped forward.

The hatchling lunged.

Tiny teeth sank into Victor’s wrist.

He cursed and ripped his arm back.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed.

Not enough to seriously injure him.

Enough to draw blood.

Victor stared at the hatchling.

The creature stood over Zee.

Protect.

The feeling crossed the Link.

Zee’s crying stopped.

Aurelia saw Victor raise the dagger.

She moved before thought.

Her hand struck his wrist.

The blade missed Zee and sliced across Aurelia’s forearm.

Blood sprayed across the blankets.

Victor froze.

Aurelia did not.

She slapped him.

The sound cracked through the room.

“You cut me.”

Victor stared at the blood.

“I did not mean—”

“No.”

Her voice trembled with rage.

“You meant worse.”

The witch rushed forward.

Victor turned toward her.

“Stay back.”

She stopped.

Not from fear.

From calculation.

Aurelia held Zee tighter.

“You will have to kill me first.”

Victor looked at his wife.

Then his son.

Then the hatchling.

Something inside him shattered.

He hated what he was about to do.

That did not stop him.

“Aurelia…”

Tears filled his eyes.

“Forgive me.”

He struck her with magic.

A dark violet force hit Aurelia across the chest and threw her onto the bed.

Zee slipped from her arms.

The witch screamed.

The hatchling leaped.

Victor caught Zee before he hit the floor.

For one terrible moment...

Father held son again.

Zee stared up at him.

Crimson eyes.

Tiny fangs.

Small hands.

Victor remembered the first time.

He remembered saying *my son*.

Then Aurelia screamed his name.

“VICTOR!”

He closed his eyes.

And drove the dagger into Zee’s chest.

Silence.

The entire world seemed to stop.

The hatchling shrieked.

A sound too large for his tiny body tore from him as teal-and-gold mana exploded through the nursery.

Aurelia crawled from the bed.

“No.”

Victor opened his eyes.

The dagger remained inside Zee.

Blood spread across the infant’s clothes.

Crimson.

Ordinary-looking.

Terrible.

Zee’s mouth opened.

No cry came.

His heartbeat stumbled.

Once.

Twice.

Then stopped.

Aurelia reached him.

Victor did not resist when she tore Zee from his arms.

She fell to the floor holding her child.

“No.”

Her fingers pressed against the wound.

“Zee.”

Nothing.

The royal witch dropped beside her.

Magic flooded her hands.

Purple light entered the wound.

Nothing happened.

“Again!”

“I am trying!”

“Again!”

The hatchling pushed himself against Zee’s side.

Fear became panic through the Dragon Link.

Where?

Gone?

Come back.

The simple emotions struck something that no newborn should have known how to answer.

But Zee did not move.

Victor stood above them.

Blood covered his hand.

His son’s blood.

He had done it.

The room blurred.

“I…”

Aurelia looked up.

The grief in her face became hatred.

“You killed him.”

Victor’s lips parted.

No words came.

Outside...

The siege stopped.

Not gradually.

All at once.

Every wolf across the northern forests collapsed.

Vampires across the world clutched their chests as the impossible heartbeat disappeared completely.

Witches everywhere felt a pressure vanish that they had not realized still lingered since Zee’s birth.

The blood-soaked clouds above Castle Darkheart turned black.

The world did not know what had happened.

It only felt the absence.

Inside the nursery, the hatchling pressed his forehead against Zee’s.

His entire body shook.

Teal-and-gold mana wrapped helplessly around the dead infant.

Aurelia sobbed.

The witch continued healing a heart that no longer beat.

Victor stared at the prophecy fulfilled by his own hand.

Or so he believed.

Then Zee’s blood moved.

One drop crawled backward across his skin.

The witch stopped.

Aurelia did not notice.

Another drop rose from the blanket.

Then another.

Victor’s face drained of color.

The blood gathered around the dagger wound.

Not flowing outward.

Returning.

The torn flesh began closing.

Slowly.

Wrongly.

Beautifully.

Zee’s tiny fingers twitched.

The crimson hatchling froze.

A feeling crossed the Link.

There.

Aurelia gasped.

“Zee?”

The infant inhaled.

The breath came violently.

His back arched.

Crimson Mana exploded through the nursery with enough force to throw every adult backward.

Victor struck the wall.

The witch crashed into the floor.

Aurelia held onto Zee with everything she had.

The dagger tore free from his chest by itself and clattered across the stone.

Zee screamed.

This time the cry was not quiet.

It rolled through Castle Darkheart.

Across the walls.

Across the battlefield.

Across forests and mountains and buried vampire halls.

His heartbeat returned.

Once.

The vampires felt it.

Twice.

The wolves lifted their heads.

Three times.

Every witch inside Castle Darkheart felt their magic shudder beneath the sudden pressure.

Zee’s wound vanished.

Completely.

No scar remained.

But something had changed.

His Crimson Mana was denser now.

Not vastly stronger.

Not transformed into some understood new state.

Simply different.

As though his body had encountered death...

And refused to remember how to remain dead.

Victor stared from the floor.

The prophecy whispered again.

*Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.*

He finally understood the horror of his mistake.

He had not prevented the prophecy.

He had become the first blade.

Aurelia rose with Zee in her arms.

The hatchling climbed against him immediately.

His tiny body pressed around Zee as though he could physically prevent death from returning.

Zee’s crying softened.

The Dragon Link carried one feeling between them.

Safe.

Victor slowly stood.

Aurelia looked at him.

“Do not come closer.”

He stopped.

The king’s face had become ash.

“I killed him.”

“Yes.”

“He came back.”

“Yes.”

Victor stared at Zee.

Fear unlike anything he had ever known entered his eyes.

Not because Zee had attacked him.

Not because Zee had threatened the kingdom.

Because Victor had just killed his own newborn son...

And death had failed to keep him.

The witch whispered,

“What is he?”

Aurelia looked at her sharply.

“No.”

The woman fell silent.

No one would answer that question tonight.

No one possessed the right.

No one possessed the knowledge.

Outside, foreign soldiers stared toward Castle Darkheart as the infant’s scream faded through the air.

The armies did not know what had happened inside.

They only knew that for several moments, the impossible presence they had feared had vanished.

Then returned.

Stronger.

And inside the nursery, King Victor Darkheart looked at the blood on his hands and realized that the first person to kill Zee...

Had also become the first person to teach his body how to survive death.

# Chapter Seven

## The Child Who Returned

No one moved for several heartbeats.

Queen Aurelia stood in the center of the ruined nursery with Zee clutched against her chest. The crimson hatchling pressed against the child as though his tiny body alone could keep death away. The eldest royal witch remained on one knee, staring at the place where the dagger wound had been.

There was no wound now.

No scar.

Only clean newborn skin beneath torn fabric and fresh blood.

King Victor Darkheart looked at his hands.

They would not stop shaking.

He had killed his son.

He knew exactly what he had felt when the dagger entered Zee’s chest. The resistance of bone. The terrible softness beyond it. The warmth of blood running across his fingers.

He had watched the child’s heartbeat stop.

And then he had watched death lose him.

Victor took one step forward.

Aurelia backed away immediately.

“Do not.”

Her voice was quiet.

That made it worse.

Victor stopped.

“Aurelia…”

“You do not get to say my name like nothing happened.”

“I know.”

“No. You do not.”

Zee stirred against her.

His crimson eyes remained open.

No golden light had entered them. No transformation announced what had happened. He was still visibly the same newborn child who had existed moments earlier.

But Aurelia could feel the difference.

His breathing had steadied far too quickly.

His heartbeat had returned stronger than before.

And his Crimson Mana now clung closer to his body, less like random leakage and more like something that had learned where danger came from.

The royal witch noticed too.

She opened her mouth.

Then remembered what had happened when everyone tried to explain Zee.

She said nothing.

Victor looked at his son.

“Is he hurt?”

Aurelia laughed once.

It was hollow.

“You are asking me if the child you stabbed is hurt?”

Victor flinched.

The hatchling hissed.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered over his crimson scales.

Danger.

The feeling passed through the Dragon Link.

Zee responded with simple unease.

Aurelia felt him tense.

The hatchling moved closer.

Safe.

The answer came without words.

Zee relaxed.

Victor watched it happen.

Even now, part of him searched for meaning.

He hated that part.

He hated that the prophecy had taught him to look at every movement and wonder whether it proved something.

The witch finally stood.

“My Queen, we need to move.”

Aurelia looked toward her.

“The passage?”

“Opened.”

Victor’s eyes sharpened.

“What passage?”

No one answered.

He understood anyway.

“You planned to flee.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“I planned to survive you.”

The words cut deeper than any blade.

Victor looked toward the broken nursery wall.

Beyond it came the distant thunder of the siege.

For several seconds, he appeared almost exhausted enough to collapse.

Then the king returned.

“You cannot leave the castle.”

Aurelia stared at him.

“Watch me.”

“There are armies outside every road.”

“Then I will find another road.”

“You do not understand what waits beyond these walls.”

“I understand exactly what waits inside them.”

Victor’s face tightened.

“Aurelia, listen to me.”

“No.”

“This is larger than us.”

“You made it larger than us when you put a dagger in our son.”

“I was trying to prevent—”

“You were trying to control what you feared.”

Victor fell silent.

Because she was right.

Aurelia adjusted Zee against her chest and moved toward the hidden passage.

Victor stepped into her path.

The crimson hatchling growled immediately.

Zee’s mana pulsed.

Victor saw it.

Then, slowly, he moved aside.

Aurelia stopped.

She had expected a fight.

Victor looked at Zee one last time.

“I do not know what to do with this.”

Aurelia’s voice softened only slightly.

“Then do nothing.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

“For once, do nothing.”

She entered the hidden passage.

The witch followed.

The hatchling remained with Zee.

Victor stood alone in the nursery.

A few moments later, the stone floor slid back into place.

His family was gone.

He had never felt more like a king.

He had never felt less like a father.

---

Outside Castle Darkheart, the battlefield had changed.

The attacking armies had heard Zee’s scream.

Not all of them recognized it as a child.

Some thought the fortress had unleashed a weapon.

Others claimed a demon had awakened.

Still others swore the earth itself had cried out.

The truth reached no one.

Only rumor did.

A line of soldiers from the southern kingdoms refused to advance.

Their commander rode before them.

“Forward!”

No one moved.

The commander drew his sword.

“I said forward!”

One soldier pointed toward Castle Darkheart.

“We felt it stop.”

The commander’s expression hardened.

“What?”

“The thing.”

Another soldier whispered, “Whatever was born there.”

The men around him nodded.

“For a moment it was gone.”

“And then it came back.”

The commander looked toward the castle.

He had felt it too.

He refused to admit that.

“Fear is not permission to abandon formation.”

A soldier near the front crossed himself.

“That was not fear.”

The commander raised his sword.

“It was an order.”

An arrow came from the walls.

It struck him through the neck.

The formation broke.

Not into retreat.

Into chaos.

The kingdoms had marched together because they feared the same newborn.

Now they could not agree on what the newborn had become.

---

Deep beneath the eastern mountains, vampires gathered in silence.

The impossible heartbeat had vanished.

Then returned.

That disturbed them more than anything before it.

One ancient vampire paced the edge of the blood chamber.

“It died.”

Another shook his head.

“You do not know that.”

“I felt it disappear.”

“And now?”

The first vampire stopped.

The heartbeat remained distant.

Steady.

Unfamiliar.

Present.

He whispered, “Now it is back.”

No one spoke.

An elder seated in the shadows finally said, “Then we have learned nothing.”

A younger vampire looked toward him.

“Nothing?”

“Nothing except that whatever happened in Castle Darkheart has become more dangerous to misunderstand.”

That was the closest anyone came to wisdom.

---

In the northern forests, the wolves changed direction.

Not all of them.

Not together.

But enough for hunters to notice.

Some packs that had spent the night tearing through villages suddenly retreated into the wilderness. Others began circling paths leading toward Darkheart territory. A few simply lay down and refused to move.

No alpha could explain it.

No shaman could interpret it.

The madness remained.

But beneath it, instinct had begun searching for something.

---

Beneath Castle Darkheart, Aurelia moved through darkness.

The hidden passage was narrow enough that her shoulders brushed the walls. The witch walked ahead with a small blue flame floating above her palm, guiding them deeper through forgotten stone.

Zee slept again.

Aurelia could not understand how.

She had watched him die.

Every time she closed her eyes, she saw the dagger.

Every time she opened them, he was alive.

Her mind could not reconcile the two truths.

The crimson hatchling remained awake.

He had not looked away from Zee since the resurrection.

His fear had changed too.

He now reacted to every footstep, every shift in the stone, every breath from the witch.

The Dragon Link carried the same simple intention again and again.

Stay.

Stay.

Stay.

Zee responded with warmth.

Near.

The hatchling relaxed only slightly.

The witch glanced back.

“My Queen.”

“What?”

“There is something ahead.”

Aurelia stopped.

The passage opened into an older tunnel.

Not a royal corridor.

Something beneath that.

The walls were rough.

Unworked.

Ancient roots had cracked through the stone.

Cold air moved from somewhere deeper underground.

The witch raised her flame.

A figure stood at the far end of the tunnel.

Aurelia’s body went rigid.

The hatchling growled.

The figure lifted both hands slowly.

“I am not armed.”

The voice belonged to a man.

Aurelia narrowed her eyes.

“Who are you?”

He stepped into the blue light.

Dark travel clothes.

Gray hair.

A scar beneath one eye.

No royal crest.

No obvious weapon.

He looked first at Aurelia.

Then at Zee.

His expression changed.

Not recognition.

Shock.

Fear.

Exactly what everyone else felt.

“Is that him?”

Aurelia stepped back.

“You have one chance to answer me.”

The man lowered his eyes.

“My name is Ser Caldrin Marr.”

The witch stiffened.

Aurelia noticed.

“You know him?”

“By reputation.”

“That is rarely good.”

Caldrin gave a humorless smile.

“No.”

He looked toward the passage behind them.

“You cannot continue east.”

“Why?”

“Foreign scouts found the old drainage tunnels hours ago.”

Aurelia’s grip tightened around Zee.

“How do you know?”

“Because I killed the three men who found them.”

Silence.

The hatchling watched him.

Caldrin looked toward Zee again.

He did not kneel.

He did not praise him.

He did not pretend to understand him.

“What happened up there?”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“Nothing you need to know.”

Caldrin studied the blood on her clothes.

Then the torn fabric around Zee’s chest.

He understood enough.

“The king?”

Aurelia said nothing.

That was answer enough.

Caldrin exhaled.

“Then Castle Darkheart has two enemies now.”

The witch looked toward him.

“What do you want?”

“To survive the siege.”

“And helping us does that?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

Caldrin’s gaze shifted toward Zee.

“Because I have seen kings kill children for less.”

Aurelia held his stare.

He continued.

“And I have buried enough of them.”

The tunnel shook from another impact above.

Dust fell.

Caldrin looked toward the ceiling.

“You have minutes before the eastern passages become unusable.”

Aurelia made a decision.

“Show us another way.”

The witch looked at her.

“My Queen—”

“If he wanted Zee dead, he had opportunity before announcing himself.”

Caldrin nodded once.

“There is a route beneath the old burial vaults.”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“Victor uses those.”

“Not the oldest ones.”

He turned.

“Follow me.”

They moved deeper beneath the castle.

---

Victor did not discover the empty nursery for long.

He had remained there after Aurelia fled, staring at the blood-covered dagger on the floor.

Eventually Captain Vale entered.

The captain stopped upon seeing the room.

Blood.

Broken stone.

No queen.

No prince.

No dragon.

His eyes went to Victor.

“What happened?”

Victor did not answer.

Vale looked at the dagger.

Then at the blood on Victor’s sleeve.

Understanding came slowly.

His expression changed from confusion to horror.

“You did it.”

Victor looked up.

Vale’s voice lowered.

“You actually did it.”

“He survived.”

The captain stared.

Victor repeated it.

“He survived.”

Vale looked toward the empty cradle.

“You stabbed him?”

“Yes.”

“And he survived?”

“He died.”

Silence.

Victor’s voice cracked.

“Then he came back.”

Captain Vale took one step away from his king.

For the first time in all their years together, the movement was not tactical.

It was fear.

Not of Zee.

Of Victor.

“You killed your own son.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“I know.”

“No.”

Vale shook his head.

“You keep saying that as if knowledge is punishment enough.”

Victor stepped toward him.

“Careful.”

The captain laughed.

It was bitter.

“There it is.”

“What?”

“The king.”

Victor’s eyes narrowed.

“You hide behind him whenever the father cannot survive what he has done.”

The words struck.

Vale did not stop.

“Twelve kingdoms came here to murder your child.”

“I know.”

“And you decided to beat them to it.”

“That is not what happened.”

“That is exactly what happened.”

Victor’s voice rose.

“You did not hear the prophecy.”

“No.”

“You did not watch him stop falling stone.”

“No.”

“You did not feel the world change when he was born.”

Vale stared at him.

“Neither did you understand any of it.”

Victor froze.

Vale continued.

“You feared what you could not explain.”

“And now?”

“Now your wife has fled with your heir.”

Victor’s face hardened.

“Find her.”

Vale did not move.

“Captain.”

“You want me to bring them back?”

“Yes.”

“For protection?”

Victor said nothing.

Vale laughed again.

“I thought so.”

The king stepped closer.

“You will obey.”

The captain held his gaze.

“For House Darkheart?”

“Yes.”

Vale’s expression changed.

“Then I will find the queen.”

Victor relaxed slightly.

Vale continued.

“But I will not deliver that child to your execution chamber.”

The room went still.

Victor’s voice became cold.

“You are refusing your king.”

“I am serving my kingdom.”

“You do not decide what that means.”

“Neither do prophecies carved into dead bone.”

Victor’s hand went to his sword.

Vale’s did not.

For several seconds, the two men stood facing one another.

Then the eastern tower shook violently.

A horn screamed from outside.

A soldier rushed into the nursery.

“My King!”

Victor turned.

“The eastern wall has been breached.”

Everything changed.

Kingdom before family.

War before fear.

Victor drew his sword.

“How large?”

“Not enough for cavalry. Infantry are forcing through.”

Victor looked toward Vale.

“Find Aurelia.”

Then he ran for the walls.

Vale watched him go.

He waited until the footsteps disappeared.

Then he looked at the hidden passage.

“Find the queen.”

The soldier beside him waited.

“Sir?”

Vale’s eyes hardened.

“We are going to.”

He moved toward the passage.

“But not for the king.”

---

The breach became a slaughter.

Foreign soldiers poured through a gap barely wide enough for three men at once.

Darkheart defenders met them with spears.

Bodies piled until the dead became part of the barricade.

Victor entered the fighting without hesitation.

His sword cut through the first invader’s shoulder.

Dark violet magic blasted another into broken stone.

A third reached him with an axe.

Victor ducked and drove his blade beneath the man’s ribs.

Blood covered the king.

Again.

Different blood.

That mattered less than it should have.

The High Marshal shouted from above.

“They are widening the breach!”

“Collapse the upper wall!”

“Our men are beneath it!”

“Move them!”

“There is no time!”

Victor looked toward the breach.

More enemy soldiers were coming.

If they entered the inner courtyard, the siege would become street fighting.

Thousands of civilians waited beyond the second gate.

Victor made the decision.

“Collapse it.”

The marshal stared.

“My King—”

“Do it!”

Darkheart witches raised their hands.

Purple and blue mana struck the damaged tower supports.

Stone cracked.

Defenders realized what was happening.

Some escaped.

Many did not.

The eastern wall collapsed.

The breach vanished beneath thousands of tons of black stone.

Enemy soldiers screamed beneath it.

So did Darkheart men.

Then silence.

Victor stood in the dust.

The castle held.

At terrible cost.

His generals looked at him.

Some with loyalty.

Some with fear.

Victor understood something then.

A king survived by making choices other men could not.

He had always believed that.

The danger was how easily that belief could excuse anything.

He looked toward the tower where his son had been.

Empty now.

For one moment, the prophecy became distant.

He saw only Aurelia’s face.

*You are condemning him for surviving a future that has not happened.*

Victor closed his eyes.

Then a scout approached.

“My King.”

Victor turned.

“What?”

“We found blood in the lower passages.”

His heart stopped.

“Whose?”

“We do not know.”

Victor began moving before the scout finished.

“Take me there.”

---

Deep below, Caldrin led Aurelia through a narrow burial tunnel.

The air had grown colder.

The witch’s blue flame flickered.

Behind them, distant footsteps echoed.

Someone was following.

Caldrin stopped.

“Give me the child.”

Aurelia’s eyes turned murderous.

“No.”

“So I can fight.”

“I said no.”

The hatchling growled.

Caldrin looked at him.

“I am beginning to understand why everyone likes you.”

The dragon hissed.

The witch whispered, “They are closer.”

Caldrin drew a short sword from beneath his cloak.

Aurelia looked at him.

“You said you were unarmed.”

“I said it when I needed you not to stab me.”

Despite everything, she almost laughed.

Almost.

The footsteps approached.

Caldrin moved forward.

Then a familiar voice echoed through the tunnel.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia froze.

Captain Vale stepped into the blue light.

Three guards stood behind him.

Caldrin raised his sword.

Vale drew his own.

Aurelia moved between them.

“Stop.”

Vale looked toward Zee.

Relief crossed his face.

“He is alive.”

Aurelia’s expression darkened.

“You know.”

“The king told me.”

The hatchling growled.

Vale lowered his sword.

“I am not here for him.”

Aurelia studied him.

“Then why are you here?”

“To get you out.”

She said nothing.

Vale continued.

“The eastern wall nearly fell. Victor is occupied.”

“For now.”

“Yes.”

“And afterward?”

Vale looked toward Zee.

“Afterward, the king will search every stone in this kingdom.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Then we need to leave Darkheart territory.”

Vale shook his head.

“Impossible tonight.”

“Then what?”

“There is one place Victor will not search immediately.”

Aurelia’s eyes narrowed.

“Where?”

Vale looked deeper into the tunnel.

“The old enemy crypts.”

The witch’s expression changed.

“Those were sealed after the Black Winter.”

“Exactly.”

Caldrin looked between them.

“What is inside?”

Vale answered quietly.

“Things House Darkheart preferred buried.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child slept.

Alive.

For now.

She had a kingdom outside trying to kill him.

A husband inside who already had.

And beneath her feet waited something the Darkhearts themselves had once feared enough to seal away.

Aurelia looked up.

“Take us there.”

The witch stared at her.

“My Queen.”

“We are out of safe choices.”

Vale nodded.

They moved.

Behind them, far through the passage, another set of footsteps entered the tunnels.

Victor had found the blood trail.

And this time, he was not carrying a dagger.

He was carrying a sword.
