# Chapter Eight

## The World Comes Below

The old enemy crypts had not been opened since the Black Winter.

Captain Vale broke the first seal with the pommel of his sword.

The sound echoed through the buried corridor like a hammer striking a coffin.

Dust poured from the archway.

Queen Aurelia stood behind him with Zee held tightly against her chest while the crimson hatchling pressed along her shoulder, his small claws tangled in the queen’s cloak. The royal witch kept one hand raised, blue-violet mana trembling around her fingers as she listened for movement beyond the stone.

Ser Caldrin Marr watched the darkness.

“Why were these sealed?”

Vale pushed against the ancient door.

“Because House Darkheart won the war.”

Caldrin glanced at him. “That does not answer the question.”

“No.”

The stone groaned.

Vale shoved harder.

“Because what we defeated refused to stay defeated.”

The door opened.

Cold air rushed over them.

The hatchling lifted his head immediately.

Fear passed through the Dragon Link.

Not the sharp terror he had felt when Zee disappeared.

Something older.

Something waiting.

Zee stirred against Aurelia.

His crimson eyes opened.

The queen looked down.

“It is all right.”

She no longer believed those words when she said them.

But Zee recognized her voice.

That was enough.

For now.

They entered.

The crypt was enormous.

Far larger than anything that should have existed beneath Castle Darkheart.

Columns disappeared into darkness overhead. Broken statues lined a sunken avenue, each depicting warriors whose faces had been deliberately carved away. Rusted chains hung from walls covered in dead runes. In the distance, black water reflected the witch’s spell-light without revealing how deep it went.

Caldrin stopped.

“This is not a crypt.”

Vale looked ahead.

“No.”

“What is it?”

“A prison.”

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“You brought my son into a prison?”

“I brought him somewhere Victor would hesitate to enter.”

“That is not the same as safe.”

“There is no safe.”

The answer silenced them.

That truth had followed Zee since the sky began bleeding.

A sound came from somewhere beyond the columns.

Stone scraping stone.

The hatchling growled.

Vale raised his sword.

Caldrin drew his own.

The royal witch strengthened her light.

Aurelia held Zee closer.

“Move.”

They continued deeper.

Behind them, far above, Castle Darkheart remained at war.

And beneath it...

Something had begun waking.

---

King Victor reached the lower passage minutes later.

He found blood first.

Aurelia’s.

Drops marked the old stones where the wound on her arm had reopened during the escape.

Victor crouched beside one.

His expression tightened.

Captain Vale had betrayed him.

Aurelia had fled.

His son had been taken into the oldest foundations of the castle.

Every part of him wanted to pursue.

Then he remembered the dagger.

The stillness after Zee’s heartbeat stopped.

The impossible breath that followed.

Victor’s hand closed around the hilt of his sword.

He would not do that again.

That certainty had formed the moment Zee returned.

Not from mercy alone.

Fear had changed shape.

Victor no longer feared only what Zee might become if allowed to live.

He now feared what trying to kill him might create.

The prophecy had warned him.

He had tested it.

Once.

That mistake would not be repeated.

But he would not allow Aurelia to disappear with something that could bring twelve kingdoms down upon House Darkheart either.

Victor rose.

“Seal every tunnel leading beyond the castle.”

The soldiers behind him exchanged glances.

“My King?”

“You heard me.”

“What about the queen?”

“She remains within Darkheart territory.”

“And the prince?”

Victor’s face hardened.

“Especially the prince.”

The commander bowed.

Victor looked into the darkness ahead.

“Send men through the southern passages.”

“How many?”

Victor considered.

Then stopped himself.

Not an army.

Not near Zee.

“Six.”

The commander looked surprised.

“Only six?”

“I said six.”

Victor stared into the tunnel.

“Do not attack the child.”

The soldiers went still.

Victor’s next words came colder.

“Do not provoke him.”

That order spread through the castle before sunset.

The king who had been the first person to kill Zee now became the first ruler to warn his own soldiers against attempting it again.

Not because he had accepted his son.

Because he had learned to fear the result.

---

Outside Castle Darkheart, the foreign armies learned something else.

The siege was failing.

Not because House Darkheart was stronger.

Because the coalition was beginning to fracture.

The twelve kingdoms had agreed that the child needed to die.

They had not agreed on who should control what remained afterward.

Some wanted the body burned.

Others wanted it studied.

One vampire-backed kingdom demanded the blood.

A northern wolf king wanted proof that the newborn’s existence had caused the madness among his packs.

Three witch courts wanted the child alive long enough to examine the strange mana witnessed during the birth.

The moment survival became politics...

Unity began dying.

Inside the largest command tent, King Orsik of Dunmere slammed his gauntlet onto a wooden table.

“We breach the western wall tonight.”

A foreign general shook his head.

“And lose another two thousand men.”

“Then lose them.”

“They are not your soldiers.”

“They will be dead either way if that creature grows.”

Across the table, Lady Maevra of the Ash Coven watched them with visible contempt.

“You continue calling him a creature because it makes your fear sound noble.”

Orsik glared at her.

“You lost your magic when he was born.”

“No.”

The witch’s expression sharpened.

“I could not reach it.”

“That distinction will comfort the dead?”

“It comforts truth.”

“Truth is that something happened.”

“Yes.”

“And the child was at its center.”

“Perhaps.”

Orsik laughed.

“You witches hide cowardice behind uncertainty.”

Maevra leaned forward.

“And kings hide stupidity behind certainty.”

Hands moved toward weapons.

A vampire envoy seated near the rear of the tent smiled.

This was more familiar.

Fear dividing prey.

King Orsik noticed.

“You find this amusing?”

The vampire’s smile faded.

“No.”

“You people felt him.”

The tent grew quieter.

The vampire looked toward Castle Darkheart.

“Yes.”

“What did you feel?”

He considered lying.

Instead, he said, “A heartbeat that did not belong inside my blood.”

“Whose?”

“I do not know.”

“Was it the child?”

“I do not know.”

Orsik struck the table again.

“Does anyone know anything?”

No one answered.

That was the truth none of them wanted.

They had marched thousands of soldiers across kingdoms to destroy something they did not understand.

Then a runner entered.

“My lords.”

Orsik turned.

“What?”

“Movement beneath the eastern ridge.”

“How many?”

“We do not know.”

“Darkheart troops?”

The runner hesitated.

“No.”

The vampire envoy stood.

“What did you see?”

The soldier swallowed.

“Something came out of the ground.”

---

In the enemy crypts, Aurelia heard the first scream.

It came from ahead.

Human.

Short.

Then silence.

Vale stopped walking.

“That was not one of ours.”

Caldrin looked back. “You sound disappointed.”

“It means someone else found another entrance.”

The witch dimmed her light.

“How?”

“Siege damage,” Vale said. “Or the foreigners knew more about the old tunnels than we thought.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child remained awake.

Too awake.

His crimson eyes moved slowly through the darkness.

The hatchling’s body had gone rigid.

Danger.

Closer now.

Not one thing.

Many.

Vale whispered, “Stay behind me.”

Aurelia almost laughed.

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

This time, she obeyed.

They entered a wider chamber.

Bodies covered the floor.

Foreign scouts.

Six, perhaps seven.

All dead.

No visible wounds.

Their faces were frozen in expressions of terror.

Caldrin crouched beside one.

“No blood.”

The witch stepped closer.

“What killed them?”

Caldrin turned the body.

Nothing.

No cuts.

No broken bones.

No burns.

Vale looked toward the far side of the chamber.

An ancient door stood open.

Black mist crawled beneath it.

“That.”

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“What was imprisoned here?”

Vale did not answer.

She looked at him.

“Captain.”

“My grandfather called them Hollow Men.”

Caldrin stood.

“That sounds comforting.”

“They are not men.”

The mist thickened.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Violet mana gathered around her.

“What are they?”

Vale’s grip tightened around his sword.

“Things that learned how to wear people.”

The first one stepped through the doorway.

It wore the body of a dead soldier.

Almost.

Its joints bent incorrectly.

Its smile stretched too far.

Its eyes were empty black pits.

The hatchling screamed.

Zee’s Crimson Mana surged.

The Hollow thing stopped.

For the first time, it looked uncertain.

Then more shapes emerged behind it.

Three.

Five.

Nine.

Caldrin whispered, “How many did your ancestors bury?”

Vale answered without taking his eyes off them.

“Enough.”

The first creature rushed forward.

Vale met it with steel.

His sword passed through its chest.

The body folded around the blade as though empty.

Then one black hand closed around his throat.

Caldrin struck from the side.

The creature twisted toward him.

The royal witch released a blast of violet force.

The Hollow thing flew backward and struck a column.

It stood immediately.

“Magic works,” she said.

“Not well enough,” Vale choked.

The others came.

Aurelia backed toward the wall.

The hatchling spread his tiny wings.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed violently around him.

One Hollow creature turned toward Zee.

Everything changed.

The thing ignored the adults.

It moved toward the child.

Aurelia felt the shift instantly.

“No.”

The witch stepped between them and cast.

A binding spell wrapped around the creature’s limbs.

It tore through the spell.

Caldrin intercepted it.

Its hand struck his chest and threw him across the chamber.

Vale cut through another.

Two more replaced it.

The Hollow creature kept coming.

Zee watched.

He did not understand monsters.

He understood Aurelia’s fear.

He understood the hatchling’s panic.

He understood something approaching.

Danger.

His heartbeat accelerated.

Crimson Mana thickened around him.

The creature reached.

The hatchling lunged first.

Newborn claws struck its face.

Teal-and-gold Dragon Mana burst against black flesh.

For the first time...

The Hollow creature screamed.

Not from pain.

From recognition.

The sound stopped everyone.

The creature recoiled from the hatchling.

Then looked at Zee again.

Something in its stolen face changed.

Hunger.

Aurelia saw it.

“Get away from him!”

The Hollow thing attacked.

Zee’s Crimson Mana erupted.

Not outward.

Inward.

Across his skin.

The creature’s hand touched him.

Then froze.

Blackness spread across Zee’s blanket.

Aurelia screamed.

The witch reached for the creature.

“Do not touch it!”

Too late.

The Hollow thing began draining something from Zee.

Not blood.

Not mana alone.

Warmth.

Life.

The child’s body went cold against Aurelia.

The Dragon Link exploded with terror.

Gone?

No.

No.

Stay.

The hatchling bit into the Hollow creature’s wrist.

Teal-and-gold mana flooded through the contact.

The creature shrieked again.

Zee reacted.

Instinct met threat.

His vampire nature reached first.

Tiny fangs extended.

Aurelia felt him turn.

Before she could understand what he was doing, Zee bit down into the Hollow creature’s hand.

The chamber went silent.

The creature convulsed.

Black essence flowed toward Zee.

Not willingly.

The Hollow thing tried to pull away.

It could not.

Crimson Mana wrapped around its arm.

The essence entered Zee.

His body seized.

Aurelia nearly dropped him.

“Zee!”

The creature collapsed.

Its stolen human shape withered inward until nothing remained but black ash.

Everyone stared.

Zee released the dead hand.

His crimson eyes remained open.

Something dark moved briefly beneath his skin.

Then Crimson Mana consumed it.

The blackness vanished.

Zee inhaled sharply.

Warmth returned to his body.

The witch stared in horror.

“What did he just—”

“Do not,” Aurelia snapped.

No explanations.

Not now.

The remaining Hollow creatures stopped attacking.

Every one of them looked toward Zee.

Then they retreated.

Not from the adults.

From him.

Vale watched them disappear beyond the ancient doorway.

Caldrin pushed himself upright, one hand pressed against his ribs.

“That seems bad.”

Aurelia looked down at her son.

Zee was breathing normally again.

Yet his Crimson Mana had changed.

Only slightly.

A thin black-red edge now appeared whenever it moved across his skin.

Gone within seconds.

Present long enough to be real.

The hatchling pressed his forehead against Zee.

Safe?

Zee’s tiny hand found him.

Safe.

For the moment.

The royal witch approached carefully.

“My Queen.”

“No theories.”

“I was going to say we need to leave.”

Aurelia looked toward the open doorway.

The Hollow creatures had vanished.

Vale wiped blood from his mouth.

“They will come back.”

Caldrin frowned. “Why?”

Vale looked at Zee.

“Because everything does.”

---

By nightfall, the story escaped the crypts.

Not the truth.

Never the truth.

A wounded foreign scout reached the coalition camp babbling about dead men walking beneath Castle Darkheart.

Another claimed a crimson-eyed infant had devoured a shadow.

A third insisted the dragon hatchling breathed gold fire.

None of them had seen the same thing.

None of them agreed.

That did not stop the rumors.

The child had survived death.

The child commanded monsters.

The child ate souls.

The child had awakened something under the castle.

Every retelling became worse.

Kingdoms that had marched to destroy Zee became more determined.

Others became afraid to approach him at all.

The first bounty appeared that night.

Not from a king.

From merchants.

Ten thousand silver crowns for proof of Zee Darkheart’s death.

Twenty thousand if the body remained intact.

By morning, assassins would hear.

By the end of the week, hunters would come.

Not armies.

Individuals.

Patient people.

Cruel people.

People who did not care about prophecies or kingdoms.

Only payment.

The world had learned something from the siege.

Armies were too loud.

Fear would become clever next.

---

Aurelia emerged from the lower crypts shortly before dawn.

Not into Castle Darkheart.

Into the forest beyond the western cliffs.

Captain Vale had known one forgotten exit.

The tunnel opened behind a waterfall half a mile from the fortress walls.

Cold dawn air struck Aurelia’s face.

She stopped.

For the first time since Zee was born, there was no ceiling above him.

No castle.

No nursery.

No execution chamber.

Only sky.

The hatchling looked upward.

He had never seen open sky either.

His tiny wings spread instinctively.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered around him.

Zee followed his movement.

The Dragon Link carried something new.

Wonder.

Aurelia felt tears rise unexpectedly.

Caldrin emerged behind them.

“We cannot remain here.”

She knew.

The armies were east.

Darkheart patrols were everywhere.

Assassins would come soon.

Victor would search.

The world would keep moving.

Aurelia looked toward Castle Darkheart in the distance.

Smoke rose from its broken towers.

Her kingdom.

Her husband.

Her home.

All behind her.

She looked down at Zee.

His crimson eyes stared up at the bleeding colors of sunrise.

He had lived three days.

In those three days, the heavens had rained blood.

The world had marched against him.

His father had killed him.

He had returned.

And something buried beneath House Darkheart had already tried to consume him.

Aurelia tightened the blanket around him.

“Your life will not always be this.”

Vale looked away.

Caldrin said nothing.

Even Aurelia knew it was a lie.

The hatchling curled against Zee.

The Dragon Link carried a simple feeling between them.

Go.

Aurelia looked west.

Beyond the mountains lay kingdoms that had not yet chosen whether to fear Zee.

Among them...

One kingdom had refused to send soldiers to Castle Darkheart.

House Vesper.

Aurelia did not know whether that meant safety.

She had stopped believing in safety.

But it meant a direction.

“West,” she said.

Vale nodded.

Caldrin adjusted his sword.

The witch pulled up her hood.

Behind them, Castle Darkheart continued burning beneath siege fire.

Ahead, the ancient world waited.

And for the first time, Zee Darkheart left the kingdom of his birth.

Not as a prince beginning a royal journey.

As a hunted child.

The world had tried an army.

It had failed.

Now it would begin sending everything else.

# Chapter Nine

## The Road Without Banners

They did not use the king’s road.

Captain Vale refused it before the sun had fully risen.

“The armies will watch every bridge, every village, every trade crossing.”

Caldrin glanced toward the distant line of smoke rising from Castle Darkheart.

“And Victor?”

“He knows the same roads I do.”

Aurelia adjusted Zee against her chest.

“Then where?”

Vale pointed toward the western forest.

“There are old hunting paths beyond the cliffs. They will slow us.”

“Slow is better than found.”

Vale nodded.

They entered the trees.

The forest swallowed them quickly.

Ancient oaks grew so close together that daylight reached the ground only in broken shafts. Moss covered stones larger than houses. Roots twisted across the earth like sleeping serpents. Somewhere far off, water moved beneath rock.

Zee remained awake for much of the morning.

The world outside Castle Darkheart seemed to hold him differently.

No walls.

No ceiling.

No constant echo of siege weapons.

Wind moved across his face for the first time.

Leaves shifted overhead.

Birds called from branches.

The crimson hatchling reacted to everything.

He snapped at falling leaves.

Stumbled after drifting insects.

Growled at a squirrel.

Then hurried back toward Zee whenever he wandered more than a few steps away.

The Dragon Link had changed since the crypts.

Not dramatically.

But enough.

Distance now carried discomfort.

Nearness brought relief.

When the hatchling moved too far ahead, Zee became restless.

When he returned, Zee relaxed.

Aurelia noticed.

“So you truly cannot leave him.”

The hatchling looked up at her.

He probably understood nothing except tone.

Then Zee reached toward him.

The hatchling climbed onto Aurelia’s cloak and settled near the child.

Caldrin watched from several paces away.

“I have seen warhounds less devoted.”

Vale looked at him.

“He is not a hound.”

“I noticed the wings.”

The witch almost smiled.

Almost.

The sound of distant horns killed the moment.

Everyone stopped.

Vale raised one hand.

“Down.”

They moved behind a ridge covered in fern and stone.

The horns sounded again.

Closer than before.

Aurelia lowered herself carefully.

“Darkheart?”

Vale listened.

“No.”

“How can you tell?”

“Victor uses three-note calls. Those are northern.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Wolf kingdom.”

Vale nodded.

The witch’s expression tightened.

“How did they get this far west?”

“They were already surrounding the castle.”

“No,” Vale said. “These are not siege troops.”

He looked through the trees.

“These are hunters.”

Aurelia’s arms tightened around Zee.

The world had changed tactics quickly.

Too quickly.

---

The hunters came on foot.

Seven of them.

No banners.

No armor bright enough to catch sunlight.

Every man wore gray hide over leather and carried a short spear, curved knife, and bow.

The leader walked with his nose slightly raised.

Wolf-blood.

Not transformed.

Not fully beast.

But enough.

He stopped near a patch of disturbed earth.

“There.”

One hunter crouched.

“Five adults.”

“Four,” the leader corrected.

He touched the ground.

“And something small.”

Another man frowned.

“Dragon?”

“Maybe.”

The leader looked west.

“They are moving slowly.”

A younger hunter smiled.

“Then we catch them before dark.”

The leader did not smile.

“You saw the castle.”

“So?”

“You saw what happened when everyone rushed.”

The younger hunter’s grin faded.

The leader stood.

“We are not soldiers.”

His gaze moved through the forest.

“We do this properly.”

He removed a black leather pouch from his belt.

Inside rested small iron needles.

Each tip had been coated in pale paste.

The youngest hunter looked uneasy.

“What poison?”

“Sleep first.”

“And if that fails?”

The leader closed the pouch.

“Then pain.”

---

Vale found the first trap before anyone stepped into it.

A wire stretched between two roots.

Nearly invisible.

He crouched.

“Hunters.”

Caldrin moved beside him.

“Recently placed.”

Vale nodded.

The witch looked around.

“They are ahead of us?”

“No.”

Vale touched the wire.

“Beside us.”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“We are surrounded.”

“Not yet.”

A small sound came from the trees.

The hatchling snapped his head toward it.

Danger.

The feeling hit Zee.

He began squirming.

Aurelia looked down.

“What is it?”

The hatchling hissed toward a cluster of brush.

Vale drew his sword.

“Stay behind me.”

The arrow came from the opposite direction.

It struck Vale beneath the shoulder.

He grunted and staggered.

“Vale!”

Caldrin dragged him behind a tree.

Another arrow struck the trunk where his head had been.

The witch raised both hands.

Blue-violet mana spread outward into a curved barrier.

Three more arrows hit it.

One shattered.

Two stuck halfway through.

She stared.

“They are treated.”

Vale looked at the arrow buried in his shoulder.

His breathing had already changed.

“Numb.”

Caldrin snapped the shaft.

“Poison.”

Aurelia looked around.

“Can you heal him?”

“Not while they are shooting at us.”

The hatchling growled again.

Zee’s Crimson Mana thickened around his body.

Aurelia felt warmth rise beneath the blanket.

“No.”

She lowered her voice.

“Stay calm.”

Zee did not understand the words.

He understood her fear.

That made calm impossible.

Another arrow struck the magical barrier.

Then another.

The hunters were testing it.

Caldrin looked toward the witch.

“How long?”

“Against arrows?”

“Yes.”

“Long enough.”

“Against whatever comes after the arrows?”

She glanced at him.

“Less long.”

He drew two knives.

“Good.”

Then vanished into the trees.

Aurelia stared.

“Where is he going?”

Vale grunted.

“To make them regret standing still.”

---

The first hunter never saw Caldrin.

A hand covered his mouth.

A blade entered beneath his ribs.

Caldrin lowered him silently.

Then moved.

The second hunter heard something.

Turned.

Saw nothing.

“Renn?”

No answer.

He raised his bow.

Caldrin stepped from behind the tree and struck him across the throat with the hilt of his knife.

The man collapsed.

Not dead.

Unconscious.

Caldrin took his bow.

Across the clearing, the wolf-blooded leader smelled blood.

He turned.

“Spread.”

Too late.

Caldrin’s stolen arrow struck one hunter in the thigh.

The man shouted.

Formation broke.

The witch seized the moment.

Her barrier collapsed inward.

Then burst outward.

Blue-violet force tore through the trees.

Two hunters were thrown off their feet.

Vale forced himself upright despite the poison.

“Go.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“You cannot even hold your sword.”

“Then I will throw it.”

Another arrow came.

The hatchling moved before anyone else.

He leaped from Aurelia’s shoulder.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed.

His tiny wings opened.

For the first time, they caught air properly.

Not flight.

A jump made longer.

The arrow passed beneath him.

The hatchling landed hard, rolled through leaves, and sprang up furious.

The hunter who fired froze.

“What in the—”

The hatchling charged.

The man lowered his bow, uncertain whether to laugh or defend himself.

That hesitation cost him.

Tiny claws caught his face.

He screamed.

The hatchling clung on stubbornly.

“Get it off!”

A second hunter reached for him.

Zee felt Zareth’s fear through the Link.

Sharp.

Immediate.

Danger.

Something inside Zee answered.

Not magic first.

Instinct.

Predator.

His pupils narrowed.

His small fangs lengthened.

Crimson Mana gathered along his hands.

Aurelia felt the shift.

“Zee?”

He turned toward the hunter threatening the hatchling.

The forest sound changed.

No thunder.

No great explosion.

Only a pulse.

The hunter stopped moving.

His body locked.

Not frozen by ice.

Held.

The man’s arm remained raised halfway toward the hatchling.

His eyes widened.

“What—”

The hatchling escaped his reach and scrambled away.

Zee’s mana flickered.

The hunter collapsed to his knees.

The effect vanished instantly.

The witch stared.

Aurelia looked at her.

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“Your face did.”

A scream came from deeper in the forest.

Caldrin emerged dragging the last conscious hunter by the collar.

The wolf-blooded leader remained missing.

Vale noticed.

“Where is the pack leader?”

Caldrin let the prisoner fall.

“Gone.”

“That is bad.”

“I thought so too.”

Aurelia looked around.

The hatchling ran back to Zee.

The Dragon Link flooded with relief.

Near.

Safe.

His crimson scales were scratched but intact.

Aurelia touched his side carefully.

“You reckless little thing.”

He chirped at her.

Vale swayed.

The witch caught him.

“We need shelter.”

Caldrin looked toward the unconscious hunters.

“And them?”

Vale forced his eyes open.

“Leave them.”

Aurelia stared.

“They came for my child.”

“Yes.”

“And they will come again.”

Vale looked at her.

“Probably.”

“Then why leave them?”

“Because every corpse teaches the next hunter something.”

Caldrin nodded.

“Alive, they report confusion.”

“Dead, someone studies what killed them.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

Already the world had begun learning from him.

Vale was right.

She hated that he was right.

“Take their poison.”

Caldrin smiled faintly.

“Now you are thinking like a fugitive queen.”

“I am still a queen.”

“Of course.”

“Remember that.”

His smile vanished.

“Yes, Your Majesty.”

They left the hunters behind.

---

The wolf-blooded leader watched from half a mile away.

He had retreated the moment the child’s strange force locked his man in place.

Not from cowardice.

From discipline.

He had been hired to confirm three things.

Whether the child lived.

Whether the queen had escaped.

Whether the dragon hatchling remained with him.

He had confirmed all three.

The contract had not required death.

Not yet.

He crouched beside a stream and cleaned blood from his hand.

Then removed a narrow strip of parchment.

He wrote only six words.

**THE CHILD LIVES. THE QUEEN FLEES.**

He hesitated.

Then added:

**DO NOT APPROACH HIM CARELESSLY.**

The message left by raven before sunset.

By midnight, three kingdoms would receive copies.

One would increase the bounty.

One would hire witches instead of hunters.

One would decide that capturing Aurelia was easier than capturing Zee.

The hunt changed again.

---

They found shelter inside the ruins of an old roadside monastery.

Its roof had collapsed in places. Roots grew through the chapel floor. The altar had been split down the middle, but the underground storeroom remained dry.

The witch removed Vale’s armor.

The poison had spread along his shoulder in dark veins.

Aurelia sat beside him while Zee slept nearby wrapped in several blankets.

The crimson hatchling refused sleep.

He lay beside Zee with golden eyes fixed on every entrance.

Caldrin returned from checking the perimeter.

“No movement.”

“For now,” Vale muttered.

The witch pressed both hands around the wound.

Blue-violet mana sank into his shoulder.

He grimaced.

“What poison?”

“Wolfroot mixed with grave-milk.”

Caldrin frowned.

“That sounds expensive.”

“It is.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

“So someone paid well.”

“Yes.”

The queen’s expression darkened.

“They did not come with banners.”

“No.”

“They were not soldiers.”

“No.”

She looked toward Zee.

“The armies failed.”

Caldrin understood.

“So the world is learning.”

Aurelia said nothing.

That possibility frightened her.

Not because Zee could not survive.

She had watched death fail.

But now survival had consequences.

Every enemy would bring a new method.

Every method would reveal something.

And every revelation would travel.

Vale opened his eyes.

“We cannot keep moving randomly.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“House Vesper.”

He nodded.

“How far?”

“If we stay off the roads? Twelve days.”

Caldrin laughed quietly.

“With half the western kingdoms hunting us?”

“Maybe fifteen.”

The witch looked toward Zee.

“He will not survive fifteen days without proper shelter.”

Aurelia’s expression changed.

Everyone looked at her.

She knew what they were thinking.

Zee could return from death.

That did not mean suffering had become meaningless.

He could starve.

Freeze.

Be captured.

Be taken from her.

Aurelia’s voice hardened.

“He will not be used as proof that hardship no longer matters.”

No one argued.

Vale slowly sat upright.

“There is a village two days west.”

“Friendly?”

“No.”

Caldrin raised an eyebrow.

“Excellent.”

Vale ignored him.

“It belongs to no crown directly. Traders, deserters, mercenaries.”

Aurelia frowned.

“Bandits.”

“Some.”

“Assassins?”

“Probably.”

“Wonderful.”

“But supplies will be available without questions if we pay.”

Aurelia looked toward the ruined altar above them.

Royal jewels still lined the inside of her traveling cloak.

Enough to purchase horses.

Food.

Information.

Perhaps betrayal too.

“Then we go.”

---

That night, Zee woke hungry.

Aurelia fed him beside a small hidden fire.

The hatchling watched.

When Zee finished, the child looked toward the dragon.

Hunger.

The simple feeling passed.

Aurelia blinked.

“You are hungry too.”

The hatchling chirped urgently.

Caldrin opened one eye from across the room.

“Finally.”

He tossed a strip of raw rabbit toward him.

The hatchling sniffed it.

Then ate greedily.

Vale managed a weak laugh.

“So dragons do not eat gemstones.”

“Someone tried that?”

Aurelia looked offended.

“The kitchen staff panicked.”

Caldrin smiled.

For a few minutes, the ruined monastery felt almost peaceful.

Zee made a soft sound.

The hatchling moved beside him.

Their heads rested near one another.

Comfort.

Warmth.

Safe.

Aurelia watched them.

Then the fire dimmed.

Every adult looked up.

The witch stood.

“I did not do that.”

Cold spread through the underground room.

The hatchling woke instantly.

A low growl escaped him.

Zee’s Crimson Mana stirred.

Something scratched across the stone floor above.

Slowly.

Once.

Twice.

Then stopped.

Caldrin drew his sword.

Vale reached for his despite the bandaged shoulder.

Aurelia lifted Zee.

The scratching came again.

Not from above this time.

From behind the wall.

The witch’s face went pale.

“There is nothing behind that wall.”

Caldrin looked at her.

“Apparently there is now.”

The stones bulged inward.

One cracked.

A black claw pushed through.

Not human.

Not wolf.

Not vampire.

The hatchling hissed.

Zee stared.

The claw ripped a second stone loose.

A smell entered the room.

Rot.

Smoke.

And something sweet beneath both.

Vale whispered,

“That is not one of the hunters.”

The wall burst inward.

A creature crawled through.

Long-limbed.

Skin stretched black over bone.

Two mouths opened along its face.

Neither contained a tongue.

Blue fire burned inside its chest.

The witch stepped backward.

Caldrin raised his sword.

“What is that?”

No one answered.

The creature looked past every adult.

Directly at Zee.

Then both mouths smiled.

The armies had failed.

The hunters had failed.

Now something else had found him.

# Chapter Nine

## The Road of Teeth

The western road had been abandoned before Aurelia ever reached it.

That was the first thing Captain Vale noticed.

No merchants.

No pilgrims.

No wagons.

No patrols from nearby villages.

Only wheel ruts hardened in old mud and a line of overturned carts left beneath a stand of black pines.

Caldrin crouched beside one of them.

“Too clean.”

Aurelia shifted Zee higher against her shoulder.

“What does that mean?”

“No bodies.”

The royal witch scanned the tree line.

“Maybe whoever attacked them took the dead.”

Caldrin stood.

“Maybe.”

The crimson hatchling pressed against Zee beneath Aurelia’s cloak.

The two had grown quieter since leaving Castle Darkheart.

Not calmer.

More aware.

The Dragon Link had begun carrying new flashes between them.

Not words.

Shapes.

Cold.

Movement.

The direction of fear.

Zee turned his head toward the forest.

The hatchling did the same.

Vale saw it.

“You both felt something?”

The hatchling’s scales tightened along his spine.

Zee’s Crimson Mana stirred.

Caldrin drew his sword.

That was answer enough.

Something moved between the trees.

Fast.

Low.

Then another shape crossed behind it.

Aurelia stopped.

“How many?”

Vale whispered, “Pack.”

The first wolf stepped onto the road.

It was enormous.

Larger than any natural wolf.

Its fur was gray-black and soaked with old blood. One ear had been torn away. Its yellow eyes fixed on Zee before moving to the dragon hatchling.

Then came the second.

Third.

Sixth.

Tenth.

The pack spread across the road and tree line until retreat vanished.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Violet mana gathered around her wrists.

“Werewolves?”

Vale studied them.

“No.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Then what?”

Vale’s expression darkened.

“Wildbloods.”

The alpha growled.

A sound answered from deeper in the forest.

Dozens more.

Aurelia tightened her hold around Zee.

“Explain quickly.”

“Wolves born too close to old magic,” Vale said. “Not shifters. Not beasts anymore either.”

The alpha took one step forward.

Then stopped.

Its nostrils flared.

It smelled Zee.

Something passed through the entire pack.

Confusion.

Hunger.

Fear.

The wolves lowered their bodies.

Not submission.

Preparation.

The attack came all at once.

Vale met the first wolf with his sword.

Steel cut across its shoulder.

The wound barely slowed it.

Caldrin drove his blade through another’s jaw.

The witch released a violet shockwave that threw three wolves into the trees.

More replaced them.

Aurelia backed toward the overturned carts.

The hatchling climbed from beneath her cloak.

“No.”

He ignored her.

Tiny crimson wings spread.

Teal-and-gold mana crawled along his scales.

Zee felt the intention.

Protect.

He reached toward the hatchling.

The Dragon Link answered with something simple.

Together.

A wolf leaped.

The hatchling screamed.

Teal-and-gold fire burst from his mouth.

Not large.

Not controlled.

But hot enough to strike the wolf across the face.

It crashed into the road, smoking.

The pack recoiled.

For one moment.

Then the alpha charged.

Vale moved to intercept.

Too slow.

The wolf hit him like a battering ram and threw him into a tree.

Aurelia turned.

The alpha came for Zee.

Zee stared at it.

His crimson eyes widened.

The wolf scent entered him.

Predator.

Pack.

Territory.

Threat.

His own wolf nature answered.

Not with transformation.

With instinct.

A low growl came from the newborn’s chest.

Every Wildblood stopped.

The sound was too small to matter.

Yet it did.

The alpha’s ears flattened.

Zee growled again.

His Crimson Mana spread into the air.

The pack began whining.

Aurelia stared.

The alpha fought whatever instinct had seized it.

Then lunged anyway.

The hatchling attacked first.

He slammed into the wolf’s muzzle and bit down.

The alpha shook violently.

The hatchling flew sideways.

Zee screamed.

The Dragon Link flooded with pain.

The world around him narrowed.

He could feel the hatchling’s fear.

His anger answered before thought.

Crimson Mana erupted from Zee’s body.

Not as a wave.

As pressure.

The alpha collapsed mid-step.

Every wolf on the road dropped with it.

No bones broke.

No blood spilled.

They simply flattened against the earth as though the air itself had become too heavy to resist.

The witch stared.

Vale pushed himself upright.

Caldrin stopped fighting.

Aurelia looked down at her son.

Zee was crying now.

Furious.

The hatchling crawled back toward him.

The moment their bodies touched, the pressure vanished.

The wolves gasped.

Several immediately fled.

Others limped backward.

The alpha remained.

Its eyes fixed on Zee.

Not hunger anymore.

Recognition.

Something in the newborn’s scent had changed.

Or perhaps the wolf had simply noticed what it had ignored before.

Zee was not prey.

The alpha lowered its head.

Then turned away.

The rest of the pack followed.

Within moments, the road was empty again.

Caldrin stared after them.

“I preferred the dead men in the crypt.”

Vale coughed.

“You say that now.”

Aurelia ignored both of them.

She looked at Zee.

“What did you do?”

The child hiccuped.

The hatchling nudged his cheek.

Safe.

Zee relaxed.

The royal witch approached carefully.

“My Queen…”

Aurelia glanced at her.

The woman corrected herself immediately.

“I do not know.”

“Good.”

The witch almost smiled.

Almost.

Vale walked toward the place where the alpha had fallen.

He crouched and touched the earth.

No spell mark.

No scorch.

Nothing.

Only deep impressions where claws had dug into the road.

“He did not cast.”

Caldrin looked at Zee.

“No.”

Vale stood.

“He commanded.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“You do not know that either.”

“No.”

Vale sheathed his sword.

“But the wolves believed he did.”

That mattered.

Perhaps too much.

---

The road grew worse by afternoon.

They left it.

Caldrin led them into the foothills where ancient hunting paths wound between dark trees and limestone ridges.

Aurelia’s body began failing before sunset.

She refused to admit it.

The royal witch noticed anyway.

“You need rest.”

“We need distance.”

“You gave birth days ago.”

“I remember.”

“You were wounded.”

“I remember that too.”

“You cannot keep walking.”

Aurelia stopped.

Her eyes hardened.

“Then carry me when I fall.”

The witch said nothing after that.

Zee slept.

The hatchling did not.

He rode against Aurelia’s shoulder, staring constantly into the woods.

Something had changed after the Wildblood attack.

His protectiveness had become sharper.

More deliberate.

He had felt Zee die once.

Now every danger seemed to carry the memory of absence.

The Dragon Link repeated one instinct again and again.

Stay close.

Zee answered even while sleeping.

Warmth.

Near.

The bond quieted.

Caldrin stopped suddenly.

Everyone froze.

Vale whispered, “What?”

Caldrin pointed toward the ground.

A footprint.

Human.

Then another.

Fresh.

Vale followed the trail with his eyes.

“Not ours.”

The witch lowered her voice.

“Soldiers?”

Caldrin shook his head.

“Too light.”

“Scouts?”

“No armor marks.”

Aurelia looked toward the trees.

“Assassins.”

Caldrin smiled without humor.

“Probably.”

The first arrow came from above.

It struck the witch’s barrier.

Violet light flashed.

“Down!”

Vale pulled Aurelia behind a rock.

Three more arrows hit the barrier.

The fourth passed through.

Not because the shield failed.

Because the arrowhead carried a seal etched into black metal.

It disrupted the spell on contact.

The witch stared.

“Anti-magic iron.”

Caldrin cursed.

Figures appeared along the ridge.

Six.

No banners.

No armor.

Mercenaries.

One raised a crossbow.

“Alive if possible!”

Another called back.

“The queen too?”

“Not required!”

Aurelia’s face went cold.

The bounty had already traveled.

Faster than expected.

Vale drew his sword.

“They are not soldiers.”

Caldrin unsheathed both blades.

“That makes them worse.”

The mercenaries descended.

They knew what they were doing.

One targeted the witch.

Two went for Vale.

Two spread wide to cut off Caldrin.

The last stayed behind with the crossbow.

No one charged Aurelia directly.

Not yet.

They wanted the defenders separated first.

The witch cast.

Violet force struck one mercenary.

He threw a black metal disk into the ground.

Her spell collapsed around it.

Caldrin saw.

“Runes!”

“They prepared for witches!”

“Of course they did.”

The world was already learning.

That frightened Aurelia more than the attack itself.

These men had heard reports.

They had adapted.

The next hunters would know even more.

Vale blocked a sword strike.

Caldrin buried a blade beneath another mercenary’s ribs.

The witch tried a different spell.

The black disk disrupted that too.

The crossbowman aimed.

At Zee.

Aurelia saw it.

“No!”

The bolt fired.

The hatchling reacted.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed.

He spread his wings in front of Zee.

The bolt struck him.

The tiny dragon screamed.

Aurelia screamed with him.

The projectile had pierced one wing.

The Dragon Link flooded Zee with pain.

Sharp.

Hot.

Wrong.

Zee woke instantly.

His crimson eyes opened.

The hatchling fell from Aurelia’s shoulder.

Blood stained his crimson scales.

Zee stared.

The mercenary reloaded.

Something inside Zee shifted.

Not power arriving from nowhere.

Instinct finding a path.

His vampire senses sharpened.

He heard the crossbow string tighten.

He heard the man’s heartbeat.

He smelled blood from the wound in Zareth’s wing.

He smelled every living body around him.

Six rhythms.

Five.

Four.

His perception narrowed until the forest seemed suddenly too slow.

Crimson Mana gathered around his eyes.

The crossbowman fired again.

Zee turned his head.

The bolt stopped inches from his face.

Not suspended by force this time.

Caught.

Aurelia stared.

Zee’s tiny hand was wrapped around the shaft.

No newborn should have possessed the reflexes.

No newborn should have possessed the grip.

The mercenary stared too.

That hesitation killed him.

Caldrin’s throwing knife struck his throat.

He fell.

The remaining mercenaries broke.

One ran.

Vale caught him.

Another surrendered.

Caldrin did not care.

The witch turned toward the hatchling.

“Let me see him.”

Zee began crying.

The sound was different.

Not fear.

Rage.

The hatchling’s blood touched Zee’s hand.

Crimson Mana reacted immediately.

It crawled toward the wound.

The witch stopped.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia looked.

Teal-and-gold Dragon Mana flickered around the damaged wing.

Zee’s Crimson Mana touched it.

For a moment, the two powers met.

They did not merge.

They did not become the same.

The teal-and-gold remained Zareth’s.

The crimson remained Zee’s.

But Zee reacted to what he felt through the Link.

Pain.

Torn flesh.

Heal.

His mana tightened around his own fingers.

Something inside his blood seemed to study the injury without understanding it.

Then the hatchling’s wound began closing faster.

Not instantly.

Not completely.

But faster than before.

The witch stared.

Aurelia looked at Zee.

He had not healed Zareth.

Not exactly.

Something about their bond had pushed his own dragon vitality harder.

The hatchling’s breathing steadied.

Zee stopped crying.

Safe?

The hatchling nudged his hand.

Safe.

Caldrin approached with blood on both swords.

“You should see this.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

One mercenary remained alive.

Vale held him on his knees.

The man was young.

Younger than Aurelia expected.

Terrified.

Caldrin pulled a folded parchment from his coat.

A bounty notice.

A rough sketch of Zee covered the center.

Crimson eyes.

Fangs.

A dragon beside him.

Below it:

**THE DARKHEART TRIBRID**

**TWENTY THOUSAND SILVER CROWNS ALIVE**

**TEN THOUSAND DEAD**

**ADDITIONAL PAYMENT FOR BLOOD, TEETH, OR CONFIRMED MAGICAL REMAINS**

Aurelia stopped breathing.

Vale read over her shoulder.

His face changed.

“Who issued this?”

The mercenary spat blood.

“Does it matter?”

Caldrin pressed a blade beneath his chin.

“Yes.”

The man laughed nervously.

“Half the continent will issue one by winter.”

Aurelia stepped forward.

“Who paid you?”

The mercenary looked at Zee.

Fear crossed his face.

Not because Zee threatened him.

Because the child existed.

“A broker in Red Hollow.”

“Working for whom?”

“I do not know.”

Caldrin increased pressure.

“You expect us to believe that?”

“I swear.”

The man swallowed.

“Contracts are being sold everywhere.”

“Kings?”

“Some.”

“Witches?”

“Yes.”

“Vampires?”

“Yes.”

“Wolves?”

The mercenary hesitated.

“Some packs are paying for information.”

Vale’s expression darkened.

Aurelia looked at the parchment again.

Three days old.

Zee was three days old.

And the world had already turned his body into currency.

She tore the bounty in half.

Then again.

And again.

The pieces fell into the dirt.

“Let him go.”

Caldrin looked at her.

“My Queen?”

“Let him go.”

Vale frowned.

“He knows our direction.”

“Exactly.”

Aurelia stepped toward the mercenary.

The man recoiled.

She looked down at him.

“You will go back.”

“To whom?”

“Everyone.”

Her voice remained calm.

“You will tell every broker, king, witch, vampire, hunter, and bastard who thinks my son is worth silver that they failed.”

The mercenary stared.

Aurelia continued.

“And tell them something else.”

Her eyes hardened.

“The price is too low.”

Caldrin smiled.

Vale released the man.

He ran.

No one stopped him.

The story would travel.

Not accurately.

Stories never did.

But it would travel.

The Tribrid lived.

The dragon lived.

The first bounty had failed.

And whoever came next would come prepared for what the mercenaries had learned.

---

That night, they made camp inside the ruins of an abandoned shrine.

No fire.

No songs.

No guards standing openly.

Only darkness.

The witch slept first.

Vale watched the eastern approach.

Caldrin watched the west.

Aurelia sat against a broken statue with Zee in her arms and the hatchling curled across her lap.

The injury in his wing had nearly closed.

Too quickly.

Aurelia touched the repaired membrane gently.

The hatchling opened one eye.

“You almost died for him.”

The tiny dragon blinked.

“You are both insane.”

He chirped.

Zee stirred.

Aurelia smiled despite herself.

For a few breaths, there was peace.

Then Zee’s eyes opened.

He looked toward the darkness outside the shrine.

His vampire hearing caught something distant.

A heartbeat.

Then another.

Then another.

Not human.

Too slow.

Too deep.

He did not understand what he heard.

But the wolf inside him recognized the scent carried by the wind.

Predator.

The hatchling lifted his head.

The Dragon Link tightened.

Danger.

Aurelia saw both infants react.

Her smile vanished.

“Vale.”

The captain stood immediately.

“What?”

Caldrin rose too.

The royal witch woke.

Aurelia looked toward the tree line.

“We are not alone.”

A growl answered from the darkness.

Not wolf.

Not Wildblood.

Something larger.

Two pale eyes opened between the trees.

Then four more.

Then eight.

Caldrin drew his sword.

“I suppose sleeping was too ambitious.”

Vale stepped in front of Aurelia.

The creatures began moving toward the shrine.

Zee watched them come.

Three days old.

Already hunted by kingdoms.

Already hunted by mercenaries.

Now hunted by something with no interest in money at all.

And beneath his skin, the First Natural Tribrid remembered every danger that had touched him.

The world had learned to hunt differently.

So had Zee.

# Chapter Ten

## The Things in the Trees

The growl came again.

Low.

Wet.

Too deep to belong to any wolf Aurelia had ever heard.

Captain Vale moved in front of the ruined shrine entrance with his sword raised while Caldrin circled toward the broken western wall. The royal witch stood behind them, both hands already glowing with violet mana.

Aurelia remained near the fallen statue with Zee held close.

The crimson hatchling climbed onto her shoulder and spread his wings.

Teal-and-gold mana moved beneath his scales in thin currents.

The eyes beyond the trees multiplied.

Pale.

Unblinking.

Watching.

Caldrin whispered, “Not Wildbloods.”

Vale answered, “No.”

“Good.”

“That was not reassurance.”

Something stepped into the moonlight.

It looked almost like a wolf.

Almost.

Its front legs were too long.

Its ribs pushed visibly beneath hairless gray skin.

Its jaw split farther back than any natural animal’s should have, exposing rows of narrow teeth slick with black saliva.

Two more emerged behind it.

Then five.

Then twelve.

The royal witch’s expression tightened.

“Gravehounds.”

Aurelia looked toward her.

“You know these?”

“I know the stories.”

Caldrin glanced back.

“I am rapidly developing a hatred for stories.”

The witch ignored him.

“They hunt burial grounds. Battlefields. Plague pits. Anywhere death gathers long enough.”

Vale studied the pack.

“Then why are they here?”

The nearest Gravehound lowered its head.

Its nostrils flared.

Toward Zee.

Aurelia’s stomach tightened.

Caldrin answered quietly.

“They smelled someone who died.”

Silence.

The hatchling growled.

The Gravehound pack erupted forward.

Vale met the first one with steel.

His blade struck the creature’s shoulder and cut nearly to bone.

It did not slow.

The hound twisted and snapped at his throat.

Vale barely blocked with his forearm guard before kicking it away.

Caldrin drove both swords into another creature’s ribs.

Black blood spilled.

The animal screamed.

The sound made every other hound more violent.

The royal witch cast.

Violet chains burst from the ground and wrapped around three Gravehounds.

They tore through the first layer.

Not the second.

She clenched both hands.

The chains tightened and dragged the creatures down.

“Move!” she shouted.

Aurelia ran toward the rear of the shrine.

No exit.

Only broken stone and a collapsed wall.

The hatchling suddenly hissed.

Danger.

Left.

Aurelia turned.

A Gravehound had climbed over the ruined roof.

It dropped.

The hatchling launched himself from her shoulder.

Teal-and-gold fire struck the creature across the face.

The Gravehound hit the floor beside Aurelia and rolled.

Still alive.

Still moving.

Zee woke.

His crimson eyes opened.

The smell hit him first.

Rot.

Blood.

Something old in the Gravehound’s flesh.

His vampire instincts reacted.

His wolf nature reacted faster.

Threat.

Pack hunter.

Predator.

But there was something else now.

A memory.

Not a thought.

A bodily memory.

Falling stone.

The Hollow creature.

Pain through the Dragon Link.

The mercenary’s crossbow.

His body recognized danger before his newborn mind could.

The Gravehound lunged.

Aurelia turned to shield Zee.

The creature never reached them.

Zee’s Crimson Mana slammed into it.

The hound stopped in midair and crashed sideways into the broken wall hard enough to crack stone.

Aurelia stared.

The Gravehound rose again.

Its body bent wrong.

Bones shifted beneath its skin.

Then it came back.

Caldrin shouted from across the shrine.

“They do not stay down!”

Vale cut the throat of another.

It kept biting.

The witch changed spells.

Instead of striking the creatures, she sealed the doorway with violet fire.

Two hounds ran directly through it.

Their skin burned.

They did not care.

Caldrin cursed.

“What kills them?”

The witch shouted back, “Enough damage!”

“Excellent!”

A Gravehound slammed into him.

He disappeared beneath it.

Vale rushed forward.

Aurelia saw blood.

The hatchling saw it too.

His fear flashed through the Link.

Zee felt it.

Pain.

Friend.

Danger.

His heartbeat accelerated.

The sounds around him sharpened.

Every Gravehound heartbeat.

Every breath.

Every claw scraping stone.

Too many.

His body had learned the rhythm of predators.

The Wildblood attack had taught him pressure.

The mercenary ambush had sharpened his reflexes.

Now something else began forming.

Recognition of movement.

Not intelligence.

Instinct.

The closest Gravehound shifted its weight before attacking.

Zee reacted before it moved.

Crimson Mana snapped around its legs.

The creature crashed face-first into stone.

The second changed direction.

Zee’s head turned before the hound did.

A burst of force struck it through the side.

The third hesitated.

That hesitation mattered.

The crimson hatchling attacked.

He bit into the Gravehound’s neck and released teal-and-gold fire directly into the wound.

The creature screamed.

This time...

It stayed down.

The witch saw.

“Inside!”

Vale looked toward her.

“What?”

“Burn them from inside!”

Caldrin emerged from beneath the hound pinning him.

Blood ran from his forehead.

“Would have appreciated that earlier.”

He stabbed through the open mouth of the next creature.

The witch cast into the wound.

Violet fire erupted beneath its skin.

The Gravehound collapsed.

Now they had a method.

The fight changed.

Vale drove steel deep enough to create openings.

Caldrin forced jaws wide.

The witch burned through flesh from within.

The hatchling struck where the creatures were already wounded.

Aurelia stayed moving.

Always keeping Zee away from the nearest threat.

But the pack kept coming.

Then the largest Gravehound entered.

The alpha.

It did not rush.

It walked.

Its skin was almost black.

Old scars covered its body.

One eye had been replaced by a pale milky membrane.

Its jaw opened.

Human teeth rested among the animal ones.

Caldrin looked at it.

“I hate that.”

Vale breathed hard.

“Agreed.”

The alpha ignored them.

It stared at Zee.

Then lowered itself.

Not in submission.

In hunger.

The scent of death clung to Zee.

Not because he was dead.

Because death had touched him and failed.

The alpha could smell the contradiction.

It charged.

The witch cast first.

The alpha tore through her binding.

Vale attacked.

The creature struck him aside.

Caldrin went low.

Its claw ripped across his shoulder.

The hatchling launched himself.

The alpha caught him in its jaws.

Zee screamed.

The Dragon Link exploded.

Pain.

Terror.

Darkness.

The hatchling’s wing bent under the pressure.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed wildly.

Zee’s Crimson Mana surged.

The alpha tightened its bite.

Something inside Zee changed.

His attention narrowed entirely onto the creature.

The world around him disappeared.

Only the heartbeat remained.

Slow.

Heavy.

There.

Zee reached.

Not with hands.

With instinct.

The alpha froze.

Its heartbeat stumbled.

Aurelia felt Zee’s small body tense.

The witch stared.

The Gravehound’s chest convulsed.

Its blood shifted beneath the skin.

Not controlled.

Pulled.

The alpha released the hatchling.

Black blood burst from its mouth.

The creature collapsed.

The hatchling fell.

Aurelia caught him with one arm while still holding Zee with the other.

The remaining Gravehounds stopped.

Their alpha lay dead.

Not burned.

Not cut apart.

Something inside it had simply failed.

The pack backed away.

One by one, they disappeared into the trees.

No one chased them.

The shrine fell silent.

Caldrin sat against a broken column.

“Was that him?”

The witch looked at Zee.

“I do not know.”

Vale coughed.

“You say that often.”

“I have learned.”

Aurelia looked down at her son.

His crimson eyes were still fixed on the dead alpha.

Something black moved beneath the Gravehound’s skin.

Then its blood began leaking toward Zee.

Slowly.

Thin threads.

Aurelia stepped back.

“No.”

The blood stopped.

For a moment.

Then Zee’s Crimson Mana reached toward it.

Not deliberately.

Automatically.

The essence entered him.

His body stiffened.

The smell of grave soil and death filled the shrine.

The hatchling whimpered.

Zee’s fangs lengthened slightly.

His heartbeat changed.

Then the blackness inside the absorbed essence met the Crimson Mana.

It began burning away.

Not disappearing.

Changing.

The witch watched with wide eyes.

She said nothing.

The dark threads beneath Zee’s skin turned crimson-black.

Then settled.

The transformation ended.

Zee exhaled.

The dead alpha began decomposing.

Fast.

Within moments, only bones remained.

Caldrin stared.

“Well.”

Vale looked toward him.

“That is all you have?”

“I am injured.”

Aurelia ignored them.

She touched Zee’s cheek.

“What did you take?”

He blinked.

He did not know.

Neither did she.

The hatchling pressed close.

The Dragon Link carried one simple thing.

Alive.

Zee answered.

Alive.

---

They left the shrine before dawn.

No one wanted to remain near the bones.

Caldrin’s shoulder required binding.

Vale limped.

The royal witch had burned through too much mana and needed rest.

Aurelia was exhausted beyond words.

Zee slept.

The hatchling did not.

The road west continued.

But something followed them now.

Not physically.

A story.

A merchant caravan found the Gravehound bones by midday.

They found black blood on the shrine walls.

They found signs of witchfire.

They found a dead alpha stripped down to bone in a way no hunter could explain.

By sunset, the nearest village heard that the Tribrid child had killed a Gravehound pack.

By midnight, the story changed.

The child commanded death-hounds.

By morning, it changed again.

The child ate monsters and stole what made them strong.

None of the witnesses had actually seen Zee.

That did not matter.

The bounty increased.

So did the fear.

And somewhere far ahead, beyond three mountain passes and a river dividing kingdoms, House Vesper received its first reliable report that Queen Aurelia Darkheart was traveling west.

Not alone.

King Lucien Vesper read the message twice.

Then handed it to the boy standing beside him.

Prince Rez Vesper.

Blue-white mana shimmered faintly around the young prince’s fingers.

Rez read the final line.

**The Darkheart child lives.**

He looked up.

“What do we do?”

King Lucien turned toward the western gates.

“We open them.”

# Chapter Eleven

## The Kingdom That Said Yes

House Vesper did not close its gates.

That alone made it different.

Every kingdom Aurelia had passed near since leaving Castle Darkheart had doubled its patrols. Some barred roads. Others searched wagons. Villages displayed bounty notices bearing Zee’s face, each drawing worse than the last.

House Vesper did the opposite.

Its border fires remained lit.

Its bridges remained open.

Travelers still crossed beneath the silver banners of the kingdom without being dragged from horses and questioned about a newborn child.

That did not mean Vesper was peaceful.

The outer walls were enormous.

Soldiers watched every road.

Witches stood beside archers.

War beasts slept beneath covered stone pens near the gates.

This was not softness.

It was confidence.

Caldrin noticed first.

“They know we are coming.”

Vale looked toward the distant towers.

“Yes.”

Aurelia adjusted Zee beneath her cloak.

“Then why have they not sent soldiers?”

The royal witch answered quietly.

“Perhaps they do not intend to stop us.”

Caldrin frowned.

“That would be new.”

The crimson hatchling lifted his head.

The Dragon Link carried curiosity.

Not fear.

That mattered.

They approached the first Vesper checkpoint.

Six soldiers waited.

No weapons drawn.

The officer at the center stepped forward.

“Queen Aurelia Darkheart?”

Vale’s hand moved toward his sword.

The officer noticed.

“You may keep it.”

Vale did.

Aurelia looked at the man.

“Who asks?”

“Captain Soren Vesper.”

“And what do you want?”

“To escort you.”

“Where?”

“To the capital.”

Caldrin laughed quietly.

“That sounds very much like arrest.”

Captain Soren looked at him.

“If this were an arrest, you would already be surrounded.”

Caldrin glanced toward the ridges.

Then smiled.

“We are surrounded.”

“Yes.”

Aurelia’s eyes narrowed.

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“Why have they not attacked?”

Soren looked toward the bundle in her arms.

“Because our king ordered them not to.”

The hatchling moved beneath the cloak.

Soren saw the crimson snout.

He did not reach for a weapon.

He did not kneel.

He simply stared for one second longer than polite.

Then looked back to Aurelia.

“You will be safe inside the capital.”

Aurelia’s expression became cold.

“I no longer believe anyone who says that.”

Soren nodded.

“That is reasonable.”

The answer surprised her.

He continued.

“Then do not believe me.”

“Believe the gates are open.”

“Believe no bounty hunter has crossed them alive.”

“Believe King Lucien has refused every demand to surrender you.”

“Beyond that, decide for yourself.”

Vale studied him.

“Why?”

Soren looked toward the road.

“That answer belongs to the king.”

Aurelia hesitated.

Then she looked down at Zee.

Three days of running.

Blood.

Monsters.

Mercenaries.

Gravehounds.

Her body could not keep this pace much longer.

Zee needed shelter.

Even temporary shelter.

She nodded.

“Take us to Lucien.”

---

The Vesper capital rose from a valley of white stone and dark rivers.

It was nothing like Castle Darkheart.

Darkheart had been built upward, black towers clawing at the sky.

Vesper spread outward.

Terraced walls followed the land instead of dominating it. Silver banners hung from towers shaped like open hands. Bridges connected districts divided by narrow rivers. Marketplaces remained crowded despite rumors of war.

People saw Aurelia’s escort.

They saw the guards.

They saw the queen beneath her hood.

Some recognized her.

Whispers began.

Then someone noticed the dragon hatchling.

A child pointed.

Aurelia tensed.

No one attacked.

No one ran.

People stared.

That was all.

For Zee, it was the first crowd that did not immediately become danger.

He watched from Aurelia’s arms.

Crimson eyes curious.

The hatchling looked too.

The Dragon Link carried something unfamiliar.

People.

Noise.

Smell.

Food.

Zee responded with hunger.

The hatchling chirped.

Aurelia almost laughed.

“You two have survived armies and monsters, and this is what interests you.”

Food.

The feeling returned.

Caldrin heard the chirp.

“I agree with the dragon.”

“No one asked you.”

“I am wounded.”

“You have mentioned.”

“Because no one appreciates me.”

Vale looked toward him.

“I appreciate silence.”

Caldrin sighed.

The tension eased.

Only slightly.

Then the palace gates opened.

King Lucien Vesper waited inside.

He wore no armor.

No crown either.

Only a dark blue coat embroidered with silver thread.

Beside him stood a boy.

Perhaps seven years old.

Dark-haired.

Sharp-eyed.

Blue-white mana moved faintly around his fingers before disappearing.

Prince Rez Vesper.

Aurelia stopped.

Lucien descended the palace steps alone.

No guards followed.

“Aurelia.”

She did not bow.

“Lucien.”

His eyes moved toward Zee.

Then the hatchling.

He took in both.

No fear entered his face.

Interest did.

Concern.

But not fear.

That alone nearly made Aurelia distrust him more.

“You know what happened?” she asked.

“Some of it.”

“How much?”

“Enough to know most reports are nonsense.”

Caldrin muttered, “Finally.”

Lucien continued.

“I know the sky bled.”

“I know wolves lost control.”

“I know vampires felt something in their blood.”

“I know witches briefly struggled to reach their own power.”

“I know your son has visible vampire traits, wolf blood, witch nature, and mana no one recognizes.”

Aurelia’s grip tightened.

Lucien saw it.

“I did not say I understand him.”

She relaxed slightly.

“Good.”

“I do not.”

He looked toward Zee.

“And I do not need to understand a child before deciding not to murder him.”

Silence.

Aurelia stared at him.

Behind Lucien, Rez watched Zee carefully.

Not with fear.

With fascination.

Lucien stepped aside.

“You may enter.”

Aurelia did not move.

“Why?”

“Because twelve kingdoms marched against a newborn.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No.”

Lucien looked toward the silver banners above the palace.

“Because House Vesper does not decide innocence by majority vote.”

Aurelia studied him.

“And if Zee becomes dangerous?”

Lucien answered without hesitation.

“Then we deal with what he does.”

“Not what frightened men imagine he might do.”

The words hit Aurelia harder than she expected.

For a moment, she could not speak.

Then Rez moved.

He stepped from behind his father.

Lucien looked down at him.

“Rez.”

“I know.”

The boy stopped several feet from Aurelia.

His attention remained on Zee.

The hatchling raised his head.

Teal-and-gold mana flickered.

Rez’s blue-white mana reacted instinctively.

Aurelia tensed.

Lucien lifted one hand.

“Rez.”

The mana vanished.

Rez looked annoyed.

“I was not attacking.”

“I know.”

The boy looked toward Aurelia.

“Can he hear me?”

Aurelia frowned.

“He is a newborn.”

Rez nodded.

“That was a stupid question.”

Caldrin coughed to hide a laugh.

Rez ignored him.

He looked at the hatchling.

“And that one?”

“He cannot speak either.”

Rez considered.

“Good.”

Aurelia raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“People talk too much.”

Lucien closed his eyes briefly.

“My son.”

“What?”

“Try hospitality.”

Rez looked back at Zee.

Then held out one finger.

He did not touch him.

He simply waited.

Zee stared.

The crimson hatchling watched.

The Dragon Link carried uncertainty.

New.

Zee moved.

His tiny hand reached out.

Aurelia almost pulled him back.

Then stopped.

Zee’s fingers closed around Rez’s.

Blue-white mana flickered.

Crimson Mana answered.

The two powers touched.

Neither consumed the other.

Neither changed.

They simply existed together for one brief moment.

Rez’s eyes widened.

Zee blinked.

The hatchling chirped.

Something quiet passed through the courtyard.

No prophecy.

No revelation.

No ancient certainty.

Only the beginning of a relationship no one yet understood.

Rez smiled.

“He is warm.”

Aurelia laughed.

A real laugh.

The first in days.

Then a horn sounded from the outer walls.

Everyone turned.

Captain Soren appeared at the courtyard entrance.

“My King.”

Lucien’s expression changed.

“What?”

“Riders at the eastern gate.”

“How many?”

“Three.”

“Banner?”

“None.”

Caldrin sighed.

“Assassins.”

Soren shook his head.

“Worse.”

Vale looked toward him.

“What is worse than assassins?”

Soren’s face hardened.

“They are carrying royal seals.”

Lucien looked toward Aurelia.

“Which kingdoms?”

“Twelve.”

The courtyard went silent.

The coalition had found her.

Lucien’s jaw tightened.

“What do they demand?”

Soren answered.

“Queen Aurelia and the Tribrid child.”

Rez still held Zee’s hand.

Lucien looked at his son.

Then at Aurelia.

Then toward the eastern walls.

“Tell them no.”

Soren nodded.

“They also say refusal will be considered an act of war.”

Lucien smiled without humor.

“Then they finally understand where we stand.”

He turned toward the palace.

“Raise the shields.”

The Vesper bells began ringing.

Soldiers moved.

Witches took their positions.

Blue-white ward fires ignited along the upper walls.

Aurelia stared at Lucien.

“You would risk your kingdom for him?”

Lucien looked back.

“No.”

Her expression changed.

Then he continued.

“I would risk my kingdom for the right to decide what kind of kingdom it is.”

Outside the city, twelve royal riders waited for an answer.

Inside, Zee Darkheart entered the first kingdom that had chosen not to fear him before knowing him.

And before the sun set, House Vesper would discover exactly what accepting the First Tribrid cost.
