# Chapter Twelve

## The Price of Sanctuary

House Vesper raised its shields before the twelve riders reached the outer court.

The transformation of the capital was immediate.

Silver bells rang from tower to tower. Market gates closed. Civilian bridges lifted. Ward-stones buried along the terraced walls awakened in sequence, throwing layered barriers over the city like translucent glass. Soldiers abandoned peacetime posts and moved into practiced formations while witches took positions along the upper battlements.

No panic.

No confusion.

House Vesper had prepared for the possibility that mercy would become war.

King Lucien stood beneath the palace archway watching the defenses come alive.

Queen Aurelia remained several steps behind him with Zee in her arms and the crimson hatchling pressed against his side.

Prince Rez had not moved far.

He stayed close enough to see Zee, but not so close that Aurelia would mistake curiosity for intrusion.

Captain Vale watched the eastern gate.

Caldrin watched everyone.

“The shields are impressive,” he said.

Lucien glanced toward him. “You sound surprised.”

“I am generally surprised when something survives first contact with politics.”

Vale muttered, “One day someone will kill you for talking.”

Caldrin smiled. “Many have tried.”

Aurelia barely heard them.

Her attention remained on the riders.

Twelve.

One for each crown that had marched against Castle Darkheart.

They were admitted through the first gate but stopped before the second.

No one entered the inner capital armed.

That included diplomats carrying threats.

Lucien descended the palace steps.

“I will speak with them there.”

Aurelia looked at him. “Alone?”

“No.”

Rez straightened.

Lucien looked over one shoulder. “You stay.”

Rez frowned.

“I did not say anything.”

“You were about to.”

“That is unfair.”

“It is accurate.”

For the first time, Lucien smiled.

Then the expression disappeared.

He looked toward Aurelia.

“You may remain here.”

“I am coming.”

“Aurelia.”

“They crossed kingdoms demanding my son.”

“That is precisely why you should remain behind the inner shield.”

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“I spent the last several days being told where I should stand.”

Lucien considered arguing.

Then chose wisdom.

“Very well.”

They walked together toward the eastern court.

The hatchling climbed higher against Aurelia’s shoulder.

Zee stirred.

The Dragon Link carried a faint pulse.

Crowd.

Strangers.

Unease.

The hatchling answered.

Close.

Zee settled.

Rez watched from the palace steps until Lucien disappeared beyond the second gate.

Then he looked toward Captain Vale.

“Does everyone always tell queens what to do?”

Vale considered.

“Only men who enjoy dangerous lives.”

Rez nodded seriously.

“That makes sense.”

---

The twelve riders stood beneath the shadow of Vesper’s eastern wall.

They wore no weapons now.

Only royal colors.

Their expressions ranged from anger to fear to weary resignation.

The eldest stepped forward.

King Lucien stopped before him.

“You delivered your demand.”

The rider bowed.

“My king requests your answer.”

Lucien looked at him.

“You rode across half a continent for a word you already know.”

The envoy’s jaw tightened.

“Then say it.”

“No.”

The answer echoed beneath the stone arch.

The other riders shifted.

One stepped forward.

“House Vesper understands the consequences?”

“Yes.”

“You shelter the Darkheart child?”

“I shelter a queen and her newborn son.”

“He is not merely a child.”

Aurelia’s voice cut in.

“He is exactly that.”

Every envoy looked toward her.

One stared at Zee.

Another at the hatchling.

A third visibly recoiled when Zee opened his crimson eyes.

The eldest rider recovered first.

“Queen Aurelia, the coalition offers you safe passage if you surrender the boy.”

Lucien laughed once.

The sound carried no humor.

“You threatened my walls to repeat the same offer she already refused?”

The envoy ignored him.

“Aurelia, kingdoms are burning because of what happened when he was born.”

“Kingdoms are burning because frightened rulers marched armies across them.”

“The wolves—”

“Are not my son’s army.”

“The vampires—”

“Do not answer to him.”

“The witches—”

“Have their magic.”

The envoy’s patience broke.

“And yet everything happened at his birth.”

Aurelia stepped closer.

“Yes.”

The admission surprised them.

She continued.

“And none of you know why.”

Silence.

“You saw signs.”

“You heard rumors.”

“You gathered frightened witnesses.”

“Then you turned uncertainty into certainty because certainty made murder easier.”

The eldest envoy looked toward Lucien.

“You agree with this?”

Lucien answered calmly.

“I agree that fear does not become knowledge because twelve crowns share it.”

Another rider spoke.

“And if the child kills someone?”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“Then judge what he does.”

“After?”

“Yes.”

The rider stared.

“That may be too late.”

Lucien answered.

“That argument can justify killing anyone.”

The envoys fell silent.

Then the youngest among them reached into his coat.

Vesper soldiers immediately raised bows.

“Careful,” Lucien said.

The rider slowly removed a parchment.

“No weapon.”

He unfolded it.

“Then hear the coalition’s final decree.”

Caldrin, standing near the rear of the court, muttered, “There is always a final decree.”

Vale elbowed him.

The envoy read.

“Any kingdom, settlement, fortress, coven, blood court, clan, merchant house, or sovereign territory providing refuge to Zee Darkheart will be considered hostile to the Twelve Crowns.”

The court went still.

“Trade will cease.”

“Borders will close.”

“Caravans will be seized.”

“Allies will be warned.”

“Any individual aiding the child may be lawfully hunted beyond coalition territory.”

Aurelia’s face changed.

Not fear.

Understanding.

This was bigger than an army now.

They were trying to make survival itself illegal.

The envoy rolled the parchment closed.

“Surrender him, and all sanctions end.”

Lucien looked toward the walls surrounding his kingdom.

Markets.

Homes.

Temples.

Thousands of people whose lives would become harder because of one decision made by their king.

For the first time since Aurelia arrived, his confidence became heavier.

He understood the price.

That mattered.

Aurelia saw it.

“Lucien.”

He looked at her.

“You do not owe us this.”

“No.”

“If you send us away now, I will understand.”

Rez had followed after all.

He stood beneath the inner arch, just far enough away to pretend he had obeyed.

Lucien saw him.

His son.

His kingdom.

His responsibility.

Then he looked at Zee.

The newborn knew none of this.

Could not understand sanctions.

Crowns.

War.

He merely stared back.

Lucien turned to the envoys.

“House Vesper rejects the decree.”

The eldest rider exhaled.

“Then you choose the child over peace.”

“No.”

Lucien’s expression hardened.

“You keep pretending those are the only choices.”

He stepped closer.

“I choose sovereignty.”

“I choose judgment based on action rather than fear.”

“I choose not to teach my son that twelve frightened rulers can make murder righteous by signing the same parchment.”

Rez stopped smiling.

He understood that part.

Lucien continued.

“If your kings wish to close borders, let them.”

“If merchants wish to abandon us, let them.”

“If your armies come, they will find our walls.”

The envoy stared.

“And the Tribrid?”

Lucien looked toward Zee.

“He remains under Vesper protection until Queen Aurelia chooses otherwise.”

Aurelia closed her eyes briefly.

The rider bowed.

“Then the Twelve Crowns have their answer.”

They left.

No swords drawn.

No blood spilled.

Yet everyone in the courtyard understood that a larger war had just begun.

Not with armies.

With isolation.

---

The first consequences arrived before sunset.

Three merchant houses suspended trade.

A grain convoy turned around at the northern border.

Two neighboring lords recalled ambassadors.

Messages flooded the palace.

One Vesper noble demanded Zee’s immediate removal.

Another accused Lucien of sacrificing generations of diplomacy for a stranger’s child.

A third warned that winter stores would not survive if the sanctions spread.

Lucien read every letter.

He destroyed none.

Rez found him hours later in the council chamber.

Stacks of parchment covered the table.

“Are we in trouble?”

Lucien looked up.

“Yes.”

Rez blinked.

He had expected reassurance.

Lucien leaned back.

“Kings who tell their children everything will be fine are usually lying.”

Rez walked closer.

“Because of Zee?”

“Because of the choices surrounding him.”

“That sounds like yes.”

Lucien nodded.

“In part.”

Rez looked at the letters.

“Do you regret letting them in?”

Lucien was silent for longer than Rez liked.

Then:

“No.”

“Even if people get angry?”

“Yes.”

“Even if we lose money?”

“Yes.”

“Even if there is war?”

Lucien looked at him.

“That answer becomes harder.”

Rez absorbed this.

“But still no?”

Lucien smiled faintly.

“Still no.”

Rez nodded.

Then turned toward the door.

“Where are you going?”

“To see Zee.”

“Rez.”

“I will not use magic.”

Lucien closed his eyes.

“That is not the only possible problem.”

Rez was already gone.

---

Aurelia had been given rooms overlooking the western gardens.

She did not sleep.

Again.

Zee rested in a cradle beside her bed.

Zareth—the name still unknown to everyone within Vesper—slept curled tightly against him.

The crimson hatchling’s injured wing was nearly healed.

Aurelia watched the two newborns breathe.

The silence felt unnatural after days of running.

A knock came.

Vale opened the door.

Rez stood outside holding a wooden toy wolf.

Aurelia raised an eyebrow.

“Your father knows you are here?”

“Yes.”

Vale looked at him.

Rez sighed.

“He knows I was going to come here.”

“That was not the question.”

Rez walked past him.

Aurelia almost smiled.

“What is that?”

He held up the carved wolf.

“It was mine.”

“You are giving it to Zee?”

Rez nodded.

“He cannot use a sword.”

Aurelia stared at him.

“I should hope not.”

“So this seemed better.”

He placed the wolf beside the cradle.

The dragon hatchling opened one eye.

Rez froze.

The hatchling sniffed the toy.

Then bit it.

Rez looked offended.

“That is not for you.”

The hatchling chewed harder.

Zee stirred.

The Dragon Link carried satisfaction.

Aurelia laughed quietly.

Rez looked at her.

“He ate my gift.”

“He is a dragon.”

“That is not an excuse.”

“It may be.”

Rez sat beside the cradle.

For a few moments, none of them spoke.

Then Zee opened his eyes.

Rez looked at him.

“Everyone is angry because you are here.”

Aurelia’s smile faded.

“Rez.”

“He cannot understand me.”

“That does not make it kinder.”

Rez considered.

Then corrected himself.

“Everyone is afraid because they do not understand you.”

Aurelia watched him.

“That is better.”

Rez extended one finger.

Zee took it.

Crimson Mana flickered faintly.

Rez’s blue-white mana responded beneath his skin but did not manifest.

The hatchling watched.

No danger.

Only familiarity beginning.

Aurelia looked at the three of them and allowed herself one fragile breath of hope.

Then the palace bells rang.

Not war bells.

Alarm bells.

Vale stood immediately.

Caldrin burst into the room a moment later.

“We have a problem.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

“What kind?”

“The quiet kind.”

That was worse.

“Someone entered the palace.”

Vale drew his sword.

“From where?”

Caldrin looked toward Zee.

“We do not know.”

Aurelia stood.

“Who?”

“We found one guard asleep.”

“Drugged?”

“No.”

“Dead?”

“No.”

Caldrin’s expression tightened.

“He cannot remember the last hour.”

Rez’s face changed.

“Magic?”

“Maybe.”

Aurelia moved toward Zee.

The hatchling was already awake.

His body went rigid.

The Dragon Link carried something cold.

Near.

Vale looked toward the corridor.

“No one leaves this room.”

Caldrin drew both blades.

“Too late.”

A whisper came from somewhere inside the walls.

Not words.

Breathing.

Then a small black needle struck the nursery door from the other side.

Everyone stared at it.

A second needle followed.

Then a third.

The metal began dissolving the lock.

Aurelia lifted Zee.

Vale moved in front of her.

Caldrin smiled without humor.

“The armies failed.”

The door cracked.

“So they sent someone patient.”

# Chapter Thirteen

## The Silent Knife

The nursery door opened without making a sound.

Captain Vale struck first.

His sword cut through empty air.

Nothing stood beyond the threshold.

The corridor was vacant.

Caldrin stepped beside him.

“That is irritating.”

Rez remained near Aurelia.

His blue-white mana had begun gathering around his fingertips despite Lucien’s warning.

Aurelia noticed.

“Rez.”

“I know.”

“You clearly do not.”

“I am not using it.”

“You are glowing.”

“That is different.”

The crimson hatchling hissed.

Everyone stopped.

He was staring upward.

Ceiling.

Vale looked up.

A shadow moved.

Fast.

Something dropped.

Caldrin pushed Aurelia aside.

A figure landed where she had been standing.

Black cloth.

No armor.

No visible face.

One thin blade in each hand.

The assassin moved immediately.

Not toward Aurelia.

Not toward Vale.

Toward Zee.

Rez reacted.

Blue-white mana exploded from his palm.

The assassin twisted.

The spell struck the wall and froze a section of stone beneath a layer of pale frost.

Rez stared at his own hand.

“I missed.”

Caldrin blocked the first blade.

Vale caught the second.

The assassin used both men as leverage, kicked off the wall, and landed behind them.

Too fast.

Aurelia moved.

The assassin followed.

The hatchling launched himself.

He bit into the assassin’s sleeve.

The attacker spun and struck him away with the flat of a blade.

The dragon crashed into the bed.

Zee screamed.

The Dragon Link flooded with pain.

Rez’s expression changed.

Blue-white mana surged violently.

This time he did not miss.

A narrow bolt struck the assassin in the shoulder.

The figure hit the floor.

Caldrin was on them immediately.

One sword at the throat.

Vale kicked both blades away.

“Do not move.”

The assassin laughed.

A woman’s voice.

“You think I came alone?”

Vale’s face changed.

Then the windows shattered.

Three more assassins entered.

The room erupted.

Lucien’s guards rushed from the corridor.

One assassin threw a black powder into the air.

The nearest soldiers collapsed.

Not dead.

Sleeping.

The second went for Rez.

Lucien arrived in time to intercept.

Dark blue mana crashed through the room and sent the attacker through a table.

“Rez!”

“I am fine!”

“You are not supposed to be here!”

“That feels less important now!”

Lucien looked ready to argue.

Then another assassin attacked.

He turned and fought.

Aurelia backed toward the wall.

Zee in one arm.

The hatchling scrambling back toward him.

The first captured assassin moved.

Caldrin saw too late.

She bit down.

Something cracked between her teeth.

Poison.

Caldrin grabbed her jaw.

“No.”

She smiled.

Black veins spread across her neck.

Aurelia looked away.

The assassin convulsed.

Then went still.

Caldrin cursed.

“No answers.”

Vale blocked another strike.

“Survive first!”

The room became too crowded.

Too many blades.

Too much magic.

Zee heard everything.

Heartbeats.

Footsteps.

Steel.

Breathing.

The vampire senses that had begun emerging on the road sharpened again beneath danger.

One heartbeat moved differently.

Slower.

Not fighting.

Waiting.

Zee turned his head.

A fifth assassin stood outside the shattered window.

Hidden.

Watching.

Crossbow.

The weapon lifted.

Aurelia did not see.

Zee did.

The bolt fired.

His body reacted before thought.

Crimson Mana snapped outward.

The bolt changed direction.

Not stopped.

Turned.

It struck the wall.

The assassin froze.

Zee stared at them.

The attacker reloaded.

The hatchling saw now.

Through the Dragon Link came a simple image.

There.

Rez followed the hatchling’s gaze.

“Window!”

Lucien turned.

The assassin fired.

Rez cast first.

Blue-white mana froze the crossbow.

The weapon shattered in the attacker’s hands.

Caldrin threw a blade.

The assassin vanished below the window.

Vale rushed forward.

“Roof access!”

Two guards followed.

The battle inside ended quickly after that.

One assassin died.

One escaped.

One surrendered only after Lucien broke both weapons and pinned them beneath a containment spell.

The final attacker tried to reach Zee again.

Aurelia moved backward.

The assassin lunged.

Zee’s wolf nature reacted.

Not with a growl this time.

With scent.

He recognized the attacker’s blood before the blade reached him.

Fear.

Adrenaline.

Poison.

Something foreign beneath it.

His tiny fangs extended.

Crimson Mana surged.

The assassin stopped in place.

Not frozen by spell.

Held by pressure.

Lucien stared.

Rez stared.

The attacker strained.

Could not move.

Zee began crying.

The pressure increased.

Aurelia whispered, “Zee.”

He heard her voice.

The force released.

The assassin collapsed.

Caldrin kicked the weapon away.

Silence followed.

The nursery was destroyed.

Again.

Lucien looked around.

Then at Aurelia.

“I apologize.”

Caldrin blinked.

“For what?”

“The hospitality.”

Aurelia laughed.

It came from exhaustion more than amusement.

“You are still doing better than my husband.”

No one answered that.

---

The surviving assassin was taken below the palace.

Lucien questioned them personally.

No torture.

Not yet.

Aurelia remained present.

Vale too.

Caldrin leaned against the wall with his arms folded.

The assassin sat chained to a stone chair.

Young.

Male.

No crest.

No obvious allegiance.

Lucien placed the black needle from the nursery door on the table.

“What is this?”

The assassin smiled.

“You know.”

“I want to hear you say it.”

“Sleepvenom.”

“Made where?”

No answer.

Caldrin spoke.

“West coast.”

The assassin looked toward him.

Caldrin smiled.

“Thank you.”

Lucien continued.

“Who hired you?”

Silence.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“You failed.”

The assassin looked at her.

“Today.”

Vale’s hand moved toward his sword.

Aurelia raised one hand.

“No.”

She studied the man.

“You are not afraid of death.”

“No.”

“Good.”

His smile faltered.

“Then tell me what you are afraid of.”

Silence.

Aurelia saw it.

Tiny.

But there.

“Whoever hired you.”

The assassin looked away.

Caldrin straightened.

“That is useful.”

Lucien leaned forward.

“Name.”

The man’s jaw tightened.

He said nothing.

Then a sound came from inside his chest.

A click.

Caldrin moved first.

“Back!”

The assassin convulsed.

Dark symbols appeared beneath his skin.

Aurelia stepped away.

Lucien raised a shield.

The man’s body collapsed inward.

Not exploding.

Erasing.

Within seconds, the chair was empty except for chains and ash.

Vale stared.

“What was that?”

Lucien’s expression darkened.

“A death seal.”

Caldrin crouched near the ash.

“Triggered by questioning?”

“Possibly.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“Witch work?”

Lucien answered carefully.

“Yes.”

“Which witches?”

“I do not know.”

She nodded.

No one pretended certainty.

That had become a rule of survival.

Caldrin touched the ash with the tip of a knife.

“Someone spent a great deal of money making sure these people could not talk.”

Vale frowned.

“So not bounty hunters.”

“No.”

Lucien looked toward the ceiling above them.

“Something organized.”

Aurelia’s expression tightened.

The physical hunts had changed again.

Armies.

Mercenaries.

Monsters.

Now assassins trained to infiltrate fortified palaces and die without revealing employers.

The world was learning faster.

So was Zee.

---

That night, Lucien moved Aurelia and Zee into an older section of the palace.

No windows.

Two exits.

Four layers of wards.

Rez objected to being excluded.

Lucien ignored him.

Zee lay awake in a new cradle.

The crimson hatchling curled beside him.

Their Link remained restless.

Images now came occasionally.

Not clear memories.

Simple impressions.

Window.

Blade.

Pain.

Friend.

The hatchling showed Zee the place where the assassin had stood.

Zee answered with the sound he remembered.

Heartbeat.

Neither understood what the other was truly doing.

But the bond had grown.

Outside the room, Lucien spoke quietly with Aurelia.

“This cannot continue.”

Her face hardened.

“You are sending us away.”

“No.”

“Then what?”

“We stop waiting for the next attack.”

Aurelia stared.

“You want to hunt them.”

“I want to know which roads are no longer safe.”

“That sounds similar.”

Lucien looked toward the sealed door.

“Zee is too young to remain at the center of a palace under constant siege.”

“There is nowhere else.”

“There may be.”

Aurelia’s expression changed.

“Where?”

Lucien hesitated.

“Northwest of Vesper territory is an old sanctuary.”

Caldrin, standing nearby, frowned.

“I dislike that word.”

“It was built before my grandfather’s reign.”

“For what?”

“Children born into dangerous bloodlines.”

Vale raised an eyebrow.

“That sounds extremely convenient.”

“It is not.”

Lucien looked toward him.

“It has been abandoned for twenty years.”

Caldrin smiled.

“Better.”

Aurelia crossed her arms.

“Why abandoned?”

Lucien did not answer immediately.

That told them enough.

Vale sighed.

“What happened there?”

“Something killed the caretakers.”

Silence.

Caldrin looked delighted.

“Perfect.”

Aurelia stared at Lucien.

“And you are suggesting I take my newborn son there?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I am suggesting we investigate it first.”

That was different.

Aurelia looked toward Zee’s door.

“What if it is not safe?”

Lucien answered.

“Then we make it safe.”

The plan began there.

Not escape.

Not hiding blindly.

Preparation.

For the first time since Zee’s birth, the people protecting him would choose where the next danger happened.

That mattered.

---

Far away, inside a chamber lit by red candles, a woman received news of the failed assassination.

She wore no crown.

No royal colors.

Only black robes stitched with silver thread.

A messenger knelt before her.

“All five failed.”

“Dead?”

“Four.”

“The fifth?”

“Gone.”

The woman’s expression did not change.

“And the child?”

“Alive.”

A pause.

“Again.”

The messenger lowered his eyes.

“Yes.”

She walked toward a table covered in reports.

Blood Rain.

Wolf madness.

Vampire disturbance.

The siege.

The resurrection rumor.

The Gravehound shrine.

The failed mercenary ambush.

Vesper sanctuary.

None offered answers.

Only patterns.

She touched Zee’s crude bounty sketch.

“Stop sending killers.”

The messenger looked up.

“My Lady?”

“They teach us nothing if they die before observing him.”

“What do you want instead?”

She smiled faintly.

“Eyes.”

“Spies?”

“Scholars.”

The messenger hesitated.

“Witches?”

“Some.”

“Why?”

The woman looked at the child’s crimson eyes drawn badly across the parchment.

“Because everyone keeps asking how to kill him.”

She folded the report.

“I want to know what survival is doing to him.”

The hunt had changed again.

And somewhere inside House Vesper, Zee Darkheart slept beside his dragon, unaware that the next enemy coming for him would not arrive with a blade.

They would arrive with questions.

# Chapter Fourteen

## The Sanctuary That Failed

House Vesper sent no banners.

That was Lucien’s first decision.

No royal carriage.

No mounted guard dressed in blue and silver.

No obvious procession announcing that Queen Aurelia Darkheart and the most hunted child in the known kingdoms had left the capital.

They departed before dawn under rain.

Aurelia rode beneath a dark traveling cloak with Zee secured against her chest and the crimson hatchling tucked close beneath the same heavy fabric. Captain Vale rode beside her. Caldrin took the lead. The eldest royal witch followed behind while four Vesper soldiers traveled in plain leather armor without crests.

King Lucien came too.

That surprised everyone except Rez.

Prince Rez Vesper had argued for nearly an hour when told he would remain behind.

He lost.

Then argued again.

He lost more loudly.

Now he stood atop the western wall of Vesper’s capital, arms folded, watching the group disappear into the rain.

His blue-white mana flickered around his fingers.

“You promised,” he muttered.

Lucien had promised nothing.

Rez had chosen to remember the conversation differently.

Far below, Lucien glanced once toward the wall.

He could barely see his son through the rain.

Aurelia noticed.

“You could have stayed.”

“So could you.”

“That is different.”

“Every parent believes that.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

He slept through the movement of the horse.

The crimson hatchling did not.

His head remained outside Aurelia’s cloak, golden eyes scanning the trees. His injured wing had healed almost completely, though he still favored it whenever he shifted.

The Dragon Link remained restless.

Zee slept.

Zareth watched.

Whenever distance opened even slightly between their bodies, unease moved through them both.

Near.

Stay.

Together.

Aurelia had begun recognizing the pattern even if she could not feel the Link herself.

“They hate being separated.”

Lucien looked toward the hatchling.

“I noticed.”

“Someone tried taking him from Zee yesterday.”

“What happened?”

“He screamed until every lamp in the room shattered.”

Lucien raised an eyebrow.

“Which one?”

“Both.”

Caldrin looked back from the front of the line.

“That should simplify childcare.”

Vale ignored him.

The road narrowed.

The Vesper foothills rose ahead, thick with pine forests and old stone formations covered in moss. No villages remained this far northwest. No farm smoke. No roadside shrines.

Only forest.

That was intentional.

The sanctuary had once been built far from major roads.

Lucien explained as they rode.

“It was established during my grandfather’s reign.”

“For dangerous children?” Aurelia asked.

“For children other kingdoms considered dangerous.”

“There is a difference.”

“Yes.”

Lucien’s expression tightened.

“Some were born with unstable magic. Others belonged to hunted bloodlines. A few were heirs whose enemies found children easier to assassinate than kings.”

Caldrin glanced back.

“A lovely place.”

“It was.”

“What happened?”

Lucien remained silent for several strides.

Then:

“One winter, every caretaker died.”

Vale looked toward him.

“At once?”

“Over three nights.”

“Children?”

“Gone.”

Aurelia frowned.

“Gone how?”

“No bodies.”

“Tracks?”

“None.”

“Blood?”

“Yes.”

Lucien looked ahead.

“A great deal.”

Caldrin sighed.

“And this is the safer option.”

“No.”

Lucien’s voice hardened.

“It is the option we can investigate without placing ten thousand Vesper civilians around Zee.”

That answer ended the argument.

The sanctuary appeared near midday.

It sat between two ridges beneath towering pines.

Old gray walls surrounded a manor built partially into the mountainside. Ivy had overtaken the northern towers. Iron gates leaned crooked beneath twenty years of rust.

No birds nested there.

No animals crossed the road.

The hatchling noticed immediately.

His body stiffened.

Zee woke.

Crimson eyes opened.

Aurelia slowed her horse.

“What is it?”

The hatchling stared at the manor.

The Dragon Link carried something unfamiliar.

Not danger.

Not yet.

Empty.

Zee responded with unease.

Lucien raised one hand.

Everyone stopped.

“From here, we walk.”

Caldrin dismounted.

“Because horses are difficult indoors?”

“Because something frightened every animal away.”

Caldrin stopped smiling.

They entered through the broken gate.

The courtyard was covered in weeds.

Children’s toys remained where they had fallen decades earlier.

A wooden sword.

A stone doll.

A little iron ring used for rolling games.

Aurelia stared at them.

“Twenty years.”

Lucien nodded.

“No one took anything.”

Vale crouched near the old fountain.

“Someone has been here.”

Lucien turned.

“How recently?”

Vale touched disturbed moss.

“Days.”

Caldrin drew his sword.

The Vesper soldiers followed.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Aurelia remained behind them with Zee.

The hatchling climbed onto her shoulder.

They entered the manor.

Dust covered the entrance hall.

Not evenly.

Footprints crossed it.

Many.

Bare feet.

Small.

Aurelia’s stomach tightened.

“Children?”

Vale shook his head.

“Too narrow.”

Caldrin looked toward the ceiling.

“Not all footprints belong to feet.”

A scraping sound came from above.

Everyone raised their weapons.

Nothing moved.

Lucien whispered, “Stay together.”

They crossed into the central hall.

Old portraits lined the walls.

Children.

Dozens.

Every age.

Every race.

Witch children.

Wolf-blooded children.

Pale vampire-born descendants.

Humans.

Others Aurelia did not recognize.

Every portrait had been scratched across the face.

Not by age.

Deliberately.

The royal witch approached one.

“These scratches are fresh.”

Lucien’s expression darkened.

“Someone is using this place.”

Zee stirred.

His vampire hearing caught something.

Far beneath them.

Heartbeat.

One.

Then another.

Then dozens.

He turned his head downward.

The hatchling reacted through the Link.

Below.

Aurelia followed Zee’s gaze.

“What?”

Lucien noticed.

“He hears something.”

Caldrin crouched and pressed one ear to the floor.

Nothing.

Vale did the same.

Then shook his head.

Zee could hear farther.

Deeper.

Something scratched beneath the floor.

Everyone heard that.

Vale stepped backward.

“Now I hear it.”

The floor collapsed.

Three Vesper soldiers disappeared.

Aurelia screamed.

Lucien grabbed her and pulled her back.

Black shapes erupted through the opening.

Not monsters.

Children.

At least they had once been.

Thin bodies climbed over broken stone with impossible speed.

Their skin was gray.

Their eyes clouded white.

Their mouths had been sewn shut with black thread.

The royal witch froze.

“Oh, gods.”

The first child-creature attacked.

Vale blocked.

His sword stopped inches from its throat.

He hesitated.

That nearly killed him.

The creature slammed into his chest and knocked him down.

Caldrin struck it with the flat of his blade.

“Do not think of them as children!”

“They are children!”

“Then find out later!”

The manor filled with movement.

More emerged from below.

Lucien cast.

Dark blue mana struck the floor in a ring around Aurelia, creating a barrier.

The creatures hit it.

Some bounced away.

Others clung to it with skeletal fingers.

Zee stared.

Not afraid.

Confused.

They smelled wrong.

Alive.

But not fully.

The hatchling hissed.

One creature pressed its face against the barrier.

Its white eyes fixed on Zee.

Something changed.

Every creature stopped.

The room went silent.

Lucien kept the barrier raised.

Vale pushed himself upright.

Caldrin whispered, “Why did they stop?”

The creature nearest Zee tilted its head.

The black stitches across its mouth began tearing.

Slowly.

Blood ran down its chin.

Aurelia looked away.

The mouth opened.

The voice that emerged did not belong to a child.

“Three.”

Everyone froze.

The creature looked at Zee.

“Three.”

Another repeated it.

Then another.

Soon the entire hall whispered.

“Three.”

“Three.”

“Three.”

Aurelia’s grip tightened.

“Do not listen.”

The nearest creature crawled closer.

Lucien strengthened the barrier.

It did not attack.

It placed one palm against the magical wall.

Then pointed toward Zee.

“Not one.”

The royal witch’s face drained.

Caldrin looked toward her.

“Do not.”

“I was not going to explain.”

“Good.”

The creature trembled.

Then screamed.

Every child-thing in the hall collapsed.

A black sigil ignited beneath their skin.

Lucien recognized it.

“Back!”

The same kind of death seal used on the assassin.

But larger.

Older.

The sigils burned across dozens of bodies.

Aurelia shielded Zee.

Nothing exploded.

Instead, the creatures began turning to ash.

One after another.

The nearest reached toward Zee before its fingers disappeared.

Its final sound was barely human.

“Run.”

Then it vanished.

Ash filled the hall.

Silence returned.

Lucien lowered the barrier.

No one moved.

Vale looked toward the pit beneath the floor.

“What was done here?”

Lucien’s expression became murderous.

“This was not what killed the sanctuary.”

Caldrin looked at the ash.

“No.”

“Someone came afterward.”

The royal witch crouched near the remains.

She examined the black residue without touching it.

“Those children were altered.”

Aurelia’s voice hardened.

“By whom?”

“I do not know.”

“Can you tell what they were?”

“Some witches.”

She pointed toward another pile.

“Some wolf-blooded.”

Another.

“Possibly vampire.”

Lucien stared at the old portraits.

A sanctuary for hunted children.

Abandoned.

Then repurposed by someone experimenting on them.

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

Suddenly the assassins made more sense.

The scholars.

The questions.

Someone did not simply want Zee dead.

Someone wanted to understand combinations of blood.

Caldrin saw the thought forming.

“Do not jump too far.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“I know.”

He nodded.

Good.

No certainty.

Only pattern.

Then a scream came from below.

Human.

Adult.

Alive.

Vale raised his sword.

Lucien looked toward the collapsed floor.

Caldrin smiled grimly.

“Well.”

He stepped toward the opening.

“The sanctuary has a basement.”

---

They descended.

The lower level was not part of the original manor.

That much was obvious.

The stone changed.

So did the air.

Iron tables lined the walls.

Broken chains lay across the floor.

Glass vessels contained dried remains of substances no one recognized.

Notes had been burned.

Most.

Not all.

The royal witch picked up a surviving fragment.

“Blood ratios.”

Lucien looked toward her.

“Whose?”

“No names.”

Caldrin examined another.

“Physical responses to mixing.”

Vale frowned.

“Mixing what?”

“Blood.”

Aurelia’s expression went cold.

The scream came again.

Farther ahead.

They followed.

A man lay chained inside the final chamber.

Middle-aged.

Emaciated.

Alive.

Barely.

Lucien approached.

“Who are you?”

The prisoner lifted his head.

His eyes focused on Aurelia.

Then Zee.

Terror consumed him.

“No.”

Aurelia stopped.

The man pulled against his chains.

“No, no, no.”

Caldrin crouched.

“You know him?”

“No!”

“Then why are you afraid?”

The prisoner looked at Zee.

“Because they wanted him.”

Silence.

Aurelia stepped forward.

“Who?”

The man began crying.

“They said there would be one.”

Lucien’s expression hardened.

“Who said?”

“I do not know their names.”

“Describe them.”

“Witches.”

“Which coven?”

“They never gave one.”

“Symbols?”

The prisoner shook his head.

“They removed them.”

Aurelia stared.

“How long have you been here?”

“I do not know.”

Caldrin looked at the man’s condition.

“Months.”

The prisoner whispered, “They were preparing.”

“For what?”

His eyes went to Zee again.

“For something they had not found yet.”

The room chilled.

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“My son?”

“I do not know.”

“Then stop looking at him as though you do.”

The man flinched.

“You asked.”

“And you answer only what you know.”

Lucien glanced toward her.

Good.

Fear would not be allowed to become false certainty again.

The prisoner closed his eyes.

“They took children with mixed blood.”

“Witch and wolf.”

“Some.”

“Vampire and witch?”

“Yes.”

“Wolf and vampire?”

“I think.”

Caldrin’s expression darkened.

“And what happened?”

“Most died.”

Silence.

The hatchling moved closer to Zee.

The prisoner looked toward him.

“They wanted combinations.”

The royal witch whispered, “Why?”

“I do not know.”

The man opened his eyes.

“But they kept saying the same thing.”

Aurelia waited.

“What?”

“That nature had limits.”

He looked toward Zee.

“And one day something would be born that did not.”

No one spoke.

Not prophecy.

Not knowledge of Zee.

Theory.

Obsession.

Someone had been searching for impossible blood before Zee existed.

That did not mean they predicted him.

It meant his birth had given monsters a new target.

Lucien turned toward Vale.

“We destroy this place.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“After we learn everything we can.”

He nodded.

The prisoner began laughing weakly.

Caldrin frowned.

“What?”

“You are too late.”

Lucien’s face changed.

“Why?”

The prisoner stared toward the corridor.

“They came back yesterday.”

Aurelia froze.

“For what?”

“To clear everything.”

Caldrin looked around.

“Then why leave you?”

The prisoner smiled through cracked lips.

“Because I am bait.”

A sound clicked behind them.

The royal witch shouted.

“DOWN!”

The entire underground chamber ignited.

Black magical fire raced across the walls.

Lucien threw up a shield.

The ceiling cracked.

Aurelia fell.

Zee slipped in her arms.

The hatchling launched himself toward him.

Through the Dragon Link came one overwhelming command.

Hold.

Zee reacted.

Crimson Mana exploded.

The collapsing ceiling stopped.

Not all of it.

Enough.

Stone hovered over Aurelia.

Lucien stared.

The royal witch screamed.

“MOVE!”

Everyone ran.

Zee’s mana strained.

The stones began falling again.

Caldrin grabbed Aurelia.

Vale carried the prisoner.

Lucien held the rear.

The hatchling stayed beside Zee.

They reached the stairs seconds before the laboratory collapsed.

The manor shook.

Flames erupted from the lower windows.

Everyone spilled into the courtyard.

Then the sanctuary began falling in on itself.

Lucien stared at it.

Twenty years of secrets vanished beneath fire and stone.

The prisoner coughed.

“They will know.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“Know what?”

“That you came.”

“How?”

He smiled weakly.

“They always know.”

Then he lost consciousness.

Aurelia looked at the burning manor.

The sanctuary was gone.

So was any chance of using it.

The world had hunted Zee with armies.

Then monsters.

Mercenaries.

Assassins.

Now someone had begun preparing places before he ever arrived.

Not because they understood him.

Because they understood fear, blood, and opportunity.

Aurelia held Zee tighter.

“We go back to Vesper.”

Lucien nodded.

Caldrin looked toward the smoke.

“No.”

Everyone turned.

He pointed toward the ridge.

A rider stood there.

Watching.

The figure wore black.

No crest.

The moment Caldrin moved, the rider turned and vanished into the forest.

Vale cursed.

Lucien’s face hardened.

“They found us.”

Caldrin sheathed his sword.

“They never lost us.”

# Chapter Fifteen

## The Eyes Behind the Hunt

They did not return by the same road.

Lucien changed the route twice before sunset.

No fires.

No visible camp.

No repeated trails.

The prisoner from the sanctuary remained unconscious across one Vesper soldier’s horse while the royal witch worked periodically to stabilize him.

Aurelia rode in silence.

Zee slept.

The crimson hatchling did not.

Something about the rider on the ridge had changed him.

Through the Dragon Link, he kept sending Zee the same crude image.

Black.

Far.

Watching.

Zee could not understand a spy.

He understood the feeling behind it.

Seen.

Aurelia noticed the hatchling looking backward every few minutes.

“So do I.”

Lucien glanced toward her.

“What?”

“The feeling.”

She looked behind them.

“No matter where we go, someone is watching.”

Lucien did not offer reassurance.

He had stopped offering reassurance he could not prove.

“We assume they are.”

Vale nodded.

“That changes travel.”

Caldrin looked back.

“It changes everything.”

The royal witch spoke from beside the prisoner.

“He is waking.”

They stopped beneath a low ridge.

The man coughed violently.

Lucien dismounted.

“What is your name?”

The prisoner stared at him.

“Theron.”

“Family name?”

“None worth using.”

Caldrin smiled faintly.

“I like him already.”

Aurelia remained mounted.

“Theron.”

He looked at her.

“The people who held you.”

His face tightened.

“What did they call themselves?”

“Nothing.”

“Never?”

“They used numbers.”

Lucien frowned.

“For rank?”

“I think.”

“What numbers?”

“First Hand. Second Hand. Third Hand.”

Caldrin’s expression changed.

“That is not a coven structure I know.”

The royal witch shook her head.

“Nor I.”

Aurelia asked, “Did they worship anything?”

“No.”

“Serve a king?”

“Not openly.”

“A god?”

“I never heard prayer.”

“Demons?”

Theron looked uncertain.

“No.”

Good.

No premature answer.

Lucien crouched.

“What did they want from you?”

Theron laughed weakly.

“My blood.”

“What are you?”

“A witch.”

“Only?”

Theron’s smile vanished.

“My mother was wolf-blooded.”

Vale looked toward the others.

Another mixed line.

Theron continued.

“I never transformed.”

“Did they care?”

“No.”

“They cared that the blood was there.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

Three complete natures.

Born together.

No wonder anyone obsessed with mixed blood would want him.

Not prophecy.

Not destiny.

Opportunity.

Lucien stood.

“What did they do?”

Theron looked away.

“They exposed us to things.”

“What things?”

“Blood.”

“Whose?”

“Vampire.”

“Monster.”

“Demon.”

The royal witch’s expression tightened.

“Trying to force adaptation.”

Theron looked at her.

“Yes.”

Aurelia’s voice hardened.

“Did it work?”

“Sometimes.”

Silence.

Caldrin’s eyes narrowed.

“What does sometimes mean?”

Theron looked toward the ground.

“Long enough to regret it.”

No one asked more.

Not yet.

The road continued.

---

They reached the Vesper border after midnight.

No attack came.

That made everyone more nervous.

At dawn, the capital appeared.

The gates opened.

Rez was waiting.

Lucien saw him from fifty yards away.

His expression changed.

“Why is he outside the walls?”

A Vesper captain rode forward.

“My King.”

“Why is my son outside the walls?”

“He refused to wait inside.”

Rez heard.

“I am standing behind the first gate.”

Lucien pointed toward the city.

“Inside.”

Rez crossed his arms.

“No.”

Aurelia looked at Lucien.

“Good luck.”

He glared at her.

“This is not funny.”

“It is a little.”

Rez ignored his father and looked toward Zee.

The crimson hatchling immediately recognized him.

The Dragon Link carried something new.

Known.

Not family.

Not yet.

But known.

Zee opened his crimson eyes.

Rez smiled.

“You came back.”

Lucien dismounted.

“We need to speak.”

“I know.”

“No, you do not.”

Rez looked toward the unconscious prisoner.

“Who is that?”

Lucien closed his eyes.

Aurelia laughed quietly.

“Definitely your son.”

---

The palace council met before noon.

Lucien.

Aurelia.

Vale.

Caldrin.

The royal witch.

Three Vesper ministers.

Theron, once he was strong enough to sit.

Rez was excluded.

He listened outside the door.

Lucien knew.

He allowed it.

The map on the table had changed.

Red markers represented known bounty routes.

Black represented assassination attempts.

Silver represented coalition kingdoms.

Now Lucien added another marker.

White.

Unknown.

He placed it over the sanctuary.

“Someone used the abandoned sanctuary for experiments involving mixed supernatural blood.”

One minister frowned.

“For how long?”

“Unknown.”

“Before Zee was born?”

“Yes.”

Aurelia leaned forward.

“That matters.”

The minister looked toward her.

“Because they were not preparing specifically for him.”

“Exactly.”

Caldrin nodded.

“They were preparing for possibility.”

Theron sat wrapped in blankets near the fire.

“They believed nature could be forced.”

The royal witch asked, “Forced into what?”

“No one told us.”

“Did they succeed with anyone?”

Theron’s face became distant.

“One girl survived longer than the others.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

“What was she?”

“Witch and wolf.”

The witch’s eyes narrowed.

“What happened?”

“They gave her vampire blood.”

Silence.

Lucien looked toward Theron.

“And?”

“She changed.”

Aurelia’s expression sharpened.

“Into what?”

“I do not know.”

Not *a Tribrid.*

Not certainty.

Theron continued.

“She became violent.”

“Stronger.”

“Faster.”

“Then she began dying.”

“From the vampire blood?”

“Maybe.”

“From the wolf blood?”

“I do not know.”

“Magic rejection?”

“I do not know.”

He slammed one weak fist against the chair.

“I do not know.”

The room went quiet.

Aurelia softened slightly.

“Enough.”

Theron nodded.

Lucien looked toward the map.

“Whoever did this may now know Zee exists.”

“They do,” Caldrin said.

Aurelia turned.

“You sound certain.”

“They sent the assassins.”

“Possible.”

“They burned the sanctuary.”

“Possible.”

“They watched us leave.”

“Likely.”

Caldrin sighed.

“You have become difficult.”

“Fear nearly killed my son.”

Her voice stayed calm.

“I prefer difficult.”

Lucien looked between them.

“She is right.”

He tapped the map.

“We separate fact from assumption.”

He began listing.

“Fact: someone experimented on mixed bloodlines.”

“Fact: the sanctuary was used.”

“Fact: a black-robed rider observed us.”

“Fact: assassins using witch death seals attacked the palace.”

“Not fact: same organization.”

Caldrin nodded reluctantly.

“Fine.”

“Not fact: they predicted Zee.”

“Not fact: they understand what he is.”

“Not fact: they know about his resurrection.”

Vale looked toward him.

“Rumors already spread.”

“Yes.”

“Then assume they heard.”

“Assume.”

Lucien’s finger moved toward the black markers.

“Do not build strategy on certainty we do not possess.”

Aurelia looked toward Zee sleeping in a guarded chamber above.

For the first time, the people around him were learning the same lesson his enemies refused to learn.

Observe.

Do not invent.

Survive what is real.

---

Later that afternoon, Zee fed.

Then slept.

Then woke hungry again.

For all the wars surrounding him, he remained a newborn.

That contrast had begun affecting Aurelia strangely.

One hour, she discussed spies and blood experiments with kings.

The next, she cleaned milk from Zee’s chin.

The hatchling watched every feeding with unbearable interest.

“No.”

Aurelia moved the bottle away from him.

The dragon chirped.

“No.”

Another chirp.

“You eat meat.”

The hatchling stared at the milk.

Zee felt the hunger through the Link.

The infant turned toward the dragon.

Hungry.

The hatchling answered.

Yes.

Aurelia looked between them.

“You are conspiring.”

Rez sat nearby.

“He wants some.”

“Thank you.”

“I am helping.”

“You are not.”

Rez took a second small cup from the tray.

Aurelia stared.

“Do not.”

Rez poured a little milk onto a saucer.

The hatchling attacked it.

Milk went everywhere.

Rez laughed.

Aurelia covered her face.

“This is a prince?”

“We do not know that.”

Rez looked at the hatchling.

“He acts like one.”

“How?”

“Entitled.”

The dragon sneezed milk onto him.

Rez stopped laughing.

Aurelia did not.

The sound startled Zee.

Then he made one too.

Small.

Barely a laugh.

But real.

Everyone froze.

Aurelia stared.

Rez stared.

The hatchling licked milk from his snout.

Zee made the sound again.

Aurelia’s eyes filled with tears.

Not sadness.

Something rarer now.

Joy.

For a few minutes, no one hunted him.

No prophecies.

No armies.

No experiments.

Only a child laughing because a dragon had sneezed on a prince.

Then the door opened.

Lucien entered.

His face erased the moment.

Aurelia stood.

“What?”

“A message.”

“From whom?”

“We do not know.”

Rez frowned.

“That happens a lot now.”

Lucien ignored him.

He handed Aurelia a small piece of parchment.

No seal.

No signature.

Only seven words.

**WE DO NOT WANT HIM DEAD YET.**

Aurelia read it twice.

Her expression turned cold.

Caldrin appeared behind Lucien.

“There is another line.”

Aurelia turned the parchment over.

Three more words.

**LET HIM GROW.**

Silence.

Rez’s blue-white mana flickered.

Lucien took the parchment back.

“They are studying him.”

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“Or trying to frighten us.”

“Yes.”

“Or both.”

“Yes.”

She looked toward Zee.

The infant was still smiling faintly.

The hatchling leaned against him.

The message changed nothing about what Zee knew.

Nothing about what he felt.

But it changed the adults around him.

Some enemies wanted him dead.

Others wanted him alive.

That distinction was not comforting.

Sometimes being wanted alive was worse.

---

Far beyond House Vesper, the woman in black received a report.

“The sanctuary burned.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

“One prisoner escaped.”

Her expression changed.

“Which?”

“Theron.”

“Did he reach Vesper?”

“We believe so.”

The woman looked toward a series of glass containers lining the chamber wall.

Inside each rested small samples of blood labeled only by number.

Some dark.

Some pale.

Some nearly black.

None crimson.

A man beside her asked, “Should we recover him?”

“No.”

“He knows too much.”

“He knows fragments.”

“That may be enough.”

She smiled faintly.

“Let him speak.”

“Why?”

“Because frightened kings are useful when they believe they have discovered something themselves.”

The man looked uneasy.

“And the child?”

“Do not touch him.”

“For how long?”

The woman looked toward a fresh report.

**Subject survived army siege.**

**Subject survived confirmed cardiac death — unverified witness chain.**

**Subject displayed reactive force manifestation.**

**Subject demonstrated abnormal predatory perception.**

**Subject potentially absorbed foreign essence.**

She tapped the final line.

“Until we know whether every attempt to destroy him teaches us more about him…”

She paused.

“…or teaches him more about us.”

The man lowered his head.

“And if he keeps evolving?”

The woman looked toward the empty crimson vial prepared on the table.

“Then eventually…”

She smiled.

“…we stop observing from a distance.”

---

That night, Zee dreamed.

Nothing complicated.

Red light.

Warmth.

Aurelia’s voice.

The hatchling beside him.

Then something else.

A shape.

Black.

Watching from far away.

The image had not come from Zee.

It came through the Dragon Link.

The hatchling was awake.

He remembered the rider.

Zee felt his fear.

He responded instinctively.

Not with language.

Not with reassurance.

With presence.

Here.

The hatchling moved closer.

Together.

Their heartbeats settled.

Outside the room, Vale stood guard.

Beyond him, Vesper soldiers patrolled halls layered with wards.

Farther still, the Twelve Crowns tightened sanctions.

Bounty hunters studied new reports.

Witch factions argued.

Vampire courts listened for Zee’s heartbeat.

Wolf packs continued changing beneath instinct they did not understand.

And somewhere beyond all of them, unseen hands began collecting every story about the First Natural Tribrid.

Zee had survived the world trying to kill him.

Now he had entered a more dangerous stage.

The world had begun trying to learn him.

# Chapter Sixteen

## The Winter Hunt

The first snow came early.

It fell over House Vesper in thick white sheets that softened rooftops, buried roads, and turned the surrounding forests into something deceptively peaceful.

Zee had been in Vesper for three weeks.

Three weeks without an army at the gates.

Three weeks without a dagger entering the nursery.

Three weeks without a monster climbing through a wall.

It was the longest uninterrupted stretch of his life.

Aurelia did not trust it.

Every morning she woke before dawn and checked Zee’s breathing.

Every night she inspected the windows herself, tested the wards with the royal witch, and refused to sleep until Captain Vale confirmed the corridors had been cleared.

Lucien never mocked her.

He understood too well what fear could turn into when ignored.

Rez, meanwhile, had decided that Zee was his.

Not in the political sense.

In the way children claimed friendships long before adults had time to define them.

He visited constantly.

He brought toys.

He brought stories Zee could not understand.

He brought food for the crimson hatchling and then complained when the hatchling preferred stealing from his plate instead.

The dragon had also grown.

Not dramatically.

But enough that Aurelia could no longer tuck him comfortably beneath one arm.

His crimson scales had deepened in color. Teal-and-gold mana appeared more often whenever he became excited or protective, threading over his body like fire beneath glass.

Rez had begun calling him Red.

The hatchling hated it.

Everyone knew because he bit Rez every time.

“Then stop calling him that,” Aurelia said.

Rez rubbed his wrist.

“He needs a name.”

“He has one somewhere.”

“Then he should tell us.”

“He cannot speak.”

“That sounds like his problem.”

The hatchling hissed.

Zee laughed.

The sound was still rare.

But it had become easier.

Aurelia watched from beside the fire as Rez sat on the floor near Zee’s cradle, offering the hatchling a strip of roasted meat with one hand while protecting his sleeve with the other.

For a few minutes, the world looked almost kind.

Then every ward in the western palace wing went dark.

Lucien entered the room before the final light disappeared.

“Vale.”

The captain was already moving.

Caldrin drew both blades.

The royal witch raised her hands.

Nothing happened.

Her expression changed.

“My magic.”

Aurelia stood immediately.

“Gone?”

“No.”

The witch tried again.

“It is there.”

“But?”

“I cannot reach it.”

The room froze.

Aurelia looked at Zee.

His Crimson Mana remained calm.

No pressure.

Nothing resembling his birth.

The witch understood the thought.

“It is not him.”

Caldrin walked toward the window.

“Someone outside.”

The snow-covered courtyard appeared empty.

Then one footprint formed.

No person.

Just a footprint.

Another appeared beside it.

Then another.

Moving toward the palace.

Vale’s face hardened.

“Invisible.”

Lucien raised one hand.

His mana answered.

Dark blue light gathered around his fingers.

“So only selected wards.”

The royal witch nodded grimly.

“Something is suppressing witchcraft.”

Rez stood.

Blue-white mana appeared around his hands.

“That is not suppressing mine.”

Lucien looked sharply at him.

“Do not test it.”

“I already did.”

“Rez.”

“I am helping.”

“You are seven.”

“That has never stopped anyone from attacking me.”

Lucien had no immediate answer.

Caldrin looked toward the courtyard.

“More footprints.”

Not one intruder.

Several.

They crossed the snow without bodies.

Aurelia lifted Zee.

The hatchling climbed beside him.

The Dragon Link carried immediate tension.

Hidden.

Near.

Zee’s vampire senses sharpened.

Heartbeats.

He heard them.

Six.

No.

Nine.

Spread across the courtyard.

His head turned slowly.

Aurelia followed his gaze.

“He hears them.”

Vale nodded.

“Good.”

Caldrin smiled.

“Finally, invisibility has a disadvantage.”

The first window shattered.

Nothing entered.

At least nothing visible.

Vale swung.

His sword struck metal.

A body flickered into sight for half a heartbeat.

White cloak.

Bone mask.

Then vanished again.

Caldrin attacked the empty space beside him.

A cry answered.

Blood hit the floor.

Visible.

The intruders did not stay unseen once wounded.

“Hit the blood,” Caldrin shouted.

More glass broke.

The hunters entered.

They carried no banners.

No royal seals.

Their weapons were silver-white and etched with seals Aurelia did not recognize.

The royal witch tried magic again.

Nothing.

One hunter threw a chain.

Vale cut through it.

The pieces landed on the floor and began moving on their own.

They wrapped around his boots.

He fell.

Lucien cast.

Dark blue mana struck one hunter directly and threw them through the wall.

Rez followed.

Blue-white force froze the moving chains around Vale.

The captain shattered them with the pommel of his sword.

Aurelia backed toward the interior chamber.

The hatchling growled.

Zee listened.

Heartbeats.

Nine.

Then eight.

Then seven.

He began tracking them instinctively.

One behind Lucien.

Zee cried out.

Lucien turned.

The invisible blade missed his throat.

He struck the attacker.

A second heartbeat moved toward Rez.

The hatchling saw the disturbance in the snow first.

He lunged.

Teal-and-gold fire exposed the hunter’s cloak.

Rez ducked beneath a blade and slammed blue-white mana into the attacker’s chest.

The figure struck the ceiling and collapsed.

Aurelia stared.

The children were learning too quickly.

That frightened her.

Because danger was the teacher.

One hunter remained outside.

Zee heard that heartbeat differently.

Steady.

Not attacking.

Waiting.

The same pattern from the palace assassin.

Observer.

His Crimson Mana stirred.

The hunter outside raised something.

Not a crossbow.

A small glass sphere.

Caldrin saw it.

“Down!”

The sphere shattered against the floor.

White smoke filled the room.

Not poison.

Cold.

Impossible cold.

The fire died.

Ice spread across stone.

The royal witch collapsed to one knee.

“I cannot feel my hands.”

Aurelia wrapped Zee inside her cloak.

The hatchling shivered.

The Dragon Link flooded with cold.

Zee reacted.

His wolf blood resisted first.

Heat rose beneath his skin.

His vampire blood slowed what should have been panic.

Crimson Mana pushed outward.

Not attacking.

Insulating.

Warmth formed around him.

Then around the hatchling.

The Dragon Link carried relief.

Near.

Warm.

Aurelia felt the temperature shift against her arms.

She looked down.

Zee’s body had adapted faster than hers.

Not because he understood the cold.

Because something inside him refused to let it win.

The hidden observer moved closer.

Zee heard the heartbeat.

He turned toward it.

His eyes fixed on empty air.

The hunter stopped.

Zee growled.

The sound came deeper than before.

The snow outside the broken window compressed beneath invisible feet.

The hunter backed away.

Then ran.

Caldrin reached the window.

“Let them go.”

Vale looked toward him.

“What?”

“They came prepared.”

“For witches.”

“For invisibility.”

“For cold.”

Caldrin looked toward the forest.

“And one stayed outside to watch.”

Lucien’s expression hardened.

“They were testing us.”

“No.”

Aurelia looked at Zee.

“They were testing him.”

Silence.

The royal witch finally managed to reach her mana again.

The suppression faded with distance.

She rubbed warmth into her fingers.

“Whoever they are, they now know cold does not affect him normally.”

Lucien looked toward the shattered windows.

“They also know he can hear what he cannot see.”

Vale stood.

“And track movement without sight.”

Caldrin sheathed one blade.

“Which means the next group will change methods.”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

The pattern had become undeniable.

The world hunted Zee.

Each failure became information.

Each survival became preparation for the next attempt.

Outside, the surviving hunter disappeared into the snowy forest.

Zee watched the empty tree line.

He could not know he had been observed.

He only knew the danger had gone.

For now.

The hatchling pressed against him.

Safe?

Zee relaxed.

Safe.

Temporarily.

---

The captured hunters carried nothing identifying them.

No coin.

No names.

No letters.

No crests.

But their masks were made from the same pale bone.

Lucien laid one on the council table.

Theron stared at it.

His face changed.

Aurelia noticed.

“You know it.”

Theron shook his head too quickly.

Caldrin smiled without humor.

“That was convincing.”

Theron looked away.

Lucien leaned forward.

“Speak.”

The former prisoner swallowed.

“I saw masks like that once.”

“Where?”

“At the sanctuary.”

The room went still.

“When?”

“Months ago.”

“Who wore them?”

“I never saw faces.”

“What did they do?”

Theron looked toward the mask.

“They collected survivors.”

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“Survivors of what?”

“The experiments.”

Silence.

Vale frowned.

“Why?”

“I do not know.”

Theron rubbed his hands together.

“They came after each trial.”

“If someone lived longer than expected, they took them somewhere else.”

Caldrin’s expression sharpened.

“Where?”

“I never found out.”

Lucien looked toward Aurelia.

The sanctuary.

The assassins.

The masked hunters.

Still not enough to prove a single organization.

But closer.

Aurelia tapped the mask.

“They did not try to kill Zee.”

Vale nodded.

“They incapacitated the room.”

“Tested his senses.”

“His response to cold.”

“His defenses.”

Caldrin looked toward the door.

“And withdrew once they had enough.”

Theron whispered, “They are measuring him.”

The room fell silent.

Aurelia stared toward the upper floor where Zee slept.

“They will not do it again.”

Lucien looked at her.

“You cannot guarantee that.”

“No.”

Her eyes hardened.

“But I can stop giving them easy opportunities.”

Vale understood first.

“You want to move him.”

“Yes.”

“To where?”

Aurelia looked toward Lucien.

“Somewhere they cannot prepare for.”

Caldrin smiled faintly.

“That rules out every known sanctuary, palace, fortress, and road.”

“Exactly.”

Lucien leaned back.

“What are you proposing?”

Aurelia looked toward the winter map.

Mountains.

Forests.

Old borders.

Unclaimed regions.

Dangerous places civilized armies avoided.

“If safety attracts hunters…”

She paused.

“Then we stop looking for safety.”

# Chapter Seventeen

## The Place Without a Crown

They left Vesper territory six days later.

This time, not even the palace servants knew.

Lucien told the court Aurelia remained inside the western wing under heavy guard.

Rez was furious when he learned he would not be going.

His argument lasted long enough that Lucien threatened to lock him inside his room.

Rez responded by reminding his father that he knew three secret passages.

Lucien discovered four that afternoon.

In the end, Rez stood beside Zee’s cradle the night before departure.

He held the wooden wolf the hatchling had nearly destroyed weeks earlier.

One ear was gone.

The tail had teeth marks.

Rez placed it beside Zee.

“This time it is yours.”

The hatchling looked at it.

Rez pointed.

“No.”

The dragon looked at him.

“No.”

The hatchling took the wolf anyway.

Rez sighed.

Zee laughed.

Rez looked toward him.

“I will see you again.”

Zee reached.

Rez gave him one finger.

Crimson Mana flickered.

Blue-white answered faintly.

No danger.

Familiar.

Rez smiled.

“You better remember me.”

Aurelia watched from the doorway.

“He will.”

Rez looked at her.

“You do not know that.”

“No.”

She smiled softly.

“But I think he will.”

That was enough.

---

The place Aurelia chose had no kingdom.

No crown.

No walls.

No trade road.

It lay north of Vesper, beyond a mountain range so old the maps disagreed on its name.

Caldrin knew the region.

That worried everyone.

“Why do you know it?” Vale asked.

“I have had an interesting life.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one you are getting.”

The journey took eleven days.

Snow became ice.

Ice became black stone.

The forests thinned until twisted trees clung to cliffs under constant wind.

No armies followed.

No bounty hunters appeared.

No masked observers crossed their path.

The silence should have comforted Aurelia.

Instead it felt like warning.

Even the hatchling became uneasy.

The Dragon Link carried distant impressions.

High.

Cold.

Open.

Then something else.

Territory.

Not theirs.

Zee felt it too.

His wolf instincts stirred.

Vale looked toward the mountains.

“What lives here?”

Caldrin shrugged.

“Depends how unlucky we are.”

Aurelia glared.

“You brought us.”

“You chose the destination.”

“You knew the road.”

“I never claimed the destination was friendly.”

The royal witch muttered, “One day I will turn you into something small.”

Caldrin smiled.

“I have been threatened with worse.”

They reached the valley at dusk.

It was enormous.

Black mountains surrounded a frozen lake.

Steam rose from cracks in the earth.

No human settlement existed.

No castle.

No shrine.

No ruins.

Just wilderness.

Aurelia dismounted.

“This.”

Vale looked around.

“This is your plan?”

“No roads.”

“No walls.”

“No known sanctuary.”

Caldrin nodded.

“No people.”

The hatchling spread his wings.

The wind caught him.

For one terrifying second, Aurelia thought he would be thrown backward.

Instead he beat his wings.

Once.

Twice.

Then lifted.

Only a few feet.

Unsteady.

Wild.

But flying.

Zee saw him.

The Dragon Link erupted with joy.

Up.

The hatchling climbed another foot.

Then crashed into the snow.

Caldrin laughed.

Aurelia covered her mouth.

Vale shook his head.

The hatchling emerged furious.

Snow covered his face.

Zee laughed so hard he hiccuped.

The little dragon glared at him.

Then sneezed.

Teal-and-gold sparks burst from his nose.

Zee laughed harder.

For several moments, the valley felt alive.

Then the ground moved.

Everyone froze.

Not an earthquake.

Something beneath the frozen lake.

Vale drew his sword.

Caldrin stopped smiling.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Aurelia lifted Zee.

The hatchling ran back toward him.

The ice cracked.

A line spread across the lake.

Then another.

Something massive moved beneath it.

The hatchling stared.

The Dragon Link carried fear.

Big.

Zee’s heartbeat accelerated.

A shadow passed below the ice.

Long.

Too long.

The frozen surface exploded.

A creature rose from the lake.

Its body resembled a serpent covered in dark blue scales and ice-white bone plates. Four long limbs ended in claws large enough to tear horses apart. Antler-like horns curved from its skull.

Water poured from its jaws.

Its eyes opened.

Silver.

The royal witch whispered, “Frost Wyrm.”

Caldrin exhaled.

“Unlucky, then.”

The beast roared.

The valley shook.

Vale moved forward.

“Get Aurelia back.”

“There is nowhere back.”

The Frost Wyrm climbed onto the ice.

It smelled them.

Its head moved.

Vale.

Caldrin.

The witch.

Aurelia.

Then the hatchling.

The creature stopped.

The crimson dragon stared back.

Something ancient passed between them.

Not recognition.

Species.

Rival.

The hatchling spread his small wings and growled.

Caldrin looked at him.

“I admire the confidence.”

The Frost Wyrm charged.

The witch cast.

Violet force struck its skull.

The beast barely moved.

Vale and Caldrin separated.

Aurelia ran toward the rocks.

The Wyrm followed.

Not them.

Zareth.

The hatchling realized too late.

It snapped at him.

The Dragon Link flooded Zee.

Fear.

Run.

Pain coming.

Zee reacted.

Crimson Mana burst outward.

The Frost Wyrm stumbled.

Not enough.

Its claw came down.

The hatchling tried to fly.

Too slow.

The claw struck.

He disappeared into the snow.

Zee screamed.

Aurelia turned.

“No!”

The Dragon Link became pain.

Then anger.

Then something deeper.

Zee’s wolf nature surged.

His vampire senses sharpened.

His witch mana flooded outward.

All three existed already.

All three answered at once.

The air around him darkened crimson.

The Frost Wyrm turned.

Its silver eyes fixed on Zee.

The newborn stared back.

The beast roared.

Zee roared too.

Small.

But not human.

The sound carried three instincts at once.

Predator.

Magic.

Blood.

The Wyrm stopped.

Its head tilted.

Zee’s Crimson Mana pressed against it.

The beast resisted.

Unlike the Wildbloods.

Unlike the Gravehounds.

This creature was ancient enough, strong enough, and territorial enough not to simply submit.

It attacked.

The royal witch shouted.

Aurelia ran.

The Wyrm’s jaws opened.

Zee reached instinctively toward the heartbeat inside it.

Too deep.

Too strong.

He could feel it.

Could not control it.

The Wyrm struck.

Then teal-and-gold fire exploded across its eye.

The hatchling lived.

He flew badly.

One wing bent.

Blood covered his side.

But rage kept him airborne.

He attacked again.

The Wyrm snapped toward him.

Zee felt the movement through the Link.

His mana reacted.

The air around the Wyrm’s head compressed.

Its bite missed.

Vale climbed onto its side and drove his sword between bone plates.

Caldrin attacked the rear leg.

The witch cast directly into the exposed wound.

The Frost Wyrm screamed.

Its blood hit the snow.

Zee smelled it.

Cold.

Ancient.

Powerful.

His vampire nature responded violently.

Hunger.

Aurelia felt him shift.

“No.”

Zee stared at the blood.

The Dragon Link carried the hatchling’s pain.

The Wyrm struck him again.

That decided it.

Zee reached.

Crimson Mana touched the spilled blood.

The blood moved.

Not all of it.

A thin stream.

It crossed the snow.

Entered Zee’s mouth.

Aurelia froze.

The effect was immediate.

Cold tore through his body.

His skin paled.

Crimson Mana surged.

The absorbed blood carried something built for frozen oceans, deep winters, and survival beneath ice.

Zee’s body reacted.

Rejected pieces.

Kept others.

Changed them.

His breath misted.

Then crimson frost appeared across Aurelia’s sleeve where his fingers rested.

The royal witch stared.

Not white frost.

Not the Frost Wyrm’s power copied.

Crimson ice.

Thin.

Alive with Zee’s mana.

The Frost Wyrm sensed it.

For the first time...

The ancient beast looked afraid.

Zee inhaled.

Cold no longer hurt him the same way.

The adaptation settled.

Incomplete.

New.

His first true Crimson Evolution had begun.

The Frost Wyrm roared and retreated toward the lake.

No one followed.

It crashed through the ice and vanished beneath black water.

Silence returned.

The hatchling landed badly beside Zee.

He collapsed.

Aurelia knelt.

“Come here.”

The dragon crawled toward Zee instead.

The Dragon Link carried one thing.

Together.

Zee touched his scales.

Crimson frost appeared briefly beneath his fingertips.

The hatchling stared.

Then sneezed teal-and-gold sparks.

The frost shattered.

Caldrin looked at the broken red crystals.

“What do we call that?”

Aurelia looked at him.

“We do not.”

“Why not?”

“Because we do not understand it.”

He nodded.

“Fair.”

Vale stared toward the frozen lake.

“We chose this place because no one else would come here.”

Caldrin looked at the blood on the snow.

“That may still be true.”

The witch looked toward Zee.

“But now we know why.”

Aurelia stood with her son.

The valley had nearly killed them within minutes of arrival.

No armies.

No assassins.

No politics.

Only the world itself.

And Zee had survived differently again.

They built camp beneath the cliffs.

For the first time, no foreign eyes watched.

No king issued orders.

No bounty hunter tracked the road.

Only mountains surrounded them.

For several weeks, perhaps months, this place might belong to no crown.

That did not make it safe.

But it gave Zee something he had never had.

Room to grow.

---

Three months passed.

Winter deepened.

Zee learned to crawl before he learned fear of heights.

The hatchling learned to fly before he learned restraint.

Aurelia learned never to leave food unattended.

Vale built defenses.

The royal witch taught Aurelia how to recognize magical disturbances.

Caldrin disappeared for days at a time and returned with meat, information, and stories nobody believed.

Zee grew.

Not peacefully.

Never peacefully.

The mountains tested him constantly.

Cold storms.

Predators.

Thin air.

Unstable ground.

Once, a cliff cat entered camp and nearly dragged him from a blanket before the hatchling attacked it.

Another time, Zee crawled too close to a thermal fissure and instinctively coated his hands in Crimson Mana before touching burning stone.

Each danger changed him slightly.

His body learned.

His senses sharpened.

His Crimson Mana became easier to summon under stress.

His crimson frost appeared whenever intense cold threatened him.

Not Frost Wyrm magic.

Something new.

His.

The first evolution born from absorbed blood.

Then spring came.

And with it...

A rider.

Caldrin spotted him first.

One man.

Half-dead.

Vesper colors hidden beneath a torn cloak.

Vale met him beyond camp.

The rider collapsed from the saddle.

Aurelia rushed forward.

“Who are you?”

The man looked up.

“Vesper messenger.”

Her blood went cold.

“Lucien?”

“Alive.”

“Rez?”

“Alive.”

She exhaled.

Then saw his face.

“What happened?”

The messenger coughed blood.

“The Twelve Crowns broke the sanctions.”

Aurelia frowned.

“What does that mean?”

“They stopped isolating Vesper.”

“Why?”

The rider looked toward Zee.

Now older.

Crawling beside the crimson dragon.

“Because they are no longer afraid of House Vesper sheltering him.”

Vale’s expression hardened.

“Why not?”

The messenger swallowed.

“They are afraid of what he is becoming out here.”

Silence.

Caldrin looked toward the mountains.

“How did they find us?”

The messenger’s eyes filled with dread.

“They did not.”

Aurelia froze.

“Then how do they know?”

Old.

Near.
