# Crimson Dynasty — Chapters Thirty-Six & Thirty-Seven

# Chapter Thirty-Six

## The House That Bought Dragons

Lady Morcant’s estate had no walls.

That was the first thing Zee disliked about it.

The second was the silence.

They reached the old quarry road near sunset and left the horses beneath a ridge thick with dead cedar. Beyond the trees, black farmland spread toward a manor built directly into the side of a pale stone hill.

No towers.

No soldiers on visible patrol.

No banners identifying the owner.

Nothing about the place looked important enough to hide stolen supernatural bloodlines.

Caldrin studied it from the ridge.

“Expensive.”

Zee frowned.

“It looks empty.”

“That is what makes it expensive.”

Ner crouched beside him.

“How?”

“People with real money pay to make danger look boring.”

Rez nodded.

“That is unfortunately true.”

He was adjusting his new sword belt again.

It had been five days since Zee accidentally changed him.

Five days of relearning reach, weight, stride, balance, stamina, and the humiliating fact that some horses now looked considerably larger than he remembered.

Rez hated all of it.

He had also improved frighteningly fast.

Seventeen years of memory did not make his ten-year-old body stronger than it was.

It did tell him exactly how to train it.

Zee looked toward him.

“Your belt is crooked.”

Rez looked down.

It was.

He fixed it.

“You saw nothing.”

Ner smiled.

“I saw everything.”

Rez pointed toward him.

“You have been waiting five days for revenge.”

“I waited seven years.”

“That is worse.”

Aurelia turned from the estate.

“Quiet.”

All three immediately stopped.

Zareth remained farther up the ridge, crimson body partially hidden beneath dark trees. He could not approach openly.

A Dragon Crown Prince landing beside a secret blood estate would announce them before anyone reached the front door.

The Dragon Link carried his displeasure.

**Bad plan. No bite. Too far.**

Zee answered silently with a simple image.

Wait.

Zareth sent one back.

Biting Caldrin.

Zee almost laughed.

Caldrin looked over.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“I dislike when you say nothing while looking at the dragon.”

“You should.”

Mara crouched beside Aurelia.

The former Khell broker had become increasingly nervous the closer they came to Morcant’s territory.

Aurelia noticed.

“You have been here.”

Mara did not answer.

Vale’s expression hardened.

“Mara.”

“Yes.”

Zee looked at her.

“You said you knew one buyer.”

“I did.”

“You did not say you delivered here.”

Mara’s jaw tightened.

“I delivered here.”

Aurelia became very still.

“What?”

“Blood.”

“People?”

Mara looked away.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“People?”

“Yes.”

Zee felt his horns warming.

Rez touched his sleeve.

Not restraining.

Reminder.

Zee breathed.

The heat steadied.

Aurelia’s voice became almost too calm.

“Veyrath?”

“Once.”

“How many?”

“Two.”

“When?”

“Six years ago.”

“Alive when you left?”

“Yes.”

Aurelia’s hands curled.

“You knew this.”

“I knew two captives bearing Veyrath markers came here six years ago.”

“And you waited until now?”

“I told you Morcant bought Veyrath.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No.”

Mara did not defend herself.

That helped her more than excuses would have.

“I was not a good person then.”

Aurelia’s stare sharpened.

“That sentence does not return anyone.”

“I know.”

Zee watched Mara.

He had expected anger to sound louder.

Instead, guilt seemed to make her quieter.

Ner asked, “What did Morcant do with them?”

Mara swallowed.

“I never stayed long enough to know.”

Caldrin studied the manor.

“Then tonight becomes educational.”

Aurelia turned toward everyone.

“We are not storming the estate.”

Zee opened his mouth.

“No.”

He closed it.

Rez looked amused.

Aurelia continued.

“We confirm who is inside.”

“Where they are kept.”

“How many guards.”

“What protections.”

“Then we move.”

Zee looked toward the darkening sky.

“What if Khell arrives first?”

“We adapt.”

“What if Morcant moves them?”

“We adapt.”

“What if—”

“Zee.”

He stopped.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“I want them out too.”

That quieted him.

Not because she was Queen.

Because this was her family.

Her blood.

Her hope.

He nodded.

Aurelia looked toward Mara.

“How do we enter?”

Mara pointed toward the quarry behind the estate.

“Deliveries go below.”

Vale frowned.

“Of course they do.”

Caldrin smiled.

“I was worried we might use a normal door.”

---

The quarry entrance was hidden behind a curtain of dead vines.

No spell concealed it.

Only neglect.

That bothered Ner.

“Why hide something important this badly?”

Mara whispered, “Because most people who find it do not leave.”

Rez looked toward her.

“You really need to improve your comforting stories.”

They descended.

Aurelia.

Vale.

Caldrin.

Mara.

Zee.

Rez.

Ner.

Zareth remained outside, tracking them through the Dragon Link as far as distance allowed.

The tunnel smelled of limestone, iron, old blood, and witchcraft.

Zee’s vampire senses sharpened.

Heartbeats ahead.

Many.

He stopped.

“Twenty-three.”

Vale looked back.

“Guards?”

“Some.”

“How many?”

Zee listened.

“Eight walking.”

“Others slow.”

“Sleeping?”

“No.”

He frowned.

“Too weak.”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

Captives.

The tunnel opened into an underground gallery.

Glass chambers lined the walls.

Empty.

Mostly.

One held dark feathers floating in preserving liquid.

Another contained shed wolf claws.

Another displayed strips of scaled hide that Zee refused to inspect closely.

Ner’s Golden Mana stirred beneath his gloves.

“This is a collection.”

Mara looked sick.

“Yes.”

Rez stared toward a cabinet containing labeled blood vials.

“Not research.”

Caldrin looked around.

“No.”

“Ownership.”

Zee hated the room immediately.

Aurelia did too.

They continued.

Voices approached.

Vale pulled Zee and Ner into a side alcove.

Rez moved beside them.

Two guards passed.

Human.

Armed.

One complained about Khell.

“Shipment should have arrived already.”

The second answered, “Morcant is furious.”

“How many?”

“Four.”

Zee looked at Aurelia.

Four.

The remaining captives who had traveled with Khell.

Maybe.

The guards continued.

“Old woman says she wants all seven reunited before auction.”

Zee’s heart stopped metaphorically—not literally, never literally.

All seven.

Aurelia’s face changed.

Not hope now.

Certainty of one thing.

Someone had deliberately brought them together.

The guards disappeared around the corner.

Aurelia whispered, “Auction?”

Mara went pale.

“That is new.”

Caldrin glanced toward her.

“Meaning?”

“Morcant collects.”

“She does not sell.”

Ner looked toward the distant corridor.

“Then someone changed the deal.”

Rez’s eyes narrowed.

“Khell.”

Possibly.

Not certainty.

They moved faster.

The next chamber answered the question.

Seven iron doors.

Three open.

Four closed.

Names had been written above them in chalk.

Not true names.

Numbers.

One.

Two.

Three.

Four.

Five.

Six.

Seven.

Zee hated that more.

Aurelia approached the first closed door.

Her hand stopped inches from it.

Something inside moved.

A heartbeat.

Weak.

Dragon.

Witch.

Both.

Aurelia inhaled sharply.

“Open it.”

Ner approached the lock.

Golden Mana began gathering.

Mara caught his wrist.

“No.”

Everyone turned.

Ner’s face hardened.

“Remove your hand.”

Mara did immediately.

“The lock is linked to the prisoner.”

Aurelia looked toward her.

“If broken incorrectly?”

“The restraint tightens.”

“Can you open it?”

“No.”

Caldrin examined the frame.

“Can we remove the door?”

“Same result.”

Zee touched the wall.

“What about the room?”

Mara looked at him.

“What?”

“If the lock controls the door…”

He pointed toward the stone beside it.

“…then we do not use the door.”

Caldrin smiled.

“My influence.”

Aurelia looked toward Vale.

Vale sighed.

“Quietly.”

They began removing stone.

Not with explosions.

Not magic at first.

Caldrin found the mortar seams.

Vale worked a narrow blade into them.

Rez used controlled Blue-White cold to weaken specific sections.

Ner shaped Golden Mana into thin wedges.

Zee listened to the heartbeat inside.

Slow.

But steady.

When enough stone loosened, Zee pulled.

The block shifted.

Crimson scales spread across his fingers under the strain.

They removed another.

Then another.

A gap opened.

Darkness beyond.

A face appeared.

Male.

Older than Aurelia.

Gaunt.

Long dark hair streaked with gray.

Deep red eyes opened slowly.

Aurelia stopped breathing for one terrible moment.

The man stared through the gap.

Confusion.

Then disbelief.

His lips moved.

No sound.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“Theron?”

The man’s face broke.

Not magically.

Emotionally.

“Aurelia?”

Zee looked at his mother.

He had never heard anyone say her name like that.

Not Queen.

Not Veyrath.

Not Darkheart.

Little sister.

Aurelia tore the remaining stone out herself.

Witch Mana shattered mortar.

Dragon strength followed.

The opening widened.

She climbed through.

Theron Veyrath tried standing.

His legs failed.

Aurelia caught him.

For several seconds, no one else existed.

Theron held her as though checking whether she was real.

“You lived.”

Aurelia’s voice broke.

“So did you.”

He laughed once.

Weak.

“You got old.”

Aurelia pulled back.

“You look terrible.”

“That is more like you.”

Zee smiled despite the room.

Then Theron noticed him.

His gaze moved past Aurelia.

To Zee.

Crimson eyes.

Horns.

Scales.

Ten years old.

Theron stared.

Aurelia followed his gaze.

“My son.”

Theron looked back at her.

“You had a child?”

“Yes.”

“With Victor?”

Aurelia’s expression changed.

“That conversation is longer.”

Theron looked toward Zee again.

Dragon scent.

Veyrath blood.

Something else.

Several something elses.

His eyes narrowed.

“What is he?”

Zee crossed his arms.

“Zee.”

Theron blinked.

Rez smiled.

Ner looked delighted.

Aurelia almost laughed.

“This is Zee.”

“My son.”

“That answer is enough for now.”

Theron nodded slowly.

Then his face changed.

“The others.”

Aurelia looked toward the remaining cells.

“Alive?”

“Three here.”

“Four coming.”

“Yes.”

“You know?”

Theron’s expression darkened.

“Khell has been using me to identify Veyrath blood for years.”

Zee remembered the broker’s words.

One captive could identify their blood by scent.

Theron.

Aurelia looked as if she wanted to kill someone with her bare hands.

Theron grabbed her wrist.

“No.”

She looked at him.

“Not because he deserves mercy.”

His eyes sharpened.

“Because he is bringing four more of ours.”

That mattered.

Aurelia breathed.

Controlled.

“Who are the three?”

Theron looked toward the other occupied cells.

“Two Veyrath descendants.”

“One Dragon-Witch.”

“Family?”

“Distant.”

“Names?”

“Later.”

Footsteps echoed.

Many.

Mara looked toward the corridor.

“Too late.”

The estate had discovered them.

Vale drew his sword.

Caldrin smiled.

“Finally.”

Aurelia helped Theron against the wall.

“You stay here.”

Theron laughed weakly.

“I remember you being easier to order.”

“I was six.”

“You were never easy.”

Zee looked toward Rez.

“Sounds familiar.”

Rez glared.

Ner whispered, “Historically.”

Rez elbowed him.

Then the first alarm bell rang.

Zareth heard it outside.

The Dragon Link erupted.

**Fight?**

Zee looked toward the ceiling.

Aurelia saw his face.

“Tell him to wait.”

Zee frowned.

“Why?”

“Because we do not know what happens if an entire Dragon crashes through a manor built over prisoners.”

Zee sent the thought.

Wait.

Zareth answered with furious reluctance.

The first guards entered the gallery.

Aurelia turned.

Her grief disappeared beneath power.

“Alive if possible.”

Caldrin sighed.

“You say that every time.”

The fight began.

---

Lady Morcant came downstairs herself.

That told Zee more about her than the guards did.

She did not hide behind them.

She walked through the gallery while the battle still moved around her, dressed in dark green robes with silver embroidery and carrying no visible weapon.

Older.

White hair.

Black eyes.

Witch.

Powerful.

Vale fought two guards near the entrance.

Rez controlled another with Blue-White Mana, using his smaller body rather than fighting against it.

Ner kept the occupied cells behind a Golden barrier.

Caldrin had already disarmed three people.

Aurelia stood in front of Theron.

Zee stood beside her.

Morcant looked at Theron.

Then Aurelia.

Her eyebrows rose.

“Oh.”

Aurelia’s voice became ice.

“Lady Morcant.”

“You are difficult to purchase.”

Zee’s horns heated instantly.

Rez shouted from across the chamber.

“Control!”

Zee breathed.

Morcant noticed.

Her gaze shifted toward him.

Interest.

No recognition of everything he was.

Only visible traits.

“Your son?”

Aurelia stepped slightly forward.

“Yes.”

“Veyrath.”

“Partly.”

Morcant smiled.

“Enough.”

Zee hated her immediately.

Theron struggled upright.

“Morcant.”

She looked toward him.

“You look healthier than expected.”

“I hope your disappointment kills you.”

Morcant smiled.

“Still charming.”

Aurelia’s magic gathered.

“Open the cells.”

“No.”

“Then I open them.”

“You cannot without injuring the occupants.”

Ner spoke from behind his Golden barrier.

“I can.”

Morcant finally noticed him.

Pure Golden Mana shone around both hands.

Her expression changed.

“What are you?”

Ner looked offended.

“A person.”

Zee smiled.

Rez shouted, “Long story!”

Morcant raised one hand.

The floor sigils activated.

Every closed cell tightened.

Theron screamed.

Aurelia turned.

The prisoners inside cried out.

Ner’s Golden Mana surged.

“Stop!”

Morcant looked toward him.

“Open one lock and all four restraints contract.”

Ner froze.

Good trap.

Different problem.

Zee listened.

Heartbeats.

Pain.

Magic.

His own instincts began overlapping again.

He hated it.

He forced himself to focus.

One sound.

Rez’s voice.

“Zee!”

He looked.

Rez pointed toward the ceiling.

“Control lines!”

Zee saw nothing.

Ner did.

Golden Mana rose.

Thin magical connections became visible between Morcant’s ring and the four cells.

Not one lock.

One control source.

Ner smiled.

“There.”

Morcant’s expression changed.

She closed her fist.

Too late.

Rez struck first.

Blue-White Mana snapped around Morcant’s wrist and forced her hand open.

Ner sealed the space around the ring.

Aurelia attacked.

Violet witchcraft tore it free.

Zee caught the ring.

Morcant stared.

The object burned his palm.

He nearly dropped it.

Crimson scales spread.

The heat decreased.

Adapt.

He closed his fist.

The ring cracked.

All four cells unlocked.

Theron laughed.

“That was expensive.”

Morcant’s face twisted.

For the first time, she lost composure.

“You stupid child.”

Zee looked at the broken metal in his hand.

“People say that a lot.”

She cast.

Black-green witchcraft struck him squarely in the chest.

Zee flew backward.

Pain exploded through his ribs.

He hit the wall.

Hard.

Stayed conscious.

Stayed alive.

Always.

His body repaired what it could while he pushed upright.

Aurelia’s face transformed with rage.

Morcant saw it.

Too late.

Aurelia hit her with enough witchcraft to crack the floor.

Morcant countered.

The collision shook the gallery.

Dragon energy surfaced beneath Aurelia’s magic.

Dark crimson-red flashed through violet.

Morcant’s eyes widened.

“Dragon-Witch.”

Aurelia advanced.

“You should have learned what you were buying.”

The next spell broke Morcant’s defense.

Vale disarmed the remaining guards.

Caldrin put a blade to Morcant’s throat.

Aurelia stopped him.

“Alive.”

Caldrin sighed dramatically.

Theron laughed again.

“I like him.”

“You should not,” Aurelia said.

“Everyone says that,” Caldrin replied.

The battle ended.

Ner opened the remaining cells safely.

Three captives emerged.

Weak.

Bruised.

Alive.

Not seven.

Not yet.

But alive.

Aurelia stood among them.

For ten years, Zee had known his mother as someone who had lost almost everything behind her.

Now three pieces of that past were breathing in front of her.

Then Theron looked toward the far corridor.

“We need to leave.”

Aurelia turned.

“Khell.”

“He will know Morcant lost the estate.”

“How?”

Theron looked toward the shattered control ring.

“That ring was linked to his transfer contract.”

Caldrin frowned.

“So destroying it warned him.”

“Yes.”

Zee looked guilty.

Theron pointed at him.

“No.”

Zee blinked.

“What?”

“I know that face.”

Aurelia almost smiled.

Theron continued.

“You freed four people.”

“Whatever consequence follows belongs to the person who built the cage.”

Zee stared.

He liked his uncle immediately.

Aurelia looked toward the ceiling.

“Zareth.”

Zee grinned.

Finally.

He sent one thought through the Link.

Come.

The manor roof exploded.

Everyone ducked.

Stone rained into the gallery.

Zareth’s enormous crimson head appeared through the opening.

Teal-and-Gold Mana rolled between broken beams.

The Dragon Prince looked extremely pleased.

Aurelia stared at the destroyed ceiling.

“I said come.”

Zee looked at Zareth.

The Link answered:

**Came.**

Rez laughed.

Ner covered his face.

Theron Veyrath stared upward at the Crown Prince of Drakonis.

Then at Zee.

Then Aurelia.

“I have many questions.”

Aurelia sighed.

“So does everyone.”

They left Morcant’s estate with four Veyrath survivors.

Lady Morcant bound.

Mara under guard but no longer treated as a prisoner.

And one new certainty.

Theron Veyrath lived.

Four more captives were still moving with Damaris Khell.

The rescue had begun.

It was not finished.

---

# Chapter Thirty-Seven

## The Brother She Buried

They did not return to Vesper.

Theron refused.

Not because of Lucien.

Not because of House Vesper.

Because Khell was moving.

Every hour mattered.

They established temporary shelter inside an abandoned stone monastery two miles from Morcant’s estate.

Zareth guarded the courtyard.

Vale secured the roads.

Caldrin questioned Morcant.

Mara checked old trade maps.

Ner helped the rescued captives recover without using more Golden Mana than necessary.

Rez trained.

Of course he did.

Zee found him in the courtyard shortly after midnight.

Rez was practicing the same sword sequence over and over.

Shorter stance.

Lower center.

Adjusted reach.

Again.

Again.

Again.

Zee leaned against a column.

“You are tired.”

Rez did not stop.

“So are you.”

“I am not swinging a sword.”

“You should be.”

Zee frowned.

Rez completed the sequence.

Turned.

Started again.

His ten-year-old body moved more naturally now.

Not perfectly.

But better.

“You are getting fast.”

“I was already fast.”

“You fell off a chair yesterday.”

Rez stopped.

“That was one time.”

“Ner says twice.”

“Ner is a liar.”

Zee smiled.

Then looked toward the monastery door.

Theron slept inside.

Or tried to.

Aurelia had not left his side for hours.

Rez noticed Zee’s expression.

“You okay?”

“Yes.”

Rez stared.

Zee sighed.

“I do not know.”

“Better.”

Zee walked into the courtyard.

“I have an uncle.”

“Yes.”

“My mother has a brother.”

“Yes.”

“She thought he was dead.”

“Yes.”

“He thought she was dead.”

“Yes.”

Zee looked toward him.

“That is horrible.”

Rez lowered the sword.

“Yes.”

No joke.

No correction.

Just truth.

Zee sat on the courtyard wall.

“Can you imagine?”

Rez looked at him.

“Losing my brother?”

Zee nodded.

Rez’s expression changed.

He sat beside him.

“I prefer not to.”

Zee remembered the night his power changed Rez.

*I can’t lose my best friend.*

*I wish I could stay with him.*

He looked at Rez’s younger face.

“I still feel bad.”

Rez groaned.

“We are not doing this every night.”

“I changed seven years.”

“You changed my body.”

“Same thing.”

“No.”

Rez tapped Zee’s forehead.

“The years are here.”

Then tapped his own chest.

“And here.”

“You did not take them.”

Zee looked at him.

Rez continued.

“I remember being seven.”

“I remember watching you grow.”

“I remember every stupid thing you did.”

“There are many.”

“Exactly.”

Zee smiled faintly.

Rez nudged him.

“My body is ten.”

“I hate parts of that.”

“I also enjoy parts.”

Zee blinked.

“You do?”

Rez looked offended by his own admission.

“I heal from training faster.”

“That might be you being ten.”

“I know.”

“I can climb palace walls again without everyone screaming about royal dignity.”

“Lucien still screams.”

“That is different.”

Zee laughed.

Rez smiled.

Then:

“And I get more time.”

Zee stopped.

Rez looked toward his younger hands.

“I do not know what this means long-term.”

“No one does.”

“But if this body keeps aging normally…”

He looked at Zee.

“I have years ahead I had already passed once.”

Zee had not thought about it that way.

Rez continued.

“I am angry you changed me without meaning to.”

Zee flinched.

“I know.”

“I am also still here.”

Both could be true.

Zee leaned his shoulder against Rez’s.

“Older brother.”

Rez smiled.

“Still.”

“You are ten.”

“I will stab you.”

“Historically.”

Rez shoved him off the wall.

Zee landed laughing.

The sound reached the monastery.

Aurelia heard it.

So did Theron.

Her brother lay on a narrow bed inside what had once been a prayer room.

He smiled faintly.

“You have a strange child.”

Aurelia looked toward the courtyard.

“You have no idea.”

Theron studied her.

“I would like one.”

Aurelia looked back.

“One what?”

“An idea.”

She sighed.

“You need rest.”

“I spent six years in a cage.”

“I have rested enough.”

“You were tortured.”

“Yes.”

“Starved.”

“Yes.”

“Used to identify your own blood for traffickers.”

His expression darkened.

“Yes.”

Aurelia sat beside him.

“Then stop pretending you are fine.”

Theron smiled.

“You sound like Mother.”

Aurelia’s face changed.

The room went quiet.

Theron looked away.

“Sorry.”

“No.”

She touched his hand.

“Say her name if you want.”

“I cannot tonight.”

Aurelia nodded.

Some wounds could be survived only in pieces.

Theron looked toward the doorway.

“Tell me about Zee.”

Aurelia almost laughed.

“That could take several years.”

“I appear to have time.”

“Do not joke like that.”

“Why?”

“Because I buried you in my head once.”

Theron’s smile disappeared.

Aurelia continued.

“I will not do it again.”

He squeezed her hand.

“Then do not.”

Silence.

Finally Aurelia began.

“He was born during Blood Rain.”

Theron stared.

“I heard stories.”

“They were not enough.”

“Witch?”

“Yes.”

“Vampire?”

“Yes.”

“Wolf?”

“Yes.”

Theron slowly sat straighter.

“All naturally?”

“Yes.”

“From birth?”

“Yes.”

“And Dragon?”

“Dormant.”

Theron stared toward the courtyard.

“Four blood natures.”

“Yes.”

“Three awake at birth.”

“Yes.”

“Then the rumors—”

“The world calls him the First Natural Tribrid.”

Theron nodded slowly.

“That remains accurate.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“You understand?”

“I understand blood classification.”

“Not him.”

“No one understands him.”

That sounded correct enough.

Theron continued.

“His Dragon nature came from you.”

“Yes.”

“The Drakonis prince?”

“Catalyst.”

“Not source.”

“Correct.”

“Link?”

“Unknown.”

Theron leaned back.

“Good.”

Aurelia frowned.

“Good?”

“You said unknown.”

She smiled faintly.

“Zee appreciates that too.”

Then Theron’s expression darkened.

“Victor.”

Aurelia went still.

“What about him?”

“He is Zee’s father.”

“Yes.”

“How did he take the birth?”

Aurelia looked away.

Theron knew immediately.

“Aurelia.”

“He was afraid.”

“Of Zee?”

“Yes.”

“Of you?”

“Eventually.”

Theron’s jaw tightened.

“What did he do?”

She did not answer.

Theron read enough in her silence.

His Dragon nature surfaced.

Dark red scales appeared along his wrist.

“Aurelia.”

“He hurt Zee.”

“How?”

“Do not.”

“Aurelia—”

“He killed him.”

The room died into silence.

Theron stared.

“What?”

Aurelia’s voice became flat.

“Once.”

“My son returned.”

“And death never reached him again.”

Theron’s face went through disbelief, rage, confusion.

Aurelia stopped him before questions multiplied.

“No.”

“You do not need to understand tonight.”

“Neither do I.”

“Victor does not.”

“Zee does not fully.”

Theron stood too quickly.

His legs nearly failed.

Aurelia caught him.

“I am going to kill Victor.”

“No.”

Theron stared.

“He murdered your child.”

“And failed to keep him dead.”

“That is not a defense.”

“I did not say it was.”

Theron breathed hard.

Aurelia guided him back onto the bed.

“Victor’s story is not tonight’s enemy.”

Theron looked toward her.

“Khell is.”

“Yes.”

“Four Veyrath captives.”

“Yes.”

“Then Victor gets to continue breathing until later.”

Aurelia gave him a look.

Theron smiled weakly.

“I am compromising.”

“You have not changed.”

“No.”

Then his eyes drifted toward the courtyard again.

“Zee knows?”

“Not every detail.”

“But enough?”

“He knows Victor fears him.”

Theron shook his head.

“Children should not know that kind of father.”

Aurelia looked toward the moonlit doorway.

“Zee knows many things children should not.”

That truth hurt both of them.

---

Lady Morcant began talking before dawn.

Not because Caldrin tortured her.

He did not need to.

He placed Khell’s broken transfer contract on the table and told her that Damaris would assume she betrayed him if she remained silent.

Morcant lasted twenty minutes.

Khell had moved the remaining four Veyrath captives southeast.

Not toward another estate.

Toward a mobile auction.

A private sale conducted aboard three river vessels that traveled between neutral territories.

No permanent address.

No stable jurisdiction.

Buyers came to the boats.

The boats came to no one.

Mara knew them.

“The Red Passage.”

Vale frowned.

“Vampire route?”

“Originally.”

“Now?”

“Anyone with enough money.”

Aurelia stood over the map.

“Where?”

Morcant remained bound across the room.

“Lower Marrow River.”

“How long?”

“Day and a half.”

Zee stood beside Aurelia.

Rez.

Ner.

Theron, despite every order that he remain in bed.

Zareth watched through a broken monastery window.

Theron pointed toward the river.

“Khell will expect pursuit.”

Caldrin nodded.

“Yes.”

“So he will divide cargo.”

Mara looked at him.

“Not if the auction requires all four.”

“Why would it?”

Morcant smiled bitterly.

“Because one of them is worth more than the others.”

Aurelia turned.

“Who?”

Morcant looked at Theron.

“You should know.”

Theron’s face hardened.

“I do not.”

“She smells like you.”

Silence.

Theron slowly went pale.

Aurelia noticed.

“Who?”

He looked toward her.

“No.”

“Theron.”

“No.”

Zee watched his uncle.

Fear.

Real fear.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“Who?”

Theron whispered:

“Seraphine.”

Aurelia froze.

Rez looked toward Zee.

Ner stopped breathing for a heartbeat.

Zee asked quietly, “Who is Seraphine?”

Neither sibling answered immediately.

Then Aurelia said:

“Our sister.”

The world changed again.

Zee stared.

“You have a sister?”

Theron looked sick.

“She was eight when we separated.”

Aurelia’s eyes filled.

“I thought she died with the eastern nest.”

“So did I.”

Morcant watched them.

“She did not.”

Aurelia turned toward her so sharply that Witch Mana flashed around the room.

“You saw her?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Six years ago.”

“Alive?”

“Yes.”

“After that?”

“I bought her.”

Theron surged forward.

Vale caught him.

Aurelia did not move.

That was worse.

Morcant continued quickly.

“Khell refused to complete the sale.”

“Why?”

“Theron.”

Everyone looked toward him.

Morcant smiled without humor.

“He discovered they shared blood.”

“He realized she could identify Veyrath lines even more accurately.”

Theron looked physically ill.

Khell had kept siblings as tools without allowing them to know.

Aurelia stepped toward Morcant.

“Where is she now?”

“The Red Passage.”

“Certain?”

Morcant hesitated.

Aurelia’s eyes turned lethal.

“Yes.”

One word.

Enough.

Aurelia turned toward the map.

“We leave now.”

Theron stood.

“So do I.”

“No.”

His head snapped toward her.

“Aurelia.”

“You can barely stand.”

“My sister is alive.”

“She is my sister too.”

“Then you understand.”

“Yes.”

Aurelia faced him.

“Which is why I will not rescue Seraphine only to watch you die trying to reach her.”

Theron’s expression hardened.

Zee watched.

Then stepped between them.

Both adults looked down.

“I have an idea.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

“That sentence has ruined many days.”

Zee ignored her.

“Theron comes.”

She opened her mouth.

“But not into the fight.”

Theron looked offended.

Zee continued.

“He knows Khell.”

“He can identify people.”

“He knows Seraphine’s scent.”

Theron nodded.

“But he stays with Vale until we know where she is.”

Vale frowned.

“I am apparently everyone’s keeper.”

Rez raised one hand.

“Welcome.”

Zee continued.

“Zareth scouts the boats from above.”

The Dragon Link sent approval.

“Ner finds magical cages.”

Ner nodded.

“Rez controls the deck.”

Rez smiled.

Aurelia looked toward him.

“What do you do?”

Zee grinned.

“Whatever goes wrong.”

Caldrin laughed.

“That may be the most accurate assignment.”

Aurelia stared at her son.

Ten.

Still ten.

Still young enough that she wanted to carry him away from every road.

Old enough that he had begun thinking in people rather than powers.

Roles.

Strengths.

Limits.

Not throwing himself at everything first.

Progress.

Dangerous progress.

She looked toward Theron.

Then the river.

Then Zee.

“Fine.”

His eyes widened.

“Really?”

“Do not make me regret it.”

Rez laughed.

“She says that to everyone now.”

Aurelia pointed toward him.

“You are still grounded.”

Rez stared.

“I am Crown Prince.”

“Physically ten.”

Rez looked betrayed.

Ner covered his mouth.

Theron watched all of them.

For the first time since leaving Morcant’s cage, something like life returned to his expression.

“You raised a strange family.”

Aurelia looked toward Zee.

Rez.

Ner.

Zareth.

Then her brother.

“Apparently.”

---

They reached the lower Marrow River by night.

Three ships moved beneath a moonless sky.

Black hulls.

No flags.

Red lanterns burning along their decks.

The Red Passage.

Zareth circled high above.

The Dragon Link brought Zee images.

Guards.

Chains.

Cages below deck.

Many heartbeats.

One felt different to Zareth only because Zee had given him Theron’s scent from a piece of cloth.

Related.

Veyrath.

Zee stood on the ridge overlooking the river.

Aurelia beside him.

Theron behind.

Mara pointed toward the center vessel.

“That is Khell’s.”

Rez adjusted his smaller sword.

Ner removed his gloves.

Pure Golden Mana flickered.

Vale drew steel.

Caldrin smiled.

Zee’s horns warmed.

Not instability.

Not loss of control.

Anticipation.

He breathed.

Focused.

Listened.

The heat remained his.

Aurelia noticed.

“You good?”

Zee looked at her.

“Truth?”

“Yes.”

“I am scared.”

Aurelia’s expression softened.

“Good.”

He frowned.

“Rez says that too.”

“Because fear is useful when it tells the truth.”

Zee looked toward the ships.

Someone his mother had mourned for years might be inside.

Seraphine Veyrath.

His aunt.

Another person Zee had never known existed.

Another piece of Aurelia’s life returning from the dead without actually returning from death at all.

No resurrection.

No rewritten history.

Only survival finally discovered.

Zee smiled faintly.

“Then I am very useful.”

Aurelia laughed once.

The center ship rang its auction bell.

Buyers began boarding.

Theron’s face hardened.

“They are selling her tonight.”

Zee looked toward Zareth overhead.

The Dragon Link tightened.

Ready.

Then toward Rez.

Ner.

Aurelia.

Vale.

Caldrin.

The hunted prince had spent ten years learning what it felt like when strangers came to take people from him.

Tonight, for the first time, Zee Darkheart would board a slave ship for someone he had never met simply because she belonged to someone he loved.

He drew his blade.

“Let’s go get my aunt.”

# Crimson Dynasty — Chapters Thirty-Eight & Thirty-Nine

# Chapter Thirty-Eight

## The Red Passage

The first rule of boarding a slave ship was apparently not to look like someone about to board a slave ship.

Caldrin informed them of this while painting dirt across Zee’s face.

Zee recoiled.

“What are you doing?”

“Improving you.”

“You made me dirty.”

“You were already dirty.”

“That was travel dirt.”

Caldrin stared.

“I apologize for disrespecting the distinction.”

Rez stood nearby in plain clothes, his smaller sword hidden beneath a dark coat. Ner wore gloves over his hands, every trace of Pure Golden Mana buried.

Aurelia had changed too.

No royal clothing.

No Darkheart symbols.

No visible witch crown.

Her hair was tied back, her Dragon nature buried so deeply Zee could barely feel its presence even knowing what to look for.

Theron remained beneath the ridge with Vale.

He hated that arrangement.

Everyone knew.

“I can walk.”

Vale folded his arms.

“You nearly fell mounting the horse.”

“I had been imprisoned for six years.”

“Yes.”

“So perhaps sympathy.”

“No.”

Theron looked toward Aurelia.

“She always chooses terrible people.”

Aurelia did not even turn.

“Victor was enough. I learned.”

Zee winced.

Rez whispered, “That was brutal.”

Ner nodded approvingly.

Above them, Zareth circled behind thick clouds.

The Dragon Link remained tense.

**Boats. People. Blood.**

Zee closed his eyes.

“Which ship?”

An image came.

The center vessel.

Lower deck.

Four distinct presences surrounded by many others.

Not enough for Zareth to identify blood.

Enough to know where people were confined.

Zee opened his eyes.

“Center.”

Mara nodded.

“Khell’s vessel.”

Aurelia looked toward her.

“You are certain?”

“The center ship always carries the broker.”

“Always?”

Mara corrected herself immediately.

“It did when I worked these routes.”

Aurelia nodded.

Better.

Truth precise enough to trust.

The three black ships drifted slowly down the Marrow River.

Red lanterns hung along their decks.

Small boats ferried wealthy buyers toward them.

No kingdom flags.

No royal insignia.

That was the point.

No crown could be blamed for what happened on water nobody claimed.

Zee watched men and women climb onto the center vessel.

Witches.

Vampires.

Humans.

One wolf-blooded noble.

Everyone dressed too well.

Everyone pretending this was business.

His fangs sharpened.

Rez touched his shoulder.

“Control.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

“You say that every time.”

“Because you keep needing it.”

Ner looked toward Rez.

“You sound seventy.”

Rez glared.

“I lived seventeen years.”

“Historically.”

Rez took one slow breath.

“I am saving all of this.”

“For when?”

“When I am taller again.”

Ner smiled.

“That assumes you grow faster than me.”

Zee laughed.

Aurelia looked at them.

“Are we finished?”

All three answered at once.

“Yes.”

Zareth sent amusement through the Link.

Aurelia sighed.

Then pointed toward the river.

“We go in two groups.”

“Caldrin, Mara, Rez.”

Rez nodded.

“You board through the buyer entrance.”

Zee frowned.

“Why Rez?”

“Because no one there expects Crown Prince Rez Vesper to look ten.”

Rez smiled.

Finally.

Aurelia continued.

“Zee, Ner, and I use the maintenance skiff beneath the stern.”

Ner looked toward her.

“And Zareth?”

Aurelia glanced upward.

“He waits.”

The Dragon Link exploded with rejection.

**No.**

Zee looked up.

“He says no.”

“I assumed.”

“He says he can help.”

“He can help by not setting the ship on fire while prisoners are below deck.”

A pause.

Then:

**Small fire.**

Zee covered his mouth.

Aurelia narrowed her eyes.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Zee.”

“He said small fire.”

Rez laughed first.

Aurelia looked toward the sky.

“Tell him if he burns that ship before I give the signal, I will personally send him back to his mother.”

The Link went silent.

Zee smiled.

“He understands.”

“Good.”

They moved.

---

Rez boarded the Red Passage as a servant.

He hated that less than being treated like an actual child.

Caldrin played the role of minor merchant.

Mara acted as broker.

That part required very little pretending.

The guard at the boarding ramp barely looked at Rez.

“Boy carries?”

Caldrin handed him a small case.

Rez accepted it with exaggerated effort.

Caldrin nearly smiled.

The guard waved them through.

The moment they crossed onto the deck, Rez changed.

Not visibly.

Inside.

Seventeen years of training settled behind ten-year-old eyes.

He counted guards.

Doors.

Stairs.

Weapons.

Possible exits.

Two vampires on deck.

Three witches.

Six humans.

One buyer carrying silver restraints.

One servant watching too carefully.

Mara whispered without moving her lips.

“Khell’s people use red cord on the wrist.”

Rez glanced.

Three guards.

Two servants.

One man near the stern.

Red cord.

Good.

Caldrin murmured, “Do not stare.”

“I am not.”

“You stare professionally.”

“That is not a thing.”

“It is now.”

The auction bell rang again.

A buyer laughed nearby.

“Veyrath, they say.”

Another answered.

“Real?”

“Supposedly.”

Rez’s jaw tightened.

“Dragon blood?”

“Better.”

“Dragon mixed with witch.”

Rez looked toward the river instead.

If he turned now, he would hit someone.

Caldrin noticed.

“Later.”

Rez nodded.

The buyers moved toward the lower auction chamber.

Rez followed.

---

Beneath the stern, Zee discovered that infiltration through a maintenance hatch was far less impressive than stories made it sound.

The hatch smelled terrible.

Ner climbed through first.

He immediately looked back.

“I hate this plan.”

Zee whispered, “You agreed.”

“I was younger then.”

“That was ten minutes ago.”

“A lot has happened.”

Aurelia entered last.

The maintenance corridor was narrow enough that Zee’s horns scraped the overhead beams twice.

He stopped.

“This place was designed badly.”

Ner looked back.

“It was designed for people without horns.”

“Exactly.”

Aurelia pushed both forward.

They descended.

Zee listened.

Heartbeats above.

Below.

Ahead.

Many.

Then four weak rhythms behind iron.

“Here.”

Aurelia stopped.

“Certain?”

“Yes.”

The corridor ended at a locked service door.

Ner removed one glove.

Pure Golden Mana gathered around his fingertips.

Zee looked at him.

“Careful.”

Ner raised an eyebrow.

“You are telling me that?”

“Yes.”

“That is alarming.”

Ner touched the lock.

Golden Mana moved through it.

Not forcing.

Reading.

The mechanism opened.

No alarm.

Ner smiled.

Zee frowned.

“You are pleased with yourself.”

“Yes.”

“Annoying.”

“You would be worse.”

True.

The next chamber contained cages.

Not cells.

Cages.

Seven spaces arranged around a central platform.

Three empty.

Four occupied.

Aurelia stopped at the entrance.

Zee had seen his mother angry.

Terrified.

Heartbroken.

He had never seen her look like this.

The four captives were alive.

Barely.

An old man lay curled inside the first cage.

A woman with silver-red hair occupied the second.

A younger Dragon-blooded man sat shackled in the third.

And in the fourth...

A woman lifted her head.

Dark red eyes.

Long hair nearly white from stress and age that Zee could not guess.

Thin.

Scarred.

Alive.

Aurelia whispered:

“Seraphine.”

The woman stared.

Nothing happened.

No recognition.

Then Aurelia stepped closer.

“Seraphine.”

Her voice broke.

The captive’s eyes widened.

She stood too quickly and stumbled against the bars.

“No.”

Aurelia reached the cage.

“It is me.”

“No.”

“Seraphine.”

“No.”

Tears appeared instantly.

“You are dead.”

Aurelia wrapped both hands around the bars.

“So are you.”

Seraphine laughed once.

Then sobbed.

“Aurelia?”

“Yes.”

The word barely left Aurelia before Seraphine reached through the bars.

Aurelia caught her hands.

For several breaths, Zee forgot where they were.

Forgot the auction above them.

Forgot Khell.

Forgot guards.

He watched his mother become someone’s sister.

Not queen.

Not survivor.

Not Dragon-Witch.

Little flame.

Seraphine pressed her forehead against the iron.

“You got old.”

Aurelia laughed through tears.

“You too.”

“I hate you.”

“I know.”

“You left.”

“You told me to run.”

“I was eight!”

“So was I!”

Seraphine stared.

Then laughed again.

It hurt to hear.

Zee looked toward Ner.

Ner’s eyes had gone wet.

He immediately looked away.

Zee did not tease him.

Not this time.

Then Seraphine noticed Zee.

Her face changed.

She stared at the horns first.

Then the Crimson scales.

Then Aurelia.

“Aurelia…”

“My son.”

Seraphine looked back at Zee.

Zee lifted one hand awkwardly.

“Hi.”

Seraphine stared.

Ner whispered, “Powerful introduction.”

Zee elbowed him.

Seraphine laughed weakly.

That seemed to decide something.

“He looks like trouble.”

Aurelia wiped tears from her face.

“He is.”

Zee frowned.

“Mother.”

Seraphine looked at him again.

“What is your name?”

“Zee.”

Her expression softened.

“I am Seraphine.”

“I know.”

“Apparently.”

He stepped closer.

“I came to get you out.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“We came.”

Zee nodded.

“We.”

Better.

Seraphine looked between mother and son.

Then her face hardened.

“Khell.”

Aurelia’s grief vanished.

“Where?”

“Above.”

“Does he know we are here?”

“No.”

A voice came from the doorway.

“Yes.”

Everyone turned.

Damaris Khell stood there.

He did not look like a blood broker.

That annoyed Zee.

He looked ordinary.

Middle-aged.

Expensive coat.

Dark beard.

No visible supernatural traits.

No theatrical weapon.

Just a man who had built a fortune by turning people into inventory.

Six guards stood behind him.

Khell looked at Aurelia.

Then Zee.

Then Ner’s uncovered hand.

His expression became very still.

“Well.”

Zee hated that word.

Khell smiled.

“Tonight has become valuable.”

Aurelia moved in front of the cages.

“You have exactly one chance.”

“To?”

“Open them.”

Khell looked toward Seraphine.

“I spent years assembling this collection.”

“They are people.”

“To you.”

Ner’s Golden Mana ignited.

“To everyone.”

Khell looked at him.

Interest sharpened.

“Pure.”

Zee stepped in front of Ner.

“No.”

Khell’s eyes moved toward him.

Crimson.

Horns.

Scales.

Fangs visible now.

He frowned.

“I know you.”

Zee’s expression hardened.

“No, you do not.”

“The Darkheart child.”

“That is not knowing me.”

Khell smiled.

“Fair.”

Then he lifted one finger.

Every cage ignited with red runes.

The captives screamed.

Aurelia turned.

Khell backed into the corridor.

“One step and the restraints constrict.”

Ner’s face tightened.

“Again?”

Zee looked toward him.

“We are getting good at these.”

“This is not the time.”

“I know.”

Khell smiled.

“I assume Morcant failed.”

Aurelia stared.

“She is alive.”

His smile vanished.

Interesting.

Caldrin’s voice sounded from behind Khell.

“And disappointed.”

Khell turned.

Too late.

Caldrin’s blade touched his back.

Rez stood behind him.

Mara beside Rez.

The guards spun.

Blue-White Mana exploded.

Rez changed the corridor in one move.

Two guards were thrown into the wall.

A third lost footing as Blue-White frost spread beneath him.

Caldrin disarmed a fourth.

Mara drew a short blade and held it against Khell’s ribs.

Khell stared at her.

“You.”

Mara looked at him.

“Me.”

“You were paid.”

“I was.”

“You profited.”

“I did.”

“You do not get to become righteous because guilt became inconvenient.”

Mara’s face hardened.

“No.”

She pressed the knife harder.

“But I can become useful.”

Khell smiled.

Then vanished.

Not magic.

Trapdoor.

The floor beneath him dropped.

Caldrin swore.

Mara nearly fell after him.

Rez grabbed her.

Zee heard Khell landing below.

Alive.

Running.

Aurelia turned toward the cages.

“Let him go.”

Zee stared.

“What?”

“For now.”

“He has—”

“Our family is here.”

That decided it.

Ner moved toward the runes.

“I can break them.”

Seraphine grabbed the bars.

“No.”

Ner stopped.

“Why?”

“They are linked.”

“Everything here is linked.”

Fast.

Done.

Thin.

Barely.

Smiled wider.

Then at Ner.

Then at Rez.

His eyes shifted toward the metal pillar.

Small.

Quick.

Ner saw.

With his eyes.

Pillar.

Lower rune.

Ner followed.

Khell relaxed slightly.

Mistake.

Toward the ceiling.

Enough.

Vampire speed.

The other grabbed the boy’s coat.

Khell slashed.

Blood.

Pain.

“What?”

Khell’s.

Release.

Furious.

Defeated.

Not the mastermind behind every hunt.

“Not my decision alone.”

Seraphine’s expression became cold.

“Good.”

“You think this changes anything?”

“It changed them.”

Khell said nothing.

Zee turned away.

The answer surprised Aurelia.

Years ago, Zee would have needed the final word.

Needed violence to feel complete.

Now he understood something else.

Sometimes defeating an enemy mattered less than what you carried away from them.

Tonight, they carried people.

Names.

Family.

Proof that House Veyrath was not as dead as Aurelia had believed.

And a new problem.

Because seven rescued Veyrath survivors could no longer disappear quietly.

By sunrise, buyers would talk.

The River Market would talk.

The Ashen Talons would hear.

Drakonis might hear.

Victor might hear.

The world would learn that Aurelia Veyrath had stepped out of hiding.

Zee stood beside his mother as the three Red Passage ships drifted toward Vesper-controlled waters.

He looked at Theron.

Seraphine.

The other survivors.

Then Rez.

Ner.

Zareth.

His family had become larger in a single week.

That should have made him feel safer.

Instead, Zee understood exactly what it meant.

More people to love.

More people the world could threaten.

But also—

more people who could stand beside him when it tried.

And this time, the world had not hunted Zee Darkheart.

Zee had hunted it back.

He had found what it took.

And he had brought them home.

# Crimson Dynasty — Chapters Forty & Forty-One

# Chapter Forty

## The Last Year of Childhood

House Vesper did not celebrate the return of House Veyrath.

Not publicly.

Lucien refused.

Too many people had escaped the Red Passage.

Too many buyers had seen Aurelia.

Too many brokers had heard the Veyrath name spoken aloud.

Trying to pretend nothing had happened would not protect anyone.

But announcing seven rescued survivors to every crown in the known world would be worse.

So Vesper did what it had always done best.

It made room.

Quietly.

Seven members of Veyrath blood had entered the rescue.

Seven returned free.

No cages.

No contracts.

No owners.

Theron walked through Vesper’s gates beside Aurelia instead of behind chains.

Seraphine came two steps later, glaring at every tower as though personally deciding whether she approved of the kingdom.

The others followed beneath Vesper protection.

Some wanted names restored.

Others did not.

One refused to sleep indoors.

Another refused to allow anyone to close a door behind him.

One of the rescued women spent the first night sitting in a garden until sunrise because grass beneath bare feet was apparently something captivity had made precious.

No one tried to hurry them.

Freedom did not make people whole by sunset.

It only gave them the right to decide what came next.

Zee understood that better than he expected.

He stood on the eastern balcony three days after their return and watched Theron argue with a healer below.

“You are supposed to use the cane,” the healer said.

“I am using it.”

“You are carrying it.”

“That counts.”

“It absolutely does not.”

Theron looked toward Aurelia for support.

She was sitting beneath an old cedar with Seraphine.

She did not help.

“Use the cane.”

Theron looked betrayed.

“You used to like me.”

“I used to be eight.”

“Children have better judgment.”

Seraphine snorted.

“You spent half our childhood throwing him out of trees.”

Theron pointed toward her.

“She remembers.”

Aurelia smiled.

Zee watched that smile longer than he meant to.

Ner leaned against the balcony beside him.

“You are doing it again.”

Zee looked over.

“What?”

“Watching your mother to make sure she is still happy.”

Zee frowned.

“I am not.”

Ner raised one eyebrow.

At ten, Nereus Azrion had somehow mastered the exact look Aurelia used when Zee lied badly.

Zee hated that.

“She lost them.”

Ner looked toward the garden.

“She found them.”

“That is not the same.”

“No.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner understood.

Finding people who had survived did not erase the years they were gone.

It did not erase cages.

Did not erase House Veyrath breaking apart.

Did not erase Victor.

Did not erase anything.

It simply meant grief had been wrong about one thing.

Some of them had lived.

Zee rested his arms against the stone railing.

“I thought getting them back would fix her.”

Ner was quiet.

Then:

“That was stupid.”

Zee turned sharply.

Ner continued before he could argue.

“Not because you wanted it.”

“Because people are not broken doors.”

Zee frowned.

“You have been spending too much time with my mother.”

“She likes me.”

“She likes everyone more than me.”

“That is because you are difficult.”

Zee shoved him.

Ner shoved back.

Neither moved much.

Behind them came Rez’s voice.

“If you both fall off that balcony, I am not explaining it.”

Zee looked back.

Rez crossed the room carrying two wooden practice blades.

His current body had stopped looking strange to Zee weeks ago.

That surprised him more than the magic itself had.

Rez was simply Rez.

Ten.

Fast.

Annoying.

His sword balance had settled.

His stride belonged to him again.

He tossed one blade toward Zee.

Zee caught it.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“I am busy.”

“You are staring at your mother from a balcony.”

“That is busy.”

Rez pointed the second blade toward the courtyard.

“Training.”

Ner smiled.

“I will watch.”

Rez looked at him.

“You are training too.”

Ner’s smile vanished.

“That seems unnecessary.”

“You told me yesterday my left side was slow.”

“It is.”

“Prove yours is better.”

Ner sighed.

“This friendship is exhausting.”

Zee looked toward the courtyard below.

Aurelia noticed the three boys.

“Do not break anything.”

Rez shouted down, “That depends on Zee.”

Zee looked offended.

“You changed age because of him,” Seraphine called from beside Aurelia. “I have known the boy three days and already believe that.”

Zee stared.

Aurelia had told her.

Of course she had.

He looked toward Rez.

“You told her?”

Rez shrugged.

“She is family.”

Seraphine cupped her hands around her mouth.

“And it is funny.”

Zee’s crimson eyes narrowed.

Seraphine smiled sweetly.

Zee liked her.

That was becoming a problem.

---

Damaris Khell did not receive a dramatic execution.

That disappointed Caldrin.

He admitted it freely.

The decision belonged to the seven people his trade had harmed directly.

Aurelia refused to take that choice from them.

Khell was tried under Vesper law for trafficking, illegal imprisonment, blood trade, magical coercion, and the purchase and sale of living supernatural captives within routes protected by Vesper treaties.

Morcant was charged separately.

Neither became a mystery.

Neither revealed a hidden throne behind the world.

Khell had buyers.

Morcant had money.

They had both profited from people other kingdoms preferred not to notice.

That was enough evil without making it grander.

Khell was sentenced to permanent confinement beneath Vesper wards after the surviving captives rejected immediate execution.

Not mercy.

Control.

They wanted names.

Ledgers.

Routes.

Buyers.

People still missing.

Khell knew too much to die quickly.

Morcant's estate was stripped of every captive holding, collection ledger, restraint design, and blood contract Vesper could identify.

Several kingdoms protested the seizure.

Lucien sent each protest back with copies of purchase records.

Most became suddenly quiet.

Mara was not pardoned.

That mattered too.

She had helped destroy Khell’s ownership structure.

She had helped free people.

She had also once carried people into cages.

Both truths remained.

Lucien offered her no clean absolution.

Instead, she agreed to testify, identify routes, locate former buyers, and help Vesper dismantle trafficking paths she had once used.

Theron hated her.

Seraphine hated her differently.

One of the other rescued Veyrath survivors refused to be in the same room with her.

Mara accepted all three responses.

Zee asked her once whether she expected forgiveness.

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then why stay?”

“Because leaving would be easier.”

Zee thought about that.

Then nodded.

Sometimes doing better did not mean being rewarded for it.

Sometimes it simply meant refusing to keep being worse.

---

The first rumor reached Vesper nine days later.

House Veyrath lives.

The second changed it.

Aurelia Darkheart is Veyrath.

The third became nonsense.

Aurelia had raised a hidden army of Dragon-Witches beneath Vesper.

The fourth claimed Zee had hatched from a Dragon egg.

The fifth insisted Zareth was actually Zee’s brother.

Zee nearly choked when Rez read that one aloud.

“No.”

Ner took the parchment.

“It gets worse.”

“How?”

“It says Queen Aurelia laid both eggs.”

Zee stared.

Zareth’s amusement exploded through the Dragon Link.

“No.”

Rez was already laughing.

Seraphine took the rumor sheet.

She read it once.

Then looked toward Aurelia.

“Mother would have enjoyed this.”

Aurelia covered her face.

Theron laughed until the healer threatened him.

Rumors were spreading.

That part could not be stopped.

House Veyrath was no longer safely dead in the imagination of the world.

Some survivors wanted that.

Theron did.

He refused to live under another name.

Seraphine did not.

Not yet.

She wanted the right to exist before she wanted recognition.

The other survivors divided between them.

Aurelia did not force unity.

House Veyrath had survived destruction.

It did not need to survive by becoming another cage.

Some stayed in Vesper.

Some planned eventually to leave.

Some wanted to search for more blood.

Others wanted nothing to do with Veyrath politics ever again.

Family grew.

It did not become simple.

Zee liked that.

He was learning simple answers were usually suspicious.

---

Near the end of autumn, Aurelia found Zee alone in the old training yard.

He was sitting on the ground with one knee raised, staring at his hands.

No Mana.

No scales spreading.

No horns burning.

Just hands.

Aurelia sat beside him.

“You are quiet.”

“I can do that.”

“Rarely.”

Zee looked toward her.

She smiled.

He looked away again.

“What are you thinking?”

“Rez.”

Aurelia waited.

Zee continued.

“I keep thinking about what I did.”

She did not tell him to stop.

That helped.

“I do not want to do it again.”

“Then do not.”

He frowned.

“You say that like I know how.”

“No.”

Aurelia looked toward the empty yard.

“I say it because not understanding a power does not mean you should poke it until someone suffers.”

Zee’s mouth twitched.

“That sounded like Caldrin.”

“Then I am deeply ashamed.”

He laughed.

Then became serious.

“What if it happens anyway?”

“Then you take responsibility for what happens.”

He looked at her.

“Not blame for everything.”

“Responsibility for what is yours.”

She touched one of his hands.

“Those are different.”

Zee thought of Khell.

Mara.

Morcant.

The hunters.

All the people whose choices had once felt like something Zee should somehow have prevented simply by existing differently.

He had spent years believing danger around him belonged to him.

Now he knew better.

Not completely.

Enough to start.

Aurelia continued.

“Fear is not control.”

“I know.”

“No.”

She looked at him.

“You are beginning to.”

Zee frowned.

“Same thing.”

“It is not.”

He sighed dramatically.

Aurelia smiled.

“You tried suppressing every Dragon reaction after Rez changed.”

Zee looked down.

“They got worse.”

“Yes.”

“Then Rez told me to listen.”

“And?”

“I hate when Rez is right.”

Aurelia laughed.

Zee smiled.

Then touched one developing horn.

“Sometimes the heat means anger.”

“Sometimes danger.”

“Sometimes Zareth.”

“Sometimes you.”

“Sometimes nothing I understand yet.”

Aurelia nodded.

“And now?”

“Now I notice before I explode.”

“Usually.”

Zee glared.

“Mother.”

“Usually is progress.”

He leaned against her.

At ten, he still did that.

Still fit beneath her arm.

Still allowed himself to.

Aurelia wrapped him close.

Zee listened to her heartbeat.

Not because his vampire nature forced him.

Because it was hers.

Steady.

Alive.

One day the world would take things from him no power could restore.

He did not know that future yet.

But he had already learned enough not to mistake survival for control over everything.

Some losses could not be undone.

Some people could only be protected while they were here.

That knowledge did not make him calm.

It made him present.

“Mother?”

“Yes?”

“I am glad they lived.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

“So am I.”

“It does not fix what happened.”

“No.”

“But it matters.”

“Yes.”

Zee nodded.

That was enough.

---

Winter came early.

By the first snowfall, Rez had stopped training as though his body were something borrowed.

It was simply his.

He ran the western wall beside Zee and Ner every morning.

He complained when they cheated.

They cheated anyway.

Ner’s Golden Mana had begun developing precision rather than merely power. He could form thin barriers instead of massive spheres, thread Mana through damaged wards, and strike hard enough to remind everyone that rare did not mean delicate.

Zareth spent increasing stretches in Drakonis.

That had been difficult at first.

For Zee.

Not Zareth.

The Dragon Crown Prince had obligations.

Family.

Training.

Politics.

A kingdom that expected to know the young prince who had spent much of his earliest life beside a Darkheart child.

Zee hated the first three-week absence.

He slept badly.

Checked the Dragon Link constantly.

Pretended he did not.

When Zareth returned, he brought no apology.

Only a stolen Drakonis ceremonial banner tied around one horn.

Zee laughed for ten minutes.

The Link had changed too.

Distance no longer made it disappear entirely.

It stretched.

Thinned.

Carried impressions rather than clarity.

But it endured.

Zareth had his own life.

Zee was learning that love did not require keeping someone within reach every second.

He disliked the lesson.

Still learned it.

---

On the final night of the year, the core four climbed onto the western roof.

It had become tradition without anyone deciding it was.

Zee sat near the edge.

Ner beside him.

Rez sprawled behind them.

Zareth occupied half the roof.

Snow gathered along his crimson scales and melted whenever Teal-and-Gold Mana warmed beneath them.

Below, Vesper celebrated quietly.

Not Zee.

Not Veyrath.

Not victory.

The year ending.

That felt better.

Rez threw a small piece of ice at Ner.

Ner caught it with Golden Mana.

Then sent it back twice as fast.

It struck Rez in the forehead.

Rez sat up.

“That was magic.”

“Yes.”

“We said no magic.”

“You said no magic.”

“That is what we means.”

Ner looked toward Zee.

“Does it?”

“No.”

Rez stared at both.

“You are terrible people.”

Zareth sent through the Link:

**Agree.**

Zee looked at him.

“You are included.”

The Dragon Prince immediately withdrew agreement.

Zee laughed.

Then silence settled naturally.

No danger.

No alarm.

No approaching hunter.

Just the four of them.

Zee looked over Vesper.

He remembered being carried into these walls as an infant while kingdoms wanted his blood.

Remembered cages.

Assassins.

Frost.

Dreams.

The Vault.

His mother becoming a Dragon beneath the moon.

Sevran stepping from her past.

Rez changing because Zee lost control.

The Red Passage.

Theron.

Seraphine.

He had spent childhood running because adults believed the safest direction was always away.

Sometimes they were right.

Sometimes running had kept him alive.

But Zee was not the child Aurelia once carried between kingdoms anymore.

He had chased Khell.

Walked into Morcant’s estate.

Helped free people he had never met.

Learned to stop before rage chose for him.

Learned that fear could warn instead of rule.

Learned that family made him vulnerable.

Learned that family also made him harder to isolate.

Ner nudged his shoulder.

“What?”

Zee realized he had been staring.

“Nothing.”

“You look weird.”

“That is rude.”

“You are smiling at the city.”

Rez sat up.

“He does that when he is thinking too much.”

Zee turned.

“You both know too much about me.”

Rez smiled.

“That seems like your problem.”

Zareth lowered his head beside them.

The Link carried warmth.

Home.

Not a word.

Not exactly.

But close.

Zee looked at the three of them.

Then toward the rooms below where Aurelia sat with Theron and Seraphine.

House Veyrath breathed again.

Vesper still stood.

Drakonis still claimed its prince.

Victor still lived in Castle Darkheart.

The world still hunted what it feared.

Nothing was solved forever.

Zee was glad.

He did not want his life finished at ten.

Snow fell harder.

He reached one hand toward it.

A flake landed against a Crimson scale and vanished.

For the first ten years of Zee Darkheart’s life, the world had tried to decide what kind of creature he would become before he was old enough to decide anything for himself.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Sleeping Dragon.

Prince.

Monster.

Abomination.

Weapon.

Miracle.

Threat.

Zee looked at his hand.

Then closed it.

The world could keep its names.

Childhood ended without a crown.

Without a prophecy.

Without another enemy appearing at the gate.

It ended with a boy sitting beside the people who had survived it with him.

A boy who knew more about himself than before.

A boy whose enemies knew more about him too.

A boy no longer small enough to carry away every time danger came.

Zee Darkheart had survived childhood.

And childhood had not survived him unchanged.

---

# Chapter Forty-One

## The Boys Who Hunt Back

Five Years Later

The vampire hit the ground hard enough to split the frozen earth.

Zee landed on him a heartbeat later.

At fifteen, there was nothing small about the impact.

The vampire rolled.

Zee’s claws caught only snow.

“Left!”

Ner’s voice.

Zee moved without looking.

A silver chain cut through the space where his throat had been.

Rez came through the trees on the opposite side.

His sword flashed once.

Blue-White Mana followed.

The chain froze from end to end.

The vampire holding it swore.

Rez smiled.

“Should have let go.”

He twisted his wrist.

The frozen chain snapped.

Ner raised both hands.

Pure Golden Mana spread between the surrounding trees—not a wall, but six thin planes of light angled precisely enough to close every escape without trapping the four boys inside.

The vampire looked around.

Then upward.

Mistake.

Zareth dropped through the winter canopy.

Fifteen years had turned the Crown Prince of Drakonis into something the forest itself seemed too small to contain.

His crimson Dragon body struck the clearing with controlled force.

Snow exploded outward.

Teal-and-Gold Mana burned beneath his scales.

Wings wider than entire cottages folded along his sides.

The fleeing vampire stopped.

Zee stood.

He was taller now.

Lean rather than bulky, but built by years of running, fighting, climbing, hunting, and surviving things designed to break him.

His horns had grown with him.

Crimson-black curves swept farther back from his temples now, still not fully mature but impossible to hide beneath ordinary hair.

Permanent Crimson scales patterned more of his body than they had at ten—along the sides of his neck, shoulders, ribs, forearms, and portions of his temples.

His fangs had matured.

So had the way people reacted when they saw them.

The vampire stared.

Recognition arrived.

Not from Zee’s face.

From everything else.

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“Yes.”

The vampire backed away.

“You are Darkheart.”

Rez walked into the clearing.

At fifteen, his current body moved with absolute familiarity.

No hesitation.

No recalculation.

His sword belonged in his hand.

His balance belonged beneath his feet.

Blue-White Mana moved around him with the kind of precision that came from years of choosing how to use what he already knew differently.

The vampire looked at him.

“Vesper.”

Rez inclined his head.

Ner stepped from between the trees.

His Golden Mana dimmed around the barriers but did not disappear.

He had grown taller too, his features sharper, confidence sitting on him more naturally now.

He wore no gloves.

Had not for years unless secrecy required them.

The vampire saw the Gold.

His expression worsened.

“Azrion.”

Ner smiled.

“You know all our names.”

“Everyone knows your names.”

Zee’s smile faded slightly.

That still felt strange sometimes.

Five years ago strangers had called him the Darkheart child.

Now hunters whispered Zee Darkheart before he entered rooms.

Some stories claimed he could tear souls out through blood.

False.

Some said he had killed armies.

Very false.

One tavern story insisted he turned into a black Dragon during every full moon.

Zareth had enjoyed that one.

Zee had not.

The vampire looked upward toward Zareth.

“And Drakonis.”

The Dragon Prince lowered his head.

The evolving Link pressed a clear intention against Zee.

**He smells afraid.**

Zee answered with an image.

Good.

Not because fear pleased him.

Because this vampire had spent six months trafficking missing village children between two border territories.

Fear seemed appropriate.

Zee looked toward the unconscious man beneath his boot.

“Where are the others?”

The vampire spat blood.

“Go to hell.”

Ner sighed.

“We rode three days for this.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

“Want me?”

“No.”

Zee crouched.

The vampire flinched.

Interesting.

Zee did nothing magical.

He simply looked at him.

“Six children disappeared from Deren Village.”

No response.

“Two from wolf territory.”

Still nothing.

“One human boy was found in a ditch.”

The vampire’s heartbeat changed.

Zee heard it.

His Wolf instinct noticed the scent shift.

His Vampire nature counted the pulse.

His Witch Mana stayed quiet.

Dragon heat moved gently beneath his scales.

Controlled.

No overlap.

No surge.

No accident.

Zee tilted his head.

“You did not kill him.”

The vampire stared.

Rez looked toward Zee.

“You sure?”

“No.”

The vampire smiled faintly.

Zee continued.

“But that bothered you.”

The smile vanished.

“There.”

Ner folded his arms.

“You always get creepy when you do that.”

Zee glanced toward him.

“You like it.”

“I did not say that.”

“You looked impressed.”

“I was looking at the prisoner.”

Rez sighed.

“Can both of you flirt after we find the children?”

Silence.

Zee turned.

Ner turned.

Rez blinked.

“What?”

Zee’s face warmed.

That was irritating.

Crimson Dragon energy responded faintly beneath the scales along his neck.

Ner saw.

His mouth almost smiled.

Almost.

“We were not flirting,” Zee said.

Rez looked between them.

“Fine.”

Ner added, “We were not.”

Zareth sent a burst of unmistakable amusement through the Link.

Zee looked upward.

“Do not start.”

The vampire stared.

“You people are insane.”

Rez looked down at him.

“That is rude.”

Then the other captured vampire groaned.

Back to work.

Zee crouched again.

“Where?”

The vampire refused to answer.

So Zee looked toward Ner.

Ner stepped closer.

Not to unlock anything.

His Golden Mana had become far more than a key over five years.

Thin lines of light spread from his fingers and passed over the vampire’s coat.

Not through flesh.

Across objects.

Metal.

Leather.

Dust.

Then stopped at one pocket.

Ner reached inside.

The vampire lunged.

Rez’s sword touched his throat immediately.

Ner removed a black wooden token.

A symbol carved into it.

Wolf territory.

Rez recognized it.

“Old mill.”

Ner nodded.

“North road.”

The vampire’s heartbeat betrayed him.

Zee smiled.

“Thank you.”

The man swore.

Zareth sent Zee an image.

Mill.

Trees.

Smoke.

Then another.

Movement to the west.

Zee looked up sharply.

“Zareth found it.”

Rez sheathed his sword.

“Alive?”

The Link carried distant heartbeats.

Small.

Many.

Zee’s expression hardened.

“Yes.”

Ner dropped the Golden barriers.

“Then why are we still talking?”

They moved.

---

The old mill sat beside a frozen river two miles north.

They did not approach from one side.

They had stopped doing that years ago.

Zareth stayed high enough to track exits.

Rez circled west.

Ner went east.

Zee took the river.

No one needed to explain the plan.

They had used versions of it dozens of times.

Zee moved across the ice without breaking stride.

At fifteen his vampire speed had become less wild.

More economical.

His Wolf nature handled balance.

Witch Mana softened impact.

Crimson Dragon durability absorbed whatever neither prevented.

He reached the mill wall.

Stopped.

Listened.

Nine captives.

Three guards.

One vampire.

Two humans.

One heartbeat inside the upper office.

Different.

Wolf.

Zee frowned.

Not every person inside belonged to the same enemy.

Good to remember.

He touched the stone.

A faint vibration moved through his horns.

The Dragon nature had become stronger over five years.

Far stronger.

Still unfinished.

The ridges beneath his shoulder blades had developed too.

Visible now beneath thin clothing when his Dragon energy surged.

Sometimes they hardened enough that Aurelia would stare at them and refuse to guess what came next.

No wings.

Not yet.

The Vault’s old judgment remained lodged inside Zee’s memory.

Four.

Three awake.

Whatever counted as complete had still not happened.

Zee did not force it.

He had learned better than that.

He sent an image through the Dragon Link.

Nine.

Zareth answered.

**Roof clear.**

Not words.

Not quite.

Intent sharpened by fifteen years of familiarity.

Rez appeared through a crack in the western wall.

Ner’s Gold glimmered once from the east.

Ready.

Zee entered.

The first guard never saw him.

Zee caught the man’s wrist before the knife cleared leather.

Turned.

Dropped him.

Second guard came from behind.

Rez intercepted.

Blue-White Mana struck the floor.

The man slipped.

Rez's pommel hit his jaw.

Down.

The vampire lunged toward the rear door.

Ner closed it with a Golden plane.

The vampire rebounded.

Zee caught him.

“Children.”

The vampire snarled.

“You think saving nine matters?”

Zee’s face changed.

“Yes.”

The vampire hesitated.

That answer had not been dramatic enough.

Good.

Zee tightened his grip.

“Where is the wolf upstairs?”

The vampire smiled.

“Not ours.”

There.

Zee released him just enough for Rez to bind him.

Then took the stairs.

He found a girl in the upper office.

Sixteen, maybe.

Wolf.

Bruised.

Armed with half a broken chair leg.

She swung the moment Zee entered.

He caught it.

“Stop.”

She snarled.

“Get away from me.”

“I am not with them.”

“Everyone says that.”

Fair.

Zee released the chair leg and stepped back.

She saw the horns.

The scales.

Recognition hit.

Not reassurance.

Fear.

“You.”

Zee stopped.

He knew that tone.

Not *Zee.*

Not a person.

A story.

“The Tribrid.”

He hated that less than monster.

Still not enough.

“My name is Zee.”

The girl stared.

Below them something crashed.

Ner shouted, “Rez!”

Rez shouted back, “That was not me!”

Zareth roared outside.

The girl flinched.

Zee sighed.

“That is Zareth.”

Her eyes widened.

“Drakonis?”

“Yes.”

Another crash.

Zee added, “Probably him.”

The Dragon Link sent offense.

The girl slowly lowered the wood.

“You came for them?”

“For everyone.”

Her expression changed.

“I am not one of the kidnapped children.”

“I know.”

“You know?”

“You smell like wolf territory.”

She stared.

“That is invasive.”

Zee blinked.

Then laughed.

“Sorry.”

That disarmed her more than any display of power could have.

“My brother is downstairs,” she said.

Zee’s smile disappeared.

“Which one?”

“Little.”

“Brown hair.”

“Scar over his chin.”

Zee listened.

Found the heartbeat.

“Alive.”

The girl almost collapsed.

She caught herself against the desk.

Zee did not touch her without permission.

Another lesson.

“They took him four days ago.”

“I followed.”

“They caught me yesterday.”

Zee nodded.

“So this was your hunt too.”

She looked at him.

He understood.

The world did not revolve around him.

Five years had made that truth instinctive.

He gestured toward the stairs.

“Come on.”

---

By midday the missing children were outside.

All alive.

Cold.

Hungry.

Terrified.

Alive.

Ner used Golden Mana only when one restraint refused to open normally.

Rez organized blankets and water before anyone asked.

Zareth remained at a distance because several children were more frightened of a massive Dragon than reassured by him.

He did not take offense.

Much.

The Dragon Link carried mild insult anyway.

Zee sat beside the smallest boy from wolf territory.

The boy kept staring at his horns.

Finally:

“Do they hurt?”

“Sometimes.”

“Can I touch one?”

Zee looked toward Aurelia in his memory.

Then toward the boy.

“Why?”

The child shrugged.

“I want to know if it feels like bone.”

Zee smiled.

“Okay.”

The boy touched the horn carefully.

“Hard.”

“Yes.”

“Cool.”

“Sometimes.”

The girl upstairs—his sister—stood nearby watching.

Her suspicion had not vanished.

Good.

Trust should not always be instant.

A rider appeared on the southern road.

Then another.

Local guards.

Not Vesper.

Not Zee’s.

They had their own authorities.

Their own responsibilities.

Zee stood.

The lead guard saw him.

Stopped.

The entire patrol slowed.

Recognition again.

One whispered something.

Zee heard.

“Darkheart.”

The leader dismounted carefully.

“We received reports of fighting.”

Rez approached.

“Trafficking ring.”

Ner pointed toward the captives.

“Three perpetrators alive.”

The guard looked between the boys.

Then toward Zareth.

Then back to Zee.

“You did this?”

The girl from wolf territory answered first.

“They did.”

Zee looked at her.

She shrugged.

“Truth.”

The guard’s expression became complicated.

Fear.

Relief.

Political calculation.

Zee knew that face too.

He had seen it on kings.

Hunters.

Village leaders.

People deciding whether Zee Darkheart was a threat before remembering he had just saved children.

The guard bowed.

Not deeply.

Not royal.

Respect without submission.

“Thank you.”

Zee blinked.

That still happened rarely enough to surprise him.

“You are welcome.”

The guard looked toward the prisoners.

“We take custody.”

Rez asked, “Under whose authority?”

“Border Council.”

Rez nodded.

“Send the records to House Vesper and the wolf council.”

The guard looked at him more closely.

“Prince Rez.”

“Yes.”

Recognition there too.

Different.

Political.

Established.

Rez no longer needed age explained to anyone who mattered.

He was simply fifteen-year-old Rez Vesper, Crown Prince, and apparently terrifying to bureaucrats.

The guard nodded quickly.

“Of course.”

Ner whispered to Zee.

“He likes that.”

Rez heard.

“I do.”

Zee smiled.

Then the rescued wolf girl approached.

“What happens to you now?”

Zee frowned.

“What do you mean?”

“You go home?”

“Eventually.”

“You are not from here.”

“No.”

“Then why were you hunting them?”

Zee looked toward the children.

Simple question.

Complicated answer.

Because someone had asked Vesper for help.

Because trafficking routes crossed old Veyrath maps.

Because Rez had pushed for intervention at council.

Because Ner found inconsistencies in missing-person wards.

Because Zareth spotted one transport wagon from the sky.

Because five years had taught them not every battle needed to begin at their own doorstep.

Zee shrugged.

“They were hurting people.”

The girl stared.

“That is it?”

“Is that not enough?”

She had no answer.

Zee turned away.

Across the frozen field, Ner was helping a child tie a blanket correctly.

His hair had fallen into his eyes.

He pushed it back impatiently.

Zee looked a little too long.

Ner glanced up.

Caught him.

Zee immediately looked elsewhere.

Too late.

A small smile appeared on Ner’s face.

Not mocking.

Worse.

Knowing.

Zee’s horns warmed.

Not danger.

He glared at them as though they had betrayed him personally.

Rez appeared beside him.

“You should really learn a different reaction.”

Zee did not look over.

“I do not know what you are talking about.”

“Of course.”

“Say anything and I will throw you in the river.”

Rez smiled.

“Fifteen years old and still terrible at lying.”

Zee elbowed him.

Rez elbowed back.

Zareth’s amusement crossed the Link.

Zee looked around at all three of them.

Fifteen.

Five more years of arguments.

Missions.

Training.

Scars.

Victories.

Mistakes.

No longer children adults carried from danger.

Not adults either.

Not finished.

Not close.

The world had changed around them.

Veyrath lived openly enough now that some kingdoms acknowledged its survivors.

Drakonis had learned to share its Crown Prince with a bond it still did not fully understand.

Vesper had become harder, richer, and more politically important after years of refusing to surrender the people under its protection.

Victor remained at Darkheart.

The black-robed observers remained somewhere beyond sight.

Hunters still came.

Bounties still appeared.

Stories about Zee multiplied faster than truth.

But something fundamental had reversed.

At ten, Zee had begun walking toward the world.

At fifteen, the world had started learning what that meant.

He looked toward the captured traffickers.

Then the rescued children.

Then Ner.

Rez.

Zareth.

Zee Darkheart smiled.

The boy they had once hunted was gone.

What stood in his place was still fifteen.

Still learning.

Still afraid of some things.

Still capable of making terrible decisions when angry.

Still his mother’s son.

Still Rez’s brother.

Still Ner’s best friend.

Still linked to Zareth by something neither kingdom could name.

But prey?

No.

That part of childhood was over.

And the world was beginning to understand the difference.
