# Chapter Forty

## The Last Night of Ten

The seven Veyrath survivors entered House Vesper through the eastern gates without chains.

That mattered more to Aurelia than banners ever could.

No herald announced them.

No musicians played.

No court gathered to stare at people who had spent too many years being examined, measured, purchased, restrained, and discussed as though blood could make a person into property.

King Lucien had offered ceremony.

Theron refused before Aurelia could answer.

Seraphine had been less polite.

“If anyone makes me stand beneath a banner while strangers clap because I escaped a cage, I am leaving.”

Lucien had looked at Aurelia.

Aurelia had looked at her sister.

Then said, “No ceremony.”

So Vesper simply opened its gates.

Seven survivors walked through.

Theron used a cane because his body still carried the damage of years beneath Damaris Khell.

He hated the cane.

Everyone knew.

He also used it.

Mostly.

Seraphine walked beside him with her chin raised and one hand hidden beneath her cloak whenever unfamiliar soldiers came too close. She did not like closed formations. She did not like locked rooms. She did not like people approaching from behind.

She did, however, like insulting Theron.

That became obvious before they reached the palace.

“You are limping badly.”

“I am walking.”

“You are performing a slow collapse with interruptions.”

Theron glared.

“I protected you when you were little.”

“You also dropped me into a stream.”

“You bit me.”

“You deserved it.”

Aurelia laughed.

Zee stopped walking.

Not because anything was wrong.

Because his mother laughed differently around them.

He had heard Aurelia laugh thousands of times.

At him.

At Rez.

At Ner.

At Zareth breaking things and pretending not to understand.

At Caldrin saying something he should not have said in front of royalty.

But this laugh came from somewhere older.

A version of Aurelia Zee had never known.

Seraphine noticed him staring.

“What?”

Zee blinked.

“Nothing.”

“That is never true when a child says it.”

“I am ten.”

“Yes.”

“That means I am allowed.”

Seraphine looked at Aurelia.

“He argues exactly like you.”

Aurelia’s smile widened.

“No.”

Theron stopped beside them.

“He argues like Father.”

Silence.

Then Theron realized what he had said.

Something old passed across Aurelia’s face.

Not anger.

Memory.

Seraphine looked away first.

Zee watched his mother carefully.

Aurelia inhaled.

Then touched Theron’s arm.

“Sometimes he does.”

The moment passed without being erased.

That was how it worked now.

Happiness did not destroy grief.

Grief did not prevent happiness.

Both were allowed to remain.

Zee was learning that.

Slowly.

---

The seven Veyrath survivors were offered rooms.

Three accepted.

One chose the gardens.

One asked for quarters near the outer walls where the windows opened fully.

Another requested no Veyrath colors, no family symbols, and no discussion of rebuilding anything.

Lucien agreed without argument.

The seventh spent two hours examining every lock in her room before finally sleeping.

Freedom turned out to be inconvenient that way.

People wanted different things.

Aurelia had once imagined finding surviving Veyrath blood would mean gathering everyone beneath one name again.

She stopped imagining that after the first day.

Theron wanted the name.

Proudly.

Angrily.

He had spent years hearing captors use Veyrath like a product classification.

He wanted it back as something they could not own.

Seraphine wanted nothing to do with becoming part of another House structure.

“I escaped one cage,” she told Theron. “I am not volunteering for a prettier one.”

“A House is not a cage.”

“It can be.”

“A family needs structure.”

“A family needs people.”

Theron opened his mouth.

Seraphine pointed at him.

“If you say tradition, I will break your cane.”

Theron looked at Zee.

“Do you see what I endured?”

Zee nodded solemnly.

“Yes.”

Seraphine looked offended.

Zee continued.

“Both of you seem exhausting.”

Aurelia nearly choked on her drink.

Theron stared.

Seraphine laughed so hard she had to sit down.

That was the first evening they ate together.

No council.

No strategy.

No maps.

No enemies.

Just food.

Aurelia at the center.

Theron beside her.

Seraphine across from them.

Zee near his mother.

Rez and Ner at the other side of the table because both had invited themselves.

Zareth remained outside the open terrace because even Vesper’s reinforced dining chamber had limits.

Through the Dragon Link came one offended impression.

**Excluded.**

Zee looked toward the terrace.

“You are the size of the room.”

Zareth sent an image of the terrace wall being removed.

Aurelia pointed without looking.

“No.”

Zee stared at her.

“You did not even know what he said.”

“I know him.”

Zareth huffed smoke.

Seraphine watched.

“You truly understand each other?”

“Sometimes.”

“What did he say?”

“He wants the wall gone.”

Seraphine studied the wall.

“That would improve the room.”

Aurelia slowly turned.

Seraphine smiled.

“What?”

Theron laughed.

Zee liked his aunt more every hour.

---

Damaris Khell's fate did not become Zee’s decision.

That mattered.

The people Khell had imprisoned had spent too many years having decisions stolen from them already.

Lucien brought the matter before the seven survivors.

Aurelia attended.

Zee did not.

He wanted to.

At ten, curiosity still competed violently with patience.

But when Aurelia told him, “This belongs to them,” he understood.

So he waited outside with Ner and Rez.

Zareth slept in the courtyard sun.

Rez practiced a sword sequence.

His movements no longer carried the awkwardness that had followed Zee’s uncontrolled magic.

He moved like himself.

Because he was himself.

Ten.

His feet landed correctly.

His balance flowed naturally.

His Blue-White Mana threaded along the blade with clean precision.

Ner watched.

“You dropped your shoulder.”

Rez did not stop.

“No, I did not.”

“You did.”

“I know what my shoulder did.”

“Apparently not.”

Rez completed the sequence.

Then pointed the blade at him.

“Come prove it.”

“No.”

“Coward.”

“Efficient.”

Zee sat on the stone railing between them.

“You did drop it.”

Rez turned.

“You were not watching.”

“I heard it.”

“You heard my shoulder?”

“I heard your foot change.”

Rez stared.

Zee smiled.

Zee caught it.

“Fight me.”

“Coward.”

“Efficient.”

Ner looked delighted.

“I am changing both of you for the worse.”

His horns warmed faintly as he raised the sword.

Not anger.

Not danger.

Excitement.

He noticed.

Let the sensation exist.

Did not push it away.

Did not feed it.

Just listened.

Warm.

Steady.

His Dragon nature had become easier when he stopped treating every reaction like an enemy invading his body.

Rez saw his scales remain still.

“Better.”

Zee nodded.

Then attacked.

The council doors opened before the first clash.

Aurelia emerged.

All three boys stopped.

“Prison?”

“For now.”

The survivors had decided execution would give him silence too quickly.

Khell possessed routes.

Names.

Buyers.

Accounts.

People still missing from dozens of bloodlines that had nothing to do with Veyrath.

He would spend whatever remained of his life answering questions beneath Vesper wards.

Not because he mattered more than he did.

Because the information did.

Lady Morcant would face separate judgment for her estate, her collection, and the people she had purchased.

Nothing about either of them reached backward into Zee’s birth.

Nothing explained Victor.

Nothing explained the Vault.

Nothing explained Blood Rain.

They were simply people who had chosen to profit from suffering.

Sometimes evil was disappointingly ordinary.

Zee looked toward Aurelia.

“And Mara?”

“Testifying.”

“Free?”

“No.”

“Prison?”

“Not exactly.”

He frowned.

Aurelia continued.

“She will help identify routes, buyers, holding sites, and brokers she once worked with. Vesper will decide her final sentence after that.”

“Do they forgive her?”

Aurelia looked toward the closed chamber.

“Some may never.”

Zee nodded.

That made sense.

Mara helping destroy Khell’s ownership contract had mattered.

Mara once helping put people into those contracts also mattered.

One good choice did not eat every bad choice that came before it.

But neither did the past make every future choice meaningless.

Zee looked down at the practice sword.

“People are complicated.”

Rez snorted.

“You just discovered that?”

Zee swung at him.

Rez blocked.

Ner stepped out of range.

“I am not getting involved.”

Zee and Rez both looked at him.

Ner sighed.

“Fine.”

Pure Golden Mana formed around his hands.

The training session became unfair immediately.

---

Rumors escaped Vesper before winter.

That part no one could prevent.

The River Market talked.

Buyers talked.

Guards talked.

Morcant’s seized ledgers traveled through royal courts.

Khell’s surviving brokers ran in several directions carrying different versions of the same truth.

House Veyrath lived.

Not as it had once existed.

Not united.

Not restored.

But alive.

The rumor changed every time it crossed a border.

Some claimed an entire Dragon-Witch army had been hiding beneath Vesper.

Some claimed Aurelia had secretly conquered Drakonis.

One version insisted Zee had been born from a Dragon egg hidden beneath Castle Darkheart.

Rez read that one aloud during breakfast.

Zee stopped chewing.

“What?”

Ner took the parchment.

“It gets worse.”

“How?”

Ner’s mouth twitched.

“Apparently Zareth hatched from the same egg.”

Zee stared at him.

“That is not how eggs work.”

Zareth, outside the terrace, sensed Zee’s outrage.

The Dragon Link sent amusement.

Rez continued reading.

“Oh, wait. Queen Aurelia laid the egg.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

Theron started laughing.

Seraphine took the page.

“Who writes this?”

“People who have never seen a Dragon,” Aurelia muttered.

Seraphine read farther.

“Victor supposedly tried to marry the Dragon Queen afterward.”

Aurelia snatched the parchment.

“Burn it.”

Zee fell sideways laughing.

For one morning, rumor became something they could laugh at.

But beneath the ridiculous stories sat a serious truth.

Veyrath could no longer disappear completely.

Some Dragon Houses began asking cautious questions.

Two witch kingdoms quietly requested confirmation.

Vesper answered neither.

Drakonis sent no public statement at all.

Zareth’s mother sent Aurelia a private message.

Not accusation.

Not recognition.

Only an invitation to speak when Aurelia chose.

Aurelia did not choose yet.

Victor sent nothing.

That bothered Zee more than a letter would have.

He did not say so.

Aurelia knew anyway.

---

Zareth left for Drakonis before the first heavy snow.

Not forever.

Not even long.

Three weeks.

Zee hated it.

He acted like he did not.

Everyone noticed.

The morning Zareth departed, the Dragon Prince stood in Vesper’s outer field while Drakonis guards waited high above.

His crimson body had grown significantly over ten years, though he remained young by Dragon standards.

Teal-and-Gold Mana flickered along his scales.

Zee stood beneath his lowered head.

“You could stay another week.”

The Link brought an image.

Dragon Queen.

Training court.

Drakonis banners.

Duty.

Zee frowned.

“I know.”

Another impression.

**Come?**

Zee looked toward Aurelia.

She stood several yards away.

He knew the answer.

Not this time.

Zareth needed time in his kingdom that was not built around Zee.

Zee rubbed one hand against the scales along Zareth’s snout.

“You are coming back.”

Zareth sent offense.

As though the question itself were insulting.

Then an image came.

Vesper roof.

Zee.

Rez.

Ner.

Him.

Return.

Zee smiled.

“Fine.”

Zareth pushed his forehead gently against Zee’s chest.

Then pulled away.

He launched.

Wind tore across the field.

Zee watched until crimson disappeared into cloud.

Then continued watching.

Ner came to stand beside him.

“He is gone.”

“I know.”

“You can stop staring.”

“I am not staring.”

Ner said nothing.

Zee looked at him.

“Do not do the face.”

“What face?”

“My mother's face.”

“I have no idea what you mean.”

“You absolutely do.”

Ner smiled.

They walked back toward Vesper.

That night Zee slept badly.

The Dragon Link had not vanished.

Distance thinned it.

Turned clear impressions into faint emotional weather.

Zareth remained there.

Far away.

Alive.

His own.

Not Zee’s possession.

Not something Zee had to keep within arm’s reach to love.

Zee hated learning that lesson.

He learned it anyway.

When Zareth returned three weeks later, he landed on the western roof carrying half a Drakonis ceremonial banner tangled around one horn.

Zee laughed until his ribs hurt.

Zareth refused to explain.

The Link supplied only fierce satisfaction.

Rez examined the banner.

“You stole this.”

Zareth growled.

Ner looked at the embroidery.

“That belongs to the Dragon Crown.”

Zareth looked away.

Zee smiled.

“He definitely stole it.”

The Link delivered:

**Acquired.**

Zee laughed harder.

---

On the last night of Zee’s tenth year, snow fell over Vesper.

Not blood.

Just snow.

Zee sat on the western roof beside Ner and Rez.

Zareth occupied most of the space behind them.

Below, Aurelia sat inside with Theron and Seraphine.

Zee could hear them laughing through the stone.

He could have listened harder.

He did not.

Some conversations belonged to other people.

Five years earlier that would have been difficult for him to accept.

Tonight it felt almost natural.

Ner shaped a small sphere of Pure Golden Mana between both hands.

Not a key.

Not a lockpick.

A tiny bird formed from light.

Its wings opened.

It flew once around Zee’s horns.

Then landed on Rez’s head.

Rez stared upward.

“Ner.”

“What?”

“Remove it.”

“It likes you.”

“I do not care.”

The golden bird pecked his hair.

Zee laughed.

Rez swatted.

The bird vanished and reappeared behind him.

Ner smiled.

Zee watched.

“You have been practicing that.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because not everything I do needs to open something.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner’s smile softened.

The answer mattered.

“Good.”

Rez finally caught the Mana bird.

It dissolved into Gold around his fingers.

“There.”

Ner stared.

“You killed him.”

“It was magic.”

“He had dreams.”

“You made him twenty seconds ago.”

Zareth’s amusement rolled through the Link.

Zee leaned back against the Dragon’s foreleg.

His head fit naturally between two scales.

The sky above Vesper was dark and enormous.

The world beyond it larger still.

Ten years.

His entire life.

Ten years of people trying to decide what he was before he could decide anything himself.

The First Natural Tribrid.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Dragon sleeping beneath all three.

Darkheart.

Veyrath.

Prince.

Monster.

Weapon.

Child.

Zee looked toward his hands.

He had hurt people.

Saved people.

Failed people.

Changed Rez without meaning to.

Learned not to touch that strange power again simply because curiosity demanded answers.

He had learned that fear could warn him.

That anger could speak without commanding.

That his horns heating did not automatically mean he needed to attack.

That scales spreading could be information.

That surviving something did not mean he had won.

That sometimes the most important part of defeating someone like Khell was not what happened to Khell.

It was who walked away free.

Zee looked toward Rez.

Then Ner.

Then Zareth.

More people to lose.

That still frightened him.

More people to stand beside him.

That mattered too.

Ner nudged him.

“You are doing the thinking face.”

“I do not have a thinking face.”

Rez answered, “You do.”

Zee frowned.

“You both know too much.”

“That is what happens when people grow up together,” Ner said.

Zee looked at him.

For some reason, the words stayed.

Grow up together.

He smiled.

“Then I know too much about you too.”

Ner raised an eyebrow.

“Name one thing.”

“You pretend not to be scared by deep water.”

Ner’s face changed.

Rez sat upright.

“He does?”

“Zee.”

“You hate pears.”

“That is not secret.”

“You sleep on your left side when you are angry.”

Ner stared.

Zee smiled wider.

“You pull your sleeves over your hands when you lie.”

Ner immediately looked down.

His sleeves were covering both hands.

Rez started laughing.

Ner shoved Zee.

Zee shoved back.

Soon all three were wrestling badly on a snow-covered roof while Zareth shifted just enough to prevent any of them from falling.

No enemy came.

No horn sounded.

No prophecy appeared.

No stranger stepped from darkness.

Childhood did not end because the world demanded one more sacrifice.

It ended because time moved.

Because people grew.

Because Zee had survived long enough to become someone different from the infant Aurelia once carried between kingdoms.

Later, when the others had gone inside, Zee remained on the roof with Aurelia.

She wrapped a cloak around his shoulders.

He leaned against her.

Still ten.

Still her son.

Aurelia rested her cheek against his hair between his horns.

“You are getting too tall for this.”

“No.”

“No?”

“I decided.”

She smiled.

“Powerful law.”

Zee listened to her heartbeat.

Steady.

Familiar.

Home.

“Mother?”

“Yes?”

“Do you think I am different?”

“From when?”

“When I was little.”

Aurelia looked down at him.

“You are little.”

Zee groaned.

She laughed.

Then became serious.

“Yes.”

“Better?”

“Different.”

He frowned.

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the true one.”

Zee considered.

“Am I worse?”

“No.”

“More dangerous?”

“Yes.”

He smiled slightly.

Aurelia tapped one horn.

“That was not praise.”

“I know.”

She held him closer.

“You are learning to choose.”

Zee looked across Vesper.

At the kingdom that had sheltered him.

At the roofs where he had grown.

At the roads that had carried hunters toward him.

At the roads he had finally begun using to go the other direction.

The world had spent ten years hunting Zee Darkheart.

It had not succeeded in making him small.

It had not succeeded in making him simple.

It had not succeeded in making him alone.

Snow settled across the city.

Zee closed his eyes against Aurelia’s shoulder.

For one final night, childhood was allowed to end quietly.

And then time moved forward.

# Chapter Forty-One

## What Survived

Five Years Later

The mercenary screamed before Zee touched him.

That was new.

Zee stopped halfway across the ruined bridge.

Wind tore through the mountain pass hard enough to snap loose cloth from the stone railings, carrying snow through the gorge in white sheets.

The mercenary backed away.

“No.”

Zee tilted his head.

“You have not heard what I want.”

“I know who you are.”

“That was not the question.”

The man looked past him.

His fear worsened.

Rez stood on the broken eastern arch with his sword lowered at his side.

Fifteen.

Vesper blue hidden beneath a travel coat.

Blue-White Mana moved along the edge of his blade in a thin, controlled line.

No wasted light.

No wasted movement.

Ner occupied the western side of the bridge.

Pure Golden Mana formed three narrow planes behind the remaining mercenaries, cutting off escape routes without blocking the mountain villagers trapped behind them.

At fifteen, Ner no longer needed enormous barriers to prove what Gold could do.

Precision had become more dangerous than spectacle.

And above them—

Zareth dropped through the snowstorm.

The Crown Prince of Drakonis hit the bridge on four claws.

Stone cracked.

Everyone swore.

Zee did not.

He had told him not to break the bridge.

The Dragon Link carried immediate innocence.

**Already cracked.**

Zee looked toward him.

“You made it worse.”

The Link returned an image of the bridge collapsing before Zareth landed.

A hypothetical defense.

Rez shouted over the wind, “Can you argue with him after we finish?”

Zee looked back.

“Probably.”

Ner raised one hand.

A Golden plane snapped sideways.

A mercenary who had tried slipping past him struck it face-first.

“Definitely later.”

The man Zee had been approaching drew a knife.

Zee sighed.

“There.”

The mercenary attacked.

Five years ago Zee would have met speed with speed.

Now he stepped half a pace aside.

Nothing more.

The blade passed his ribs.

Zee caught the wrist.

Crimson scales brightened along his forearm.

His horns—larger now, sweeping backward from his temples in juvenile crimson-black arcs—warmed faintly.

Not rage.

Not danger worth fearing.

Information.

The man’s pulse jumped.

Left shoulder injured.

Breathing uneven.

Weight favoring his right leg.

Zee’s Wolf nature read the stance.

His Vampire senses counted the heartbeat.

His Witch Mana remained quiet until needed.

Something older and hotter moved beneath all three.

Dragon.

Still not fully awake.

Much less asleep.

Zee twisted.

The knife fell.

The mercenary hit the bridge.

Zee kept him there with one boot.

“Where are the villagers?”

The man laughed through pain.

“You came too late.”

Zee’s expression did not change.

Across the bridge, Rez looked toward a cave opening cut into the northern cliff.

He raised two fingers.

Ner saw.

Golden Mana threaded toward the rock.

Not through the cave.

Around it.

Feeling pressure.

Movement.

Space.

He looked back.

“Seventeen heartbeats.”

Zee listened.

Found them.

“Eighteen.”

Ner frowned.

“One is very weak.”

Rez’s sword came up.

“Then we are not late.”

The mercenary under Zee’s boot stopped smiling.

Zee looked down.

“Thank you.”

“I did not tell you anything.”

“Your face did.”

Ner called, “That sounded dramatic.”

Zee looked toward him.

“It worked.”

“Barely.”

Zareth’s amusement pushed through the Link.

Zee ignored him.

The remaining mercenaries moved at once.

Bad choice.

Rez stepped from the arch.

Blue-White Mana struck the bridge in four narrow lines.

Not freezing the entire surface.

Only the places where feet would land.

Two men slipped.

Rez reached the first before he recovered.

Sword hilt to the jaw.

Turn.

Elbow.

The second came from behind.

Rez ducked without looking.

He knew Zee was there.

Zee’s Crimson Mana hit the attacker sideways.

Rez never broke stride.

Five years of fighting together had removed most explanations from battle.

Ner sealed the southern edge.

A crossbowman fired at him.

Ner did not block the bolt.

He shifted one Golden plane three inches.

The bolt struck it at an angle and changed direction.

It buried itself in the mercenary captain’s shoulder.

Ner winced.

“I meant the wall.”

Rez laughed.

“Good shot.”

“It was not a shot.”

“Still counts.”

A third mercenary charged Ner.

Zee moved instinctively.

Stopped himself.

Ner saw.

Good.

He did not need rescuing every time something came near him.

Pure Golden Mana condensed around Ner’s fist.

He struck once.

The man left the ground.

Zee stared.

Ner flexed his hand.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“I am not.”

Rez looked between them while disarming another attacker.

“Oh, no.”

Zee turned.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That was obviously something.”

“Busy.”

Zee narrowed his eyes.

Ner looked toward Zee.

For half a heartbeat their eyes held too long.

Something warm moved beneath Zee’s scales.

Not Dragon.

Or perhaps not only Dragon.

He looked away first.

Zareth felt the emotion through the Link.

A pulse of delighted curiosity returned.

Zee immediately pointed at the Dragon.

“Do not.”

Ner frowned.

“Do not what?”

“Nothing.”

Rez laughed.

The last mercenary tried running.

Zareth lowered his head.

The man stopped.

Slowly turned.

Zareth’s Teal-and-Gold Mana pulsed beneath scales now thick enough to catch snow without melting it unless he wanted.

At fifteen, he was enormous.

Not fully grown.

Not close by Dragon standards.

Still large enough that the mercenary had to lean backward to see his face.

Zareth showed teeth.

The man dropped his weapon.

Rez nodded.

“Efficient.”

The Dragon Link carried deep satisfaction.

---

The captives had not been taken because of Zee.

That was why he had come.

Three mountain villages had been fighting over winter pasture rights for generations.

Then a mercenary company realized kidnapping children from all three and selling them back separately could make each village blame the others.

Ugly.

Simple.

Profitable.

Nothing about it required prophecy.

Nothing about it required Darkheart blood.

The world had always possessed horrors that did not need Zee to exist first.

The core four had learned to choose some of those fights anyway.

Zee entered the cave first.

Not because he had to.

Because the weakest heartbeat was fading.

Crimson Mana moved beneath his boots.

He crossed the stone too quickly for ordinary sight.

The cages were crude.

Iron.

No enchanted ownership contracts.

No ancient runes.

No grand mystery.

Just locks.

Ner arrived seconds later.

His eyes went immediately toward the weakest captive.

A little girl wrapped in torn wool.

“Cold.”

Rez entered behind him.

“I have blankets outside.”

“Bring them.”

Rez turned without argument.

Zee crouched beside the cage.

The girl looked at his horns.

Then his eyes.

Then the scales that now patterned portions of his temples and neck in permanent Crimson.

Her face tightened.

Fear.

Zee stopped reaching for the lock.

“My name is Zee.”

She stared.

He waited.

That was another thing five years had taught him.

Being able to act did not always mean acting first was best.

The girl whispered, “Darkheart?”

“Yes.”

Her eyes widened.

One of the older boys in another cage pushed himself backward.

“The monster prince.”

Zee's jaw tightened.

The name still worked.

Less than before.

Not never.

Ner crouched beside him.

“People also call him irritating.”

Zee looked over.

“That is not helping.”

“It helped me.”

The girl’s mouth twitched.

Barely.

Good.

Zee looked back.

“We are taking you home.”

“Which village?”

“Whichever one is yours.”

She swallowed.

“They said our village would not pay.”

Zee’s expression changed.

“That is not your problem.”

The words came easily now.

Five years ago he might have promised revenge.

Might have described what he would do to the mercenaries.

Today the girl needed something else.

“Your village does not have to buy you back.”

Ner’s Golden Mana touched the first lock.

It opened.

Then the next.

And the next.

He could have broken all of them at once.

He chose precision.

Rez returned carrying blankets.

He moved through the cages distributing them with the practiced authority of a Vesper prince who had spent years learning that leadership often looked less like speeches and more like noticing who was cold.

Zareth stayed outside.

Not because he had been ordered.

Because frightened children did not need a massive Dragon filling the cave entrance.

The Link carried impatience.

Then concern.

Then an image.

Sky.

Movement.

Zee stood.

“What?”

Rez looked toward him.

“Zareth?”

Zee closed his eyes for half a heartbeat.

The Link sharpened.

Three riders approaching from the north.

Vesper colors.

No.

Not Vesper.

One gray.

One green.

One white.

Local kingdoms.

Good.

Zee opened his eyes.

“Officials.”

Rez sighed.

“Worse.”

Ner smiled.

“You enjoy politics.”

“I enjoy winning politics.”

“You enjoy hearing yourself talk.”

“That too.”

They brought the captives out.

Eighteen.

All alive.

One barely conscious.

Ner carried her.

Zee noticed that.

Five years ago he would have reached automatically.

Now he did not.

Ner was capable.

More than capable.

The girl’s head rested against his shoulder while Golden Mana warmed the air around her without touching her skin.

Zee looked too long again.

Rez appeared beside him.

“You are doing it.”

Zee immediately looked away.

“I do not know what you mean.”

“Sure.”

“Say something and I will throw you off the bridge.”

Rez smiled.

“You have been threatening that for five years.”

“One day.”

“Try.”

Zee shoved him lightly.

Rez shoved back.

Same age.

Same current life.

No qualifiers.

Just Rez.

Their boots skidded in the snow.

Ner looked over.

“Can both of you behave?”

“No,” they answered.

The arriving officials saw them before reaching the bridge.

All three slowed.

The woman in green recognized Zareth first.

That was understandable.

Then Rez.

Vesper.

Then Ner.

Gold.

Then Zee.

Her expression changed.

Not confusion.

Recognition.

The kind Zee had spent five years learning to read.

Fear.

Calculation.

Curiosity.

The stories arrived before he did now.

Some called him protector.

Some called him butcher.

Some swore he could drink an army dry.

Some claimed no prison could hold him twice.

One particularly ridiculous northern story insisted his horns grew every time he lied.

Ner still referenced that whenever convenient.

The woman dismounted.

“Zee Darkheart.”

Not child.

Not creature.

Name.

He preferred that.

“Yes.”

Her gaze moved toward the captives.

“You found them.”

Rez answered.

“We found everyone registered missing from the three villages.”

The official looked toward him.

“Prince Rez.”

He nodded.

Then toward Ner.

“Azrion.”

“Nereus.”

Her gaze shifted toward Zareth.

She bowed more carefully.

“Crown Prince Drakonis.”

Zareth lowered his head once.

His own choice.

Then back to Zee.

“We were told the mercenaries numbered twenty.”

“They did.”

Her eyes moved toward the prisoners.

“How many dead?”

Zee looked.

“None.”

That surprised her.

It surprised people often.

The monster stories had grown faster than Zee’s actual appetite for killing.

“None?”

“They surrendered.”

One prisoner groaned from the bridge.

Rez added, “Eventually.”

The official looked toward Zee’s bloodied knuckles.

He noticed.

“Not mine.”

Ner looked over.

“It is mostly not his.”

Zee stared.

“Ner.”

“What?”

The official almost smiled.

Almost.

She looked toward the children.

“What happened here?”

Zee answered simply.

“They were being sold back to their families.”

“By whom?”

Rez handed her a captured ledger.

“Names.”

Routes.

Payments.

No prophecy.

No grand conspiracy.

A crime.

Evidence.

A consequence.

The woman accepted it.

“We take custody.”

Rez’s expression became political.

“Joint custody.”

She looked at him.

“Vesper has no authority here.”

“Vesper provided the request that brought us.”

“Your request came from one village.”

Ner interrupted.

“Two.”

The official looked toward him.

Ner nodded toward the children.

“The second sent a request through a witch courier three days later.”

“How do you know?”

“I read it.”

Rez smiled.

“And Drakonis airspace was crossed during the abduction.”

Zareth’s Teal-and-Gold Mana pulsed once.

The official looked toward the Dragon Prince.

Then back at the three boys.

Zee almost felt sorry for her.

Almost.

She exhaled.

“Joint custody.”

Rez smiled.

“I enjoy diplomacy.”

Ner muttered, “You enjoy winning.”

“Yes.”

---

They left the mountain pass after sunset.

No triumphant procession.

No songs.

No crown.

Just four fifteen-year-olds moving south while village families reunited behind them.

Zareth flew above.

Rez walked beside Zee.

Ner slightly ahead.

Snow caught in Ner’s hair.

Zee watched him brush it away.

Again, too long.

Ner looked back.

Caught him.

Neither spoke.

A strange tension passed between them.

Not uncomfortable.

Not exactly comfortable either.

New.

Zee looked toward the road.

Ner smiled to himself and continued walking.

Rez saw everything.

Of course he did.

Zee did not look at him.

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“You are thinking loudly.”

Rez laughed.

“Careful. That phrase has history.”

Zee’s expression changed.

Only slightly.

Some powers remained untouched.

He had never intentionally reached toward the strange living-age magic again.

Not once.

The boundary mattered.

The past remained fixed.

Rez’s changed life had taught Zee enough about what careless power could cost.

Some mysteries were allowed to wait until understanding arrived.

Zee rubbed one hand along the scale pattern at his forearm.

His Dragon nature stirred beneath it.

Stronger than at ten.

Far stronger.

His horns had grown.

His durability had changed.

The ridges beneath his shoulder blades had become more pronounced during surges.

Crimson Dragon energy came more easily now.

But no wings had opened.

No true Dragon form had appeared.

Whatever the Convergence Vault had once measured remained unfinished.

Four.

Three awake.

Zee could live with unfinished.

That was new too.

Above, Zareth banked east instead of south.

Zee stopped.

The Dragon Link carried a complex impression.

Drakonis.

Return tonight.

Council tomorrow.

Duty.

Zee frowned automatically.

Then caught himself.

Rez noticed.

“You knew he had to go.”

“I know.”

Ner stopped beside them.

“How long?”

Zee interpreted the Link.

“Four days.”

A flash from Zareth.

Maybe five.

Zee narrowed his eyes.

“Five.”

Ner smiled.

“You almost sounded offended.”

“I am.”

Zareth sent warmth.

Then an image.

Return.

The western roof at Vesper.

The four of them.

Zee exhaled.

“Fine.”

He raised one hand.

Zareth roared once and climbed higher.

No panic.

No desperate need to follow.

Zee missed him before he disappeared.

That was allowed.

The Dragon Prince had his kingdom.

Zee had his road.

Love did not become weaker because distance existed inside it.

Ner bumped Zee’s shoulder.

“You are getting better at that.”

“At what?”

“Not acting like Zareth leaving for four days means the end of civilization.”

“Five.”

Rez laughed.

Zee glared.

Then all three continued south.

Fifteen.

Not adults.

Not kings.

Not legends.

Not yet.

Five years had given them new scars, new habits, new arguments, and the kind of teamwork that only came from surviving enough bad plans together.

House Veyrath lived in fragments by choice.

Vesper had become a kingdom people thought carefully about threatening.

Drakonis had a Crown Prince who divided his life between two homes without belonging less to either.

Victor still sat inside Castle Darkheart.

The black-robed observers had not vanished.

Hunters still studied Zee.

Kingdoms still feared him.

Some people prayed he never crossed their borders.

Others sent requests hoping he would.

The stories had grown.

The boy inside them had grown too.

But Zee Darkheart was still only fifteen.

Still learning what his blood could become.

Still discovering which battles were worth choosing.

Still capable of looking at Ner too long and immediately pretending he had not.

Still capable of arguing with Rez over nothing.

Still listening for Zareth across the Link.

Still seeking Aurelia when the world became heavier than he wanted anyone else to see.

# Crimson Dynasty — Chapters Forty-Two & Forty-Three

# Chapter Forty-Two

## The Price of Interference

The first argument waiting for Zee Darkheart at House Vesper wore silk.

He preferred knives.

Knives were honest.

Knives did not sit beneath blue-white Vesper banners drinking expensive wine while explaining why eighteen kidnapped children should have remained somebody else's problem.

Zee stood against the western wall of the royal council chamber with his arms crossed.

His travel coat was still damp from mountain snow.

A shallow cut beneath his jaw had already closed.

Permanent Crimson scales patterned the sides of his neck, disappeared beneath his collar, then returned along both forearms.

His crimson-black horns made pretending he was an ordinary visiting prince impossible.

That was fine.

He had stopped trying years ago.

Across the chamber, six Vesper nobles argued around the council table.

King Lucien sat at its head.

Rez sat to his right.

Not behind him.

Not watching.

Participating.

The fifteen-year-old Crown Prince had changed clothes after returning from the mountains, but nothing else about him suggested rest. His black hair remained wind-tossed, and Blue-White Mana occasionally flickered around two fingers whenever someone said something especially stupid.

It had happened four times.

Zee was counting.

Councilor Darius Hane struck one palm against the table.

“The Northern Border Council has formally protested.”

Lucien said nothing.

Hane continued.

“Prince Rez entered disputed territory with armed companions, apprehended licensed contractors, seized private documents, and transferred detainees without authorization.”

Zee lifted one eyebrow.

“Licensed kidnappers.”

Every head turned.

Rez closed his eyes.

Lucien looked toward Zee.

“I was handling that.”

“I improved it.”

Ner, seated near the opposite end of the table with three recovered ledgers spread before him, whispered, “You did not.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner did not look back.

That somehow made Zee look longer.

Five years had sharpened Nereus Azrion in ways Zee was still becoming embarrassingly aware of.

His face had lost the roundness of childhood.

His Pure Golden Mana moved with restrained confidence instead of flashing at every irritation.

His hands—

Zee stopped.

Why was he looking at Ner's hands?

Rez cleared his throat.

Zee immediately faced the table.

Rez's mouth twitched.

Traitor.

Councilor Hane continued.

“The point remains. Whatever those mercenaries did, Vesper cannot simply cross every border because Zee Darkheart decides someone deserves saving.”

Zee's jaw tightened.

Lucien spoke before he could.

“They did not enter under Zee's authority.”

Hane looked toward Rez.

Lucien continued.

“They entered under mine.”

That silenced several nobles.

Rez looked at his father.

Lucien did not look back.

He was letting the statement stand.

The mission had begun with requests transmitted through Vesper.

That made the consequences Vesper's too.

Another noble, Lady Merrow, leaned forward.

“And now the Northern Council threatens to suspend grain passage through the upper roads.”

Theron Veyrath sat near the rear windows and muttered, “Then perhaps their grain should learn to walk around us.”

Seraphine, beside him, smiled.

“You would be terrible at diplomacy.”

“I survived captivity.”

“That did not make you charming.”

“It should have.”

Aurelia sat between them.

Five years of having both siblings back had not made their arguments less exhausting.

It had made her better at ignoring them.

She looked toward Zee instead.

He recognized the warning.

Do not explode at politicians.

He had received that look many times.

Zee sighed.

Rez leaned over the table.

“What exactly does the Northern Border Council want?”

Hane passed him a sealed letter.

Rez broke the wax.

Read.

His expression changed.

“Return of the prisoners.”

Ner looked up.

“Of course.”

Rez continued.

“Return of all seized property.”

“The ledgers?” Ner asked.

“Yes.”

“No.”

Several nobles looked toward him.

Ner calmly placed one hand over the nearest book.

Pure Golden Mana flickered across the cover.

“No.”

Councilor Hane frowned.

“Nereus, the documents were taken beyond Vesper jurisdiction.”

“They document the sale of children.”

“They allegedly document—”

“They document it.”

Ner looked directly at him.

“I spent six hours reading them.”

Hane's expression hardened.

“That does not make you a court.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“No.”

Golden Mana formed along the edge of one page.

Hidden writing rose from the parchment.

Names.

Payments.

Village marks.

Transfer dates.

Then vanished when Ner lowered his hand.

“It makes me capable of reading what somebody tried to hide.”

Zee smiled.

Hane did not.

Good.

Rez folded the demand.

“What else?”

Lucien answered.

“The Northern Council is sending a representative.”

“When?”

“Tomorrow.”

Rez frowned.

“They sent the complaint before the children were even back in their villages.”

Silence.

That mattered.

The mountain officials had barely taken custody before the protest arrived.

Too fast.

Zee pushed away from the wall.

“So they already knew.”

Lady Merrow looked toward him.

“Knew what?”

“That the mercenaries would be arrested.”

Rez looked at Zee.

Then the letter.

Ner stopped moving.

Lucien's eyes sharpened.

Adjusting.

Zee had been thinking hard enough for the Link to feel the weight of it.

He let the sensation pass without reaching for Zareth.

This answer belonged to him.

“I do not know.”

Ner nodded.

“Then figure it out before you become stronger.”

Zee almost laughed.

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is.”

“You are threatening me?”

“I am your best friend.”

“That is apparently worse.”

Ner smiled.

Zee looked at him.

Again too long.

Ner noticed.

Again.

This time he did not look away.

Neither did Zee.

The air shifted.

Not magic.

Something much more inconvenient.

Zee became aware that their knees were almost touching.

That Ner's face was closer than he expected.

That his eyes were warmer in firelight than Pure Golden Mana ever looked.

Zee's horns heated.

Ner glanced upward.

Then smiled.

Zee immediately looked toward the city.

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“You were going to.”

“I was.”

Zee pushed his shoulder.

Ner pushed back.

Their hands hit the stone between them at the same time.

Fingers brushed.

Neither moved.

For one heartbeat.

Two.

Then footsteps sounded below.

Both pulled away far too quickly.

Rez emerged from the tower stair.

He looked at Zee.

Then Ner.

Then the suspicious distance suddenly placed between them.

His face became unbearable.

Zee pointed.

“No.”

Rez raised both hands.

“I came to tell you dinner is ready.”

Ner stood.

“Good.”

He walked past Rez.

Rez waited until Ner disappeared down the stairs.

Then looked at Zee.

Zee stood.

“Say one word.”

Rez smiled.

“I am proud of your commitment to diplomacy.”

Zee shoved him into the wall.

Rez laughed the entire way downstairs.

---

Aurelia was awake when Zee returned to his room.

Of course she was.

She sat beside the window holding a book she had not turned a page of in several minutes.

Zee stopped.

“Were you waiting?”

“Yes.”

“I am fifteen.”

“I noticed.”

“That means you do not have to wait every time.”

“I know.”

She closed the book.

“That does not mean I won't.”

Zee walked over.

For a moment he considered sitting across from her.

Instead he sat beside her.

Then leaned against her shoulder.

Fifteen did not make that unnecessary.

Aurelia wrapped one arm around him.

Neither spoke at first.

Then:

“I hurt Renn.”

“I heard.”

“I liked it.”

“I know.”

Zee looked up.

“How?”

“You smiled.”

His stomach tightened.

Aurelia had seen.

She did not look frightened.

That mattered too much.

“Does that make me bad?”

Aurelia considered the question instead of answering quickly.

“No.”

Zee frowned.

“That was too easy.”

“I was not finished.”

Of course.

She touched one of the scales along his wrist.

“What you enjoy tells you something about yourself.”

“It does not make every choice for you.”

Zee looked toward the window.

“What if I enjoy it more?”

“Then you had better become very good at knowing why you are hurting someone.”

That answer surprised him.

No demand that he become gentle.

No lie that violence was always wrong.

Aurelia knew their world better than that.

Zee asked, “And if they deserve it?”

“People use that sentence to justify terrible things.”

His face tightened.

“Victor thought I deserved what he did.”

Aurelia went still.

There it was.

The line Zee feared crossing.

Victor had once looked at an infant and convinced himself fear was judgment.

That danger lived in certainty.

Aurelia spoke quietly.

“Then remember him.”

Zee looked at her.

“Not to become him.”

“To remember how easy it is to believe fear makes you righteous.”

Zee thought about Renn.

He had evidence.

Children.

Oaths.

A clear crime.

That had not made breaking the man's wrist necessary.

The first break stopped his casting.

The second had been because Zee wanted the scream.

He knew the difference.

That was what frightened him.

And perhaps what could protect him too.

“I broke it twice.”

Aurelia understood.

“The first time?”

“To stop him.”

“The second?”

Zee looked down.

“Because I wanted to.”

No excuse.

No monster.

No prophecy.

Just truth.

Aurelia kissed his temple beside one horn.

“Then remember that difference.”

Zee closed his eyes.

Outside, Vesper prepared for a trade dispute.

Rez was probably still arguing with Lucien over alternate grain routes.

Ner was probably pretending the tower moment had not happened.

Zareth was several kingdoms away inside Drakonis, carrying responsibilities that belonged to him alone.

The core four were not children anymore.

Not adults.

Not rulers.

Not legends.

But the world had begun bringing them problems that could not be solved by surviving until morning.

At fifteen, Zee Darkheart was learning that choosing a hunt was easier than choosing what happened when he caught what he hunted.

He could break bones.

He could spill blood.

He could frighten people who deserved fear.

And somewhere beneath the part of him that protected innocents, another part had begun enjoying what monsters sounded like when they realized the monster in front of them was stronger.

Zee did not hate that part.

Not yet.

That was the danger.

He leaned against Aurelia and listened to her heartbeat while he still could.

Then opened his eyes.

Because if Zee Darkheart was going to decide what kind of monster the world deserved—

he would have to make sure the world did not decide it for him first.

# Chapter Forty-Four

## The Kingdom That Could Not Eat Pride

The grain stopped at sunrise.

Not gradually.

Not with another warning.

Every northern wagon under compact protection turned around at the border.

By breakfast, House Vesper knew.

By noon, the markets knew.

By evening, people who had never heard the name Maelor Renn were already arguing over flour.

Rez spent most of that day in council.

Zee lasted forty minutes.

That was a personal record.

He stood near the rear windows while Vesper ministers moved stones across a trade map.

Blue represented existing supply.

White represented emergency reserves.

Red represented villages that would begin experiencing shortages first.

There were too many red stones.

Councilor Hane tapped the northern road.

“We have enough royal reserve for several weeks.”

Lucien sat at the head of the table.

“That is not the question.”

“No.”

Hane looked toward Rez.

“The question is whether we continue holding Renn while the compact remains suspended.”

Rez's expression stayed flat.

“We do.”

One of the older nobles sighed.

“Your Highness—”

“Do not.”

The room quieted.

Rez leaned forward.

“If your next sentence is that children being kidnapped matters less than grain prices, improve it before you speak.”

The noble closed his mouth.

Zee smiled.

Rez saw.

“Do not encourage me.”

“I did nothing.”

“You have the face.”

Ner sat beside three ledgers near the opposite wall.

He looked up.

“He does.”

Zee turned toward him.

“You are supposed to support me.”

“I support truth.”

“That sounds suspiciously convenient.”

Ner's mouth twitched.

Lucien ignored them.

“Western coven routes?”

Lady Merrow pointed toward the lower map.

“Available.”

“Capacity?”

“Insufficient alone.”

“River?”

“Possible.”

“Fast?”

“No.”

Rez looked toward the red stones.

“Which villages run out first?”

Lady Merrow moved three markers.

“These.”

Two sat near Vesper's northeastern edge.

The third was farther south.

Small.

Agricultural.

Ironically dependent on northern grain because the region grew medicinal plants instead of wheat.

Rez's jaw tightened.

Zee recognized that expression.

The Crown Prince was no longer discussing politics.

He was seeing people.

Good.

Lucien asked, “What do you want to do?”

Several councilors looked toward him.

Rez looked back at his father.

Not surprised.

Lucien had been doing this increasingly over the last few years.

Handing him real decisions.

Not pretend ones.

Rez touched the western route.

“Buy from the covens.”

Hane frowned.

“We already established it is not enough.”

“I know.”

Then the river.

“Lease civilian barges.”

“Expensive.”

“Yes.”

“Slow.”

“Yes.”

“Dangerous this season.”

“Yes.”

Hane stared.

Rez continued.

“Then reduce palace stores.”

Silence.

A noble blinked.

“Your Highness?”

“Royal reserve feeds the northeastern villages first.”

Lady Merrow looked toward Lucien.

Rez did not.

He was not asking permission yet.

“Vesper city takes ration reduction.”

Hane frowned.

“You cannot cut capital supply without unrest.”

“I can if the palace cuts first.”

Zee stopped smiling.

That was smart.

Rez continued.

“Publish the reductions.”

“Royal kitchens.”

“Barracks.”

“Noble allotments.”

“Mine.”

His finger touched the map.

“We do not ask outer villages to absorb a political punishment aimed at us while the palace eats normally.”

No one spoke.

Then Lucien leaned back.

“Approved.”

Rez looked toward him.

That was it.

No ceremony.

No praise.

Responsibility handed over and accepted.

Zee liked watching him become a ruler.

It was strange.

Rez could be laughing on a roof one night and restructuring Vesper food supply the next morning.

Both were real.

Both were him.

Councilor Hane sighed.

“We still need more grain.”

Ner spoke without looking up.

“The western covens have more.”

Lady Merrow frowned.

“They already stated maximum sale.”

“They stated maximum sale to Vesper.”

Everyone turned.

Ner finally looked up.

“What?”

Rez narrowed his eyes.

“What did you find?”

Ner closed one ledger and opened another.

“The covens are not refusing because they lack grain.”

“They are refusing because they do not want to be seen choosing Vesper against the Northern Council.”

Lucien's expression sharpened.

“How do you know?”

Ner pointed toward three shipping marks.

“They increased deliveries to two neutral trading Houses last week.”

Lady Merrow approached.

“How much?”

“Enough.”

Rez stood.

“So we buy through the neutral Houses.”

Hane shook his head.

“At double cost.”

“Then negotiate.”

“With whom?”

Ner looked toward Rez.

“The covens.”

Rez frowned.

“They will deny involvement.”

“Probably.”

Zee watched Ner's face.

There.

That particular little confidence.

He had a plan.

Zee knew it.

Rez knew it.

Lucien probably knew it too.

“What?” Rez asked.

Ner leaned back.

“They invited me.”

The room changed.

Zee's attention snapped fully toward him.

“Who?”

“The western coven delegates.”

“When?”

“This morning.”

“You did not tell me.”

Ner looked toward Zee.

“They did not invite you.”

“I noticed.”

Rez covered a smile.

Zee ignored him.

Lucien asked, “Why?”

Ner hesitated.

That was enough to make Zee stop being annoyed.

“Because of my Mana.”

Aurelia, who had remained silent until now, looked up.

“Specific request?”

“Yes.”

Ner handed Lucien a sealed letter.

“Their senior ward-master wants to discuss Golden boundary work.”

Zee's scales warmed faintly.

Not danger.

Protectiveness.

He noticed.

Controlled it.

Ner noticed too.

Their eyes met.

Zee looked away first.

Annoying.

Lucien read the letter.

“They want you to come without royal escort.”

Zee immediately said, “No.”

Ner immediately said, “Yes.”

They stared at each other.

Rez sighed.

“We are doing this now?”

Ner folded his arms.

“I can go to a coven meeting without Zee attached to me.”

“I am not attached to you.”

“You tried answering before Lucien finished reading.”

“That proves nothing.”

“It proves everything.”

Zee stepped closer.

“They asked specifically for no royal escort.”

“Yes.”

“That is suspicious.”

“Or political.”

“Same thing.”

Rez muttered, “Unfortunately true.”

Ner looked toward Lucien.

“I want to go.”

Zee's jaw tightened.

There.

The actual point.

Not whether Zee approved.

Ner wanted it.

His problem.

His choice.

Zee hated that.

Which meant he needed to learn from it.

He exhaled.

“Fine.”

Ner blinked.

“That easy?”

“No.”

Zee looked at him.

“I just know you will go anyway.”

Ner smiled.

“That sounds more accurate.”

Aurelia watched Zee carefully.

Progress.

Again.

Lucien tapped the letter.

“You will not go alone.”

Ner frowned.

“They explicitly requested—”

“No royal escort.”

Lucien looked toward Caldrin.

Caldrin smiled.

“I am barely royal-adjacent.”

Ner groaned.

Zee laughed.

That helped.

Until Lucien looked toward Rez.

“You go too.”

Rez straightened.

“As Crown Prince?”

“No.”

That surprised everyone.

“As Nereus's friend.”

Rez looked toward Ner.

Then Lucien.

“Why?”

“Because if this becomes negotiation, I want you there.”

“And if it does not?”

“Then stay quiet.”

Rez looked offended.

Zee laughed harder.

Lucien turned toward Zee.

“You stay.”

Zee stopped laughing.

“What?”

Aurelia's mouth twitched.

Lucien continued.

“You are the exact opposite of politically invisible.”

“That feels insulting.”

“It is factual.”

Zee looked toward Ner.

Ner tried not to smile.

Failed.

“You seem happy.”

“A little.”

“I hope the covens are terrible.”

Ner laughed.

---

Zareth returned from Drakonis that afternoon.

He came down from cloud cover over Vesper's eastern wall and landed in the training field without damaging anything.

Mostly.

One stone cracked.

Zee decided not to count it.

The Dragon Link hit him the moment Zareth touched ground.

Heat.

Drakonis.

Annoyance.

Three older Dragons arguing.

A ceremonial chamber.

A map with a red border.

Then—

Food.

Zee stared.

“You left for royal council and came back hungry?”

Zareth lowered his head.

The Link delivered offended certainty.

**Both possible.**

Zee laughed.

He rested one hand against Zareth's snout.

Five days apart had sharpened how much he missed the weight of the Link nearby.

Not desperation anymore.

Just absence finally filled.

Zareth studied him.

Then Ner.

Then Rez.

Then the map case in Caldrin's hand.

Question.

Zee sighed.

“They are leaving.”

The Dragon's attention sharpened.

An image followed.

Zee left behind.

Ner leaving.

Then amusement.

Zee glared.

“You learned too much in Drakonis.”

Zareth's Teal-and-Gold Mana warmed beneath his scales.

Rez approached.

“Good. You are back.”

Zareth turned toward him.

Rez pointed east.

“I need a Dragon opinion.”

Zee looked at him.

“You are taking him?”

“No.”

Zareth's head lifted.

Rez continued.

“I need to know whether the northern grain suspension affects Drakonis caravan routes.”

Zareth's Link shifted toward Zee.

A complicated impression.

Mountain pass.

Dragon-controlled air corridors.

Two neutral road crossings.

No northern authority.

Zee translated.

“Not directly.”

Rez nodded.

“What about Vesper merchants using Drakonis roads?”

Zareth considered.

Then sent:

Possible.

Expensive.

Political consequences.

Dragon Queen approval required.

Rez smiled.

“I knew I liked him.”

Zee frowned.

“He is not solving your grain problem for free.”

Rez stared.

“Did he say that?”

“No.”

Zareth sent approval.

Rez laughed.

Ner arrived wearing a travel coat.

Zee's eyes moved toward him before he could stop them.

Dark coat.

Gold stitching near the cuffs.

Hair tied back.

He looked—

No.

Zee looked at Zareth.

The Dragon Link instantly returned the emotional equivalent of laughter.

“I hate this bond.”

Ner stopped.

“What did he do?”

“Nothing.”

Rez smiled.

“Zareth has become very observant.”

Zee looked at Rez.

“Do you want to survive fifteen?”

Rez laughed.

Ner shook his head.

Then his expression became serious.

“We leave now.”

Zee hated those words more than expected.

Not because danger was certain.

Because he was not going.

That felt new.

For years the core four had become so practiced together that being excluded from one another's problems felt unnatural.

But that was exactly why it needed to happen.

Ner stepped toward him.

“I will be fine.”

Zee frowned.

“I did not say you wouldn't.”

“You have the face.”

“Everyone needs to stop saying that.”

Ner smiled.

Then lowered his voice.

“You really okay?”

Zee looked at him.

Close.

Too close for the courtyard to suddenly feel empty.

“I do not like not being there.”

“I know.”

“That does not mean I think you cannot handle it.”

Ner's expression softened.

“That is better.”

“Do not sound surprised.”

“I am a little surprised.”

Zee shoved his shoulder.

Ner shoved back.

Their hands brushed again.

Both noticed.

Neither moved immediately.

Rez deliberately turned toward Caldrin.

“Beautiful weather.”

Caldrin looked at the cloudy sky.

“Awful.”

“Yes.”

Ner pulled his hand away first.

“I will come back.”

Zee nodded.

“I know.”

Zareth pressed a faint impression into the Link.

Return.

Same lesson.

Different person.

Zee exhaled.

“Go before I change my mind and become unreasonable.”

Ner grinned.

“You would have to become unreasonable first.”

Zee stared.

Rez grabbed Ner by the shoulder and steered him toward the horses.

“Excellent final words.”

---

Zee lasted six hours without them before Aurelia found him training hard enough to crack stone.

Not uncontrolled.

Just angry.

She stood outside the practice ring.

“You are sulking.”

“I am training.”

“You can do both.”

Zee hit the dummy again.

Crimson Mana snapped through the wood.

He stopped before destroying it.

Progress.

Aurelia entered.

“Why are you upset?”

“I am not.”

She looked at the broken post.

Zee sighed.

“Ner wanted to go.”

“Yes.”

“So he went.”

“Yes.”

“That is good.”

“Yes.”

“I hate it.”

Aurelia smiled.

“There.”

Zee glared.

“Do not.”

She approached.

“You are learning something unpleasant.”

“What?”

“People you love will choose risks without your permission.”

He hated the sentence immediately.

“That seems badly designed.”

“Frequently.”

Zee looked down.

His horns had warmed.

He focused.

Not danger.

Not rage.

Fear.

There.

He could name it now.

That mattered.

“What if something happens?”

“Then something happens.”

Zee's face tightened.

Aurelia continued before he could reject the answer.

“You cannot protect people by reducing their lives until nothing dangerous reaches them.”

Victor lived inside that lesson whether she said his name or not.

Control.

Containment.

Fear disguised as protection.

Zee understood.

He hated understanding.

“I am not Victor.”

“No.”

Aurelia touched his cheek.

“But no one becomes someone terrible all at once.”

Zee looked at her.

“People become what they keep choosing.”

Her old words.

Still true.

He nodded.

Then asked, “Can I at least be annoyed?”

Aurelia smiled.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He hit the dummy again.

This time she laughed.

---

The western covens answered before midnight.

Not through letter.

Through Rez.

A Vesper messenger arrived at full speed carrying a sealed strip marked with Crown Prince authorization.

Lucien opened it.

Zee stood beside him.

Aurelia behind.

Zareth occupied the terrace.

The message was short.

**Negotiations accepted. Grain available. Terms changed.**

Zee smiled.

Then Lucien read the next line.

The smile vanished.

**Ner remains with coven ward-master until morning by his choice.**

Zee looked up.

“Why?”

Lucien continued.

**Boundary breach discovered beneath western grain storehouses. Golden Mana required to stabilize without destroying reserves. Rez assisting evacuation. No attack confirmed.**

Zee's horns warmed.

Danger.

Real this time.

Zareth felt it.

The Dragon Link tightened.

Aurelia read over Lucien's shoulder.

“Do not assume.”

Zee looked toward her.

“It says breach.”

“It also says no attack confirmed.”

“Something is under the storehouses.”

“Yes.”

“Ner is staying.”

“By choice.”

That was the part.

Again.

Zee paced once.

Then stopped.

“What can I do?”

Aurelia's eyebrows rose.

Not *Can I go?*

What can I do?

Better.

Lucien handed him a second note.

“Rez requested Vesper ward maps.”

Zee took it.

“Then we send them.”

He turned toward the archive corridor.

Aurelia smiled faintly.

The hunted child would have run west.

The fifteen-year-old boy was learning that sometimes protecting someone meant helping from where you were.

That lesson lasted until the second message arrived.

Then everything changed.

The western boundary beneath the grain houses had not been breached from outside.

It had been opened from within.

And the person who opened it had used Pure Golden Mana.

# Chapter Forty-Five

## Gold Does Not Belong to One Boy

Zee read the line twice.

Then a third time.

**Pure Golden Mana confirmed at breach site.**

“No.”

Lucien looked toward him.

Zee shook his head.

“Ner did not do it.”

Aurelia stood beside the council table.

“No one said he did.”

“They will.”

That was the problem.

Pure Golden Mana belonged to Nereus.

Everyone who mattered knew that.

At least everyone they trusted.

If another Golden signature appeared beneath western coven grain stores, then either the report was wrong—

or something more complicated had happened.

Zee's first instinct was to leave immediately.

He felt it.

Named it.

Then did not obey it.

“Who sent this?”

Lucien handed him the seal.

“Rez.”

Zee checked it himself.

Vesper mark.

Blue-White authentication line.

Rez.

Real.

“What else?”

“Nothing yet.”

Zareth's Link tightened.

Question.

Zee sent the concept.

Ner.

Gold.

Wrong.

Zareth's Mana flared once.

Concern.

Then an image.

Fly west.

Zee almost agreed.

Aurelia saw.

“No.”

He looked at her.

“Zareth can reach them before morning.”

“And arrive over a witch coven with a Dragon Crown Prince while they are already suspicious of Nereus?”

Zee stopped.

Bad.

Very bad.

Zareth understood too.

His irritation rolled through the Link.

Zee sighed.

“Fine.”

Lucien looked toward him.

“Go sleep.”

Zee stared.

“No.”

“Then sit.”

“I can do that.”

“Without pacing.”

Zee looked toward the floor.

He had already worn a line into the rug.

Annoying.

He sat.

For three hours.

The longest three hours of his life.

Then Rez came through the council doors just before dawn.

Alone.

Zee stood so fast the chair fell backward.

“Where is Ner?”

“Alive.”

“Where?”

“Still west.”

“Why?”

Rez crossed to the water table and drank before answering.

That alone told Zee this was bad.

“Ner found the breach.”

“I know.”

“He stabilized it.”

“I know.”

“The coven ward-master accused him of creating it.”

Zee's jaw tightened.

Rez continued.

“I stopped that from becoming an arrest.”

“How?”

“Politics.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is at four in the morning.”

Zee glared.

Rez sighed.

“The covens need Vesper grain purchases.”

“We need their supply.”

“They cannot openly imprison Lucien's protected guest without evidence.”

“And?”

“And Ner volunteered to stay until they determine what happened.”

Zee stared.

“He volunteered?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because if he leaves, it looks like guilt.”

“He does not owe them—”

“I know.”

Rez's voice sharpened.

“He knows too.”

That stopped Zee.

Rez looked exhausted.

Not frightened.

Angry.

Different.

“The problem is not that the signature resembles Ner.”

Zee's stomach tightened.

“What?”

“It is Ner.”

Silence.

Aurelia stepped forward.

“What exactly does that mean?”

Rez pulled a folded ward sheet from his coat.

“The Golden Mana in the breach matches his.”

Zee shook his head.

“That is impossible.”

Ner was unique.

Pure Gold belonged to him.

Rez looked toward Aurelia.

“The ward-master says the breach was opened approximately two days before Ner arrived.”

Zee froze.

Two days.

Impossible.

Not by Ner.

He had been in Vesper.

Everyone knew.

Aurelia asked, “Stored Mana?”

Rez nodded slowly.

“That is their working theory.”

Zee looked toward him.

“Someone took his magic.”

“Not all of it.”

“Copied?”

Rez frowned.

“Ner says no.”

Good.

That matched everything Zee knew about rare power.

No direct copying assumptions.

Rez continued.

“He thinks someone preserved a piece of Golden Mana from an older spell.”

Zee's eyes narrowed.

“When?”

“That is the problem.”

Ner had used Golden Mana publicly for years.

Barriers.

Seals.

Combat.

Rescues.

Political meetings.

Any number of people could have collected residue if they understood how.

His uniqueness had become reputation.

Reputation created vulnerability.

For once, the threat belonged to Ner.

Not Zee.

Zee's horns warmed.

Anger.

Focused.

“Who benefits?”

Rez smiled without humor.

“Now you sound like Crown Council.”

“Answer.”

“The western covens lose grain.”

“Vesper loses access.”

“Ner gets blamed.”

“Trade collapses.”

Aurelia looked toward the map.

“Which benefits the Northern Council.”

Rez nodded.

“Possibly.”

Zee frowned.

“Renn is imprisoned.”

“Renn is one councilor.”

There.

Larger world.

Not one mastermind.

Not one villain controlling every thread.

People sharing interests without sharing loyalty.

Aurelia said, “Do we have evidence?”

“No.”

Zee hated that.

Because evidence was what separated justice from whatever his anger wanted.

Rez continued.

“Ner asked for you.”

Zee looked up.

That changed everything.

“When?”

“Now.”

---

They traveled west without Zareth.

The Dragon Prince had his own problem.

A Drakonis messenger arrived before they left carrying an urgent summons tied to the same northern trade disruption. Dragon-controlled mountain roads were suddenly being pressured by merchants seeking alternate passage.

Zareth could have ignored it.

He did not.

He looked toward Zee.

The Link carried conflict.

Friend.

Duty.

Both.

Zee touched his snout.

“Go.”

Zareth hesitated.

Zee smiled faintly.

“I mean it.”

An image came.

Ner.

Danger.

Zee.

Then trust.

Zareth launched east.

Zee traveled west with Aurelia, Rez, Caldrin, and six Vesper guards.

No Dragon.

No full core four.

Different problem.

Good.

The western covens occupied a series of fortified hill settlements surrounded by cultivated fields and old stone ward towers.

Zee had visited twice before.

Neither visit ended comfortably.

Today was worse.

The coven gates opened for Rez.

Not Zee.

That was deliberate.

Zee noticed.

Did not care.

Much.

Ner stood inside the main ward hall with three senior witches around him.

He looked tired.

Golden Mana circled both wrists in thin restraint bands.

Zee stopped.

Everything inside him sharpened.

Ner saw.

“Don't.”

Zee stared at the bindings.

“They restrained you.”

“I agreed.”

“You agreed badly.”

Ner almost smiled.

One of the senior witches stepped forward.

“Prince Darkheart—”

Zee looked at her.

She stopped.

Aurelia touched Zee's arm.

Not restraint.

Reminder.

He breathed.

Anger.

Not command.

“Why is he bound?”

The witch answered carefully.

“Because until we understand how his Mana signature opened the lower ward, we cannot allow unrestricted casting.”

Ner lifted both hands.

“They are symbolic.”

Zee looked closer.

They were.

Weak enough Ner could break them instantly.

That mattered.

He had chosen to wear them.

Zee still hated them.

Ner looked toward Rez.

“You took forever.”

“It is far.”

“You are a witch.”

“I cannot teleport kingdoms.”

Ner sighed.

“Disappointing.”

Then his gaze shifted to Zee.

Their eyes held.

Something inside Zee unclenched.

“You okay?”

“Yes.”

“Truth.”

Ner looked down at the Golden restraints.

“Angry.”

“Good.”

One coven elder frowned.

“Good?”

Zee looked at her.

“He tells the truth when he is angry.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“Usually.”

Aurelia stepped toward the breach map.

“Show us.”

---

The grain storehouse sat above an old boundary chamber.

No prophecy.

No ancient destiny.

Just infrastructure.

Witch kingdoms built wards around food stores for obvious reasons.

Fire.

Poison.

Theft.

Rot.

The lower chamber contained six stone anchors.

One had been opened.

Golden residue remained inside.

Ner stood several feet away.

“It is mine.”

Zee looked toward him.

“You are sure?”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

That bothered Zee more than denial would have.

Ner crouched.

“The structure came from one of my older barrier patterns.”

“How old?”

“Years.”

Rez looked around.

“Can you tell which one?”

Ner closed his eyes.

Pure Golden Mana rose from his hands despite the restraint bands.

The coven elders tensed.

Ner ignored them.

A thin line extended toward the residue.

Touched.

His expression changed.

“Oh.”

Zee moved closer.

“What?”

“I know this.”

“From where?”

Ner looked toward him.

“Vesper.”

Everyone went still.

Rez frowned.

“When?”

“Three years ago.”

He touched the residue again.

“South wall reconstruction.”

Zee remembered.

A storm had broken part of Vesper's outer ward network.

Ner had spent three days helping rebuild it.

Dozens of workers.

Witches.

Contract laborers.

Foreign masons.

Officials.

Not secret.

Not guarded like a unique magical ritual because at thirteen they had not yet understood how valuable magical residue could become.

Ner stood.

“Someone harvested leftover Mana.”

A coven elder looked horrified.

“Can that be done?”

Ner looked at her.

“Apparently.”

Zee frowned.

“You sound annoyed.”

“I am.”

“This is your power.”

“Yes.”

“And someone used it.”

“Yes.”

His voice hardened.

“Which means I decide what happens next.”

Zee looked at him.

There it was.

Not Zee's hunt.

Ner's.

Good.

Hard.

Necessary.

“What do you want?”

Ner looked toward the six anchors.

“Find the carrier.”

“How?”

Ner smiled.

The kind of smile Zee liked for dangerous reasons.

“They preserved my Mana.”

He lifted one hand.

“So they preserved my mistakes too.”

Rez's eyebrows rose.

“That sounds useful.”

“It is.”

Ner touched the residue.

Pure Gold spread into it.

Not overpowering.

Comparing.

A tiny flicker of pale green appeared inside the Golden signature.

Zee saw.

“What is that?”

“Copper.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Metal?”

“Dust.”

Ner looked toward the floor.

“South wall reconstruction used copper binding powder.”

Rez understood.

“Meaning whoever stored the Mana took it directly from that work.”

“Yes.”

Aurelia looked toward the coven elders.

“Who had access to both Vesper reconstruction crews and northern trade interests?”

Silence.

One elder went pale.

Rez saw.

“Who?”

She hesitated.

Zee smelled fear.

Not guilt necessarily.

Fear.

Important difference.

The elder answered.

“The Brannic Trade House.”

Lucien's records had mentioned them before.

Neutral merchants.

Not villains.

Not yet.

Rez frowned.

“They supplied stone to Vesper.”

“And transport grain for the north,” the elder said.

There.

Connection.

Not proof.

Ner stood.

“I want their depot.”

The elder stared.

“You cannot simply enter a neutral merchant depot.”

Zee smiled.

Ner looked toward him.

“No.”

Zee's smile widened.

“We can ask.”

Rez laughed.

“That was not what I expected.”

Zee shrugged.

“I am growing.”

Aurelia looked suspicious.

Ner knew him too well.

“What is the second half of that sentence?”

Zee's smile sharpened.

“If they say no, we know more.”

---

Brannic Trade House said yes.

That complicated everything.

Their depot manager welcomed inspection.

Opened records.

Allowed Ner to test storage rooms.

Provided employee lists.

Offered tea.

Zee distrusted him for being cooperative.

Ner told him that was irrational.

Zee agreed.

Then kept distrusting him.

Three hours produced nothing.

No Golden residue.

No hidden containers.

No suspicious correspondence.

Rez found ordinary tax fraud.

The depot manager looked deeply embarrassed.

Rez looked delighted.

“That is not our problem today.”

“Thank you.”

“Vesper's revenue office may feel differently.”

The man stopped smiling.

Ner searched the final storage hall.

Nothing.

Zee leaned against a crate.

“So they are innocent.”

Rez answered.

“Of this.”

Ner frowned.

“Maybe.”

Zee looked toward him.

Ner was staring at the floor.

“What?”

“Copper.”

A faint dust line ran beneath one crate.

Normal.

Except Ner followed it.

To a loading door.

Then outside.

Toward wagon tracks.

He crouched.

Gold moved across the earth.

One wheel rut responded.

Not with Golden Mana.

With residue from a preservation vessel.

Ner stood.

“Transport.”

Rez looked down the road.

“Where?”

The depot manager checked records.

“That wagon left yesterday.”

“For?”

He swallowed.

“Northern Council diplomatic stores.”

Zee's face changed.

There.

Not one person.

A route.

A mechanism.

Evidence.

Ner looked toward him.

“Do not smile like that.”

“I am not.”

“You are.”

Rez sighed.

“Both of you can argue while riding.”

The diplomatic wagon was half a day ahead.

They caught it before sunset.

No dramatic chase.

No army.

One wagon.

Four guards.

One clerk.

The guards surrendered immediately when Rez identified himself.

The clerk did not.

He ran.

Zee caught him in twelve seconds.

The man tripped across a dry field.

Zee landed in front of him.

The clerk stumbled backward.

“No.”

Zee tilted his head.

People had been saying that a lot lately.

“Why did you run?”

“I panicked.”

“Badly.”

The clerk reached for a knife.

Zee sighed.

“Worse.”

He caught the wrist.

Twisted.

Stopped before bone broke.

That was deliberate.

The man stared.

Zee stared back.

He could feel how easy it would be.

One movement.

One scream.

That dark satisfaction waited.

Interested.

Zee released the wrist.

“Do not make me regret that.”

The clerk dropped the knife.

Rez arrived moments later.

Ner behind him.

Ner opened the wagon.

Inside were six preservation jars.

Five empty.

One still containing a trace of Pure Golden Mana.

Ner went completely still.

No joke.

No smile.

Someone had bottled pieces of him.

Zee looked toward the clerk.

Anger became something colder.

“Who?”

The clerk shook his head.

“I only transport.”

Rez approached.

“Names.”

“I do not know.”

Ner touched one jar.

His face changed.

“Truth.”

Zee looked at him.

“You can tell?”

“The jar was sealed against handler contamination.”

Ner studied the clerk.

“He probably never touched the contents.”

That saved the man's wrist.

Maybe more.

Rez opened the paperwork.

No buyer name.

Only a council storage mark.

Then a second seal.

The same office Renn had used.

Not Renn personally.

His administrative network.

Rez exhaled.

“This is bigger than him.”

Aurelia, arriving with Caldrin and the guards, looked at the jars.

“Not necessarily bigger.”

Rez looked toward her.

“Wider.”

Better word.

One corrupt councilor could be removed.

A bureaucracy that had learned to profit from his methods was harder.

Zee looked toward Ner.

“What do you want to do?”

Ner stared at the jar.

For once he looked fifteen.

Not powerful.

Not rare.

Not Golden.

Fifteen.

Angry that someone had taken something of his without asking.

“Break them.”

Zee nodded.

Ner lifted the first jar.

Pure Golden Mana entered it.

The preserved residue responded.

Then folded inward.

Not released.

Not reused.

Destroyed.

One jar.

Then another.

Then another.

The final trace vanished.

Ner exhaled.

Gone.

No one else would use those pieces of him.

The clerk looked terrified.

Zee turned.

“Take him.”

Rez frowned.

“To Vesper?”

“No.”

Everyone looked at Zee.

He pointed toward the western coven guards approaching from the road.

“The breach happened in their territory.”

Rez's expression changed.

Approval.

Different moral code.

Not *Zee decides everything.*

Not *Vesper owns every consequence.*

Jurisdiction mattered when it protected people instead of shielding predators.

The clerk sagged with relief.

Zee noticed.

That irritated him.

“You look happy.”

The man froze.

Zee stepped closer.

“You helped move stolen magic.”

“I did not know.”

“Maybe.”

Zee's horns warmed.

He could hurt him.

Would enjoy it if the man proved complicit.

That was exactly why he did not decide yet.

“Let them find out.”

The clerk stared.

Zee turned away.

Ner watched him.

No smile.

Something quieter.

Proud, maybe.

Zee looked toward him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You have the face.”

Ner laughed.

“Your face.”

Zee smiled.

The western covens took custody of the clerk and wagon.

The grain agreement survived.

More than survived.

By nightfall, the covens agreed to sell directly to Vesper under emergency humanitarian terms, publicly separating the trade from Northern Council pressure.

That mattered.

Rez sent the agreement home under royal seal.

Vesper villages would eat.

The Northern Council had lost one weapon.

And Nereus Azrion had discovered something ugly about reputation.

Once the world knew your power was rare enough to matter, people did not always need to possess you.

Sometimes they only needed what you left behind.

That night Ner sat beside the road fire turning a tiny sphere of Golden Mana between his fingers.

Zee sat beside him.

Not touching.

Close.

“You okay?”

“No.”

Zee nodded.

Ner looked over.

“That is all?”

“You hate when people tell you what you should feel.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“True.”

“So be angry.”

“I am.”

“Good.”

Ner looked at the Gold in his hand.

“I used to think being the only one meant no one could take it.”

Zee understood that feeling too well.

“They did not take *you.*”

Ner looked at him.

Zee continued.

“They stole residue.”

“Used it badly.”

“Blamed you.”

“Yes.”

Zee's face hardened.

“Still not you.”

Ner was quiet.

Then:

“You are getting less terrible at this.”

Zee looked offended.

“I am excellent at this.”

“No.”

“Rude.”

Ner smiled.

Their shoulders touched.

This time neither moved.

Across the fire, Rez saw.

He looked toward Caldrin.

Caldrin followed his gaze.

Rez immediately whispered, “Do not.”

Caldrin smiled.

“I said nothing.”

Rez groaned.

Zee heard.

“Stop talking about us.”

Ner looked toward him.

“Us?”

Zee froze.

Rez covered his face.

Caldrin turned away to laugh.

Zee's horns heated.

Ner looked up at them.

Then back at him.

A slow smile appeared.

Zee stared into the fire.

“I hate all of you.”

Ner leaned his shoulder more firmly against Zee's.

“No, you don't.”

Zee did not answer.

Because that was becoming the problem.

He did not.

Not even close.

And somewhere far east, the Dragon Link stirred with Zareth's distant amusement as if he had somehow felt exactly enough to become unbearable about it later.
