# Chapter Forty-Six

## The Name Beneath the Seal

The first person to recognize the Northern Council storage mark was not Rez.

It was Seraphine Veyrath.

She took one look at the copied seal after the group returned to Vesper and said, “That office has changed names three times.”

Rez stopped halfway through removing his travel cloak.

“What?”

Seraphine leaned over the council table and turned the parchment toward herself.

“The symbol beneath Renn’s administrative mark.”

Ner moved closer.

Pure Golden Mana had already exposed the layered signatures twice on the journey home, but neither he nor Rez had recognized the oldest pattern buried beneath them.

Seraphine did.

Aurelia stood beside her sister.

“You have seen it?”

“Years ago.”

Theron looked up from his chair near the fire.

“Where?”

Seraphine’s expression hardened.

“In trade documents.”

The room quieted.

That answer carried history none of them liked.

Seraphine continued.

“Not Khell’s.”

Zee watched her face.

Good.

He did not want Khell resurrected into importance simply because an old seal existed.

“Before him?”

“Yes.”

Seraphine tapped the lower mark.

“House Veyrath used neutral northern routes generations ago. This symbol belonged to a regional trade registry.”

Rez frowned.

“So Renn’s office sits on older infrastructure.”

“Probably.”

“Probably?”

Seraphine looked toward Zee.

“Your mother trained all of you to be irritating about certainty.”

Zee smiled.

“Yes.”

Aurelia almost looked proud.

Rez unfolded three additional records.

“If the registry existed before Renn, then we may be dealing with corruption inside an existing trade structure rather than something he built.”

Lucien nodded.

“Better.”

Zee looked at him.

“How is that better?”

“Because institutions can be repaired.”

Theron muttered, “That is optimistic.”

Lucien looked toward him.

“I rule one.”

“Exactly.”

Seraphine laughed.

Rez ignored them.

“What did the registry control?”

“Storage authorizations.”

“Cross-border trade exemptions.”

“Emergency provisions during famine.”

“And custody declarations for restricted supernatural materials.”

Ner’s face darkened.

“Materials.”

Seraphine looked toward him.

“That was the old word.”

“It is a bad one.”

“Yes.”

Zee watched Ner’s hand close around the edge of the table.

A few days ago, jars containing preserved pieces of his Golden Mana had traveled under that same structure.

Something inside Zee turned cold.

Not rage yet.

Something cleaner.

Attention.

He had begun recognizing that too.

Anger shouted.

This feeling listened.

Rez spread the records into a line.

“So Renn did not create the office.”

“No.”

“He used it.”

“Yes.”

“And someone else inside it helped move preserved Golden Mana.”

Seraphine nodded.

“Most likely.”

Zee looked toward Ner.

“What do you want?”

Ner did not answer immediately.

Five years ago Zee might have answered for him.

Found the culprit.

Broken something.

Called that protection.

Now he waited.

Ner traced one finger over the seal.

“I want the registry opened.”

Rez frowned.

“Publicly?”

“Yes.”

“That could expose every restricted transaction attached to it.”

“That is the point.”

Lucien leaned back.

“Not all restricted transactions are criminal.”

Ner looked toward him.

“I know.”

“Some protect refugees.”

“I know.”

“Hidden bloodlines.”

“I know.”

“Political asylum.”

“I know.”

His voice sharpened.

“I am not asking you to dump every protected name into the street.”

Lucien held his gaze.

“Then what are you asking?”

Ner looked toward Rez.

“For the office to prove which records were accessed, altered, and moved under Renn’s authority.”

Rez understood.

“An audit.”

Zee frowned.

“That sounds boring.”

Rez smiled.

“It will ruin lives.”

Zee considered.

“Less boring.”

Ner looked at both of them.

“I want to know who used my Mana.”

Not who vaguely benefited.

Not which region disliked Vesper.

Who.

Specific.

Earned.

Lucien nodded.

“Then we request a joint audit.”

Rez looked toward him.

“They will refuse.”

“Probably.”

Ner almost smiled.

Zee noticed.

Everyone had apparently become infected by Aurelia.

Lucien continued.

“If they refuse, that becomes information.”

Zee leaned against the table.

“And if they accept?”

“Then Rez goes north.”

Rez looked up.

“Me?”

“You are Crown Prince.”

“Yes.”

“And this dispute now involves trade law, Vesper citizens, political sabotage, and stolen supernatural material.”

Rez sighed.

“I liked it better when people just attacked us in forests.”

Zee smiled.

“No, you didn’t.”

“No.”

Rez looked toward the seal.

“But forests are simpler.”

Theron raised his cup.

“To simple violence.”

Aurelia stared.

Theron slowly lowered it.

“Bad toast.”

Seraphine nodded.

“Terrible.”

---

The Northern Council accepted the audit.

That made everyone more suspicious.

Especially Zee.

“They said yes too quickly.”

Rez adjusted the clasp on his formal Vesper coat.

“You distrust people when they refuse.”

“Yes.”

“You distrust them when they cooperate.”

“Yes.”

“You understand that makes diplomacy difficult.”

“I do not do diplomacy.”

“You keep coming to diplomatic meetings.”

“To protect you.”

Rez looked at him.

“I have guards.”

“They are not me.”

“That was disgustingly affectionate.”

Zee shoved him.

Rez laughed.

They stood in Vesper’s eastern departure court while a small diplomatic party prepared to ride north.

Rez would lead.

Ner would accompany him as the injured party and magical specialist.

Two Vesper legal witches would attend.

Caldrin would go because apparently nobody could stop him.

Zee was not going.

Again.

He hated the pattern.

Again.

This time Lucien did not need to explain why.

The Northern Council had agreed to receive Crown Prince Rez Vesper.

Not Zee Darkheart.

Bringing Zee would turn an audit into a threat before anyone spoke.

Zee understood.

Understanding remained irritating.

Ner approached wearing formal black and deep gold.

Zee looked.

Then looked away.

Too late.

Rez saw.

Of course.

Zee immediately said, “No.”

Rez smiled.

“I have said nothing.”

Ner stopped in front of them.

“What is happening?”

“Nothing,” Zee said.

Rez answered, “Everything.”

Zee glared.

Ner looked between them.

Then at Zee.

A faint smile appeared.

Worse.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are all terrible.”

Ner adjusted one glove.

He no longer wore them to hide his Mana regularly.

Today the gloves were ceremonial.

Zee noticed that too.

Annoying.

Ner looked toward the horses.

“We will probably be gone four days.”

Zee frowned.

“Probably?”

“Maybe five.”

“No.”

Rez stared.

“You do know you are not in charge of distance.”

“I should be.”

“That would be horrifying.”

Ner stepped closer.

“You will survive.”

Zee crossed his arms.

“Barely.”

Ner’s smile softened.

There.

That look again.

Not exactly friendship anymore.

Not only.

Zee hated not understanding things about himself almost as much as he hated not understanding his powers.

Ner touched his wrist.

Brief.

Simple.

“We will come back.”

Zee looked at the hand.

Then at him.

“Good.”

Rez made a very quiet choking sound.

Zee turned.

“I swear—”

Rez raised both hands.

“Cough.”

“You are bad at lying.”

“I learned from you.”

Ner laughed.

Then mounted.

Rez followed.

Caldrin paused beside Zee.

“Should I supervise them?”

Zee looked at him.

“Yes.”

Caldrin smiled.

“I was asking Rez.”

Rez shouted from horseback, “No!”

Caldrin mounted anyway.

The party left.

Zee watched until they passed beyond the outer road.

Then kept watching.

Aurelia appeared beside him.

“You are doing better.”

“No.”

“You did not follow.”

“That is the lowest possible standard.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her.

She smiled.

Zee sighed.

Then something huge landed behind them.

The ground shook.

Zareth.

Back from Drakonis.

Zee turned.

The Dragon Prince folded his wings and lowered his head.

The Link opened.

Drakonis council.

Border dispute.

His mother furious at three elder Dragons.

A broken ceremonial table.

Zee blinked.

“You broke it?”

Zareth sent immediate denial.

Then an image of another Dragon’s tail striking the table.

Zee laughed.

“Fine.”

The Link shifted.

Ner absent.

Rez absent.

Question.

“They went north.”

Zareth stared.

Then sent Zee an image of himself flying after them.

Zee smiled.

“No.”

The Dragon Prince looked offended.

“They need to do this.”

Zareth sent suspicion.

Zee nodded.

“I know.”

Then another image came.

Zee.

Bored.

Dangerous.

Zee narrowed his eyes.

“I am not that bad alone.”

Aurelia coughed.

Zee turned.

“You too?”

She walked away smiling.

---

By the second day, Zee stopped pretending he was not restless.

He trained.

Then stopped before training became punishment.

He spent an hour with Theron learning an old Veyrath breathing technique meant to regulate Dragon heat during partial surges.

Theron warned him it might not work properly because Zee’s Dragon nature did not exist alone.

Zee appreciated the honesty.

It helped anyway.

Crimson Dragon energy no longer jumped through his horns every time irritation sharpened.

It gathered lower.

More controlled.

More concentrated.

Seraphine watched from the courtyard wall.

“You look constipated.”

Zee opened one eye.

Theron sighed.

“Please leave.”

“I am helping.”

“You are not.”

Zee laughed and lost the breathing rhythm completely.

Theron glared at his sister.

“See?”

Seraphine smiled.

“Much better.”

Later Zee helped Aurelia review letters concerning Veyrath survivors scattered through three kingdoms.

Not lost siblings.

Not another rescue.

Just people deciding whether to use their family name publicly now that Veyrath survival was no longer rumor.

One wanted recognition.

One wanted anonymity.

Another wanted permission to visit Vesper without joining anything.

Aurelia granted all three wishes.

Zee watched.

“You are not rebuilding House Veyrath.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

“Not the way it was.”

“Theron wants to.”

“Theron wants a banner.”

From the next room:

“I heard that.”

Aurelia continued.

“Seraphine wants everyone left alone.”

“I heard that too,” Seraphine called.

Zee smiled.

“And you?”

Aurelia looked toward the letters.

“I want Veyrath to mean people have somewhere to return if they choose.”

Not command.

Not ownership.

Choice.

Zee understood why that word kept appearing in his life now.

At fifteen, strength was no longer the difficult part.

Choice was.

---

The audit turned violent on the third day.

Not because Rez attacked anyone.

Because someone tried burning the registry.

The message reached Vesper at dusk.

Zee read it once.

Then looked toward Zareth.

The Link had already sharpened.

Fire.

North.

Ner.

Rez.

Danger.

This time Zee did not ask permission.

Aurelia saw his face.

“Go.”

He stopped.

“What?”

“They asked for help.”

She handed him the second message.

Rez’s seal.

Three words beneath the emergency mark.

**Bring Zee now.**

Zee smiled.

Not because people were in danger.

Because this time he was needed.

Zareth spread his wings.

Zee looked toward the Dragon.

No riding.

Never.

“I will meet you there.”

The Link answered with challenge.

Race.

Zee grinned.

“You are going to lose.”

Zareth launched.

Zee ran for the northern gate.

The audit had finally found the person willing to burn evidence rather than let the truth survive.

And Zee Darkheart was very interested in meeting them.

# Chapter Forty-Seven

## Burn the Records

The Northern Trade Registry was already on fire when Zee arrived.

Not metaphorically.

Actual fire.

Three floors of old stone and timber burned beneath a night sky stained orange.

Witches flooded the courtyard.

Some fought the flames.

Others fought each other.

That was less helpful.

Zee hit the outer wall at full speed, ran three steps vertically with Crimson Mana beneath his boots, caught the balcony edge, and pulled himself over.

A registry guard stared.

“Darkheart?”

Zee kept moving.

“Where is Rez?”

“Inside!”

“Ner?”

“Inside!”

“Of course.”

He ran.

Behind him, a Dragon roar shook the district.

Zareth had arrived.

People screamed.

Zee reached through the Link.

No fire.

A burst of offended restraint returned.

Good.

He entered smoke.

---

Rez had commandeered the central records hall.

That was the only reason half the building still existed.

Blue-White Mana covered the support beams in controlled frost, slowing combustion without freezing the stone hard enough to fracture it.

At fifteen Rez no longer looked like a boy pretending to command adults.

He pointed.

People moved.

“East shelves out first!”

Two registry witches obeyed.

“Do not carry sealed asylum ledgers into the public courtyard!”

A clerk changed direction.

“Where?”

“Inner stone annex!”

“Your Highness, that annex is full.”

“Then make room!”

Zee found him halfway up the stairs.

Rez looked over.

Relief flashed across his face.

Then vanished under work.

“You took forever.”

“I beat Zareth.”

A roar hit the roof.

Rez looked upward.

“No, you didn’t.”

Zee smiled.

“Where is Ner?”

“Lower archive.”

Zee stopped smiling.

“Why?”

“Because the fire began there.”

“Who is with him?”

“Caldrin.”

“Good.”

Rez grabbed Zee’s sleeve before he moved.

“Listen.”

Zee looked at him.

“This is not random.”

“I assumed.”

“Someone activated internal fire wards backward.”

“Meaning?”

“They turned suppression wards into accelerants.”

Zee’s expression hardened.

“Who can do that?”

“Senior registry access.”

“Names?”

“Five.”

“Where are they?”

Rez looked toward the burning lower level.

“Three accounted for.”

“Fourth fled.”

“Fifth is missing.”

Zee understood.

“Ner thinks one is below.”

“Yes.”

Rez released him.

“Do not destroy the archive.”

Zee frowned.

“That feels specifically directed at me.”

“It is.”

“Rude.”

“Accurate.”

Zee ran.

---

The lower archive was worse.

No open flames.

Heat.

Smoke.

Magical fire moving behind walls.

Ner stood inside a ring of Pure Golden Mana with both hands raised.

The entire corridor around him glowed.

Not because his power was opening anything.

Because he was holding six magical boundaries apart at once.

Caldrin stood beside a collapsed clerk.

Alive.

Barely conscious.

Zee entered.

Ner did not look back.

“You came.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Zee stopped beside him.

“What do you need?”

That question made Ner glance over.

Only for a heartbeat.

Then back to the wards.

“Three anchor rooms.”

“Which one?”

“All.”

Zee frowned.

“I cannot be in three places.”

Ner’s mouth twitched.

“Disappointing.”

“Still joking?”

“Barely.”

Golden Mana trembled.

Zee saw the strain.

“What happens if you let go?”

“The fire crosses the archive boundaries.”

“And?”

“Everything burns.”

Zee looked around.

Records.

Protected asylum identities.

Trade histories.

Criminal ledgers.

Veyrath routes.

Witch coven treaties.

Centuries of things some people needed hidden and others needed exposed.

A mess.

“What do I do?”

Ner nodded toward the far passage.

“Find the person feeding it.”

“Heartbeat?”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“Half the building is full of terrified people.”

Fair.

Zee closed his eyes.

Listened.

Heartbeats everywhere.

Fast.

Uneven.

Smoke coughs.

Running.

Then one pattern stood out.

Slow.

Too slow.

Someone calm in a burning archive.

Zee opened his eyes.

“Found one.”

Caldrin looked toward him.

“Could be unconscious.”

“Walking.”

“Better.”

Zee ran.

---

Senior Registrar Elian Voss was destroying files by hand.

Not escaping.

Burning specific pages.

Zee stopped in the doorway.

Voss looked up.

Older man.

Gray hair.

Northern robes.

No armor.

No weapon.

One hand glowing with dull green Witch Mana.

A ledger burned between his fingers.

He dropped it.

Zee crossed the room and crushed the flame beneath his boot.

Voss stared.

“You.”

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

“You should not be here.”

Zee looked around.

“No.”

He smiled faintly.

“I definitely should.”

Voss cast.

Zee moved aside.

Green fire struck a shelf.

Zee swore.

“Rez specifically told me not to let you do that.”

Voss attacked again.

Zee closed distance.

One hand caught the wrist.

He twisted.

Not breaking.

Yet.

“Stop.”

Voss laughed.

“You think this is about children.”

Zee’s expression hardened.

“What?”

“You think Renn was the rot.”

“No.”

That surprised him.

Zee continued.

“I think Renn was one man.”

Voss’s eyes narrowed.

Good.

Zee was learning.

Voss tried pulling away.

Zee held him.

“What are you burning?”

“Things that should have remained buried.”

“Like Ner’s stolen Mana?”

Voss’s face changed.

There.

Zee’s horns warmed.

Anger.

Controlled.

“Why?”

Voss smiled.

“Because rare power belongs in hands capable of using it properly.”

Zee’s grip tightened.

“Wrong answer.”

Voss winced.

“You children stumble into forces kingdoms spent centuries controlling.”

“Gold.”

“Dragon blood.”

“Mixed blood.”

“Ancient wards.”

“You break structures because nobody taught you why they exist.”

Zee leaned closer.

“Sometimes they exist because people like you built them.”

Voss laughed.

“And sometimes monsters need boundaries.”

There it was.

Monster.

Old word.

Less power over Zee now.

Not none.

Voss continued.

“You think the world fears you because it is ignorant?”

“No.”

Zee’s answer came easily.

“Sometimes I am frightening.”

Voss stopped.

Zee smiled without humor.

“But you used kidnapped children to protect grain routes.”

“I did not.”

“Renn did.”

“Yes.”

“And you helped cover him.”

Silence.

“You stole Ner’s Mana.”

“It was residue.”

“It was his.”

“Magic has no owner once released.”

That made Zee’s expression change.

He thought of blood brokers.

Khell.

Morcant.

People reducing living parts of others into commodities.

Something inside him darkened.

Voss saw.

He smiled.

“Go on.”

Zee frowned.

“What?”

“Hurt me.”

The invitation was almost eager.

“You want to.”

Zee hated that Voss was right.

The man’s wrist rested inside his grip.

One turn.

One crack.

Easy.

Voss continued.

“Everyone knows what you are becoming.”

Zee’s Dragon energy warmed beneath his scales.

“Do they?”

“The hunted child grew teeth.”

Zee’s fangs showed.

“He always had teeth.”

Voss laughed.

Then whispered:

“Prove them right.”

Zee almost did.

That was the danger.

Not because Voss manipulated him well.

Because Zee wanted an excuse.

He could break him.

Hear the scream.

Feel that satisfaction Renn had given him.

Maybe more.

This man had stolen from Ner.

Helped bury crimes.

Was currently burning evidence that might protect people.

Zee’s hand tightened.

Then Ner’s words returned.

*If the only reason you stop is because one of us says your name, what happens when we are not there?*

Ner was not here.

Aurelia was not here.

Rez was upstairs.

Zareth was outside.

No one said his name.

Zee let go.

Voss stumbled backward.

Confusion crossed his face.

Zee looked toward the burning ledger.

“Put your hands on the wall.”

Voss stared.

“What?”

“You heard me.”

“You think restraint makes you better?”

“No.”

Zee stepped closer.

“I think I need you alive.”

That answer mattered more.

Voss tried casting again.

This time Zee hit him.

One strike.

Enough to drop him.

No pleasure.

Not because it was painless.

Because Zee chose the amount before he moved.

Voss hit the floor conscious.

Zee kicked his wand away.

“Hands.”

Voss laughed through blood.

“You are afraid of yourself.”

Zee looked at him.

“Yes.”

The honesty shut him up.

Zee bound his wrists with the man’s own belt.

Then grabbed the rescued ledgers.

“Good.”

Voss stared.

Zee smiled faintly.

“Fear can be useful.”

---

The internal fire wards shut down when Voss’s access seal was removed.

Ner did that personally.

He emerged from the lower archive pale, furious, and coated in soot.

Zee met him in the courtyard.

Ner looked toward Voss under guard.

“You found him.”

“Yes.”

“You hurt him?”

“A little.”

Ner stared.

Zee shrugged.

“He cast twice.”

“That was not my question.”

Zee looked at him.

“I wanted to.”

Ner waited.

Zee continued.

“I did not do more.”

Something in Ner's face softened.

“Without us there?”

“Yes.”

Ner smiled.

Small.

Real.

“Good.”

Zee hated how much that smile affected him.

His horns warmed.

Ner looked up.

Zee immediately said, “Different reason.”

Ner’s smile widened.

“Oh?”

Zee froze.

Caldrin walked past carrying three rescued ledgers.

“Terrible time to flirt.”

Zee’s head snapped around.

“We are not—”

Ner laughed.

Actually laughed.

Zee stared at him.

That made it worse.

Rez appeared from the building.

“What did I miss?”

“Nothing,” Zee said.

Caldrin answered, “Everything.”

Zee closed his eyes.

Zareth landed in the street beyond the courtyard.

The Link instantly flooded Zee with amused curiosity.

“No.”

The Dragon had not even done anything yet.

That did not matter.

He would.

---

By dawn the registry fire was contained.

One archive wing was destroyed.

Two damaged.

Most protected asylum records survived.

The stolen Golden Mana records survived too.

So did payment logs connecting Renn’s administrative office to preservation vessels, false grain disruptions, mercenary contracts, and three other officials.

Not an entire kingdom.

Not every Northern Council member.

Three.

Specific.

Important.

The Council suspended them before noon.

Not from morality.

From self-preservation.

Rez knew that.

He accepted it anyway.

Political consequences rarely required pure hearts.

The grain compact reopened under emergency review.

Vesper kept its alternate western routes.

That was permanent too.

Rez had no intention of allowing one neighboring council to control Vesper food supply so completely again.

He stood on the registry steps after sunrise while northern officials argued around him.

Fifteen.

Tired.

Soot on one sleeve.

Absolutely in his element.

Zee approached.

“You enjoy this.”

Rez looked over.

“What?”

“Watching politicians realize they lost.”

Rez smiled.

“Maybe.”

Zee nodded.

“Good.”

Rez laughed.

“Your morality is deteriorating.”

“Probably.”

Then Rez became serious.

“You did well.”

Zee looked toward Voss being transported under guard.

“I almost didn’t.”

“But you did.”

“He wanted me to hurt him.”

“People will.”

Zee looked over.

Rez continued.

“They will provoke you because they fear you.”

“Or because they want proof.”

“Exactly.”

Zee thought about Victor.

Again.

Fear becoming judgment.

Judgment becoming violence.

He understood the trap better now.

That did not mean he would always avoid it.

He was fifteen.

Angry.

Powerful.

And sometimes violence felt very, very good.

That truth remained.

But another truth existed beside it now.

He could choose how much.

Sometimes.

That was enough progress for one night.

Ner descended the steps behind them.

Zee looked automatically.

Rez saw.

Zee saw Rez seeing.

“Do not.”

Rez smiled.

“I am leaving.”

“Good.”

Rez walked away.

Too easy.

Zee narrowed his eyes.

He turned back toward Ner.

Ner stopped beside him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You have the face.”

“Everyone needs new material.”

Ner looked toward the rising sun.

Then toward Zee.

“You stayed.”

Zee frowned.

“Where?”

“With Voss.”

“You could have killed him.”

“Yes.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

Ner studied him.

Zee suddenly became very aware of how close they were again.

“I remembered what you said.”

Ner’s expression changed.

“What part?”

“The part about figuring it out when none of you are there.”

A quiet moment passed.

Ner smiled.

“I am glad.”

Zee looked at him.

Too long.

Again.

This time Ner looked too long too.

Neither pretended otherwise.

No confession.

No grand declaration.

Just something changing.

Slowly.

Dangerously.

Fifteen.

Ner looked away first.

“Come on.”

“Where?”

“Food.”

Zee smiled.

“Finally, something important.”

They started down the steps together.

Behind them the Northern Trade Registry still smoked.

Ahead, Rez was already arguing with a council secretary.

Zareth waited beyond the walls.

Aurelia would want the full truth when they returned.

And somewhere inside Zee Darkheart, the darker thing growing beside his mercy had learned its first real boundary.

Not every monster needed to die.

Some needed to live long enough to answer for what they had done.

And Zee was beginning to discover that restraint could be its own kind of cruelty.

He was not sure whether that realization made him better.

He was very sure he liked it.

# Chapter Forty-Eight

## The Things Kings Cannot Punch

Vesper smelled like bread again.

Zee noticed before the western gates fully opened.

Warm grain.

Yeast.

Smoke from the lower bakeries.

Something sweet from the market district.

For almost two weeks the city had smelled different.

Less food.

More rationing.

More boiled roots.

More people pretending reduced meals did not matter because House Vesper needed them to believe everything remained under control.

Now wagons rolled through three entrances carrying grain from the western covens.

Children followed them.

Adults tried pretending they were not doing the same.

Rez saw.

His expression changed.

Only slightly.

Pride looked strange on him when it had nothing to do with winning a sword fight.

Zee walked beside him.

“You did that.”

Rez looked over.

“We did.”

“No.”

Zee nodded toward the grain wagons.

“That part was you.”

Rez frowned.

“Ner found the western supply.”

“Ner found the lie.”

“You changed the routes.”

“Lucien approved them.”

“You decided first.”

Rez looked toward the city again.

Zee smiled.

“Just accept it.”

“I am accepting it.”

“You look uncomfortable.”

“I am uncomfortable because you are being sincere.”

Zee shoved him.

Rez laughed.

Ner walked several steps ahead carrying one of the recovered registry cases beneath his arm.

Zee’s eyes went toward him automatically.

Again.

This was becoming ridiculous.

Ner had soot still caught near one temple.

His coat had been cleaned badly after the registry fire.

One sleeve had a burn near the cuff.

He was arguing with Caldrin about whether Voss’s preservation jars should be destroyed immediately or kept as evidence until the Northern Council finished internal review.

Ner wanted them destroyed.

Caldrin wanted photographs, magical impressions, and documentation first.

They had been arguing for thirty minutes.

Neither had repeated an argument.

Zee had stopped understanding half of it after minute eleven.

He kept listening anyway.

Ner glanced back.

Caught Zee looking.

Again.

This time Zee did not turn away immediately.

That felt like progress.

Then Ner smiled.

Zee looked forward.

Progress ruined.

Rez whispered, “Embarrassing.”

Zee did not even bother turning.

“I will throw you into the canal.”

“You threaten that too often.”

“One day I will mean it.”

“You always mean it.”

Zareth landed beyond the palace courtyard.

His arrival scattered three pigeons, six guards, and one extremely offended horse.

Teal-and-Gold Mana rolled beneath enormous crimson wings before settling.

The Dragon Link struck Zee with immediate warmth.

Home.

Food.

Then an image of the northern registry on fire.

Zee frowned.

“You already know?”

Zareth lowered his head.

The Link delivered Drakonis couriers.

Rumor.

Northern traders.

A picture of Zee standing inside flames looking dramatic.

Zee stared.

“That did not happen.”

Ner walked up behind him.

“What?”

“Apparently someone in Drakonis says I walked through the entire burning registry while carrying six people.”

Rez smiled.

“Only six?”

Zee looked toward him.

“Do not encourage this.”

Zareth sent another image.

Zee breathing fire.

“No.”

Ner laughed.

“You should let that one spread.”

“I cannot breathe Dragonfire.”

“Yet.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner’s smile faded slightly.

Not because he was worried.

Because both of them knew the word mattered.

Yet.

Five years of Dragon development had given Zee more.

Horns.

Scales.

Durability.

Crimson Dragon energy.

Pressure beneath the shoulder blades.

Partial manifestations during extreme emotion.

But not completion.

Not wings.

Not full transformation.

Not the fourth awakening.

Zee had learned not to force that door.

Mostly.

Zareth nudged him with his snout.

The Link shifted.

Drakonis.

Problem.

Zee frowned.

“What problem?”

A richer impression followed.

Dragon council.

Merchants.

Vesper grain routes.

Northern complaints.

A map.

Three territories.

Rez’s attention sharpened.

“What?”

Zee looked toward him.

“Drakonis has traders demanding the northern suspension be punished.”

Rez sighed.

“I thought reopening the compact ended that.”

Zareth sent disagreement.

Zee translated.

“Apparently some Dragon merchants lost money when northern trade diverted.”

Rez rubbed his face.

“Of course they did.”

Ner looked toward Zareth.

“Do they want compensation?”

An image.

Gold.

A lot of it.

Rez groaned.

“Of course they do.”

Zee smiled.

“Kings cannot punch trade.”

Rez looked at him.

“That may be the wisest thing you have ever said.”

“I did not say it was fair.”

Aurelia’s voice came from behind them.

“You have been home less than three minutes.”

They turned.

She stood at the top of the palace stairs.

Theron beside her.

Seraphine leaned against one column.

Zee smiled immediately.

Aurelia noticed.

Her expression softened.

He climbed the stairs.

At fifteen he no longer ran into her arms every time he returned from a mission.

Usually.

Today he reached her and stopped.

Aurelia opened one arm.

Zee leaned into her.

No embarrassment.

No apology.

He had spent two days around politicians, burning archives, stolen Mana, and people trying to make moral certainty sound simple.

He wanted his mother.

So he took the comfort.

Aurelia kissed his temple beside one horn.

“You smell like smoke.”

“Registry.”

“I heard.”

“You always hear.”

“I am Queen.”

“That is not magic.”

“Sometimes it feels like it.”

Seraphine looked toward Zee.

“Did you kill anyone?”

Aurelia turned.

“Seraphine.”

“What?”

Zee answered.

“No.”

Seraphine nodded.

“Good.”

Then added:

“Disappointing.”

Theron laughed.

Aurelia stared at both siblings.

Zee smiled against her shoulder.

Family.

---

The first surprise arrived during dinner.

King Lucien did not attend.

That happened occasionally.

Not often.

Rez noticed before anyone else sat down.

“Where is he?”

A servant answered carefully.

“Private council, Your Highness.”

“With whom?”

The servant hesitated.

Rez looked up.

That was enough.

“With whom?”

“Representatives from House Darkheart.”

The room changed.

Zee stopped reaching for his cup.

Aurelia became completely still.

Theron’s expression hardened.

Seraphine stopped smiling.

Rez stood.

“When did they arrive?”

“An hour ago.”

“Why was I not informed?”

“The King ordered privacy.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

Zee was already standing.

Aurelia spoke.

“Sit.”

He looked at her.

“Victor sent people.”

“Yes.”

“I am not sitting.”

“You are not storming Lucien’s council chamber either.”

“I was not going to storm.”

Seraphine muttered, “He was going to storm.”

Theron nodded.

“Definitely.”

Zee glared.

Aurelia remained calm.

“Lucien will tell us when he is ready.”

Zee’s horns warmed.

Anger.

Fear.

Both.

He named them.

That helped nothing.

“Why now?”

No one knew.

That was worse.

House Darkheart had not disappeared from Zee’s life over the last five years.

Victor still ruled.

Still controlled what portions of the House could publicly say about his son.

Still rejected every attempt to place Zee near Darkheart succession rituals.

Still refused to acknowledge Zee’s expanding Dragon manifestations as anything but “corruption.”

He had not tried to kill Zee again.

Never.

That one act remained singular.

But fear had matured into policy.

Zee was permitted in Darkheart territory only under negotiated terms.

Aurelia’s authority remained contested whenever Victor wanted it contested.

Certain Darkheart nobles quietly supported Zee.

Others called him curse when they thought Vesper ears were absent.

Victor had built distance and called it order.

Zee had responded by living anyway.

But Victor rarely sent formal representatives to Vesper.

Not without reason.

Rez pushed his chair back in.

“I am going to my father.”

Aurelia nodded.

Different.

Rez belonged in that conversation.

Zee did not.

Not yet.

He hated knowing the difference.

Rez looked toward him.

“I will come back.”

Zee frowned.

“I did not ask.”

“You had the face.”

“Everyone needs to stop saying that.”

Rez left.

Ner sat beside Zee.

Not across.

Beside.

That did not help Zee think.

“Do you want to go after him?”

“Yes.”

“Will you?”

“No.”

Ner looked slightly surprised.

Zee frowned.

“Stop looking like that.”

“You are getting better.”

“I hate when people say that.”

“Why?”

“Because then I have to keep doing it.”

Ner smiled.

Zee looked down at his hands.

Crimson scales had appeared farther across his knuckles.

He breathed.

Named the feeling.

Waited.

They receded slightly.

Theron watched.

“You learned my breathing.”

“Some of it.”

“Badly.”

Zee looked toward him.

“You said I was improving.”

“I lied.”

Aurelia raised one eyebrow.

Theron corrected himself.

“I encouraged.”

Seraphine laughed.

The tension eased.

Then the dining room door opened.

Rez returned.

His face told them before he spoke.

Something had changed.

Zee stood.

“What?”

Rez looked toward Aurelia.

Then Zee.

“Victor issued a formal claim.”

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“For what?”

Rez answered.

“For Zee.”

Silence.

Not his throne.

Not land.

Not blood recognition.

Zee.

Rez placed a sealed document on the table.

“King Victor asserts that as Zee’s father, King of House Darkheart, and ruler of the kingdom where Zee was born, he retains sovereign authority over Zee until adulthood.”

Zee stared.

Ner’s face hardened.

Theron stood.

Seraphine said a word Aurelia usually disliked hearing at dinner.

Aurelia ignored it.

Rez continued.

“He is demanding Zee return to Castle Darkheart.”

“No,” Aurelia said.

Immediate.

Absolute.

Zee looked toward her.

Then the document.

“Why?”

Rez’s expression darkened.

“Because your reputation has become politically dangerous.”

Zee laughed once.

No humor.

“Now?”

“He cites the northern crisis.”

“The Veyrath resurgence.”

“Your intervention in foreign territory.”

“Reports of increasingly unstable Dragon manifestations.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

“I am more controlled than I have ever been.”

“I know.”

“What else?”

Rez hesitated.

Zee saw.

“What?”

“Victor claims House Darkheart has a right to determine whether you remain heir.”

That hit differently.

Zee had never begged for Darkheart.

But the House was his.

Birth.

Blood.

Mother.

History.

Victor deciding whether Zee belonged to it felt like someone trying to cut a piece from him and call that law.

Theron looked toward Aurelia.

“He cannot compel Vesper.”

“No.”

Rez answered.

“But he can create a succession dispute.”

Aurelia picked up the document.

Read.

Her face became colder with every line.

“He wants control.”

Zee looked at her.

Not protection.

Control.

Familiar.

The old fear wearing legal clothing.

Zee’s Crimson Mana flickered.

The candles bent.

Ner touched his wrist.

Not stopping him.

Grounding.

Zee looked down at the contact.

Then at Ner.

The Mana settled.

Aurelia saw.

She folded the document.

“Lucien’s answer?”

Rez smiled faintly.

“He told the envoys Zee is not property.”

Zee looked up.

Good.

Rez continued.

“They replied that House Darkheart considers this an internal matter.”

Seraphine laughed without humor.

“Vesper has sheltered him for most of his life.”

Theron’s scales appeared faintly along one wrist.

“They lost the right to call him internal when Victor put a blade through him.”

Aurelia’s face changed.

Zee looked away.

That old wound never needed repeating.

Rez continued.

“There is one problem.”

Zee sighed.

“There is always one.”

“Victor did not ask Vesper to send you by force.”

“Then what?”

“He invoked a royal challenge of guardianship.”

Aurelia stared.

Old Witch Kingdom law.

Ancient.

Ugly.

Zee knew enough to recognize the phrase.

“If House Darkheart proves Vesper is unlawfully preventing access to its heir, Victor can bring the matter before the Witch Crowns.”

Ner frowned.

“And they decide?”

Rez nodded.

“Potentially.”

Zee looked toward Aurelia.

“What do you want?”

Her answer was immediate.

“You do not go.”

Zee nodded.

Then:

“What do I want?”

Aurelia stopped.

Important difference.

The table went silent.

Zee looked toward the document.

For fifteen years Victor had feared him from a distance.

Controlled him from a distance.

Called him monster through walls and law and title.

Zee had spent childhood running from people who came to decide his life.

At fifteen, he could choose whether to keep running.

“I want to answer him.”

Aurelia’s face tightened.

“Zee.”

“Not alone.”

“Not by fighting.”

Her shoulders eased a fraction.

Zee continued.

“I want to stand in front of him.”

That scared her more.

He saw.

“Mother.”

“You do not owe Victor confrontation.”

“I know.”

“You do not owe House Darkheart proof.”

“I know.”

“You do not have to return simply because he finally found a law that sounds respectable.”

“I know.”

Zee took the document from her hand.

Then looked at the royal seal.

“But he keeps deciding what I am from rooms I am not in.”

His crimson eyes hardened.

“I am tired of that.”

Ner watched him.

Rez too.

Aurelia looked at the boy she once carried away from Darkheart.

Except he was not that child anymore.

Not helpless.

Not safe.

Not hers to command simply because fear told her danger was coming.

That lesson was harder for mothers.

“I come with you,” she said.

Zee smiled faintly.

“I assumed.”

Theron stood.

“So do I.”

“No,” Aurelia and Zee said together.

Theron looked offended.

Seraphine smiled.

“Beautiful.”

Theron pointed at her.

“You are staying too.”

“I did not volunteer.”

“Good.”

Rez looked toward Lucien’s empty seat.

“I will represent Vesper.”

Zee frowned.

“You have a kingdom crisis.”

“I have a Crown Prince problem.”

“You are the Crown Prince.”

“Exactly.”

Ner stood.

“I am coming.”

Zee turned.

“No.”

Ner stared.

“What?”

Zee realized how that sounded.

He corrected himself.

“You do not have to.”

Ner’s expression softened.

“I know.”

Then:

“I am coming.”

Their eyes held.

Zee smiled.

“Fine.”

Above the palace, Zareth roared.

Everyone looked toward the ceiling.

The Dragon Link flooded Zee.

Darkheart.

Castle.

Zee.

Danger.

Then unmistakable resolve.

Zee laughed.

“Apparently Zareth is coming too.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

Rez smiled.

“Of course.”

The childhood Zee had been dragged away from Castle Darkheart because adults knew he could not survive its fear alone.

At fifteen, he was choosing to return.

Not to reclaim a throne.

Not to kill Victor.

Not to prove the prophecy right.

To make one thing clear.

Victor Darkheart could fear his son.

He could reject him.

He could hate what he had become.

But he would no longer decide who Zee was without Zee standing there to answer.

And for once, the hardest fight waiting for Zee Darkheart might be the one he could not solve with his hands.

# Chapter Forty-Nine

## The Son Who Came Back

Castle Darkheart had not changed.

Zee had.

That became obvious before the gates opened.

The towers were still black stone.

The old Witch sigils still burned along the outer walls.

House banners still hung from spear-pointed battlements.

The valley below still carried the same wind.

The same smell.

Pine.

Cold iron.

Old magic.

Memory.

Zee stood at the end of the approach road with Aurelia beside him.

Rez slightly behind.

Ner on Zee’s other side.

Zareth remained above the valley, too large to land inside the outer court without turning diplomacy into architecture damage.

The Dragon Link held steady.

Watchful.

Not frightened.

Zee felt his mother’s tension anyway.

He looked over.

Aurelia’s face remained composed.

Queen.

Dragon-Witch.

Veyrath.

Darkheart by marriage and history.

But Zee knew her heartbeat.

Faster.

He touched her hand.

Aurelia looked down.

“I am fine.”

Zee raised an eyebrow.

She sighed.

“Do not.”

“You taught me.”

“That was a mistake.”

He smiled.

Then the gates opened.

Darkheart soldiers waited inside.

Some Zee recognized.

Older.

Scarred.

Different uniforms.

Five years.

Life had continued here too.

One soldier saw Zee.

His face changed.

Recognition.

Fear.

Then something almost like awe.

Zee ignored all three.

The captain approached.

He bowed first to Aurelia.

“Your Majesty.”

Then Rez.

“Crown Prince Vesper.”

Ner received a respectful nod.

Then the captain looked toward Zee.

Longer.

“Prince Darkheart.”

Zee’s expression sharpened.

Prince.

Not abomination.

Not curse.

Interesting.

“Captain.”

The man hesitated.

“You have grown.”

Zee almost laughed.

“So have you.”

The captain blinked.

Aurelia hid a smile.

They entered.

No attack.

No assassins.

No blades.

That made Zee more alert, not less.

Darkheart servants watched from halls.

Witches paused near stairways.

Whispers followed.

Zee heard all of them.

Tribrid.

Dragon horns.

Veyrath.

Victor’s son.

Monster.

Prince.

He could have listened harder.

Instead he chose one sound.

Ner’s footsteps.

Steady beside him.

That helped.

Rez noticed the technique.

Said nothing.

They reached the throne hall.

King Victor Darkheart waited.

Five years had changed him too.

More gray near the temples.

Harder face.

Heavier crown.

Still the same eyes Zee remembered from nightmares he rarely had anymore.

Victor sat beneath the Darkheart crest.

No weapon visible.

Good.

Zee stopped at the center of the chamber.

Aurelia remained beside him.

Victor’s gaze went to her first.

“Aurelia.”

“Victor.”

No warmth.

No old love offered for public consumption.

Then Victor looked at Zee.

The hall became quiet enough that Zee heard candles.

For several seconds neither spoke.

Victor stared at the horns.

The scales.

The Crimson eyes.

The boy he had once killed.

The son who had become something death could never take again.

Fear entered Victor’s face.

Older now.

More disciplined.

Still fear.

Zee saw.

For years he had imagined this moment differently.

Sometimes he screamed.

Sometimes Victor begged.

Sometimes Zee hurt him.

Sometimes he laughed.

Reality was quieter.

Victor finally said:

“You came.”

Zee looked around.

“You asked.”

“I demanded.”

Zee’s mouth twitched.

“There he is.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

Not now.

Zee controlled the smile.

Victor’s gaze moved toward Rez.

“Vesper.”

Rez nodded.

“Darkheart.”

Then Ner.

Victor’s eyes lingered on the Pure Golden Mana signature beneath his skin.

“Azrion.”

“Nereus.”

Zee immediately looked toward Ner.

Ner did not look back.

Victor noticed.

Zee hated that.

Then Victor looked upward as a distant Dragon roar shook the valley.

His face tightened.

“Drakonis.”

Zee smiled.

“Zareth says hello.”

That was not exactly what the Link said.

The actual impression involved suspicion, teeth, and the castle roof.

Close enough.

Victor’s hands tightened against the throne.

“You bring foreign princes into a House matter.”

Rez answered before Zee.

“I am here because Vesper is named in your claim.”

Victor’s eyes moved toward him.

“You are fifteen.”

Rez’s expression did not change.

“Yes.”

Nothing else.

No argument.

No explanation.

Victor waited.

Rez did not give him more.

Good.

Victor looked toward Zee.

“You have become surrounded by people who encourage your defiance.”

Zee frowned.

“I was defiant before them.”

Ner coughed to hide a laugh.

Aurelia looked toward the ceiling.

Victor’s expression hardened.

“This is not a joke.”

“No.”

Zee’s humor disappeared.

“That is why I came.”

The throne hall changed.

Zee stepped forward.

Victor watched every movement.

Fear.

Control.

Calculation.

Zee did not enjoy it.

Not yet.

“I read your claim.”

“You are my son.”

“Yes.”

“And heir of House Darkheart.”

“Sometimes.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“You mock your birthright?”

“No.”

Zee looked directly at him.

“I mock the way you remember it only when you want control.”

A murmur moved through the hall.

Victor’s face darkened.

“Clear the chamber.”

Aurelia immediately said, “No.”

Victor looked toward her.

“This concerns my son.”

“And mine.”

“House Darkheart—”

“Does not erase me.”

Silence.

Victor looked toward the assembled court.

Then seemed to reconsider.

“Everyone except the principals.”

Servants left.

Minor nobles followed.

Darkheart guards remained.

So did Rez.

Ner.

Aurelia.

Zee.

Zareth above.

Victor stood from the throne.

That was the first time Zee realized his father no longer seemed enormous.

Childhood memory had made Victor taller.

Fifteen years had corrected the illusion.

Victor descended the steps.

“You intervene in foreign disputes.”

“Yes.”

“You cross borders.”

“Yes.”

“You consort with Veyrath survivors.”

Zee looked toward Aurelia.

“They are my family.”

Victor flinched at that.

Tiny.

Enough.

“You involve yourself with traffickers, covens, Northern Councils, mercenaries—”

“Usually because they are hurting people.”

“You believe that grants you authority?”

“No.”

Zee’s answer surprised him.

Victor frowned.

Zee continued.

“I choose whether I care.”

“That is worse.”

“Why?”

“Because you have power without law.”

Rez’s expression sharpened.

Zee thought about Renn.

Voss.

Khell.

People with law.

People who used it badly.

“Law does not make people good.”

“No.”

Victor stepped closer.

“But power without law makes monsters.”

There.

Monster.

Same word.

Older conversation.

Zee’s horns warmed.

Aurelia noticed.

Ner too.

No one spoke.

Zee breathed.

“What law did you use when you killed me?”

Victor froze.

The room disappeared around the question.

Aurelia went rigid.

Rez looked toward Zee.

Ner’s expression changed.

Victor’s face lost color.

No repeated act.

No new violence.

Only the one truth between them.

Victor answered quietly.

“None.”

That surprised Zee.

He had expected justification.

Prophecy.

Fear.

The kingdom.

Anything.

Victor continued.

“I was afraid.”

Zee stared.

“That is not an apology.”

“No.”

“Do you regret it?”

Victor looked at him.

For one moment, Zee saw the father from before the prophecy.

The man who had wanted to hold his newborn son.

Then fear returned.

“I regret that I did not understand what it would create.”

Zee’s face went cold.

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

There.

Not regret for Zee’s pain.

Regret for consequence.

Victor saw the reaction.

“Do not twist my words.”

“I did not.”

Zee stepped closer.

“You regret making me harder to kill.”

Victor’s silence answered.

Something dark inside Zee smiled.

He felt it.

That same part that enjoyed Renn’s scream.

Victor deserved fear.

Zee believed that.

The temptation to step closer, show fangs, let Crimson Mana fill the room until Victor remembered exactly how powerless he had been against the thing he tried to destroy—

It was strong.

Easy.

Satisfying.

Zee’s Mana stirred.

Darkheart wards flickered.

Guards tensed.

Aurelia said nothing.

Ner said nothing.

Rez said nothing.

No one called his name.

This was his choice.

Zee let the Mana settle.

Victor noticed.

His fear changed.

Confusion.

“You could have threatened me.”

“Yes.”

“You wanted to.”

“Yes.”

Victor looked at him more carefully.

“Why didn't you?”

Zee smiled faintly.

“Because then you would make my point for me.”

Victor frowned.

“You think restraint proves you safe?”

“No.”

Zee’s smile disappeared.

“I am not safe.”

That silenced even Aurelia for a heartbeat.

Zee continued.

“I am a Vampire.”

“A Wolf.”

“A Witch.”

“Dragon is waking inside me.”

“I have been hunted since birth.”

“I fight.”

“I hurt people.”

“Sometimes I like hurting them.”

Aurelia watched.

Proud and frightened all at once.

Zee held Victor’s gaze.

“But you do not get to take everything frightening about me and call it proof that you were right.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“You are fifteen.”

“Yes.”

“You do not understand what kingdoms see when they look at you.”

Zee laughed softly.

“I have spent fifteen years being told.”

“Then listen.”

“No.”

That word landed.

Zee moved closer until only several feet remained.

“You listen.”

Victor went still.

“The world can hate me.”

“Fear me.”

“Call me monster.”

“Try to kill me.”

“Apparently they enjoy trying.”

Ner’s mouth twitched.

Zee continued.

“But you do not get to claim me because my reputation became inconvenient.”

“You do not get to decide I am your heir when it gives you authority and your abomination when it gives you distance.”

Victor’s face hardened.

“I am King of this House.”

“Yes.”

“You are its prince.”

“Yes.”

“Then you answer to me.”

Zee thought.

Then smiled.

“No.”

Darkheart wards flickered again.

Victor’s eyes sharpened.

Zee continued before anyone could mistake him.

“I answer for what I do.”

“That is different.”

“You want obedience.”

“I want order.”

“You want control.”

Victor stepped forward.

“And what would you know about control?”

Zee’s scales brightened.

Ner looked toward him.

Zee heard his own heartbeat.

Then Victor’s.

Then Aurelia’s.

Then nothing else.

“One of my best friends is alive because I learned the difference between control and fear.”

Rez’s face changed slightly.

Victor did not understand the reference.

He did not need to.

Zee continued.

“I have hurt people because I lost control.”

“I have stopped because I chose to.”

“I have walked away from men I wanted to kill.”

“Have you?”

The question struck.

Victor’s face changed.

Zee saw it.

Aurelia did too.

Victor looked away first.

Zee did not smile.

That mattered.

He could have enjoyed winning.

Part of him did.

But this was not Renn.

Not Voss.

Not a trafficker beneath his hands.

This was his father.

Ugly in a different way.

Victor returned to the throne steps.

“What do you want, Zee?”

First time.

His name.

Not boy.

Not abomination.

Not heir.

Zee.

He noticed.

“I want your claim withdrawn.”

“No.”

Zee expected that.

“Then we go before the Witch Crowns.”

Aurelia turned toward him.

Victor stared.

Rez did too.

Ner remained still.

Victor laughed once.

“You think they will side with you?”

“I do not know.”

Truth.

Victor’s expression shifted.

Zee continued.

“But I will stand there.”

“And when they ask whether Vesper has prevented you from returning?”

“I will tell them no.”

“When they ask whether Aurelia turned you against your House?”

“I will tell them no.”

“When they ask whether I am your father?”

“I will tell them yes.”

Victor waited.

Zee’s crimson eyes hardened.

“And when they ask whether I belong to you…”

Silence.

“…I will tell them no.”

The words did not shake the castle.

No prophecy answered.

No Blood Rain began.

They were only words.

That made them stronger.

Victor stared at his son.

Perhaps for the first time understanding the problem in a way prophecy never explained.

Zee had grown into someone he could no longer control through fear.

Victor looked toward Aurelia.

“You allowed this.”

Aurelia’s face became cold.

“I raised him.”

Different answer.

Victor closed his eyes.

For several seconds he looked older than his crown.

Then:

“I will withdraw the guardianship claim.”

Zee blinked.

Rez’s eyebrows rose.

Aurelia did not relax.

Victor lifted one hand before anyone spoke.

“Not the succession question.”

There.

Of course.

Zee looked toward the throne.

Then Victor.

“Keep it.”

Victor frowned.

“The throne?”

Zee shrugged.

“I did not come for it.”

That landed harder than Zee expected.

Victor had built so much fear around what Zee might take.

Power.

House.

Crown.

Perhaps hearing Zee refuse to beg for any of it unsettled him more than ambition would have.

“You are heir by blood.”

“Then blood will still be there tomorrow.”

Victor stared.

Zee turned.

Conversation over.

Victor said:

“Zee.”

He stopped.

Not because the King commanded it.

Because his father used his name again.

Victor looked at the horns.

The scales.

The son he had failed.

Fear remained.

So did something else.

Something too small to call love.

Too complicated to call regret.

“I do not know what you will become.”

Zee looked back.

“Neither do I.”

Victor’s face tightened.

The prophecy had given him terror disguised as certainty.

Zee’s answer gave him something worse.

Unknown.

Zee smiled faintly.

“That is kind of the point.”

He left the throne hall.

Aurelia followed.

Rez and Ner behind her.

Above the castle, Zareth roared once.

Not victory.

Recognition.

Zee crossed the outer courtyard beneath Darkheart banners that still belonged partly to him whether Victor liked it or not.

Ner fell into step beside him.

“You did well.”

Zee looked over.

“That sounds surprised.”

“I expected at least one broken table.”

“Rez told me kings cannot punch trade.”

Rez, behind them, called:

“That is not what I said.”

Zee smiled.

Ner bumped his shoulder.

“You wanted to scare him.”

“Yes.”

“But you didn't.”

“I think I scared him anyway.”

Ner smiled.

“Probably.”

Their hands brushed as they walked.

This time neither moved away.

Zee noticed.

Ner noticed.

Rez definitely noticed.

Zee looked over his shoulder.

Rez immediately studied the sky.

Traitor.

Aurelia waited at the gate.

Zee reached her.

For a moment neither spoke.

Then she pulled him into her arms.

Fifteen.

More dangerous.

More independent.

Still hers.

Zee held her back.

“You okay?”

“No.”

“Truth.”

Aurelia laughed quietly into his hair.

“That was the truth.”

Zee smiled.

Then she whispered:

“I am proud of you.”

His chest tightened.

“For not killing him?”

Aurelia pulled back.

“For choosing why you didn't.”

Zee looked toward Castle Darkheart.

He had returned expecting confrontation.

He left without a throne.

Without reconciliation.

Without pretending Victor had changed enough to deserve forgiveness.

Nothing was magically repaired.

Good.

Real things rarely were.

But Victor had withdrawn his attempt to control Zee’s present life.

Zee had stood inside the castle where his first death began and left because he chose to.

No one carried him.

No one rescued him.

No one decided his answer first.

The hunted child had come home.

The hunter had left.

And somewhere between those two versions of Zee Darkheart, something else had begun taking shape.

Not a king.

Not yet.

A boy learning that sometimes the most powerful thing he could take from an enemy—

was the right to define him.

Zee laughed.

There he was.

They moved.

---

The deeper forest stopped pretending to obey ordinary geography.

They passed a waterfall flowing sideways through open air.

A field of black flowers turned their petals away from Zee's blood.

A herd of eyeless six-legged creatures watched from a cliff that had not existed a minute earlier.

None attacked.

That mattered.

Zee began understanding.

“This place is not hunting us.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“It attacked after Zareth burned the tree.”

Zareth sent offense.

Ner thought.

“The antler came after the fire.”

“And the false Aurelia?” Rez asked.

Ner frowned.

“Maybe defensive behavior.”

Zee looked toward the eyes opening in distant bark.

“Or curiosity.”

The wounded hunter shook his head.

“It killed my people.”

“Did they attack first?” Zee asked.

Silence.

The man looked away.

Rez noticed.

“What did your group do?”

The hunter swallowed.

“We found one of the six-legged animals.”

Zee's face hardened.

“And?”

“We killed it.”

Of course.

Ner closed his eyes.

“Why?”

“We thought it was dangerous.”

“Did it attack?”

“No.”

Zee's darkness stirred.

Not enough to act.

Enough to judge.

The hunter continued quickly.

“Then we cut it open.”

Zareth growled.

The Link filled with disgust.

Rez's expression went cold.

“You crossed into unknown territory, killed an animal that did not threaten you, and dissected it.”

The hunter looked ashamed.

“We needed to know what it was.”

Ner stared.

“That is not how asking works.”

Zee almost smiled.

Not because it was funny.

Because the world had once used the same logic on him.

Unknown.

Dangerous.

Cut it open.

Find out afterward.

He understood this place a little better now.

Maybe.

“Where did you kill it?”

The hunter pointed uncertainly.

“No idea.”

Zee looked at the Crimson folds.

“I do.”

His new perception pulled faintly toward something.

Blood.

Not ordinary blood.

The creature's blood had touched one of the folds and left a pattern.

Zee followed.

Rez did not question.

Ner tested every turn.

Zareth mapped from above.

For once, the strange place allowed them through.

Or they stopped fighting it enough to move correctly.

Both were possible.

They found the dead creature near sunset.

Its body had not rotted.

Six legs folded beneath it.

Smooth eyeless face turned toward the ground.

A long wound opened across its abdomen.

Hunter tools lay nearby.

The forest around it was silent.

Zee approached slowly.

No threat.

No touch.

He crouched.

“I am sorry.”

Rez looked at him.

The hunter bowed his head.

Something moved beneath the earth.

The enormous eye opened again.

Not under Zee.

Ten yards away.

Watching.

Zareth lowered himself but did not attack.

Ner kept his Mana quiet.

Rez lowered his sword.

The eye remained.

Zee looked toward the hunter.

“Your weapon.”

The man hesitated.

Then handed over his hunting knife.

Zee placed it beside the dead creature.

Then the man's specimen pouch.

Inside were pieces of pale tissue taken from the animal.

Ner saw.

His face tightened.

Zee placed them beside the body too.

The forest shifted.

Not violently.

Trees straightened a fraction.

The sideways waterfall slowed.

The eye blinked.

Zee's new Crimson perception saw a fold opening nearby.

Different.

Stable.

A path.

Rez saw Zee's face.

“Exit?”

“I think.”

Ner threw a Golden sphere.

It crossed the fold.

Did not vanish.

Rolled normally through the snow beyond.

Zee smiled.

“Yes.”

The hunter started crying.

Quietly.

No one mocked him.

They crossed one by one.

Rez took the hunter first.

Ner next.

Zee waited.

Zareth remained behind him.

The Dragon Link carried a question.

The eye still watched.

Zee looked back at it.

“What are you?”

No answer.

Good.

He did not expect one.

The world did not owe him explanations simply because he survived meeting it.

Something passed through the Link from Zareth.

Old Dragon concept.

Not name.

Not certainty.

A category.

**Deep wild.**

Places older than borders.

Regions Dragons remembered only enough to avoid.

Not evil.

Not safe.

Zee nodded.

Then crossed.

Zareth followed.

The fold closed.

The forest behind them became ordinary trees.

Mostly.

The border stone stood less than a hundred yards away.

Impossible.

They had traveled for hours.

Ner looked back.

“No.”

Rez smiled tiredly.

“Do not start.”

Ner pointed.

“We were miles inside.”

“Yes.”

“That is impossible.”

Zee looked at his hands.

Crimson lines flickered once around his fingers.

Then disappeared.

“Apparently not.”

The hunter sat in the snow.

Alive.

The core four stood around him.

Bloodied.

Exhausted.

Different.

They had entered expecting a monster.

Found an ecosystem.

Provoked a territory.

Learned that some supernatural things did not fit neatly into Witch, Vampire, Wolf, Dragon, demon, curse, spell, or kingdom.

And Zee carried a new scar through his abdomen that had already begun fading into something his body would remember.

Not a copied power.

Not victory.

A new way to see when the world folded wrong.

Ner looked toward him.

“Do not experiment with that.”

Zee frowned.

“I was not going to.”

Rez stared.

Zareth sent immediate disbelief.

Zee looked offended.

“Fine.”

Ner smiled.

The wounded hunter laughed weakly.

For the first time since they crossed the border stone, the sound did not feel inappropriate.

Rez looked back toward the unknown forest.

“We tell the wolf clans to mark this entire region.”

“As forbidden?” Zee asked.

Rez thought.

“No.”

Ner looked toward him.

Rez continued.

“As inhabited.”

That was better.

Much better.

Zee looked at the forest one last time.

Kingdom maps had called the land empty.

It was not.

They simply had not understood what lived there.

The known world had not expanded because Zee conquered something.

It expanded because, for once, he had survived something without needing to own it, kill it, or understand all of it.

Beyond the trees, deeper places waited.

Older species.

Stranger laws.

Things kingdoms had never named.

Zee's Crimson eyes brightened.

Fear remained.

So did wonder.

And now that he knew how little of the world belonged to crowns—

he wanted to see all of it.
