# Chapter Fifty-Two

## The Country Without Roads

The first problem with trying to warn people about a place that folded distance was deciding where the place actually was.

The wolf clans wanted coordinates.

Rez wanted boundaries.

Ner wanted repeated measurements.

Zareth wanted everyone to stop pretending the land cared about their maps.

Zee wanted to go back.

That last opinion was unpopular.

They stood inside a long timber hall three days after escaping the deep wild, surrounded by wolf trackers, two witch surveyors, a Vesper cartographer, and one clan elder who had spent twenty minutes insisting that every region could be mapped if enough people survived measuring it.

Ner finally placed both hands on the table.

“No.”

The elder stared.

“No?”

“No.”

“You have been fifteen for exactly long enough to become disrespectful.”

Ner smiled.

“I was disrespectful before fifteen.”

Rez coughed.

Zee looked innocent.

The elder glared at all three.

Ner pointed toward the map.

“You keep asking where the boundary moved.”

“Yes.”

“We do not know.”

“You crossed it.”

“Yes.”

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“Then mark the route.”

“We tried.”

Ner slid three pieces of parchment forward.

Each held a different version of the same journey.

On the first, the path curved six miles northwest.

On the second, the same landmarks appeared nearly fourteen miles apart.

On the third, the border stone sat less than a hundred yards from where the dead six-legged creature had been found.

The elder looked between them.

“That is impossible.”

Zee smiled.

“You are going to hear that a lot.”

Rez gave him a look.

Zee shrugged.

The Vesper cartographer leaned closer.

“What if the terrain physically moved?”

Ner shook his head.

“The trees changed position without moving through the space between positions.”

The witch surveyor frowned.

“How can you know?”

Ner lifted one hand.

Pure Golden Mana formed a thin line across the map.

“I anchored spell markers.”

“Some returned behind us.”

“Some appeared above us.”

“One remained exactly where I placed it while the path around it stopped leading to the same location.”

The hall went quiet.

The elder looked toward Zee.

“And you could see these... folds?”

“After one stabbed me.”

Several wolves looked toward his abdomen.

Zee frowned.

“It healed.”

“That was not the concern.”

“It usually is.”

Rez leaned against the table.

“What matters is this: do not call the region uninhabited.”

The elder’s expression hardened.

“We lost people there.”

“Yes.”

“To something dangerous.”

“Yes.”

“And you are telling me not to seal it?”

Rez shook his head.

“I am telling you that sealing and invading are different decisions.”

One wolf captain folded his arms.

“What would you call it?”

Rez looked toward Zee.

Zee thought about the eye beneath the ground.

The false Aurelia.

The eyeless animals.

The hunter confessing what his party had done first.

Then the path opening only after the stolen remains were returned.

“Inhabited.”

The elder frowned.

“By what?”

Zee looked toward Zareth.

The Dragon Prince had remained outside because the hall was too small, but his head rested beside an open wall section built for larger visitors.

The Link carried the same old Drakonis concept.

Deep wild.

Not a species.

Not a kingdom.

Not a name.

A warning category.

“Something that was there before us.”

“That tells me nothing.”

“Then write that.”

The elder stared.

Zee continued.

“Unknown inhabitants.”

“Unknown laws.”

“Do not kill anything unless it attacks first.”

“Do not cut pieces off things because you are curious.”

The surviving hunter from the expedition stood near the rear wall.

His face tightened.

Good.

He had chosen to testify publicly.

That mattered.

Zee looked toward him.

The man stepped forward.

“We caused what happened.”

A murmur moved through the wolves.

The hunter swallowed.

“We killed one of the creatures.”

“Unprovoked.”

“We opened it.”

“Took tissue.”

“And after that... the land changed.”

One clan warrior looked disgusted.

“You expect us to believe the forest judged you?”

The hunter shook his head.

“No.”

“I expect you to believe we did something stupid inside a place we did not understand.”

That answer was better.

The elder sat back.

“What do you recommend?”

Rez answered.

“Observation posts outside the last stable landmarks.”

“No patrols crossing the line without cause.”

“Nobody alone.”

“No hunters entering for trophies.”

Ner added, “No permanent magical anchors.”

The surveyors looked toward him.

“Why?”

“Because we do not know whether the region reads anchored magic as intrusion.”

Zee glanced at him.

“That is a guess.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Ner smiled.

The elder looked toward Zareth.

“And Drakonis?”

Zee opened the Link.

Question.

The answer came slowly.

Dragon history.

Old regions.

Avoidance.

Watching from high altitude.

No nesting nearby.

No claim.

Zee translated carefully.

“Drakonis will not claim it.”

The wolf elder raised an eyebrow.

“Zareth has that authority?”

The Dragon Prince’s Teal-and-Gold Mana flared outside the hall.

The elder looked toward the massive crimson head filling half the wall opening.

“Fair.”

Rez smiled.

Then the hall doors opened.

A young wolf messenger entered breathing hard.

“Elder.”

Everyone turned.

The messenger bowed.

“Something came out.”

Silence.

Zee straightened.

“From the deep wild?”

The messenger looked toward him.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“We do not know.”

Zee smiled.

Rez immediately said, “Stop smiling.”

“I am not.”

“You absolutely are.”

The elder stood.

“Where?”

“North watch.”

“Hostile?”

The messenger hesitated.

“No.”

That changed everything.

“What is it doing?” Ner asked.

The messenger looked deeply confused.

“Waiting.”

---

The thing waiting beyond the north watch had antlers.

That was where resemblance to any known animal ended.

It stood in a field of dead winter grass beneath a gray afternoon sky, nearly nine feet at the shoulder, with six narrow legs and a body covered in pale charcoal hide that seemed smooth from a distance and patterned with fine moving lines up close.

Its head was long.

Eyeless.

But unlike the smaller creatures from the deep wild, this one possessed a split crown of black antlers that curved backward and then inward as though framing empty space above its skull.

No mouth.

No visible nostrils.

No heartbeat Zee could detect.

No blood scent.

No obvious Mana.

Wolf warriors ringed the field at a distance.

None had attacked.

Good.

The creature stood perfectly still.

Zareth landed behind the group.

The animal reacted immediately.

Its antlers changed.

Not shape.

Position.

For a heartbeat Zee saw the crown in three places at once.

Then one again.

Zareth’s Link tightened.

Recognition?

No.

Caution.

Ner moved closer.

Rez caught his sleeve.

“Not yet.”

“I am not touching it.”

“That sentence has history.”

Ner glared.

Zee listened.

Nothing.

Then the strange Crimson perception in his blood stirred.

Faint lines appeared around the animal.

Not around its body.

Through it.

Several folds crossing the same space.

Zee inhaled.

“It is not fully here.”

Rez looked over.

“Meaning?”

“I do not know.”

Ner smiled faintly.

Zee frowned.

“Do not.”

Ner lifted one hand.

Pure Golden Mana formed a tiny sphere.

Not aimed at the creature.

He released it several feet to the left.

The sphere moved normally.

Then vanished when it crossed one of Zee’s perceived lines.

Ner’s expression sharpened.

“Again.”

He formed another.

This one he sent lower.

It passed.

Another higher.

Gone.

The creature finally moved.

One step.

Every wolf raised a weapon.

Rez raised one hand.

“Hold.”

The creature’s six legs folded oddly, each joint bending in different directions, yet the movement remained smooth.

It approached Zee.

Only Zee.

He did not move.

Aurelia was not here to tell him not to.

That made the choice more important.

Ner whispered, “Zee.”

“I know.”

Zareth’s Link filled with readiness.

Rez moved half a step closer.

The animal stopped six feet away.

Its antlers shifted again.

The air between them folded.

Zee saw a landscape.

Not around them.

Inside the space between the antlers.

Black grass.

Silver rain falling upward.

A distant mountain hanging upside down in a violet sky.

Then something moved across that landscape.

Hundreds of pale creatures.

Migrating.

Zee’s eyes widened.

Ner stepped closer despite Rez.

The image sharpened.

Not illusion.

A view.

Somewhere else.

The creature lowered its head.

One antler touched the ground.

The field beneath it changed.

Only a circle several feet across.

Winter grass became black.

For one heartbeat.

Then normal again.

Zee felt pressure against his bones.

Same impossible almost-language as before.

Not words.

Need.

Movement.

Blocked.

Danger.

Rez looked at Zee.

“You are getting something.”

“Not language.”

“What?”

Zee focused.

Images arrived.

A migration path.

Animals moving through deep wild folds.

Then a rupture.

Fire.

Not Dragonfire.

Different.

White-green.

A section of folded terrain collapsing.

Creatures scattering.

One route closed.

Then—

A thing Zee recognized.

Not species.

Structure.

A tower.

Human-made.

Built at the edge of unfamiliar land.

Ner saw only Zee’s face.

“What?”

“Someone built something.”

“Where?”

“I think inside.”

Rez frowned.

“Inside the region?”

Zee nodded slowly.

The antlered creature raised its head.

The view vanished.

Then it turned north.

Took three steps.

Stopped.

Looked back without eyes.

Zee stared.

Rez sighed.

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“It wants us to follow.”

“We do not know that.”

Ner looked toward the creature.

“Yes, we do.”

Rez turned.

“How?”

Ner pointed.

The animal had taken another three steps.

Stopped again.

Zareth’s Link supplied dry amusement.

Rez closed his eyes.

“Fine.”

The wolf elder, who had arrived with them, looked horrified.

“You are not going back in there.”

Zee turned.

“Probably.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the true one.”

The elder stared toward the creature.

“What if this is bait?”

Rez answered.

“Then we find out before sending anyone else.”

The elder looked toward him.

“You are all fifteen.”

Rez nodded.

“Yes.”

Nothing else.

The elder seemed to realize age was not going to win the argument.

Ner stepped toward the antlered creature.

It did not retreat.

“Whatever happened inside affected the migration.”

Zee nodded.

“And whatever caused it looks like something built.”

Rez’s expression darkened.

That was important.

The deep wild had not come looking for kingdoms.

Someone from the known world may have gone farther in.

Zareth lifted his wings.

Question through the Link.

Go?

Zee looked toward the others.

Rez sighed.

Ner smiled.

Of course.

Zee turned toward the wolf elder.

“Keep everyone outside.”

“You cannot order me.”

“No.”

Zee looked toward the strange creature.

“But if we are right, the thing inside may be dangerous because somebody already ignored the warning.”

The elder's face tightened.

Then he nodded.

“Six hours.”

Rez frowned.

“What?”

“If you are not back in six hours, we do not send anyone after you.”

Zee smiled.

“Good.”

The elder blinked.

“You agree?”

“Yes.”

Rez looked toward him.

Zee continued.

“If this place folds people wrong, adding more bodies is stupid.”

Ner nodded.

“There is hope for you.”

Zee shoved him lightly.

The antlered creature started walking.

This time they followed.

The line between mapped kingdoms and everything beyond them opened without a door.

One step was winter field.

The next was black grass beneath silver rain.

No transition.

No warning.

No border stone.

Zee looked back.

The wolves were gone.

The sky had changed.

And the creature had already moved fifty yards ahead.

Rez drew his sword.

Ner’s Gold gathered around his hands.

Zareth spread enormous wings.

Zee’s Crimson lines returned around the world.

This time, they had not entered the deep wild because they were lost.

Something inside had asked for help.

Or something close enough to asking that Zee Darkheart was willing to find out.

And if someone from the kingdoms had brought fire into a place older than their maps—

then the monsters might not be the things with antlers.

# Chapter Fifty-Three

## The Men Who Built a Sun

Silver rain fell upward.

Zee hated it immediately.

Not because it was dangerous.

Because every drop that struck his skin rolled toward the sky instead of the ground.

His hair slowly became wetter from underneath.

“That is disgusting.”

Rez looked over while trying to keep his footing on black grass that leaned away from him.

“Of all the things here, that bothers you?”

“Yes.”

Ner tilted his head.

“It is actually fascinating.”

“You would say that.”

A droplet struck Ner's chin and slid upward along his cheek.

He smiled.

Zee stared.

Then realized he was staring.

Then became irritated with himself because even impossible rain could apparently become a Ner problem.

Rez saw.

He said nothing.

That was worse.

Zareth moved overhead.

His crimson body crossed a violet sky where two mountain ranges hung at different angles, one below and one suspended sideways in the distance.

Through the Link came tactical impressions.

Antlered creature ahead.

Large herd farther east.

Fire-light beyond ridge.

Movement.

Human-sized.

Zee looked toward Rez.

“There are people.”

Rez’s expression sharpened.

“How many?”

Zareth sent scattered points.

Twelve.

Maybe more below ground.

Ner frowned.

“Human?”

Zee waited for the Link.

No certainty.

“Two legs.”

Rez sighed.

“Useful.”

They followed the antlered creature across a landscape that made direction meaningless.

The black grass ended at a cliff.

Except the cliff extended horizontally into open air.

The creature walked onto it.

Zee stopped.

“No.”

Ner looked toward him.

“You are scared of heights?”

“No.”

“You have Zareth as a best friend.”

“I am scared of walking on walls that think they are floors.”

Rez stepped beside him.

“Reasonable.”

The antlered creature continued.

Its six legs adhered to stone as if gravity agreed with it.

Zareth banked nearby.

The Link delivered an image of the same path from above.

Except from Zareth's angle, the cliff was level ground.

Zee frowned.

“This place is rude.”

Ner smiled.

“Move.”

He stepped onto the vertical stone.

Nothing happened.

His body rotated without rotating.

One heartbeat Zee watched Ner standing sideways.

The next Zee’s mind accepted the surface as ground.

Ner looked back.

“Come on.”

Zee hated that Ner looked good while doing impossible things.

He stepped.

The world shifted.

Rez came next.

No comment.

His face suggested comment would happen later.

They crossed.

At the far end, the smell reached Zee.

Smoke.

Metal.

Blood.

Not much blood.

Oil.

Alchemy.

Witchcraft.

And something artificial burning too hot.

Zee stopped.

“I know that smell.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“Not the whole thing.”

He inhaled.

“Spell fuel.”

Ner’s expression sharpened.

“Human-made?”

“Witch-made.”

Zareth landed nearby.

The antlered guide finally stopped.

Ahead, black grass opened into a crater.

Someone had built a camp inside it.

Not tents.

Structures.

Metal supports drilled into pale stone.

Wooden platforms.

Ropes.

Crates.

Three portable ward pylons.

A central framework surrounded something bright.

Too bright.

White-green light burned inside an iron cage.

It resembled a tiny sun.

Zee’s Dragon nature recoiled.

Hard.

Crimson scales raced across his neck.

His shoulder ridges tightened.

Zareth snarled so violently the ground vibrated.

The Link hit Zee with pain.

Wrong-fire.

Dragon instinct hated it.

Ner stared.

“What is that?”

Rez looked toward the workers below.

“Whatever it is, they built it.”

The antlered creature lowered its head.

The black grass around its feet faded gray.

Zee understood.

“That is what damaged the route.”

Ner crouched.

Golden Mana formed along his fingertips.

He studied the distant framework without touching it.

His face changed.

“No.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“That is not producing energy.”

“What is it doing?”

Ner looked at the world around them.

“Taking structure.”

Zee frowned.

“Explain.”

“I am trying.”

Ner narrowed his eyes.

“Magic usually has an anchor.”

“Caster.”

“Object.”

“Place.”

“Blood.”

“Something.”

He pointed toward the white-green light.

“That thing is anchoring itself by forcing the surrounding space to become simpler.”

Rez looked toward the impossible mountain overhead.

“Which means?”

“It is making this place obey ordinary geometry.”

Silence.

Zee looked at the crater again.

Around the artificial light, the deep wild looked almost normal.

Ground stayed down.

Rain fell downward.

Trees grew upright.

Distances held.

A circle of kingdom logic carved into a place that did not share it.

Rez’s face hardened.

“They are not studying the region.”

“No,” Ner said.

“They are changing it.”

The antlered creature moved its head toward the eastern horizon.

Zee followed.

Far away, herds of pale animals crowded against folded terrain.

Their migration route severed by the artificial stable zone.

Zee’s darkness stirred.

This time not because he enjoyed violence.

Because someone had entered a place they did not understand and decided understanding was unnecessary if they could force it to behave.

He thought of Victor.

Different scale.

Same temptation.

Control what frightens you.

Call that safety.

Rez watched the camp.

“We need to know why.”

Zee looked at him.

“You already know enough?”

“No.”

Good.

Rez continued.

“Maybe they are preventing something worse.”

Ner nodded reluctantly.

“Possible.”

Zee did not like it.

That did not make it false.

Zareth’s Link pushed a memory.

Drakonis border engineers stabilizing volcanic ground before hatchling migrations.

Sometimes changing dangerous land saved lives.

Important distinction.

Zee exhaled.

“Fine.”

Rez smiled.

“You are learning patience.”

“Do not ruin it.”

---

They entered the camp openly.

That was Rez’s decision.

Zee hated it.

Sneaking would imply guilt if the camp was legitimate.

Attacking would be worse.

So four fifteen-year-olds and one enormous Dragon walked down the crater slope toward a group of researchers who reacted exactly as badly as expected.

Weapons came out.

Wards ignited.

Someone shouted:

“Dragon!”

Someone else shouted:

“Darkheart!”

Zee sighed.

“Of course they know me.”

Rez lifted empty hands.

“We are not attacking.”

A woman near the central framework stepped forward.

Forties.

Witch.

Dark green Mana.

Heavy coat.

Silver goggles.

Not a soldier.

Her first reaction to Zee was not fear.

It was annoyance.

“What are you doing here?”

Zee blinked.

That was new.

Rez answered.

“Investigating disappearances tied to this region.”

“You should not be here.”

Ner looked toward the artificial sun.

“That makes at least six people who should not be here.”

The woman’s eyes narrowed.

“Who are you?”

“Nereus Azrion.”

Her expression changed at the name.

Not greed.

Recognition.

Professional.

“Golden Mana.”

Ner’s face hardened.

“My name was first.”

The woman paused.

Then:

“Fair.”

She looked toward Rez.

“Prince Vesper.”

“Yes.”

Then Zareth.

She swallowed.

“Crown Prince Drakonis.”

Zareth stared.

Finally Zee.

“Zee Darkheart.”

Zee smiled.

“There.”

“What?”

“You used my name.”

The woman looked confused.

Rez covered his face briefly.

“My name is Doctor Maeven Oris.”

Zee frowned.

“Doctor?”

“Scholar.”

“That sounds safer.”

“It is not.”

Ner smiled faintly.

Rez asked, “What did you build?”

Maeven looked toward the caged light.

“A stabilization core.”

“Purpose?”

“To create a survivable research perimeter.”

Ner stared at her.

“You are rewriting local spatial behavior.”

Maeven’s expression sharpened.

“You understand it?”

“No.”

That surprised her.

Ner continued.

“I understand what it is doing.”

“Not why it works.”

Maeven looked at him differently now.

Respect.

Maybe.

“Neither do we.”

Zee laughed once.

Everyone looked at him.

“You built it anyway?”

Maeven’s face hardened.

“We lost eleven researchers before the first stable perimeter.”

Rez’s expression changed.

“Dead?”

“Missing.”

Important.

Maeven continued.

“We came here after finding evidence of rare spatial minerals beyond the western range.”

Zee looked toward the pale supports.

“Mining?”

“Research.”

Ner glanced at the crates.

Some were marked with ore weights.

Maeven saw.

“Research funds itself poorly.”

Ner’s mouth tightened.

There.

Less noble.

More complicated.

Rez asked, “Did you know you were blocking migration?”

Maeven frowned.

“What migration?”

Zee looked toward the antlered creature.

It had remained beyond the camp boundary.

Maeven saw it.

Her face went pale.

“That thing has been following us for weeks.”

“Did it attack?”

“No.”

“Did you attack it?”

Maeven hesitated.

Zee's expression cooled.

“How many?”

“Two.”

Zareth growled.

Maeven looked toward the Dragon.

“They approached the perimeter.”

Ner stared.

“So?”

“We did not know what they were.”

Zee almost laughed at the familiarity of that sentence.

Rez spoke first.

“And what happened after?”

“The terrain became more hostile.”

Zee looked toward him.

Rez looked back.

There.

Pattern.

Maeven’s face changed.

“You think it is retaliating.”

Zee shook his head.

“I think you keep calling everything retaliation because you assume it is thinking about you.”

Maeven stared.

That landed.

Zee continued.

“Maybe you built your core across where they live.”

Ner stepped closer to the framework.

“Turn it off.”

Maeven immediately said, “No.”

“Why?”

“Because if we shut it down too quickly, every stabilized boundary may collapse at once.”

Ner stopped.

That mattered.

“How many?”

“Seven field anchors.”

“How far?”

“Four miles.”

Rez cursed quietly.

They had found one camp.

The damage was larger.

Zee looked toward the antlered creature.

The pressure in his bones intensified.

Images.

Herds trapped.

Folds compressed.

One section tearing.

Not anger.

Emergency.

Ner looked at Zee.

“It is showing you something.”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Zee described it.

Maeven went pale.

“That cannot happen.”

Ner rounded on her.

“You just said you do not understand how the region works.”

Maeven stared.

Then shut her mouth.

Good.

Rez stepped toward the camp map.

“Show us the seven anchors.”

Maeven hesitated.

Rez’s voice sharpened.

“Now.”

Future king.

No shouting needed.

Maeven unfolded a field chart.

Seven stabilization points formed a rough ring.

Ner stared.

Then his face changed.

“Oh, no.”

Zee hated that phrase from him.

“What?”

Ner traced the circle.

“These are not independent.”

Maeven nodded.

“They reinforce each other.”

“No.”

Ner looked at her.

“They are tightening.”

Maeven frowned.

“What?”

“Your anchors are not holding seven areas stable.”

Pure Golden Mana flickered over the map.

The geometry became visible.

Lines pulling inward.

“They are compressing everything unstable between them.”

Rez immediately understood.

“A trap.”

“For the land itself.”

The ground shuddered.

Hard.

Zareth spread his wings.

The artificial sun brightened.

Every impossible mountain in the distance shifted at once.

The antlered creature outside the perimeter collapsed onto its front legs.

Zee felt the pressure hit his Dragon nature like a hammer.

His horns burned.

Crimson lines exploded across his vision.

Folds everywhere.

Too many.

All being dragged toward the stabilization ring.

Ner grabbed his shoulder.

“What do you see?”

Zee could barely answer.

“Everything is folding inward.”

Rez looked toward Maeven.

“How long?”

She stared at her instruments.

“I do not know.”

“Guess.”

“Minutes.”

Zee smiled without humor.

“There goes diplomacy.”

Rez pointed toward the central core.

“No one destroys anything yet.”

Zee looked offended.

“I know.”

Ner was already studying the map.

“We have to release the anchors in sequence.”

Maeven stared.

“That will collapse the perimeter.”

“Yes.”

“And kill us.”

“Maybe.”

Maeven looked horrified.

Ner continued.

“If we leave them active, you may collapse whatever this place uses instead of geography.”

“That could be worse.”

Rez took command.

“Zareth.”

The Dragon Prince looked toward him.

“Aerial anchors.”

Zareth launched.

“Ner, sequence.”

“Working.”

“Maeven, evacuation.”

She hesitated.

Rez shouted for the first time.

“Move!”

She moved.

“Zee.”

Zee looked toward him.

Rez pointed toward the Crimson lines only Zee could see.

“You tell us where reality is safe enough to stand.”

Zee smiled.

“That is a terrible job.”

“You are uniquely qualified.”

“Rude.”

“Accurate.”

The camp erupted.

Researchers grabbed equipment.

Others abandoned it.

Crates were left.

Good.

Life before ore.

Zee moved through the crater seeing folds no one else could.

“Not left!”

A team changed direction.

The ground where they would have stepped opened into silver ocean.

“Right!”

Ner shouted from the central frame.

“Anchor six first!”

Zareth’s Link flashed.

Found.

Teal-and-Gold Mana struck not the anchor itself but the support braces around it.

Careful.

Independent judgment.

The first anchor tilted.

Ner released its magical connection remotely.

The world screamed.

There was no other word.

A vibration passed through Zee’s teeth.

The black grass outside the perimeter turned white.

Maeven shouted, “That made it worse!”

Ner ignored her.

“Anchor two!”

Zee saw the folds.

“No!”

Everyone stopped.

Ner looked at him.

Zee pointed to the map.

“If two releases now, that whole side overlaps.”

Ner stared.

Then recalculated.

“You are right.”

That scared Zee.

Ner rarely said it that quickly.

“Four.”

Rez relayed.

Zareth turned midair.

The Dragon Link carried understanding.

Anchor four fell.

A section of artificial normalcy vanished.

Gravity changed.

Three researchers lifted from the ground.

Zee jumped.

Caught one.

Rez grabbed another.

Ner threw a Golden plane beneath the third and rotated it until the woman dropped safely.

Maeven stared.

“This is impossible.”

Zee shouted, “Stop saying that!”

Another tremor.

The artificial sun cracked.

White-green fire leaked through the cage.

Zareth screamed through the Link.

Pain.

Zee’s Dragon nature answered.

The fire hurt Dragons.

Not ordinary flame.

Something about forced stability cut against what Dragon magic sensed in the deep wild.

Zee’s scales spread.

He looked at the core.

Darkness stirred.

Destroy it.

Easy.

No.

Not yet.

Rez saw him.

“Zee!”

“I know!”

“Good!”

Ner shouted:

“Three and seven together!”

Zee checked the folds.

“Yes!”

Zareth hit seven.

Zee ran toward three.

Maeven shouted, “What are you doing?”

“Helping!”

“There is a release lever!”

“Where?”

“Inside the frame!”

Zee smiled.

“Of course.”

He entered.

White-green fire struck his arm.

Pain tore through him.

His Crimson scales blackened.

Did not die.

Did not stop.

His body adapted enough to keep moving.

Not immunity.

Resistance growing second by second.

The fire bit differently each time.

His Crimson Mana changed around it.

Less like a shield.

More like a refusal to let the forced stability define his blood.

Unique.

His.

Zee reached the lever.

Pulled.

Anchor three released.

At the same instant, Zareth tore seven free.

The artificial sun imploded.

Not exploded.

Light collapsed inward.

The crater disappeared.

For one heartbeat Zee stood nowhere.

No ground.

No sky.

No sound.

Then Ner’s hand caught his.

Golden Mana.

Boundary.

Rez grabbed Ner.

Zareth’s Link hit Zee like a chain of instinct.

Together.

Four points.

Not enough to control the deep wild.

Enough not to lose one another.

The world returned.

Black grass.

Silver rain upward.

No camp.

No crater.

No artificial sun.

Researchers scattered across the field.

Alive.

Maeven lay twenty yards away staring at the sky.

All seven anchors were gone.

The deep wild settled.

Slowly.

The strange mountains returned to impossible positions.

The migrating herd began moving.

The antlered creature rose.

Zee lay on his back breathing hard.

Ner’s hand was still locked around his.

Neither released.

Rez sat nearby covered in black grass.

Zareth landed with enough force to shake silver rain from the sky.

The Link flooded Zee.

Alive.

Angry.

Relieved.

Zee laughed.

Ner looked at him.

“What?”

“We fixed it.”

Rez groaned.

“We survived fixing it.”

“Same thing.”

“No.”

The antlered creature approached.

Every researcher tensed.

Zee lifted one hand.

“Do not.”

They listened.

Good.

The creature stopped near Maeven.

She stared up at it.

No weapon.

No spell.

For the first time, perhaps, no assumption.

The creature lowered its antlers.

A fold opened between them.

Maeven saw another landscape.

A migration.

Broken paths reconnecting.

Then the view closed.

Maeven whispered:

“We were in the way.”

Zee sat up.

“Yes.”

She looked toward him.

Not angry.

Ashamed.

“We thought the instability was the danger.”

Ner finally released Zee’s hand.

“Sometimes the instability is just the rule.”

Maeven nodded.

That lesson hurt her.

Good.

Lessons should.

Rez stood.

“What happens to your research?”

Maeven looked toward the destroyed equipment.

“Over.”

One of her researchers protested.

“Doctor—”

“No.”

She looked toward the migrating herd.

“We entered without understanding enough to know what damage meant.”

Then toward the surviving staff.

“We leave.”

Zee watched her.

No villain defeated.

No execution.

No glorious victory.

Just a woman realizing curiosity had become entitlement somewhere along the way.

Zee understood that danger.

He felt it himself.

He wanted to know everything about the deep wild.

Wanted to touch the folds.

Test the Crimson perception.

See what else existed beyond kingdom maps.

But wanting knowledge did not make everything his to open.

That mattered.

The antlered creature turned.

Walked toward a fold.

Then stopped.

Looked back.

Not at the researchers.

At the four.

Zee felt one final concept.

Not invitation.

Not friendship.

Recognition.

Different.

Allowed.

For now.

Then it vanished.

No door.

No spectacle.

One step here.

Next step elsewhere.

Zareth watched.

The Link carried wonder.

Ner stared at the empty space.

Rez exhaled.

“Well.”

Zee smiled.

“What?”

Rez looked around at silver rain, impossible mountains, and a herd walking through the side of a hill.

“We need better maps.”

Ner laughed.

Zee did too.

The known world had become smaller again.

Not because they had conquered the deep wild.

Because they had discovered that something could exist beyond kingdoms without asking to become one.

And somewhere beyond those folding horizons, the world continued.

Older.

Stranger.

Alive.

Waiting for no prince.

Not even Zee Darkheart.

# Chapter Fifty-Four

## The Things That Follow Rivers

The deep wild did not follow them home.

That was the first good sign.

The second was that the surviving researchers left when they said they would.

No hidden camp remained.

No replacement stabilization core appeared a week later.

No one tried turning the folded land into a kingdom.

For once, people learned before Zee had to break anything else.

He considered that progress.

The problem started with the river.

Three days after they returned to Vesper, an entire fishing village woke to find thousands of silver-black fish swimming upstream.

Not unusual by itself.

Fish did strange things.

Zee had learned not to assume every strange thing deserved him.

Then the fish climbed onto land.

That changed matters.

They did not die.

They moved.

Hundreds of sleek bodies pulled themselves through mud on narrow fin-like limbs that had not existed the day before according to every fisherman who had spent his life catching them.

They crossed the village.

Ignored people.

Ignored food.

Ignored dogs.

Then entered the western forest.

By noon, birds followed.

By evening, deer.

The next morning, a flock of black-winged creatures no one in Vesper could identify crossed the same river and went in the same direction.

Not fleeing.

Traveling.

King Lucien received six reports before breakfast.

Zee was eating when the seventh arrived.

A royal messenger entered the private dining chamber soaked to the shoulders.

“Your Majesty.”

Lucien looked up.

“What now?”

The messenger bowed.

“Something large crossed the lower Vesper.”

Rez stopped eating.

“How large?”

The messenger hesitated.

“Larger than the ferry.”

Zee smiled.

Aurelia looked toward him.

“No.”

“I said nothing.”

“You smiled.”

“That is not illegal.”

“Yet,” Rez muttered.

Ner covered his mouth.

Zareth was absent.

Drakonis had summoned him the previous night for a royal migration council concerning several Dragon territories where prey animals had begun abandoning traditional ranges.

At the time, Zee thought it unrelated.

Now he was less certain.

Lucien pushed away from the table.

“Did it attack?”

“No.”

“Damage?”

“One dock.”

“Intentionally?”

“We do not think so.”

Zee looked toward Rez.

Rez already had the same expression.

Pattern.

Not attack.

Movement.

Ner placed his cup down.

“Everything is going west.”

The messenger nodded.

“Yes.”

Aurelia frowned.

“Toward the deep wild?”

“Maybe,” Zee said.

Lucien looked toward him.

“Maybe?”

“The river route bends south before the old wolf border.”

Rez stood.

“But the migration path could still connect.”

Ner’s eyes sharpened.

“Unless the deep wild changed something outside itself.”

Silence.

Zee did not like that possibility.

Not because it meant danger.

Because they had assumed restoring the folds had finished the problem.

Maybe it had.

Maybe this was something else.

Good.

Unknown again.

Lucien looked toward the messenger.

“Any people missing?”

“No.”

“Deaths?”

“No.”

“Then no panic.”

He looked toward Rez.

“Send notice to river settlements.”

“No hunting unfamiliar migrations unless attacked.”

Rez nodded.

“Already drafting it.”

Zee looked at him.

“You were eating.”

“I can think while eating.”

“That seems arrogant.”

“It is a basic skill.”

Ner looked toward Zee.

“You cannot?”

Zee frowned.

“I hate both of you.”

Aurelia stood.

“You are not leaving until we know more.”

Zee sighed.

Then the Dragon Link struck.

Hard.

Zareth.

Far east.

Urgency.

Sky filled with wings.

Not Dragons.

Thousands of pale creatures moving above the mountains.

Then an image of a Drakonis elder pointing west.

Another.

A river seen from impossible height.

Black movement inside it.

Then Zareth himself.

Coming.

Fast.

Zee’s expression changed.

Aurelia noticed.

“Zareth?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Zee looked toward the open terrace.

“He found the same thing.”

---

Zareth arrived before noon.

Not alone.

That was new.

Three Drakonis Dragons came with him.

All young adults.

All larger than Zareth.

All armored along the chest and neck with dark ceremonial plating.

They landed outside Vesper’s eastern walls with enough controlled force to shake windows.

Zee reached the field first.

Rez and Ner behind him.

Aurelia came later.

Lucien even later because kings apparently had to finish speaking to people before running toward unexpected Dragons.

Zareth lowered his head immediately.

The Link opened.

Mountain herds.

Sky-creatures.

A river changing course for several breaths before returning.

A Dragon patrol finding black scales floating in a lake.

One final impression.

**Following something.**

Zee frowned.

“The animals are following something?”

Zareth’s head shifted.

Not exactly.

The concept changed.

**Being called.**

Ner stepped closer.

“Called how?”

Zee relayed the question.

The Link returned sensation.

Pressure.

Direction.

Compulsion?

No.

Invitation?

No.

More primitive.

A pull like migration instinct.

Rez looked toward one of the older Dragons.

“Can they speak human form?”

The Dragon’s body shifted.

Bones compressed.

Wings folded inward.

Scales receded.

A tall woman with dark red hair stepped from the transformation wearing Drakonis armor.

Zee stared.

He had known older Dragons could shift.

Still strange seeing something the size of a building become a person in seconds.

The woman looked toward Zareth first.

“Crown Prince.”

Then Rez.

“Prince Vesper.”

Ner.

“Azrion.”

Zee.

Her gaze lingered on his horns.

“Darkheart.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“Everyone gets my name right now.”

Rez muttered, “Growth.”

The Dragon woman ignored him.

“My name is Commander Varessa Drakonis.”

No relation claimed beyond House and kingdom.

Good.

The world was allowed to have people without becoming family trees.

Varessa continued.

“For two weeks, migratory patterns across Drakonis territory have changed.”

“How many species?” Ner asked.

“Twenty-seven confirmed.”

Rez whistled softly.

“Direction?”

“West.”

Zee looked toward Zareth.

The Dragon Link sent agreement.

Varessa continued.

“Predators too.”

That mattered.

Prey moved for food.

Predators followed prey.

But if predators and prey moved together—

Ner understood.

“They are not following the food chain.”

“No.”

“Do they attack each other during migration?”

“Rarely.”

Zee’s Wolf nature reacted to that.

Wrong.

Not impossible.

Wrong.

“Something is suppressing hunting instinct.”

Varessa shook her head.

“We do not know.”

Good.

She did not pretend.

Rez asked, “Why come to Vesper?”

Varessa looked toward Zareth.

“He insisted.”

Zee smiled.

Zareth’s Link carried pride.

Varessa did not.

“He believes this connects to whatever you encountered west of wolf territory.”

Ner frowned.

“We do not know that.”

“No.”

Varessa looked toward him.

“But Drakonis records contain one old pattern.”

There.

Not full explanation.

Fragment.

“What pattern?” Zee asked.

Varessa looked toward the western horizon.

“Mass migration before a region changes.”

Rez went still.

“Changes how?”

“We do not know.”

Zee sighed.

Varessa looked at him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

Ner smiled.

“She gave the correct answer.”

Varessa looked confused.

Good.

Zee continued.

“What do Dragon records actually say?”

“Very little.”

“Three events across several thousand years.”

“Each involved unrelated species moving in the same direction.”

“Each ended with the territory afterward being different.”

“Destroyed?”

“No.”

“Dead?”

“No.”

“Different how?”

Varessa hesitated.

“Maps stopped agreeing.”

Ner’s face changed.

Rez looked toward Zee.

Deep wild.

Not necessarily the same thing.

But related enough to matter.

Varessa continued.

“One record describes a mountain that became a lake.”

“Another describes a valley appearing where no valley existed.”

“The third says an entire forest migrated.”

Zee stared.

“The forest?”

“Those are the words.”

Rez looked toward Ner.

“Can forests migrate?”

Ner gave him a flat look.

“We just spent two days somewhere rain falls upward.”

“Fair.”

Zee looked toward Varessa.

“Where are the animals going exactly?”

She unfolded a Drakonis map.

Three migration lines.

Then Vesper reports.

Rez added the river settlements.

Ner added wolf territory.

The lines did not converge at the deep wild.

They converged south of it.

Farther west than any of the four had traveled.

Beyond maintained kingdom roads.

Beyond Drakonis patrol routes.

Beyond the wolf maps.

A region labeled with nothing.

Not because empty.

Because unknown.

Zee stared.

Then smiled.

Aurelia arrived in time to see.

“No.”

Zee looked toward her.

“I said nothing.”

“You smiled.”

“That is getting old.”

“You keep earning it.”

Rez leaned over the map.

“If the migration continues at current rate, whatever is happening reaches the convergence point in four days.”

Ner frowned.

“You said reaches.”

Rez looked at him.

“Wrong?”

“We do not know whether the animals are arriving.”

“Or leaving something else.”

Silence.

That was worse.

Zee looked toward Zareth.

The Link carried the same restless urge.

Go.

Find.

Understand.

This time Zee agreed.

Aurelia saw.

Her expression tightened.

“You are going.”

Not question.

“Yes.”

She exhaled.

No argument yet.

Progress on both sides.

“Who?”

Zee looked toward Rez.

Rez nodded.

Ner too.

Zareth’s wings spread.

All four.

Varessa frowned.

“You are fifteen.”

Zee looked toward her.

“So is Zareth.”

She stared at the Crown Prince.

Zareth stared back.

Varessa sighed.

“That argument is deeply irritating.”

Rez smiled.

“We get that often.”

Aurelia stepped toward Zee.

“This is not another political border.”

“I know.”

“Not a rescue we understand.”

“I know.”

“Not something you can assume wants help.”

“I know.”

She searched his face.

Zee let her.

Then:

“If it becomes too strange—”

“Mother.”

“No.”

He stopped.

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“You do not get to become older by interrupting me.”

Ner looked away to hide a smile.

Zee sighed.

“Fine.”

“If it becomes too strange, you leave.”

Zee thought of the deep wild.

Of antlers through his body.

Of false Aurelia calling him from the trees.

Of learning that retreat was not failure.

“I will.”

Aurelia did not fully believe him.

Neither did Zee.

But he meant it now.

That mattered.

---

They left before dawn.

No army.

No convoy.

The four.

Varessa and one Drakonis scout accompanied them until the final Dragon patrol line, then turned back by agreement.

After that, there were no kingdom markers.

No road.

Only migration.

The farther west they traveled, the stranger it became.

Wolves walked beside deer.

Vampires would have called the scent unbearable.

Zee did.

Thousands of heartbeats layered across valleys.

Animals that should never share space moved together without fighting.

Birds traveled at ground level.

Fish swam through flooded ditches beside hoofed creatures.

One enormous reptile with a translucent spine crossed their path, ignored Zareth completely, and continued west.

Ner stared.

“I want to study everything.”

Zee looked at him.

“That sounds dangerous now.”

“I know.”

“That did not stop you.”

“No.”

Rez smiled.

“Good. Self-awareness.”

By afternoon, the land began losing sound.

Not silence.

Distance.

A bird flapped ten feet away.

No sound.

Rez dropped a stone.

They heard it only after it struck.

Ner raised one hand.

Golden Mana pulsed.

The light appeared before the magical pressure reached them.

Zee frowned.

“Sound is slow.”

Ner corrected him.

“Maybe.”

Zee sighed.

“Of course.”

Then Zareth stopped.

The Dragon Link went rigid.

Ahead.

Something enormous crossed the horizon.

At first Zee thought it was a mountain.

Then it moved.

Not walking.

Drifting.

A black shape taller than castle towers passed behind distant hills.

No wings.

No obvious limbs.

Its upper body vanished into cloud.

Animals below did not flee.

They moved toward it.

Zee’s Vampire senses found no heartbeat.

Wolf instinct found no category.

Witch perception found no ordinary magic.

Dragon nature—

Dragon nature bowed.

Not Zee.

The blood.

Something deep inside his developing fourth nature pulled tight with instinct older than his own consciousness.

Not submission.

Recognition of scale.

Zee whispered:

“What is that?”

Zareth’s Link gave him nothing.

Not even a fragment.

For the first time since Zee had known him, Zareth had no Dragon memory to offer.

Ner’s Golden Mana flickered uncertainly.

Rez slowly drew his sword.

Then stopped halfway.

Put it back.

Zee looked toward him.

Rez stared at the moving shape.

“If that thing notices us, the sword is decorative.”

Zee laughed quietly.

Not because it was funny.

Because fear had returned.

Real fear.

The world had gotten bigger again.

And whatever crossed the horizon did not know or care that kings existed.

# Chapter Fifty-Five

## The Shepherd of Nothing

They followed the migration until night.

Not the black thing.

That would have been impossible.

It moved too slowly to judge distance and too strangely to judge speed.

Sometimes it appeared miles away.

Sometimes it seemed close enough to touch.

Then hills passed in front of it that should have been behind.

Ner hated it.

Zee could tell because Ner had gone silent.

That was always serious.

Rez noticed too.

“How bad?”

Ner looked toward him.

“I cannot decide whether it is large.”

Zee frowned.

“It is obviously large.”

“No.”

Ner pointed toward the horizon.

“You are assuming apparent size corresponds to distance.”

Rez looked again.

Then stopped smiling.

Ner continued.

“It may be closer and smaller.”

“Farther and larger.”

“Or…”

He hesitated.

Zee looked over.

“Or?”

“I do not know whether all of it occupies the same distance.”

Zee stared.

“That sentence was terrible.”

“I hated saying it.”

Zareth flew lower.

The Link carried discomfort.

The black shape crossed beneath a moon that momentarily disappeared behind it.

Then the moon reappeared inside the shape.

Not through a hole.

Inside.

Zee stopped walking.

“No.”

Rez looked toward him.

“That is your analysis?”

“Yes.”

“Strong.”

The migration continued around them.

Animals moved with strange calm.

None appeared exhausted.

None stopped to feed.

That finally bothered Zee enough to test something.

He approached a gray wolf traveling near the edge of the herd.

Ordinary wolf.

Mostly.

It looked at him.

No fear.

Zee crouched.

His own Wolf nature reached instinctively.

Not command.

Recognition.

Pack language without words.

The wolf’s mind felt—

Far away.

Not controlled.

Focused.

One need overwhelmed everything else.

West.

Not *go west.*

More like:

**home is west now.**

Zee recoiled.

Rez stepped closer.

“What?”

“They think they belong there.”

“Do they?”

“I do not know.”

Ner crouched beside the wolf without touching.

Golden Mana formed around one eye.

Not entering the animal.

Reading the magical boundary around it.

“There is no compulsion spell.”

“Sure?”

“Yes.”

“Curse?”

“No.”

“Possession?”

“No.”

Rez looked toward the herd.

“So nothing is forcing them.”

Ner frowned.

“Not magically.”

Zee stood.

“Instinct.”

“Changed instinct?”

“Maybe.”

Rez sighed.

Ner looked at him.

“You hate uncertainty.”

“I hate plans made from uncertainty.”

“That is different.”

“Barely.”

The wolf continued.

Zee let it.

---

They camped on a ridge.

Not because any of them wanted sleep.

Because moving in unknown territory at night while sound, distance, and animal behavior were all unreliable was stupid.

Rez said that.

Zee agreed reluctantly.

Zareth remained awake.

Of course.

His huge body curled around one side of the camp without enclosing it completely.

Not possession.

Protection.

The Dragon Link remained tense.

Zee sat near the fire.

Ner beside him.

Rez slept lightly several feet away with one hand near his sword.

The black shape remained visible.

It had not moved much.

Or had moved tremendously.

Impossible to tell.

Zee looked toward Ner.

“You are thinking too loudly.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“You cannot hear thoughts.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

“You have the face.”

Ner laughed.

“Everyone says that to you.”

“I am stealing it.”

“That is growth.”

Zee looked toward the distant shape.

“What are you thinking?”

Ner took his time.

“That the deep wild had rules we did not understand.”

“Yes.”

“This feels different.”

“How?”

“The deep wild reacted to boundaries.”

“To injury.”

“To intrusion.”

Ner looked toward the migration.

“This does not feel reactive.”

Zee understood.

“It is doing something.”

“Yes.”

“On purpose?”

“I do not know.”

A pause.

Then Ner looked toward Zee.

“You are not smiling.”

Zee frowned.

“Should I be?”

“You usually smile when you are scared.”

“That is not true.”

“It is.”

Zee thought.

Annoyingly, yes.

Fear often made him curious.

Alive.

Ready.

This felt different.

Not predator fear.

Not fight fear.

Smallness.

# Chapter Fifty-Six

## Nanda Parbat

Zee left Vesper before sunrise.

No note.

No guard.

No explanation.

Aurelia would have stopped him.

Rez would have demanded a plan.

Ner would have asked enough questions to make lying irritating.

Zareth would have felt the direction through the Link eventually and followed.

So Zee did something he had become increasingly interested in learning how to do properly.

He disappeared.

Not with magic.

That distinction mattered.

His Witch nature could conceal him.

His Vampire speed could carry him beyond watchtowers before guards finished blinking.

His Wolf senses could find every patrol route.

His developing Dragon durability could get him through terrain ordinary travelers would avoid.

But Zee wanted something none of those powers gave automatically.

Skill without supernatural advantage.

He had spent fifteen years surviving people who came for him with armies, spells, blood, claws, politics, monsters, and fear.

He could overpower most ordinary fighters.

That was becoming a problem.

Strength taught bad habits when strength always worked.

Renn had taught him that.

Voss had taught him more.

The deep wild taught him the rest.

There were things power could not simply crush.

There were moments when knowing *how* to kill mattered more than being strong enough to do it.

And somewhere in the mountains, according to whispers from killers who refused to say the name twice, there existed a place where people devoted their lives to exactly that lesson.

Nanda Parbat.

The League of Assassins.

Zee wanted what they knew.

Nothing more.

No ancient power.

No hidden bloodline.

No artifact.

Skill.

So he followed rumors east and north until roads stopped.

Then tracks.

Then smoke.

Then nothing.

That was when he knew he was close.

Someone had erased their presence too carefully.

Wolf instinct found the first mistake.

Not a footprint.

The absence of one.

A mountain hare had crossed fresh snow, then altered direction for no visible reason.

Something had occupied the space.

Something the animal sensed.

Zee crouched.

His Vampire hearing found no heartbeat nearby.

Good.

His Witch perception found a suppression veil.

Better.

His Dragon instincts warned that eyes watched from above.

Best.

Zee smiled.

“Found you.”

A blade touched the side of his throat.

He stopped smiling.

A voice behind him said, “No.”

Zee’s crimson eyes shifted sideways.

Black clothing.

Human heartbeat.

Steady.

He had not heard the assassin approach.

Interesting.

The assassin pressed the blade closer.

“We found you.”

Zee disappeared.

Vampire speed.

The man turned.

Too slow.

Zee caught his wrist.

Then stopped.

That was the point.

He had already cheated.

The assassin smiled beneath his mask.

“You came to learn and used magic before the first lesson.”

Zee frowned.

“How do you know why I came?”

“Because if you came to kill us, you would have tried already.”

Fair.

The man pulled free with a joint movement Zee did not recognize.

Zee’s grip broke.

Not through superior strength.

Angle.

Leverage.

Technique.

The assassin swept Zee’s knee.

Zee hit the snow.

A knife stopped above his heart.

Again.

Two failures.

Zee’s smile returned.

“Oh, I like this place.”

---

The League did not welcome him.

That made Zee like it more.

He was blindfolded.

Disarmed.

Searched.

His knives removed.

Then his spare knife.

Then the knife hidden in his boot.

Then the sliver of sharpened metal sewn into his sleeve.

The assassin searching him paused.

“How many weapons?”

Zee smiled beneath the blindfold.

“That depends what you count as a weapon.”

They removed his belt too.

Rude.

He was taken through mountain corridors by sound alone.

He counted turns.

Seven left.

Four right.

One descent.

Two climbs.

Twenty-three steps through colder air.

A waterfall somewhere behind stone.

Three doors.

One open courtyard.

Then someone hit him.

Zee blocked too late.

Wood cracked against his ribs.

He ripped off the blindfold.

A tall man stood across from him with a practice staff.

Older.

Gray at the temples.

Nothing supernatural in Zee’s senses.

Human.

Relaxed.

Dangerous.

The others bowed.

Master Assassin.

No name offered.

Zee did not ask.

The Master swung again.

Zee caught the staff.

The Master let go.

Zee’s balance shifted.

A knife handle struck the nerve beneath his elbow.

His arm went dead.

The Master swept his ankle.

Zee hit the stone.

Again.

Zee growled.

The Master looked down at him.

“You are powerful.”

“I know.”

“That is why you are easy to read.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

The Master continued.

“You enter every movement believing failure remains survivable.”

Zee went still.

Accurate.

“You rely on speed because few can punish a mistake.”

“Strength because few can resist.”

“Magic because it solves distance.”

“Instinct because it warns you faster than thought.”

The Master crouched.

“Take those away.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“That is why I came.”

For the first time, the Master looked interested.

“Good.”

Then he punched Zee in the throat.

Training began.

---

The first lesson was walking.

Zee hated it.

He could cross a room without sound using Vampire control.

The Master called that cheating.

“Again.”

Zee crossed.

One board whispered beneath his foot.

“Dead.”

Again.

This time no board.

His coat brushed stone.

“Dead.”

Again.

His breathing changed near the door.

“Dead.”

Again.

His shadow crossed a candle before his body did.

“Dead.”

Zee stared at the flame.

“You count shadows?”

“I count everything.”

That sentence stayed.

By evening Zee counted everything too.

Floor grain.

Airflow.

Loose stone.

Where people looked.

Where they never looked.

Where sound gathered.

How leather creaked before metal moved.

How weight transferred through hips before a strike.

How someone touched a hidden weapon without realizing.

The second lesson was anatomy.

The League taught bodies as maps.

Nerves.

Arteries.

Joints.

Tendons.

Bone angles.

Places where one finger could collapse balance.

Places where a knife ended a fight immediately.

Places where a knife looked fatal and was not.

Places where supernatural creatures differed.

Vampires required speed and separation.

Wolves required joint destruction before recovery.

Witches required hands, mouths, focus, or whatever channel their casting used.

Dragons required humility.

Demons required identification before engagement.

Zee learned.

Too fast.

At first they thought he memorized.

Then he demonstrated.

Blindfolded, he identified six different poisons by scent.

Three more by taste before anyone could stop him.

The poison master slapped the cup from his hand.

“You could die.”

Zee looked at him.

“No.”

The man frowned.

Zee smiled.

“Long story.”

His body rejected the first toxin violently.

The second burned for almost an hour.

By the third, his blood had begun adapting enough to slow absorption while his senses learned the chemical signature.

Not immunity.

Recognition.

The League watched.

Zee stopped letting them.

He learned countertracking by laying three false trails while leaving by a fourth route nobody noticed.

He learned disguise by changing posture before clothing.

A prince walked differently from a servant.

A servant looked at doors differently from a guard.

A frightened boy held his shoulders differently from a killer.

The Master caught him on the first attempt.

Not the third.

He learned to fight blind by smell.

Then the Master filled the room with herbs.

Zee switched to hearing.

Then bells.

He switched to floor vibration.

Then suspended ropes beneath his feet.

Zee smiled in the darkness.

Wolf instinct took over.

Air.

Pressure.

Movement.

A knife came from behind.

He moved before thought.

Caught the wrist.

Twisted.

The attacker hit the floor.

The blindfold stayed on.

“Again.”

They attacked six at once.

No magic.

No Vampire speed.

No supernatural strength beyond what he could carefully restrain.

Zee lost.

Then again.

Lost slower.

Again.

Two fell before him.

Again.

Four.

Again.

All six.

The Master watched from the doorway.

“You are adapting to them.”

Zee removed the blindfold.

“Yes.”

“What happens when they change?”

Zee smiled.

“I change faster.”

The Master attacked.

Zee lost.

---

Sword work came next.

The League corrected everything power had allowed Zee to ignore.

His reach was excellent.

His recovery was lazy.

His speed covered bad foot placement.

His strength allowed him to bind blades inefficiently.

The Master exploited all of it.

First duel:

Zee disarmed in eleven seconds.

Second:

Twenty-three.

Third:

Zee cut the Master’s sleeve before losing.

Fourth:

The Master used a short blade instead.

Zee lost.

Fifth:

Zee switched weapons mid-fight.

Closer.

Sixth:

No weapons.

Zee reached the Master’s throat.

The Master reached his heart.

Draw.

The seventh duel happened in rain.

The Master never touched him.

Neither did Zee.

For eight minutes they moved.

Read.

Feinted.

Tested.

Then Zee threw his sword away.

The Master frowned.

That hesitation was enough.

Zee stepped inside the blade.

Elbow to wrist.

Shoulder turn.

Two fingers beneath the jaw.

One knee behind the leg.

The Master hit the ground.

Zee’s knife stopped against his throat.

Silence.

The Master smiled.

“Better.”

Zee looked down.

“I could have done that yesterday.”

“No.”

The Master’s eyes sharpened.

“Yesterday you could have overpowered me.”

“Today you defeated me.”

Difference.

Zee understood.

That night he practiced throwing knives until he could strike by reflected sound.

Improvised weapons until a spoon became dangerous.

Escape until bindings stopped being meaningful unless magical.

Presence suppression until two League assassins passed within arm’s reach of him in a dark corridor without noticing he was there.

That one pleased him.

Vampire Zee learned to suppress even the predatory cues other Vampires read instinctively.

Heart rhythm.

Breathing pattern.

Blood scent.

Body temperature.

He learned how much his blood betrayed him.

How to mask it.

How to follow someone through a city by one drop of old blood on a cuff.

How to separate bloodlines by scent.

Human.

Witch.

Wolf.

Vampire.

Dragon.

Mixed.

His compulsion sharpened too.

Not because the League taught magic.

Because they taught control of attention.

Three guards looked into Zee’s crimson eyes during an infiltration exercise.

“Forget you saw me.”

All three obeyed.

The fourth deliberately looked away.

Zee’s voice dropped.

“Look at me.”

The man resisted.

Zee felt the resistance.

Pressed.

Not with Witch magic.

Vampire.

The man’s head turned despite himself.

Zee frowned afterward.

That had been new.

The Master noticed.

“You did not touch him.”

“No.”

“Did you compel him?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Zee looked toward his own hand.

“I do not know.”

The Master smiled faintly.

“Then do not depend on it.”

Good advice.

Wolf Zee became terrifying in pursuit.

No spell.

No Vampire speed.

Just patience.

Scent broken over water?

Track mud displacement.

Scent masked with ash?

Find crushed grass.

False trail?

Read animal avoidance.

Target hiding inside a crowd?

Hear fear.

Dragon Zee learned pain could be endured without announcing itself.

Scales could turn a knife.

Heat could reveal poison in metal.

His developing horns changed close combat geometry.

His shoulder ridges remained unfinished, sometimes swelling beneath his shirt when Dragon energy surged, but never opening.

No wings.

No full awakening.

Witch Zee changed most subtly.

Less power.

More placement.

One whispered spell to alter a hinge.

A breath of force to shift a blade half an inch.

A tiny sensory illusion to make someone hear one footstep where none existed.

Surgical.

The League approved.

Zee hated that he cared.

Then came the final test.

---

The Master Assassin hunted him at midnight.

No magic allowed unless Zee was discovered.

Every corridor was guarded.

Every exit trapped.

Every roof watched.

The rule was simple.

Survive until dawn.

Zee disappeared before the Master finished explaining.

At first, the hunt worked as expected.

The Master found a disturbed curtain.

A missing rooftop tile.

A footprint deliberately placed in dust.

He followed.

Then stopped.

Too easy.

He turned.

Found another trace.

Also deliberate.

The Master smiled.

Zee was countertracking.

Good.

He changed route.

For twenty minutes he found nothing.

Then one of his assassins vanished.

Not dead.

Unconscious inside a storage chamber.

No sound.

Another disappeared.

Then another.

The Master stopped hunting Zee.

He began hunting the pattern.

Wrong.

There was no pattern.

That was the lesson.

Zee used Vampire senses without Vampire speed.

Wolf instinct without pursuit.

Witch precision without visible spellwork.

Dragon endurance to remain motionless in freezing water beneath a bridge for seven minutes while two assassins searched above him.

Then ordinary assassin skill for the rest.

Hours passed.

The Master found no target.

Near dawn he entered the highest courtyard.

Empty.

Snow falling.

He stopped.

Something was wrong.

No guards.

He turned.

Nobody.

His hand moved toward his sword.

A knife touched the artery beneath his jaw.

Zee stood behind him.

Completely silent.

Not even the Master had heard him.

The Master smiled slowly.

“When?”

“Six minutes ago.”

“You were behind me six minutes?”

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“I was above you.”

The Master looked toward the roofline.

Then understood.

Zee had not survived the hunt.

He had reorganized it.

Removed observers.

Driven the Master through controlled routes.

Predicted every correction.

Then taken the final position.

The Master asked, “Why am I alive?”

Zee could feel the pulse beneath the blade.

One movement.

Done.

He enjoyed knowing that.

That was different now.

Not rage.

Not hunger.

Control.

“I came here to learn how to kill.”

The Master waited.

Zee lowered the knife.

“I already knew how to choose.”

The Master turned.

For the first time, something close to respect entered his face.

“You surpassed the lesson.”

Zee shook his head.

“No.”

He looked toward the knife.

“I made it mine.”

Then he left Nanda Parbat before sunrise.

No ceremony.

No oath.

No League membership.

No extended farewell.

He had what he came for.

Skill.

---

Aurelia knew something was wrong the moment Zee walked into Vesper.

Not because he looked injured.

He did not.

Not because his clothes had changed.

Barely.

Because she did not hear him enter.

Aurelia turned sharply in the private solar.

Zee stood three steps behind her.

She stared.

“How long have you been there?”

Her eyes narrowed.

“Zee.”

He smiled.

“Hi, Mother.”

Stopped.

Looked at Zee.

The knife on the table.

Aurelia’s hand.

Distance to the door.

Zee frowned.

“Nothing.”

Ner arrived next.

Zee’s attention cataloged automatically.

Golden Mana dormant.

Left sleeve loose enough to conceal a blade.

Weight balanced.

No injury.

Pulse slightly elevated because he had hurried.

Ner stopped.

Zee realized.

Immediately looked away.

“Sorry.”

That made Ner more worried.

Zareth landed outside.

The Dragon Link opened.

Then recoiled.

Not from Zee.

From the difference.

Sharper.

Quieter.

Predatory focus disciplined into stillness.

Zareth lowered his head.

Question.

Zee touched his snout.

“I am fine.”

Aurelia folded her arms.

“Where were you?”

Zee hesitated.

That was enough.

Rez stared.

“Yes.”

Ner’s face hardened.

“For how long?”

“That is not an answer.”

Zee looked toward him.

Automatically saw three ways to disable his casting without injuring him.

His stomach turned.

There.

That was the cost.

The League had taught him too well.

He looked at Rez.

Knee.

Wrist.

Carotid.

Blind angle.

Aurelia.

Never.

His mind still cataloged.

Weapon hand.

Heart position.

Dragon-Witch durability.

Zareth.

Eyes.

Wing joints.

Neck scales.

Zee took one step backward.

Ner noticed.

Zee looked at his hands.

“I can see it.”

Rez frowned.

“See what?”

Zee looked around the room.

Three exits.

Two hidden blades.

Four breakable sightlines.

One balcony route.

Seven objects usable as weapons.

Distances.

Timing.

Bodies.

Weak points.

Kill opportunities.

“All of it.”

Aurelia’s face changed.

Not fear.

Concern.

“Who taught you?”

Zee looked at her.

“The League of Assassins.”

Silence.

Rez blinked.

Ner stared.

Zareth’s Link erupted with anger.

“I know.”

Slowly.

Hated himself for it.

Mother.

Safe.

Still.

Good.

Silence.

The servant stared.
