# Chapter Sixty-Four

## Fire Over Drakonis

Zareth did not ask Zee to come.

The Dragon Link did not work that way.

It gave Zee heat.

Smoke.

Blood.

A mountain collapsing beneath claws.

Then Zareth’s rage.

That was enough.

Zee left Darkheart before the eastern gates finished opening.

Rez came with him.

Ner followed.

No argument.

They reached Drakonis under a red sky.

Not sunset.

Fire.

Three mountain watchtowers burned along the western ridge.

Dragons filled the air.

Not fleeing.

Fighting.

Zareth was already among them.

He struck another Dragon from the sky.

The enemy twisted.

Black armor covered its chest.

Not Drakonis.

Zee smelled foreign Dragon blood before they landed.

“Who are they?”

Rez looked upward.

“Not here to negotiate.”

Ner’s Gold spread over his hands.

“That narrows it down.”

Zee’s crimson-and-gold eyes shifted.

Slits.

The Link opened.

Zareth sent images fast.

Foreign Dragon mercenaries.

Hired.

Targeting royal nesting grounds.

Not him specifically.

Destroy hatcheries.

Break Drakonis succession strength.

Force the Dragon Queen into border concessions.

Zee’s face hardened.

“Someone hired them to hit the hatcheries.”

Rez stopped.

“That is war.”

“Yes.”

Zareth hit the ground nearby.

His true Dragon body was bloodied.

One wing membrane torn.

Still standing.

Still furious.

Zee approached.

Zareth lowered his head.

The Link carried one clear demand.

**Do not take this from me.**

Zee understood.

This was Drakonis.

Zareth’s kingdom.

His fight.

Zee nodded.

“Lead.”

The Dragon Prince’s eyes burned.

Then he turned.

Good.

---

They did not fight as rescuers.

They fought as reinforcements.

Zareth commanded the air.

Three Drakonis squadrons split at his signal.

One drove attackers high.

One cut off retreat.

One protected the lower nesting valleys.

Zee stayed on the ground at first.

Wolf senses.

Blood.

Smoke.

Movement.

He found six foreign fighters trying to enter through a narrow ravine.

Two Dragons in human form.

Four armed mercenaries.

The first man never saw Zee.

Knife.

Silent.

The second did.

Barely.

Zee caught his wrist.

Twisted.

One short movement.

Done.

The Dragon shifted halfway.

Scales spread.

Zee hit him before transformation completed.

Vampire speed.

Assassin placement.

One precise strike beneath the jaw.

Then Witchcraft.

“Still.”

Crimson force locked the Dragon’s body for one second.

One second was enough.

Zee drove him into the cliff.

The second Dragon attacked from behind.

Zee smelled the blood before hearing movement.

Wolf instinct turned him.

Claws met claws.

Dragon force slammed into Zee’s ribs.

His dark crimson-black scales held.

Pain.

Not failure.

Zee smiled.

The attacker saw the horns.

The eyes.

The heat.

Then froze.

“You.”

Zee’s expression did not change.

Recognition again.

Reputation.

Useful.

“The Crimson Demonic Dragon.”

“I really hate that name.”

The Dragon backed away.

Good.

Fear without effort.

Zee stepped forward.

The Dragon attacked anyway.

Better.

Zee caught the throat.

Vampire strength.

Wolf balance.

Dragon durability.

He drove the enemy down.

Fangs descended.

The Dragon’s eyes widened.

Zee smelled old enchanted blood in him.

Witch mixture.

Foreign.

Interesting.

He fed.

Not because necessary.

Because he wanted to know.

Dragon blood entered hot.

His evolved Dragon nature reacted immediately.

No copied flame.

No new species trait.

Just adaptation pressure.

His scales warmed.

His body recognized the foreign enchantment in the blood and rejected it before it could spread.

Zee drank until the Dragon weakened badly.

Then stopped.

The Dragon stared.

Surprised to be alive.

Zee wiped his mouth.

“Who hired you?”

Silence.

Zee crouched.

“Do not make me ask twice.”

The Dragon tried to resist compulsion by looking away.

Zee barely cared anymore.

“Answer.”

Predatory pressure entered the command.

Vampire will.

Blood recognition.

Voice.

The Dragon’s jaw tightened.

Resistance.

Strong.

Zee pushed harder.

Blood vessels burst in one eye.

The Dragon gasped.

“Lord Sevrik.”

Rez arrived behind Zee.

“Where?”

“Eastern Vale.”

“Why Drakonis?”

“Trade passage.”

“Whose passage?”

The Dragon shook.

“His.”

Zee looked at Rez.

Different attacker.

Different motive.

Good.

No grand alliance.

Just greed.

Rez’s face hardened.

“Keep him alive.”

Zee stood.

“He is yours.”

The prisoner stared at him.

Then realized Zee had decided not to kill him.

Relief.

Zee noticed.

Enjoyed that too.

---

The hatcheries survived.

Barely.

One lower nesting chamber collapsed.

No hatchlings died.

That mattered most.

Three Drakonis guards did.

Seven attackers surrendered.

Twelve died.

Five escaped.

Zareth landed on the highest ridge after the battle.

Blood covered his claws.

One side of his face was burned.

He looked older than twenty-one.

Not weaker.

More royal.

The Dragon Queen arrived behind him.

She did not ask Zee what happened.

She asked Zareth.

Good.

Zareth shifted through the Link and Dragon gestures.

Attack route.

Numbers.

Casualties.

Names.

Lord Sevrik.

Trade passage.

The Queen listened.

Then looked toward Zee.

“You fed from one.”

“Yes.”

No apology.

“Why?”

“Information.”

“And?”

Zee looked toward the surviving foreign Dragon being guarded below.

“He lived.”

The Queen’s expression changed slightly.

Not approval.

Evaluation.

Then she looked back at her son.

“What do you recommend?”

Zareth went still.

Zee did too.

This was new.

Not because Zareth had never advised.

Because the Queen asked in front of everyone.

The Crown Prince looked over the damaged ridge.

Then sent his answer.

Not revenge.

Not immediately.

Secure hatcheries.

Close western air route.

Send demands to Sevrik.

Prepare force.

If refused—

strike.

Zee smiled faintly.

Rez noticed.

Future ruler.

The Queen nodded.

“So ordered.”

Zareth’s posture changed.

Pride.

Responsibility.

Weight.

Zee knew that feeling now.

King recognized Crown Prince.

No one needed to say it.

---

They left Drakonis after midnight.

Not because everything was safe.

Because Zareth stayed.

His kingdom needed him.

Zee did not ask him to come back to Darkheart.

That would have been wrong.

The Link stretched as Zee, Rez, and Ner traveled west.

Zareth remained behind.

Still connected.

Still his own.

Rez rode beside Zee.

“You are quiet.”

“I am thinking.”

“Dangerous.”

Ner looked over.

“About Sevrik?”

Zee nodded.

Rez frowned.

“Drakonis will handle him.”

“Yes.”

“And you are going to let them.”

“Yes.”

Rez looked suspicious.

Zee smiled.

“I am King now. I understand jurisdiction.”

“That may be the scariest thing you have ever said.”

Ner laughed.

Then suddenly stopped.

Zee turned.

Ner’s face changed.

Pure Gold flashed beneath his skin.

“What?”

Ner touched his throat.

“Blood.”

“Whose?”

“I do not know.”

His voice deepened involuntarily.

A low resonance moved through the night.

Zee felt it in his own veins.

Then Ner looked toward the road ahead.

“Mine.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“What?”

Ner lifted one hand.

A thin red line had appeared across his palm.

No wound.

No blade.

Blood beaded anyway.

Rez stopped his horse.

“That is not normal.”

Ner stared at the line.

“It is calling me.”

Zee went completely still.

Not panicked.

Not loud.

Worse.

Calm.

Someone had reached into Ner’s blood from a distance.

That was enough.

The road home could wait.

Zee turned east.

Rez sighed.

“Where are we going?”

Zee’s voice became very quiet.

“To find who touched him.”

And this time he did not intend to wait for a second attempt.

# Chapter Sixty-Five

## Before They Could Try Again

The blood-call came from a ruined monastery three valleys east of Darkheart.

No active kingdom claimed it.

No road led there.

That was probably why whoever chose it believed they were safe.

They were wrong.

Ner tracked the resonance.

Zee tracked Ner.

Not because Ner was helpless.

Because blood was being pulled from him in tiny amounts every few minutes.

Not enough to kill.

Enough to map.

Test.

Measure.

Someone wanted to understand what the Witch Bloodsong had become.

Ner hated that more than pain.

“They are sampling me.”

Rez looked over.

“From this distance?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Ner’s jaw tightened.

“I do not know.”

Zee’s Wolf scent found no trail yet.

Vampire blood sense found Ner everywhere.

Too much.

Every drop taken from him left a faint path through the air like a pressure line.

Zee’s Crimson adaptations noticed the foreign influence woven around it.

Not magic he knew.

Not standard curse.

Not compulsion.

Something blood-based.

Ner stopped.

“There.”

The monastery sat below them.

Broken walls.

Collapsed tower.

No visible guards.

Rez studied the ridge.

“Too quiet.”

Zee already knew.

“Six outside.”

Ner looked over.

“You can hear them?”

“No.”

Wolf scent.

Ash.

Leather.

Old blood.

One hidden beneath stone.

Two downwind.

Three on the roof.

Zee’s assassin training filled the rest.

“Maybe more inside.”

Rez drew his sword.

“We go together.”

Zee looked at him.

“Yes.”

That surprised him.

Rez smiled.

“You are learning.”

“Do not ruin it.”

Ner flexed his fingers.

Pure Gold formed.

Then his voice dropped.

“I want whoever is doing this alive.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner’s eyes were hard.

“For now.”

Good.

His choice.

Not Zee’s.

---

The first guard disappeared without sound.

Zee took him from behind.

Pressure point.

Unconscious.

Second guard turned.

Ner whispered one note.

The man’s blood pressure dropped.

His knees hit stone.

Rez caught him before his head struck.

“Useful.”

Ner looked annoyed.

“I know.”

Third guard attacked from above.

Rez moved first.

Blue-White Mana froze the ledge.

The assassin slipped.

Zee caught him by the throat.

Not to save him.

To keep him quiet.

One squeeze.

Unconscious.

No deaths yet.

That mattered because Ner wanted answers.

The roof guards lasted less than a minute.

Then the monastery woke.

Wards lit.

Red.

Not Gold.

Blood magic.

Zee felt them immediately.

His Witch nature reacted.

One hand lifted.

“Break.”

The nearest ward cracked.

Not all.

Good.

Resistance meant structure.

Ner stepped closer.

“Wait.”

Zee stopped.

Ner studied the remaining lines.

“These are not trying to keep us out.”

Rez frowned.

“Then what?”

“Keep something in.”

Silence.

Zee smelled fear.

Inside.

Many heartbeats.

Not fighters.

Captives.

His face changed.

No longer an investigation.

Now personal morality had entered.

Ner heard it too.

“They have people.”

Rez drew his sword fully.

“Then fast.”

They entered.

---

The monastery basement held nineteen prisoners.

Human.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Two mixed-bloods Zee did not know.

All restrained.

All alive.

Thin tubes carried blood from their arms into glass channels along the walls.

Ner stopped breathing.

Zee did not.

He became cold.

A woman in white robes stood at the center.

Not afraid.

That was interesting.

She held one hand over a bowl filled with dark red liquid.

Ner’s blood.

Zee knew immediately.

The woman smiled.

“There he is.”

Ner’s voice sharpened.

“My blood.”

“Yes.”

“Give it back.”

The woman laughed.

“No.”

Zee looked at her.

No obvious weapon.

Witch.

Experienced.

Four guards.

Two hidden behind the columns.

One exit below.

Rez caught Zee’s glance.

Understood.

He moved left.

Ner moved right.

The woman watched Zee.

“You are quieter than expected.”

Zee said nothing.

“You killed a God.”

Still nothing.

“You created him.”

She pointed toward Ner.

Ner’s face hardened.

“I am standing here.”

The woman ignored him.

Mistake.

Ner spoke one word.

“Look.”

Her blood answered before her head did.

She turned toward him.

Pure Gold flashed.

Bloodsong resonance struck the bowl.

Every drop of stolen blood rose.

Not into Ner.

Away from her.

The woman’s smile vanished.

Zee moved.

Vampire speed.

Knife at her throat.

No theatrics.

“Now you can talk.”

Her guards attacked.

Rez intercepted two.

Blue-White Mana redirected the third into a pillar.

Ner’s Gold sealed the fourth inside a narrow boundary.

The hidden guards emerged.

Zee did not look.

His Wolf instincts already knew.

One clawed hand swept backward.

Caught the first across the chest.

The second tried a poisoned needle.

Zee caught his wrist without turning.

Nanda Parbat.

“Wrong hand.”

Snap.

The guard screamed.

Zee looked at the woman.

“Who are you?”

She smiled despite the knife.

“Scholar.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

“Bad answer.”

She swallowed.

“Maera Sol.”

“Why Ner?”

“Because he should not exist.”

Ner laughed once.

“No.”

Maera looked toward him.

“You died.”

“Yes.”

“And returned with Witch nature intact.”

“Yes.”

“Vampire traits.”

“Yes.”

“Voice resonance.”

Ner’s face went cold.

“Yes.”

“You are proof that—”

Zee pressed the blade closer.

“Careful.”

Maera looked toward him.

Then understood.

He was not protecting Ner from information.

He was warning her not to speak about Ner as an object.

Different.

She adjusted.

“You are proof that Zee’s blood can alter supernatural inheritance.”

Zee went still.

That was new.

Ner looked at him.

Rez did too.

Maera continued.

“We wanted to know whether it can happen again.”

Zee’s face emptied.

Behind her, nineteen captives bled into channels.

“Using them.”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

No coercion.

No remorse.

Zee’s darkness made the decision before she finished breathing.

But Ner wanted answers.

So Zee waited.

Barely.

Ner stepped closer.

“What did you learn?”

Maera smiled.

“That your blood is impossible.”

“Try harder.”

“Your Witch nature remains independent.”

“Yes.”

“The Vampire blood did not suppress it.”

“Yes.”

“And there is a third resonance inside you.”

Ner’s eyes narrowed.

“What third?”

Maera opened her mouth.

Bloodsong hit first.

Ner’s voice changed.

Not loud.

Layered.

“Tell me.”

Maera stiffened.

Her blood answered.

Not compulsion exactly.

Siren-Vampire influence carried through circulation.

She fought it.

Strong mind.

Blood ward.

Ner pushed harder.

Pure Gold formed around the effect, containing it to one target.

Precise.

Controlled.

“Tell me.”

Maera’s eyes filled with rage.

“Siren.”

Silence.

Ner froze.

Zee’s pupils shifted human for one heartbeat.

“What?”

Maera gasped as the Bloodsong released.

“Dormant bloodline.”

“Old.”

“Very old.”

“Your mother’s line carried traces.”

Ner stared.

His face gave away nothing.

Zee saw the impact anyway.

Siren.

A name finally.

Not full explanation.

Enough.

Ner looked toward the prisoners.

“What did you do to them?”

“Testing compatibility.”

Rez’s expression hardened.

“How many died?”

Maera did not answer.

Zee smelled the lie before she spoke.

“None.”

Zee smiled.

Small.

Terrible.

“Wrong.”

Maera looked at him.

He could smell death on her clothing.

Old blood.

Many sources.

“Seventeen?”

Her face changed.

There.

Zee leaned closer.

“More.”

Ner whispered:

“Zee.”

Not stop.

He looked at Ner.

Ner’s eyes were Golden and dark-red.

His expression was hard.

“I am done asking.”

That was permission only for himself.

Not Zee.

Still, Zee understood.

Maera did too.

She panicked.

Finally.

“Wait.”

Zee’s smile disappeared.

“No.”

He killed her quickly.

Knife across the throat.

No feeding.

Not every death needed appetite.

Maera collapsed.

The guards froze.

Zee looked at them.

“Anyone here by force?”

Two immediately raised their hands.

Truth.

He smelled it.

The rest did not.

Rez moved.

“Take the two.”

Ner’s Gold sealed the others.

Zee looked toward the blood channels.

Then at the captives.

His hand lifted.

Every glass line shattered at once.

Silent Witchcraft.

Ner moved among the prisoners.

Bloodsong guided him to the weakest.

Rez organized release.

Zee stood in the center.

Not helping yet.

Thinking.

The old Zee would have stopped here.

Rescue.

Capture.

Return home.

Let law decide the rest.

The twenty-one-year-old King thought farther.

“Who funded this?”

One surviving guard looked away.

Zee heard his heartbeat jump.

There.

He walked over.

“Name.”

The guard resisted.

Zee’s predatory presence filled the room.

Vampire.

Not Witch.

“Name.”

No eye contact.

The guard clenched his teeth.

Zee’s will pressed through voice and blood recognition.

Resistance cracked.

“House Veylan.”

Rez looked over.

“Where?”

“South.”

“Distance?”

“Two days.”

Ner turned.

“Zee.”

He knew that face.

Not because Zee was angry.

Because he was planning.

“What?”

“You are not going tonight.”

Zee looked toward nineteen bleeding prisoners.

Then the blood channels.

Then Maera.

“No.”

Ner relaxed slightly.

Zee continued.

“I am going tomorrow.”

Rez sighed.

“There it is.”

Ner’s jaw tightened.

“What are you planning?”

Zee answered honestly.

“To make sure they cannot do this again.”

That could mean several things.

Everyone heard the darker one.

Rez approached.

“We know one facility.”

“Funded by one House.”

“According to one guard.”

“Yes.”

Zee looked at him.

“I will verify.”

That mattered.

No reckless massacre.

No immediate assumption.

But also no waiting for House Veylan to strike twice.

The philosophy was changing.

Ner saw it.

“You are going after them before they come again.”

Zee’s eyes shifted into slits.

“Yes.”

No apology.

No guilt.

No pretending he was merely responding.

He looked toward the rescued captives.

“They already came.”

That distinction satisfied him.

For now.

By dawn, all nineteen prisoners were alive.

The two coerced guards had been separated for questioning.

House Veylan’s name had been confirmed through ledgers, payments, and blood-sealed correspondence.

No guessing.

No rumor.

Evidence.

Rez read the final document.

Then looked at Zee.

“Well.”

Zee was cleaning one knife.

“What?”

“They funded it.”

“Yes.”

“Authorized the deaths.”

“Yes.”

“Ordered continued experimentation on Ner.”

Zee’s hand stopped.

Human pupils vanished.

Slits.

Rez noticed.

“So.”

Zee sheathed the knife.

“So now I go south.”

Ner stepped beside him.

“I am coming.”

Zee looked over.

Not to protect him.

Not to stop him.

His choice.

“Good.”

Rez sighed.

“I suppose I am coming too.”

Zee smiled.

“Of course.”

Far away, Zareth remained in Drakonis handling his own kingdom’s war.

The Link carried distance, heat, and fierce attention.

Not every problem required all four physically present.

The bond remained anyway.

Zee walked toward the monastery exit.

Once, enemies attacked his people and Zee waited until blood was spilled before hunting them.

Now someone had reached for Ner once.

Zee had found the hand.

Tomorrow he intended to find the arm attached to it.

And for the first time, the difference between protection and elimination had begun to feel very small.

# Chapter Sixty-Six

## House Veylan

House Veylan expected soldiers.

Zee brought six people.

Himself.

Rez.

Ner.

Two Darkheart scouts.

And one former prisoner who knew the southern estate.

That was enough.

The Veylan manor sat behind white stone walls covered in blood wards.

Ner studied them from the tree line.

“Layered.”

Rez crouched beside him.

“Alarm?”

“Alarm. Binding. Identification.”

Zee looked toward the western wall.

“And the weakness?”

Ner smiled faintly.

“You assume there is one.”

“There is always one.”

“There are three.”

Better.

Ner pointed.

“The upper wards identify blood.”

“Lower wards identify magic.”

“The center line reacts to movement.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

“You can bypass all three?”

Zee’s eyes shifted into slits.

“Yes.”

“Without smashing the wall?”

Zee looked offended.

“I have learned subtlety.”

Ner coughed.

Rez smiled.

Zee disappeared.

---

The first guard never saw him.

Zee crossed the blood ward using presence suppression.

His Vampire heartbeat slowed.

Body heat dropped.

Crimson Mana pulled inward until the ward barely registered him.

When the movement line reacted, he froze.

Not magically.

Perfectly.

The pulse passed over him.

Nothing.

Then Wolf Zee took over.

Scent.

Oil.

Leather.

Three guards.

One hidden above.

Two below.

Zee moved between them silently.

Pressure point.

One down.

Knife handle.

Second.

The third turned.

Zee caught his mouth.

“Sleep.”

Witchcraft touched the nervous system with surgical precision.

The guard collapsed.

The fourth saw everything.

He reached for a bell.

Zee looked up.

“Don’t.”

Vampire compulsion struck before the man met his eyes.

The hand froze.

Zee climbed the wall.

“Open the gate.”

The guard resisted.

Strong blood ward.

Zee pressed.

“Open it.”

The man’s face tightened.

Then his hand moved.

The gate unlocked.

Rez entered first.

“Subtle.”

Zee smiled.

“Told you.”

Ner followed.

“Terrifying.”

“Also told you.”

---

House Veylan was not empty.

That was the problem.

Servants.

Children.

Guards.

Healers.

Stable workers.

People who had nothing to do with blood experiments.

Zee smelled them all.

His first instinct was not slaughter.

Good.

His second was to find the people who mattered.

Better.

Rez unfolded the seized monastery ledger.

“Three names.”

“Lord Veylan.”

“Lady Coris.”

“Master Alven.”

Ner’s face hardened.

“Alven signed the orders involving me.”

Zee looked toward him.

“Then he is yours to question.”

Ner nodded.

No argument.

They split.

Rez handled guards and evacuation.

Ner took the eastern archive with one scout.

Zee went upstairs.

Alone.

---

Lord Veylan was eating breakfast.

He looked up when Zee entered.

Did not panic.

Interesting.

“King Darkheart.”

Zee closed the door.

“Lord Veylan.”

The man glanced toward the window.

Two exits.

One hidden knife.

Poison ring.

Old knee injury.

Recent Vampire blood in his system.

Not enough to turn.

Enough to enhance stamina temporarily.

Zee noticed everything.

Veylan smiled.

“I wondered when you would come.”

“Then you should have left.”

“I considered it.”

“Why didn’t you?”

The man lifted his cup.

“Because kings who run lose everything.”

Zee’s expression barely changed.

“Kings who experiment on captives lose more.”

Veylan set the cup down.

“So that is what Maera told you.”

“She did not get much time.”

The smile weakened.

Good.

Veylan stood.

“We studied a phenomenon.”

“Ner is not a phenomenon.”

“No.”

Veylan looked toward the door.

“He is proof.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Careful.”

Veylan smiled again.

“There it is.”

“What?”

“The creature underneath the crown.”

Zee crossed the room without Vampire speed.

Slow.

Predatory.

“You funded seventeen deaths.”

Veylan’s expression cooled.

“Collateral.”

Zee stopped.

“That word usually means someone else paid.”

Silence.

Then Veylan moved.

Fast.

Not Human fast.

Vampire blood enhancement.

He threw the poisoned ring-blade.

Zee flicked two fingers.

The weapon turned in the air.

Passed Veylan’s face.

Embedded in the wall.

Zee kept walking.

Veylan cast.

Not Witchcraft.

Blood sigils flashed beneath his sleeves.

Foreign magic.

Zee smelled Demon residue.

“Interesting.”

The binding struck.

Crimson-black chains wrapped Zee’s arms.

Veylan smiled.

“I prepared for you.”

Zee looked down.

The chains tightened.

Pain.

Suppression.

Demon residue.

Blood magic.

All things his body had met before.

Not this exact combination.

But enough.

Crimson Adaptation stirred.

His scales darkened.

Heat rose.

The chains began smoking.

Veylan’s smile vanished.

Zee closed both hands.

“Break.”

The entire structure shattered.

Veylan backed away.

Zee grabbed him by the throat.

One-handed.

Lifted him.

No rage.

No speech.

Just strength.

Veylan choked.

Zee looked into his eyes.

“Who else knows about Ner?”

The man resisted.

Blood ward again.

Zee’s Vampire dominance pressed harder.

“Who?”

Veylan’s nose bled.

“Three Houses.”

“Names.”

Resistance cracked.

“Veylan.”

“Ors.”

“Mereth.”

Zee’s grip tightened.

“Who ordered the monastery deaths?”

Veylan’s heartbeat changed.

Fear.

Truth approaching.

“I did.”

Good.

Zee smiled faintly.

Veylan saw.

Panicked.

“Wait.”

Zee’s fangs descended.

“You had your warning.”

He fed.

Human blood mixed with foreign Vampire blood and Demonic enhancers.

Strange.

Zee’s body separated them almost immediately.

Human nourishment.

Artificial Vampire enhancement.

Demon contamination.

Three layers.

His blood sense had become frightening.

He drank until Veylan weakened badly.

Then stopped.

Not mercy.

Information first.

Veylan gasped.

Zee leaned close.

“You are going to watch your House survive without you.”

The man stared.

“What?”

Zee snapped his neck.

Final.

---

Ner found Master Alven alive.

Barely.

Golden Mana held him against a wall while blood floated in thin red strands around the room.

Rez entered just after Zee.

“What happened?”

Ner’s voice stayed calm.

“He tried to use my blood against me.”

Alven coughed.

“I almost succeeded.”

Ner looked at him.

Then hummed.

One low note.

Every stolen sample in the room trembled.

Alven screamed.

Ner’s Bloodsong pulled the samples out of their containers and into a suspended ring.

Not into himself.

Around him.

Control.

Precision.

Pure Gold separated each drop.

Zee watched.

Proud.

Not because Ner needed him.

Because he did not.

Ner looked toward Alven.

“How many people?”

The man said nothing.

Ner’s eyes darkened red beneath Gold.

“Answer.”

Bloodsong pressed through his circulation.

Alven’s body locked.

“Forty-two.”

Rez went still.

“Experiments?”

“Yes.”

“Deaths?”

“Twenty-nine.”

Ner’s face changed.

No softness.

“Why?”

“To reproduce you.”

Silence.

Zee’s darkness moved.

Ner saw.

Raised one hand.

Not to stop Zee.

To claim his own choice.

“This one is mine.”

Zee nodded.

Alven laughed weakly.

“You think killing me proves—”

Ner whispered:

“Quiet.”

His blood obeyed before his mouth did.

Silence.

Ner stepped closer.

“I am not killing you because I am unique.”

His Gold tightened.

“I am killing you because twenty-nine people died so you could satisfy curiosity.”

Alven’s eyes widened.

Ner’s voice dropped lower.

“Still.”

His heart stopped.

One command.

One Bloodsong strike.

No spectacle.

Ner released him.

The body fell.

Zee looked at him.

“You all right?”

“No.”

Good answer.

Ner looked toward Zee.

“But I do not regret it.”

Zee understood.

That mattered more.

---

They did not destroy House Veylan.

That surprised everyone.

Rez found the servants first.

Seventy-three people.

Only eleven had known what the ruling family funded.

Four had objected.

Two had secretly helped prisoners escape.

Zee heard all of it.

He did not punish bloodline.

He punished choice.

Lady Coris confessed before Ner questioned her.

She had known.

Signed payments.

Never visited the monastery.

Still guilty.

Zee sentenced her to imprisonment.

Not death.

Rez looked at him afterward.

“Why?”

“Veylan confessed.”

“Alven enjoyed it.”

“Coris enabled it.”

Different lines.

Rez nodded.

Reasoning.

Not softness.

The estate changed hands by sunset.

Not to Zee personally.

To the surviving Veylan council under Darkheart oversight until the prisoners’ families were compensated and the research network dismantled.

People whispered anyway.

House Veylan had been taken in one day.

Its lord dead.

Its secrets exposed.

Its power broken.

King Zee Darkheart had entered with six people.

The story spread faster than the truth.

By nightfall, some versions claimed Zee killed everyone.

Others said he drank the entire ruling family.

One claimed he transformed into a crimson beast with six horns.

Zee hated that one.

Rez loved it.

Ner laughed for ten straight minutes.

Then a Darkheart messenger arrived.

Blood on his coat.

“Majesty.”

Zee turned.

“What happened?”

“Eastern wall.”

“Attack?”

The messenger shook his head.

“No.”

That was worse.

He handed Zee a black metal box.

No seal.

No mark.

Only one thing inside.

A severed Dragon scale.

Zareth’s.

Zee’s face emptied.

Then the Dragon Link struck.

Pain.

Not Zareth.

Someone else forcing pain through the bond.

The world had found a new direction.

Zee stood.

No panic.

No shouting.

Just one sentence.

“Find the route.”

And everyone in the room understood that House Veylan had just become yesterday’s problem.

# Chapter Sixty-Seven

## The Hand on the Dragon Link

Zareth was not captured.

That was the first thing Zee learned.

The second was worse.

Someone had found a way to touch the Dragon Link from outside.

Not control it.

Not enter it fully.

Touch.

Enough to send pain.

Enough to make Zee think Zareth was hurt when he was not.

Enough to prove the bond had become visible to someone else.

Zareth arrived at Darkheart before midnight.

Furious.

Uninjured except for one missing shoulder scale.

The same scale inside the box.

Zee stood in the courtyard.

The Link opened instantly.

Zareth showed him what happened.

Drakonis council chamber.

A visiting envoy.

Human-shaped.

Face hidden behind white cloth.

No heartbeat Zee could detect through the memory.

The envoy asked to see the Crown Prince privately.

Zareth refused.

The figure threw powder.

Not poison.

Something that made Dragon Mana flare uncontrollably.

Then touched one scale.

Cut it free.

Escaped through a collapsing shadow.

Zareth chased.

Lost the trail.

Then pain hit the Link.

Artificial.

Inserted.

Ner listened carefully.

“So they did not hurt you.”

Zareth growled.

Zee translated.

“No.”

Rez folded his arms.

“They wanted Zee to react.”

Zee looked at the scale.

“Or prove they could reach the bond.”

Ner stepped closer.

Pure Gold traced around the metal box.

“Something is attached.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“What?”

“Not spellwork I know.”

“Blood?”

“No.”

“Dragon Mana?”

“Partly.”

Ner looked toward Zareth.

“Your scale is carrying an imprint of the Link.”

Zareth’s head snapped toward him.

Zee went still.

“Can you remove it?”

“I do not know.”

Good.

Ner studied.

Rez paced once.

“Do not destroy the scale.”

Zee looked toward him.

“Why?”

“It is bait.”

“Yes.”

“Which means destroying it might trigger whatever they expect.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“Future king.”

Rez glared.

“Current idiot.”

Ner almost laughed.

Zareth did not.

The Link had become violated territory.

Dragons understood that differently.

Zee felt his anger beneath everything.

Not fear.

Offense.

Possession of self.

Someone had touched what belonged only to them.

Zee understood.

He did not need to calm him.

He felt the same.

---

Ner discovered the first rule an hour later.

The imprint reacted to Zee.

Not proximity.

Attention.

When Zee focused directly on the scale, the hidden pattern brightened.

When he looked away, it faded.

Ner frowned.

“It is reading recognition.”

Rez looked at him.

“Meaning?”

“It wants Zee to know it is there.”

Zee leaned against the table.

“Dramatic.”

Ner stared.

“You are one to talk.”

Fair.

Zareth sent impatience through the Link.

Zee looked at him.

“You want to hunt.”

Immediate agreement.

Wolf instinct inside Zee answered.

Yes.

Rez saw.

“No.”

Zee frowned.

“No?”

“You have no trail.”

“I have the scale.”

“You have bait.”

Ner nodded.

“Rez is right.”

Zee looked betrayed.

Ner continued.

“We need to make it think the bait worked.”

Silence.

Then Zee smiled.

That one was darker.

Rez noticed.

“There.”

“What?”

“That face means you like the plan before we have one.”

“I like deception.”

“Nanda Parbat ruined you.”

“Improved me.”

Zareth’s amusement finally entered the Link.

Good.

Still them.

Ner placed both hands over the box.

“If this imprint reads Zee’s attention, I may be able to make it believe he is focused on it even when he is not.”

Rez understood.

“Fake the signal.”

“Yes.”

Zee stepped closer.

“And when someone checks?”

“We follow.”

Rez pointed.

“Not you.”

Zee’s expression cooled.

“Explain.”

“If the trap is designed for you, you are the obvious thing they will watch.”

Zee hated when logic worked against him.

Rez continued.

“Ner and I follow the magical trace.”

“Zareth takes sky.”

“You remain visible.”

Zee stared.

“At Darkheart.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

Ner looked at him.

“You are King.”

“That is not an argument.”

“It is today.”

Zee’s jaw tightened.

Zareth sent agreement.

Traitor.

Zee sighed.

“Fine.”

Rez blinked.

“That was easy.”

“I am growing.”

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“Also I already thought of another way.”

Everyone looked at him.

Of course.

---

Zee stayed publicly visible.

Very publicly.

He held court.

Annoying.

Useful.

Every visitor saw him.

Darkheart nobles watched him hear petitions, settle disputes, and threaten one merchant with seizure after the man tried bribing a border judge.

Zee barely raised his voice.

“Return the money.”

The merchant swallowed.

“I—”

Zee looked at him.

Human pupils shifted into slits.

“Return it.”

Compulsion pressed through the room.

The merchant’s resistance lasted three seconds.

Then:

“Yes, Majesty.”

Good.

Zee continued court.

Meanwhile, Ner created a false recognition pulse around Zareth’s stolen scale.

Rez followed the reaction through prepared observers.

Zareth flew high enough not to be seen from ground trails.

No one needed Zee physically.

That irritated him more than he expected.

Good.

His people were capable.

His friends were not extensions of him.

He could sit on a throne while they hunted.

Still hated it.

---

The trap led to a river shrine thirty miles east.

Not ancient.

Not divine.

Recently abandoned.

Rez entered first.

Ner behind.

Zareth remained above.

The shrine contained one person.

A woman in white cloth.

Same envoy.

She looked toward Rez.

“You are not him.”

Rez smiled.

“Disappointed?”

She moved.

Fast.

Not Human.

Ner’s Gold snapped around the doorway.

The woman hit the barrier.

Her body distorted.

Not shapeshifting.

More like her edges refused to stay fixed.

Rez drew his sword.

“What are you?”

No answer.

She touched the barrier.

It began blackening.

Ner’s face changed.

“Do not let her touch me.”

Rez moved immediately.

Blue-White Mana froze the floor beneath the woman.

She slipped.

Ner tightened the Gold.

Zareth crashed through the roof.

Careful enough not to crush Rez.

Barely.

The woman looked up.

Too late.

Zareth pinned her beneath one claw.

The Link exploded back toward Zee.

Found.

Alive.

Unknown.

Zee stood from the Darkheart throne in the middle of a tax dispute.

Everyone stopped talking.

He looked at Lord Merek.

“Continue without me.”

Merek blinked.

“Majesty?”

Zee was already gone.

Vampire speed.

---

He reached the shrine before the woman escaped.

Barely.

She had burned through half of Ner’s Golden boundary.

Rez had blood on one sleeve.

Zareth’s claw smoked where she touched him.

Zee entered silently.

The woman did not notice.

Good.

Assassin.

He stood behind her.

Knife touched the base of her skull.

“Don’t move.”

She froze.

Not from compulsion.

Calculation.

Then laughed.

“You came.”

Zee’s voice stayed calm.

“You wanted me.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“To see whether the stories were true.”

Zee’s expression changed.

That was almost disappointing.

“Which stories?”

“That you killed a God.”

“Yes.”

“That your blood changed.”

“Yes.”

“That Dragon blood lives inside the Tribrid.”

Zareth growled.

The woman continued.

“That the bond between you can be reached.”

Zee pressed the knife slightly harder.

“By you?”

“By anyone who knows where to cut.”

Ner’s face hardened.

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Bad answer.”

The woman smiled beneath the cloth.

“You are becoming visible.”

“Everyone knows me.”

“No.”

She turned her head just enough to look sideways.

“Not like this.”

Zee smelled no ordinary blood.

No heartbeat.

No Witch Mana.

No Demon signature.

Something else.

Unknown.

Good.

The world still had surprises.

He asked:

“Who sent you?”

“No one.”

Truth?

His blood sense could not tell.

Interesting.

“What do you want?”

“To test the link.”

“Why?”

“To know whether it breaks.”

Zareth’s anger hit the bond like fire.

The woman smiled.

“It doesn’t.”

Zee looked at Zareth.

Then Ner.

Then Rez.

No mastermind.

No kingdom.

No obvious political motive.

Just someone testing.

That was somehow worse.

Zee’s voice dropped.

“You cut a scale from my brother to satisfy curiosity.”

The woman shrugged.

“Yes.”

Wrong.

That line was enough.

Zee removed the knife.

Everyone noticed.

The woman smiled.

Thought mercy.

Then Zee caught her throat.

Vampire strength.

Lifted.

Her body distorted.

He held anyway.

Crimson Demonic Dragon heat surged through his palm.

The distortion stabilized.

She looked surprised.

Zee smiled.

“There.”

New weakness.

Not copied.

Observed.

He drove her against the wall.

“Tell me what you are.”

“No.”

He compelled.

“Tell me.”

Nothing.

No effect.

Interesting.

Stronger resistance.

Or no blood pathway compatible with his dominance.

Zee smiled wider.

The woman looked unsettled.

“You enjoy failure?”

“I enjoy learning.”

That answer bothered her.

Good.

She struck him.

Her palm phased through his chest—

almost.

Crimson scales flared beneath the skin.

His Demonic Dragon adaptation resisted the distortion enough to force her hand partially solid.

Zee caught the wrist.

Broke it.

She screamed.

Finally.

He liked that.

Ner watched.

No comment.

Zee leaned close.

“You touched my family.”

The woman’s breathing remained strange.

No heartbeat.

Still pain.

“Do you know what happens now?”

She smiled weakly.

“You kill me.”

“Yes.”

No threat.

Fact.

He drove the knife into her heart position.

Nothing.

No heart.

Of course.

She laughed.

Zee laughed too.

Then Wolf instinct noticed something.

Not heartbeat.

Center of movement.

Every time she twisted, her weight protected the lower left ribs.

Weak point.

Assassin Zee saw it.

He struck there.

The woman screamed louder.

Something dark spilled from the wound.

Not blood.

Liquid shadow.

Zee’s Vampire hunger reacted anyway.

Curiosity.

Ner immediately said:

“Do not.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner’s face was serious.

“We do not know what that is.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“Exactly.”

Rez groaned.

“Zee.”

For once, Zee listened.

Not because they controlled him.

Because the argument was good.

He did not feed.

He killed her another way.

Crimson Witchcraft closed around the wound.

“Burn.”

Dark crimson fire consumed the liquid shadow from inside.

The woman convulsed.

Then collapsed.

Dead.

No blood.

No drain.

No answer to species.

Permanent progress anyway.

They knew the Dragon Link could be externally sensed under certain conditions.

They knew it could not be broken easily.

They knew unfamiliar entities had begun testing Zee directly.

And Zee learned something else.

His new evolution could force certain unstable supernatural bodies into solidity through contact and heat.

Not a copied power.

Another Crimson interaction.

Useful.

Dangerous.

He stood.

Rez looked at the body.

“Who was she?”

Zee wiped his knife.

“No idea.”

Ner sighed.

“You are getting too comfortable with that.”

“Yes.”

Zareth lowered his head.

The Link carried irritation.

Then one more image.

The severed scale.

Zee looked toward him.

“You want it back.”

Immediate.

Ner smiled.

“I can remove the imprint now.”

Good.

They returned to Darkheart before dawn.

Ner cleansed the scale with Gold and Bloodsong together.

Zareth pressed it against the damaged spot on his shoulder.

Dragon healing began pulling it back into place.

Zee watched.

Then felt something at the edge of his territory.

Not the Link.

Wolf instinct.

Smoke.

Far west.

Too much.

A messenger entered seconds later.

“Majesty.”

Zee turned.

“Now what?”

The man swallowed.

“Three villages.”

“Burning.”

Rez closed his eyes.

Ner muttered something rude.

Zareth’s Link carried exhausted amusement.

Zee looked toward the western windows.

Another attack.

Another reason.

Another direction.

He did not sigh.

Did not complain.

His pupils narrowed.

“Find out who started it.”

The messenger bowed and ran.

Zee looked toward the others.

No rest.

No peace.

Fine.

The world wanted pressure.

It would get pressure back.

And slowly, almost invisibly, Zee Darkheart was beginning to stop thinking like a man waiting for danger to arrive.

He was starting to think like a King deciding which dangers should be allowed to exist at all.

# Chapter Sixty-Eight

## The Villages That Burned First

The western villages were already burning when Zee arrived.

Three.

Not one line of fire.

Three separate strikes.

Different roads.

Different timing.

Same result.

People running.

Livestock screaming.

Darkheart soldiers dragging families from houses while witches fought flames that did not behave like ordinary fire.

Zee stopped at the edge of the first village.

Smelled everything.

Wood.

Oil.

Blood.

Spell residue.

Wolf.

Human.

And something metallic beneath it.

Rez arrived beside him.

“Raiders?”

“No.”

Ner looked toward the flames.

“Magic?”

“Yes.”

Zareth circled above.

The Dragon Link pushed a sharp impression.

Fire wrong.

Not Dragon.

Not demon.

Zee’s crimson-and-gold eyes narrowed.

“Someone made the fire spread after impact.”

Rez looked toward the second village in the distance.

“Meaning they did not need many attackers.”

“Exactly.”

A scream cut through the road.

Zee vanished.

Vampire speed.

He appeared beneath a collapsing roof and caught the burning beam before it crushed a child.

Dragon durability took the heat.

His scales darkened.

He threw the timber aside.

“Run.”

The child stared at his horns.

Then moved.

Good.

Another building cracked.

Zee barely lifted one hand.

“Hold.”

Crimson Witchcraft caught the wall long enough for three people to escape.

Ner rushed past him.

Pure Gold spread across the road in precise lanes.

“Everyone inside the light! Stay between the lines!”

His voice carried more than volume.

Bloodsong resonance.

Panic softened.

Not erased.

Directed.

People moved where he told them.

Rez took over the evacuation without hesitation.

“North road closed!”

“South bridge clear!”

“Wounded first!”

“Anyone who can walk carries someone who cannot!”

He did not need a throne to sound like a king.

Zareth landed beyond the village and dragged an overturned wagon away from a trapped family with one claw.

No one waited for Zee.

Good.

That meant Zee could hunt.

---

The first attacker was still nearby.

Zee knew because fire was loud.

Fear was louder.

He shifted.

Bones changed.

Body dropped.

Dark near-black fur replaced skin.

Four legs hit the earth.

Wolf Zee.

No horns.

No scales.

No Dragon distortion.

Just Wolf.

Complete.

He ran.

Through smoke.

Across burned fields.

One scent separated from fleeing villagers.

Ash.

Leather.

Fresh fear.

Zee followed.

The trail crossed water.

He did not slow.

The attacker had tried to break scent by moving upstream.

Smart.

Zee left the river twenty yards early and circled.

Wolf instinct.

Human habits.

People always checked behind themselves after crossing.

The attacker did.

Zee was waiting ahead.

The man stopped.

Saw crimson-and-gold eyes in the dark.

His face drained.

“No.”

Zee advanced.

The man reached for a flare.

Zee lunged.

One paw struck the wrist.

Bones snapped.

The flare fell.

The man screamed.

Zee shifted back before him.

Human-shaped again.

Blood-dark coat.

Mature horns.

Slit pupils.

The attacker stared.

“You are him.”

Zee crouched.

“Who sent you?”

The man clenched his jaw.

Zee smelled poison inside one tooth.

Nanda Parbat.

Suicide capsule.

Zee caught his face before he could bite.

Two fingers.

Pressure.

The jaw locked.

The man panicked.

Zee smiled.

“Not yet.”

Vampire compulsion pushed through voice.

“Open.”

Resistance.

Strong training.

Zee pressed harder.

“Open.”

The man’s mouth obeyed.

Zee removed the poison capsule.

Dropped it.

Crushed it beneath one boot.

“Now answer.”

The attacker shook.

“Red Covenant.”

Rez arrived through the smoke.

“What is that?”

The man laughed weakly.

“Not yours.”

Zee looked at Rez.

“Useful?”

“Maybe.”

Ner reached them next.

Gold still burning around his hands.

“We got everyone out of the first village.”

Good.

Zareth’s Link carried the same from the second.

No deaths there.

One at the third.

Zee’s face changed.

One was enough.

He looked back at the prisoner.

“Why the villages?”

The man swallowed.

“To draw you west.”

Rez frowned.

“From where?”

No answer.

Ner’s eyes sharpened.

“Darkheart.”

Zee stood.

Too late.

A messenger horn sounded from the east.

Then another.

Then silence.

His castle.

Zee did not swear.

Did not shout.

He simply disappeared.

---

The attack on Castle Darkheart lasted four minutes.

That was all it needed.

The western fires were distraction.

The real target had entered through the old lower aqueduct beneath Victor’s abandoned prison wing.

Six intruders.

Not soldiers.

Assassins.

They moved directly toward the royal archive.

Not Zee.

Not Ner.

Not Rez.

Not Zareth.

Records.

Blood records.

House genealogy.

Veyrath lineage documents.

Zee arrived as the last assassin reached the archive door.

The man heard nothing.

Zee stood behind him.

“Wrong room.”

The assassin spun.

Blade.

Fast.

Zee moved less.

One wrist turn.

Knife trapped.

Elbow broken.

Knee destroyed.

The man hit stone.

Zee looked toward the five others.

All trained.

All already committed.

Good.

No speeches.

The first attacked high.

Zee ducked.

Second came low.

Wolf instinct read the movement.

He stepped outside the angle.

Third threw poison.

Zee smelled it before release.

His body already recognized the family of toxins.

He held his breath.

Flicked two fingers.

The needle reversed.

Hit the thrower.

Fourth cast.

Zee raised his palm.

The spell stopped.

Not blocked.

Stopped.

Then he closed his fist.

The magical structure collapsed.

The Witch gasped.

Zee crossed the distance.

Pressure point.

Down.

Fifth tried fleeing.

Vampire speed.

Zee appeared in front of him.

“Stay.”

Compulsion struck.

The assassin froze.

Sixth went for the archive.

Zee smiled.

That one had priorities.

He liked that.

Then killed him.

One knife.

Heart.

No wasted motion.

Rez arrived seconds later.

He looked at the six bodies and prisoners.

“Fast.”

Zee wiped the blade.

“They were not here to fight.”

Ner entered behind him.

“Then what?”

Zee opened the archive door.

Inside, one cabinet had been disturbed.

Only one.

Aurelia’s lineage records.

Veyrath.

Ner’s face hardened.

“They wanted proof.”

“Of the Dragon blood.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

“The world already saw enough.”

“Rumors are not records.”

Zee pulled one parchment free.

Aurelia Veyrath.

Dragon-Witch.

His mother.

His blood.

The attackers had come for certainty.

Not fear.

Not revenge.

Information.

Zee looked toward the surviving assassin.

“Red Covenant?”

The man’s heartbeat changed.

Yes.

Zee crouched.

“What are they?”

The assassin smiled.

“You.”

Zee’s expression did not move.

“That was stupid.”

The man continued.

“People deciding what you become next.”

Silence.

There it was.

Not one kingdom.

Not one council.

A group afraid enough to research him before attacking.

Rez asked:

“Where?”

The assassin laughed.

“Everywhere.”

Zee smelled the lie.

“Wrong.”

He compelled.

“Where?”

Resistance.

Blood ward.

Training.

Zee pressed harder.

The man’s eyes rolled toward him despite himself.

“Where?”

“Greyhaven.”

One word.

Ner looked toward Rez.

Rez nodded.

Known town.

Two days north.

Zee stood.

The assassin smiled weakly.

“You will come.”

“Yes.”

That answer frightened him.

Good.

Zee looked toward the burning villages through the western windows.

Then toward Aurelia’s record.

The philosophy shifted again.

Someone had burned three villages to reach one archive.

They had already demonstrated what they were willing to spend.

Zee did not need a second demonstration.

He looked at Rez.

“Secure the villages.”

“Ner?”

“Stay if you want.”

Ner’s eyes narrowed.

“I am going.”

Zee nodded.

No argument.

Then he looked toward Zareth through the Link.

Drakonis still recovering.

Stay.

Zareth sent immediate irritation.

Then acceptance.

His kingdom first.

Good.

Zee sheathed the knife.

“Greyhaven tonight.”

Rez stared.

“Tonight?”

“Yes.”

“Without knowing how large the Covenant is?”

Zee looked at the surviving assassin.

Then the archive.

Then smoke beyond Darkheart.

“I know enough.”

Rez did not like that answer.

He also did not say Zee was wrong.

That mattered.

Because the world had just burned Zee’s people to test how fast he would react.

And for the first time, Zee Darkheart did not intend to react.

He intended to arrive before they finished preparing the next fire.

# Chapter Sixty-Nine

## Greyhaven

Greyhaven was asleep when Zee entered.

It stayed asleep.

That was the point.

No army.

No Darkheart banners.

No declaration.

Just Zee and Ner beneath black cloaks while Rez remained outside town coordinating exits with four trusted Darkheart scouts.

The Red Covenant occupied a former hospice near the northern wall.

Twenty-three heartbeats inside.

Three Vampires.

Nine Humans.

Seven Witches.

Four Wolves.

No children.

No servants.

No innocent household staff.

Good.

Zee smelled blood beneath the building.

Stored.

Supernatural.

Dragon.

Wolf.

Witch.

Vampire.

Samples.

Ner smelled something else.

“My blood.”

Zee stopped.

“How much?”

“Not much.”

“Old?”

“Months.”

His face hardened.

“Taken from one of the monastery samples.”

So House Veylan had not been the end.

Different group.

Different purpose.

Same theft.

Zee’s pupils became slits.

Ner touched his wrist.

Not stopping him.

“Do not kill anyone until we know what they are doing.”

Zee looked over.

Reasonable.

Annoying.

“Fine.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“You hate when I am right.”

“Yes.”

---

The first room held maps.

Not kingdoms.

People.

Zee.

Ner.

Rez.

Zareth.

Theron.

Seraphine.

Lucien.

Darkheart nobles.

Drakonis officers.

Vesper routes.

Not one planned strike.

Dozens of possible ones.

Ner stared.

“They are profiling us.”

Zee moved to the wall.

Notes.

Not prophecy.

No destiny.

Patterns.

Zee responds fastest to family threat.

Rez prioritizes civilians and infrastructure.

Ner protects boundaries and blood-related victims.

Zareth returns to Drakonis under pressure.

The Covenant had studied behavior.

Zee smiled.

Ner looked toward him.

“That smile is bad.”

“They think they understand us.”

“That is why you are smiling?”

“Yes.”

Zee touched one page.

A projected strike against Vesper grain storage.

Another against Drakonis hatcheries.

Another against House Veyrath survivors.

Not executed yet.

Plans.

Preparations.

Potential.

There.

The next moral line.

No attack yet.

Not technically.

Only preparation.

Ner saw it too.

His expression tightened.

“We have evidence.”

“Yes.”

“Enough to arrest them.”

“Probably.”

Zee looked toward the next room.

“Maybe.”

Ner watched him.

“You are thinking about killing them before they act.”

“Yes.”

No lie.

No shame.

Ner breathed slowly.

“Then prove they mean to.”

Good.

Not conscience.

Standard.

Evidence.

Zee nodded.

“Agreed.”

They kept moving.

---

The basement proved it.

A Dragon scale from Zareth.

Ner’s dried blood.

Hair from Rez.

Blood from three Darkheart guards.

One of Zee’s discarded bandages from a battlefield years earlier.

Stored.

Cataloged.

Beside weapons built around each sample.

Blood-targeting needles.

Resonance disruptors.

Dragon-link interference dust.

Compulsion-resistant charms.

Crimson suppression mixtures.

Nothing complete.

Everything experimental.

One Witch stood over the workbench.

She looked up.

Saw Zee.

Stopped breathing.

He smiled faintly.

“Continue.”

She stared.

“What?”

“You were working.”

Ner stepped beside him.

“Keep going.”

The Witch looked between them.

Then reached slowly toward an alarm.

Zee barely moved one finger.

The alarm shattered.

“Not that.”

Her hands trembled.

“Who leads the Covenant?”

Silence.

Ner looked toward the blood samples.

His Bloodsong sharpened.

He hummed once.

Every vial containing his blood rang.

The Witch flinched.

“Who?”

“Council of Five.”

Rez’s voice came through the open stairwell.

“Names?”

He had entered from below after scouts secured the street.

The Witch stared.

Zee smelled the lie before it came.

“I don’t know.”

“Wrong.”

Vampire compulsion pressed outward.

No eye contact needed.

“Names.”

She resisted.

Strong charm.

Zee heard her heartbeat jump when the command hit the ward.

Interesting.

He stepped closer.

His predatory presence filled the room.

“Names.”

The charm cracked.

Not physically.

Mentally.

The Witch gasped.

“Orin Bale.”

“Mara Vess.”

“Dren Solvar.”

“High Witch Keira Morn.”

“And?”

She shook violently.

“Father Caldus.”

Rez frowned.

“Priest?”

“No.”

“Title?”

“Yes.”

No divine smell.

Good.

No God.

Not yet.

Zee looked toward the plans.

“Which attack happens next?”

The Witch began crying.

“Vesper.”

Ner’s face changed.

“When?”

“Tomorrow night.”

Rez went still.

Target.

His kingdom.

Not theoretical anymore.

“Where?”

“South aqueduct.”

“Explosives?”

“Bloodfire charges.”

Rez’s expression became cold.

Future king.

Not brother.

Different.

He turned toward the scouts.

“Send word now.”

One left immediately.

Zee looked at him.

“You want this one?”

Rez understood.

Not the Witch.

The operation.

Vesper.

“Yes.”

Good.

Zee turned back.

“Where are the Five?”

The Witch swallowed.

“Not here.”

“Where?”

“Separate.”

Smart.

No easy decapitation.

Rez looked toward Zee.

“We take the cell alive.”

Zee stared at the plans.

Burn Darkheart villages.

Break Vesper aqueduct.

Attack Drakonis hatcheries.

Target Ner’s blood.

Target Veyrath.

All prepared.

Not yet all executed.

His definition of threat shifted again.

He did not need to wait for fire anymore.

Still, Rez was right.

Living prisoners would expose the Five faster.

Zee nodded.

“Alive.”

The Witch exhaled.

Relief.

Then a door opened above.

Someone shouted.

The building woke.

---

The fight lasted six minutes.

Twenty-three members.

Three surrendered immediately.

Zee spared them.

Four tried escaping.

Rez’s scouts caught two.

Zee caught the others.

One Human fighter threw down his sword.

“Mercy.”

Zee stopped.

The man had not attacked civilians personally.

No blood scent from the burned villages.

No direct participation.

“Stay down.”

He lived.

A Vampire lunged from the balcony.

Zee caught him by the throat in midair.

The Vampire snarled.

“Monster.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

“Original.”

He slammed him into the floor.

The Vampire reached for a bloodfire capsule.

Zee saw.

Decision made.

Fangs.

He drained him.

Fast.

No speech.

No guilt.

Supernatural blood entered.

Crimson adaptation stirred.

The Vampire had consumed resistance compounds against compulsion.

Zee’s blood separated them.

Studied them.

Rewrote around them.

Another small step toward making ordinary anti-Vampire defenses less reliable.

Useful.

He dropped the body.

A Witch cast from behind.

Ner intercepted.

Pure Golden Mana folded around the spell.

Bloodsong followed.

“Still.”

The Witch froze.

Not from Zee.

From Ner.

Her blood obeyed just long enough for Rez to disarm her.

Ner’s control had become frighteningly clean.

Zee noticed.

Loved him for it.

Did not say so during combat.

Probably wise.

Two Wolves attacked together.

Zee smiled.

Then transformed.

Four-legged Wolf.

No horns.

No scales.

Just near-black fur and crimson-gold eyes.

The Wolves hesitated.

One recognized him.

“The King.”

Wrong moment to hesitate.

Wolf Zee hit them hard.

No Vampire speed.

No Witchcraft.

Just strength, balance, teeth, instinct.

He drove one down.

Circled the second.

The enemy tried fleeing.

Zee let him run ten seconds.

Then hunted.

He enjoyed the chase.

Caught him at the stairwell.

Dragged him back by the shoulder.

Alive.

Because they had agreed.

That mattered.

He shifted human again.

Blood on his mouth.

Ner looked at him.

“Show-off.”

Zee smiled.

“Worked.”

“Unfortunately.”

---

By dawn, Greyhaven knew nothing had happened.

That was how cleanly they moved.

The hospice remained standing.

The Covenant cell was gone.

Seventeen captured.

Six dead.

No civilian casualties.

No city panic.

The records belonged to Darkheart now.

Rez had the Vesper strike plan.

Ner had every sample of his blood destroyed under his own control.

Zee stood in the basement over the map of future attacks.

He could see the next step clearly.

Once, he would have waited.

Then responded.

Then hunted whoever attacked.

Now?

He had names.

Five.

Somewhere in the world.

Planning more strikes.

Rez looked at him.

“You are going after them.”

“Yes.”

“All five?”

“Yes.”

“Before they attack again.”

Zee met his eyes.

“Yes.”

Ner leaned against the table.

No surprise.

No immediate objection.

Only:

“Verify each one.”

Zee nodded.

“I will.”

That was the line now.

Not innocence until attack.

Evidence before elimination.

Different.

Darker.

Still a line.

For now.

A scout entered.

“Prince Rez.”

Rez turned.

“Vesper message.”

He read.

His face tightened.

“What?”

“The aqueduct team moved early.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

Rez folded the note.

“My father is handling it.”

Zee looked at him.

“You are going home.”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

Good.

Ner looked toward Zee.

“And us?”

Zee studied the five names on the wall.

Then one blood sample marked for House Veyrath.

He thought of Theron.

Seraphine.

Aurelia.

His people.

The next attack had not happened yet.

That used to matter more.

Now the preparations were enough.

Zee pulled the first name from the wall.

Orin Bale.

Then the second.

Mara Vess.

He folded both into his coat.

“We start verifying.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“Verifying.”

“Yes.”

“And if they are guilty?”

Zee’s expression stayed calm.

His crimson-and-gold eyes shifted into slits.

“Then they die before they get another chance.”

No one called him good.

No one called him evil.

No one needed to.

The descent had become simpler than labels.

Zee Darkheart had spent most of his life surviving people who decided what he might become was reason enough to act first.

Now, for the first time, he was preparing to do something dangerously similar.

The difference, in his mind, was evidence.

The question was how long that difference would remain enough.

# Chapter Seventy

## The First Name

Orin Bale lived in a city that worshiped discretion.

No banners.

No guards in uniform.

No royal colors.

Just money.

Old money.

Quiet money.

The kind that paid other people to become violent.

Zee preferred obvious predators.

They were easier.

He and Ner entered the city before dawn.

No army.

No escort.

Rez had returned to Vesper.

His kingdom had been targeted.

That came first.

Zareth remained in Drakonis.

His kingdom still had wounds of its own.

The core four did not need to stand in the same room to remain brothers.

Zee had learned that.

Mostly.

Ner walked beside him beneath a dark cloak.

“You are smiling.”

“No.”

“You are.”

“I like cities where everyone thinks secrets make them powerful.”

Ner sighed.

“Of course you do.”

Zee’s crimson-and-gold eyes remained human-pupiled.

Calm.

Thinking.

He had not come to kill Orin Bale.

Not yet.

He had come to prove the name.

That distinction mattered.

For now.

---

Orin owned four warehouses, two bathhouses, three blood banks, and one respectable charitable hospital.

The hospital was the problem.

Zee smelled it before they entered.

Blood.

Too much.

Not fresh violence.

Stored.

Categorized.

Separated.

Human.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Demon.

Something amphibious.

Something Zee did not recognize.

Ner stopped beside him.

“You smell it too?”

“Yes.”

“The basement.”

“Yes.”

A nurse approached.

Human.

Tired.

No fear.

No guilt.

“Can I help you?”

Zee smiled politely.

“We are looking for Lord Bale.”

“He does not visit patients.”

“I did not ask whether he did.”

The nurse blinked.

Ner stepped in before Zee frightened her unnecessarily.

“We were told he maintains a private office here.”

“Oh.”

She pointed.

“Third floor.”

“Thank you.”

They walked away.

Ner looked at Zee.

“You were about to compel her.”

“Yes.”

“She answered.”

“Yes.”

“So why?”

Zee considered.

“Habit.”

Ner gave him a look.

That bothered Zee more than criticism.

Not because Ner was judging.

Because Zee realized he had almost used domination simply because it was easier.

He filed that away.

No guilt spiral.

Just correction.

---

Orin’s office had six locks.

Zee opened none.

He entered through the window.

Ner came through the door after dismantling the wards.

They arrived at the same time.

Orin Bale looked up from breakfast.

Older Human.

Maybe fifty.

Silver hair.

Steady heartbeat.

No immediate fear.

That changed when Zee sat in the chair opposite him.

“King Darkheart.”

“Orin.”

Ner closed the door.

Orin looked toward him.

Then back to Zee.

“I assume this concerns Greyhaven.”

Zee’s expression did not move.

Confirmation one.

“You know about it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I funded part of it.”

Ner’s Gold flickered.

Orin lifted one hand.

“Before either of you decides that sentence is enough to kill me, ask what I funded.”

Zee smiled faintly.

Smart.

“Go on.”

“Research into defensive measures against supernatural coercion.”

“Compulsion?”

“Yes.”

“Blood manipulation?”

“Yes.”

“Dragon-link interference?”

Orin’s face tightened.

“No.”

Truth.

Zee smelled no fear spike around the denial.

Interesting.

Ner stepped closer.

“What about my blood?”

Orin looked at him.

“That was not my project.”

“Were you aware it existed?”

“Yes.”

“Did you stop it?”

“No.”

There.

Guilt.

Different kind.

Ner’s face hardened.

“Why?”

“Because the Covenant is not a military order.”

Zee leaned back.

“What is it?”

“A network.”

“Five principal patrons.”

“Independent cells.”

“Separate agendas.”

“Shared intelligence.”

Rez would have liked that answer.

No single mastermind.

No perfect chain.

Messier.

Real.

Orin continued.

“I paid for anti-compulsion development after three cities lost councils to Vampire domination.”

Zee’s eyes sharpened.

“Mine?”

“No.”

Truth again.

“And when Greyhaven began planning attacks?”

“I objected.”

“Not enough.”

“No.”

Orin did not defend himself.

That was unusual.

Zee looked around the office.

No hidden weapon.

One panic switch.

Orin had not touched it.

“Why stay?”

“Because leaving the Covenant means losing access to information about what the others are planning.”

Ner laughed without humor.

“And how many people did that information save?”

Orin answered:

“Three hundred and eleven.”

Specific.

Zee looked at him.

“Prove it.”

Orin opened a drawer slowly.

Placed ledgers on the desk.

Names.

Dates.

Anonymous warnings.

Cancelled raids.

Evacuated settlements.

One entry involved Vesper.

Rez had received an unexplained warning two years earlier about a Vampire nest moving through the eastern ridge.

Zee remembered.

Orin watched him read.

“I am not innocent.”

“Good.”

Zee closed the ledger.

“I hate when people waste time pretending.”

Orin’s mouth twitched.

“I funded anti-compulsion weapons.”

“Some were tested on prisoners.”

Ner said.

Orin’s face darkened.

“I learned that after.”

“And stayed.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because Mara Vess wanted to turn the Covenant into something worse.”

There.

Second name.

Zee’s attention sharpened.

“What worse?”

“Preemptive extermination.”

Silence.

Ner glanced toward Zee.

Orin continued.

“Not stopping threats.”

“Eliminating bloodlines judged likely to produce threats.”

Zee went very still.

Infants.

Possibility as guilt.

Victor.

Different century.

Same disease.

Orin saw the change.

“That is why I stayed.”

“To stop her?”

“To slow her.”

“Did you?”

“Sometimes.”

“Not enough.”

“No.”

Again.

Truth.

Zee stood.

Orin did not.

“Am I dead?”

Zee looked at him.

Six years ago he might have killed him for complicity.

Three years ago he might have fed first and asked later.

Now?

Darker did not mean simpler.

“No.”

Orin exhaled.

Zee continued.

“But your money ends today.”

Orin looked up.

“And if I refuse?”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

Slits.

Predatory pressure filled the room.

“Do you want to?”

Orin’s heartbeat stumbled.

“No.”

Good.

Zee leaned slightly closer.

“Give me everything you have on Mara Vess.”

Orin hesitated.

Then opened another drawer.

No compulsion necessary.

That pleased Zee more than forcing him would have.

Barely.

---

They left with three ledgers and one address.

Ner walked beside Zee in silence for two streets.

Then:

“You spared him.”

“Yes.”

“You wanted to kill him.”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you?”

Zee looked ahead.

“Because he is guilty of cowardice and complicity.”

“Not what Mara is planning.”

Ner nodded.

No praise.

No moral lesson.

Just understanding.

Zee looked at him.

“You expected me to kill him.”

“I expected you to consider it.”

“I did.”

Ner smiled faintly.

“I know.”

Zee’s hand brushed his.

Ner caught it.

Held.

For half a block.

Then released when they reached the city gate.

Romance did not stop the hunt.

It traveled with it.

Outside the walls, one of Zee’s Darkheart scouts waited with a sealed message.

“From Vesper.”

Zee opened it.

Rez’s handwriting.

Short.

**Aqueduct attack stopped. Lucien alive. Twelve captured. Three escaped. One name overlaps your list: Mara Vess.**

Zee smiled.

This time Ner did not ask why.

The first name had not deserved death.

The second one was becoming much harder to defend.

And somewhere south, Mara Vess was preparing to eliminate threats before they ever acted.

Zee knew exactly how dangerous that philosophy could become.

Because part of him was beginning to understand it.

---

# Chapter Seventy-One

## The Woman Who Chose First

Mara Vess lived in a monastery carved into red cliffs.

Not hidden.

Protected.

There was a difference.

Everyone nearby knew she was there.

No one approached.

Zee understood why.

Bodies hung from the cliff road.

Not fresh.

Not decorative either.

Warnings.

Each corpse wore a wooden plaque naming the crime.

**FERAL VAMPIRE.**

**CHILD-KILLER.**

**BLOOD TRAFFICKER.**

**DEMON CULTIST.**

Ner read the fourth.

“She kills monsters.”

Zee looked upward.

“So do I.”

“That is probably the point.”

The road continued.

Then the plaques changed.

**UNSTABLE WITCH BLOODLINE.**

Zee stopped.

Next.

**WOLF CHILD — PROPHECY RISK.**

His face went cold.

Next.

**MIXED BLOOD — FUTURE THREAT.**

Ner’s Golden Mana flared.

“There.”

Difference.

Not crimes committed.

Possibility.

Zee looked toward the monastery doors.

“Verified.”

Ner did not disagree.

---

Mara was waiting.

Mid-forties.

Witch.

White hair.

Black robes.

No army in the chamber.

Only six armed followers.

She smiled when Zee entered.

“King Darkheart.”

Zee said nothing.

Mara looked toward Ner.

“The anomaly.”

Ner’s voice sharpened.

“Nereus.”

Mara ignored the correction.

That irritated Zee more than it should have.

She gestured toward the table.

“Sit.”

Zee remained standing.

“No.”

Mara smiled wider.

“You know why I wanted your records.”

“To build weapons.”

“To understand what comes next.”

“There is always a next.”

“Yes.”

She leaned forward.

“And you are proof.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

“Of?”

“That power compounds.”

“Blood adapts.”

“Species change.”

“Hybrids emerge.”

“Dragons mutate.”

“Gods die.”

Ner’s face hardened.

Mara continued.

“The world is becoming less controllable.”

Zee almost laughed.

Victor would have loved her.

Mara looked at him.

“So I choose first.”

There.

Her philosophy.

Simple.

Clean.

Horrible.

“Before what?” Zee asked.

“Before danger matures.”

Ner looked toward the hanging road outside.

“Children.”

“Potential catastrophes.”

“They were children.”

“Both can be true.”

Zee’s pupils became slits.

Mara noticed.

Good.

“You understand me.”

“No.”

“I think you do.”

Mara stood.

“You have begun killing threats before they strike.”

Silence.

Ner looked toward Zee.

Not accusing.

Watching.

Mara smiled.

“You came here before I attacked Darkheart again.”

“I came because you already burned my villages.”

“And because you found future plans.”

“Yes.”

“Exactly.”

Zee’s expression stayed calm.

Mara stepped closer.

“The only difference between us is scale.”

“No.”

“What difference?”

Zee looked toward the bodies outside.

“Evidence.”

Mara laughed.

“You think evidence will save you from becoming practical?”

Zee said nothing.

That bothered him because part of the answer was no.

Mara continued.

“You killed your father.”

“Yes.”

“You killed a God.”

“Yes.”

“You drain supernatural enemies to evolve.”

“Yes.”

Ner’s eyes shifted toward him.

Mara smiled.

“You are becoming exactly what intelligent people should fear.”

Zee took one step closer.

“Then fear me.”

Her smile vanished.

“But do not use me to justify dead children.”

Silence.

Good.

---

Mara attacked first.

Appropriate.

The floor lit with black sigils.

Ner moved.

Pure Gold snapped around Zee before the spell completed.

The black structure hit the boundary and split.

Mara’s followers attacked from both sides.

Zee barely moved.

One hand.

“Down.”

Crimson Witchcraft smashed three to the floor.

The other three resisted.

Good.

Ner took one.

Gold locked the weapon arm.

Bloodsong struck circulation.

“Still.”

The follower froze.

Zee took the second through Vampire speed.

One instant standing.

Next unconscious.

Pressure point beneath the jaw.

The third was a Wolf.

He lunged.

Zee smiled.

Then shifted.

Four-legged Wolf form hit the stone.

Near-black fur.

Crimson-and-gold eyes.

No horns.

No scales.

Just Wolf.

The enemy hesitated.

Zee did not.

They collided.

Claws.

Teeth.

Weight.

No Vampire speed.

No Witchcraft.

Wolf Zee drove him across the floor.

The enemy tried turning away.

Zee caught the shoulder.

Pinned him.

Could kill.

Did not.

Not yet.

He shifted back.

Human-shaped.

Mara stared.

“Every nature complete.”

Zee straightened.

“Three always were.”

She looked toward the darker scales along his neck.

“And the fourth?”

Zee smiled faintly.

“None of your business.”

Mara cast.

This time directly at Ner.

Wrong choice.

Zee moved without thought.

Raised one palm.

The spell stopped.

He closed his fist.

It shattered.

Then his other hand flicked.

Mara flew backward through her own table.

Wood exploded.

Zee continued walking.

No hurry.

Mara rose coughing.

“You protect him because he proves your blood can make more.”

Zee’s face changed.

“No.”

She laughed.

“You love him.”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

Ner went still.

Not because it was new.

Because Zee said it here, covered in blood, while walking toward someone he intended to kill.

Both true.

Both Zee.

Mara attacked again.

Zee disappeared.

Reappeared behind her.

Knife beneath ribs.

Not fatal.

Yet.

Assassin placement.

She gasped.

Zee whispered:

“Who else did you order killed?”

Mara smiled through pain.

“Hundreds.”

Truth.

His Vampire blood sense caught no deception.

Zee pushed the knife deeper.

“How many children?”

“Enough.”

That was the answer.

No remorse.

No coercion.

No uncertainty.

Zee could kill her now.

He wanted to.

Ner said:

“Wait.”

Zee stopped.

Not because Ner commanded.

Because he trusted the reason would matter.

Ner approached.

“Where are the lists?”

Mara’s expression shifted.

Lists.

Good.

Zee smiled faintly.

Ner noticed.

“You forgot the evidence.”

“I was distracted.”

“By murder.”

“Yes.”

Mara laughed.

“You two are absurd.”

Ner looked at her.

“Where?”

She resisted.

Ner’s voice changed.

Bloodsong.

“Tell me.”

Mara had wards.

Strong.

Her blood fought the resonance.

Ner pushed with Golden precision around the command, isolating the effect from everyone else.

“Tell me.”

Blood vessels stood along Mara’s neck.

She finally gasped:

“Lower crypt.”

Ner released her.

Zee looked toward him.

“Done?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Mara understood.

Fear entered her.

Finally.

“Wait.”

Zee looked at her.

“You just spent ten minutes explaining why waiting is weakness.”

Mara’s face twisted.

“I can help you.”

“Probably.”

“Then—”

“I do not want your help.”

Zee pulled the knife free.

Mara stumbled.

Relief.

Wrong.

He caught her by the throat.

Vampire strength lifted her.

She struggled.

“Mercy.”

Zee stared.

At nineteen, he had begun asking why.

At twenty-one, he still did.

“Give me a reason.”

“I know every threat forming against you.”

“Names?”

“I can tell you.”

“Lists?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“Crypt.”

Already had it.

No new value.

Mara realized.

Fear deepened.

Zee enjoyed it.

He did not pretend otherwise.

“You are going to kill me.”

“Yes.”

“You are proving me right.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“No.”

His fangs descended.

“You killed people for what they might become.”

He pulled her closer.

“I am killing you for what you already chose.”

Then he fed.

---

Mara’s Witch blood hit hard.

Old.

Potent.

Layered with defensive rituals and traces of dozens of supernatural substances she had consumed over years trying to harden herself.

Zee drank all of it.

Not her spells.

Not her knowledge.

Her blood entered Zee and met Crimson biology.

Poison resistance stirred.

Suppression resistance.

Blood analysis.

The foreign mixtures began separating almost instantly.

His body was becoming frighteningly good at deciding what belonged.

Mara weakened.

Her hands stopped moving.

Her heartbeat slowed.

Zee did not stop until it ended.

He dropped the body.

No guilt.

No apology.

Ner watched him wipe blood from his mouth.

“You enjoyed that.”

“Yes.”

“Because she was afraid?”

“Yes.”

“Because of the blood?”

“Yes.”

“Because you killed her?”

Zee thought.

Then:

“Yes.”

Ner nodded.

No approval.

No condemnation.

He simply knew Zee.

That mattered.

---

The lower crypt held forty-seven names.

Some marked dead.

Some pending.

Some under observation.

Not all guilty.

That was the worst part.

A twelve-year-old Witch with unstable fire magic.

A Vampire child born from an old predatory bloodline.

A Wolf girl whose father had massacred a village.

A mixed-blood infant Mara believed could become dangerous.

Potential.

Nothing more.

Ner stood over the list.

“She would have killed them.”

“Yes.”

Zee’s face was unreadable.

Then he burned the list.

Not the evidence ledger beside it.

Only the kill orders.

Ner looked over.

“Why keep one?”

“Proof.”

Growth.

Darkness had not made him stupid.

# Chapter Seventy-Two

## The Man Who Wanted the King Alive

Dren Solvar did not hide.

That made Zee suspicious immediately.

Open gates.

Visible guards.

No blood wards.

No hidden fortress.

No attempt to run.

“Good.”

“I know.”

His problem.

His hunt.

Zareth remained in Drakonis.

The Link carried distant mountain heat and irritation at being excluded from a problem that specifically involved Zee’s blood.

Zee sent back amusement.

Then looked toward Ner.

“You stay outside.”

Ner stared.

“No.”

“Dren wants me alive.”

“Yes.”

“So I give him what he wants.”

“I want to see how.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

“Thirty.”

“Twenty-five.”

Quick.

---

Dren Solvar waited in the garden.

Human.

At least mostly.

Zee smelled Vampire blood in him.

Not enough to become Vampire.

Repeated doses.

Enhancement.

Other blood too.

Wolf.

Witch.

Something reptilian.

Dren had been experimenting on himself.

Interesting.

He sat beneath a white pavilion drinking tea.

“King Darkheart.”

Zee approached.

“Dren.”

“You came alone.”

“No.”

Dren smiled.

“At least you are honest.”

Zee sat opposite him.

No weapon visible.

Four guards behind Dren.

Two archers on the roof.

One Witch beneath the pavilion floor.

Three heartbeats behind the garden wall.
