# Chapter Ninety-Two

## When Choice Disappeared

The Kingdom of Rell did not care that Zee could create hybrids.

It cared that people kept leaving.

Workers.

Debtors.

Prisoners.

Servants.

Mixed families.

People born into contracts they never signed.

For three years, they had crossed Darkheart’s borders and refused to return.

Rell called them stolen property.

Darkheart called them citizens.

The difference became war.

---

The Safe Road attack happened at dawn.

Thirty Darkheart escorts.

Sixty-three travelers.

Families moving toward Southhold.

Rell soldiers struck from both sides.

By the time reinforcements arrived, fourteen Darkheart citizens were dead.

Twenty-seven were missing.

Including children.

One survivor carried a message nailed through his coat.

He was still alive when Zee read it.

**RETURN THE PROPERTY OF RELL.**

**OR RELL WILL RECLAIM WHAT BELONGS TO IT.**

Zee read it twice.

Then looked at the wounded man.

“Property?”

The survivor coughed.

“They kept saying it.”

Ner stood nearby.

His face hardened.

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Where did they take them?”

Amara answered from the doorway.

“I found the trail.”

“Where?”

“Old quarry west of the Rell border.”

Rez looked at the map.

“That is a basin.”

“Yes.”

“High walls.”

“Yes.”

“Only two exits.”

“Yes.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

“It is a trap.”

“I know.”

Ner stood.

“I am coming.”

So did Kael.

Tessa.

Amara.

Zee did not argue.

These were Darkheart citizens.

Their problem too.

---

The quarry held exactly what Zee expected.

Archers above.

Infantry below.

Witch suppressors built into the stone.

Silver traps.

Anti-Vampire compounds.

Wolf restraints.

Prepared kill lines.

And prisoners.

Witches chained with suppression iron.

Vampires fitted with silver collars.

Wolves restrained in scent-breaking cages.

Mixed families tied together.

Children among them.

General Oren Vael stood on the central platform.

Human.

No magic.

No supernatural blood.

No need.

Three hundred Rell soldiers obeyed when he lifted one hand.

That made him dangerous enough.

“King Darkheart.”

Zee walked into the basin.

“You attacked my road.”

“We recovered Rell property.”

“No.”

Oren smiled.

“Debt contracts.”

“No.”

“Inherited service.”

“No.”

“Convicted labor.”

“No.”

“Family obligations.”

Zee looked toward the prisoners.

A Vampire man held his daughter against him despite both being chained.

A Witch woman had positioned herself between two children and the soldiers.

Zee’s voice became quiet.

“People.”

Oren’s smile vanished.

“Subjects of Rell.”

“They left.”

“They had no right.”

“They chose.”

“They belong to us.”

“No.”

One word.

Absolute.

Oren stared.

“You would destabilize every labor law in the eastern kingdoms.”

Zee almost smiled.

“Good.”

Oren lifted one hand.

A soldier dragged a young Wolf girl onto the platform.

Nine.

Maybe ten.

Her knees were bleeding.

A chain circled her throat.

Amara snarled behind Zee.

Oren placed a blade beneath the girl’s jaw.

“Her father owed Rell forty-seven silver crowns.”

Zee went still.

“So?”

“The debt passed to his household.”

“She is nine.”

“She is collateral.”

“No.”

“She belongs to—”

“No.”

Oren looked directly into Zee’s eyes.

“Then kneel.”

The quarry went silent.

Zee heard the girl’s heartbeat.

Fast.

Terrified.

He could smell tears.

Wolf blood.

Old bruises.

Oren pressed the blade closer.

“Your people for obedience.”

Zee did not kneel.

Oren smiled.

Then cut her.

Not deep.

Not fatal.

Enough.

Blood ran down her throat.

The girl screamed.

And something inside Zee disappeared.

---

Later, Zee would remember every detail.

That was the worst part.

The smell of her blood.

The sound of Oren’s blade.

The first Rell soldier moving.

The moment Witchcraft exploded from Zee before he decided to cast.

“BREAK.”

The platform shattered.

Oren disappeared behind falling stone.

Zee moved.

Not strategy.

Not judgment.

Movement.

A Rell soldier raised a shield.

Zee tore through him.

Another dropped his sword.

Zee killed him too.

A third shouted:

“I surrender!”

Zee bit his throat.

Fed.

Kept feeding after the man stopped fighting.

Kael reached the prisoners with Darkheart forces.

Then looked toward Zee.

A Rell soldier was running away.

No weapon.

Retreating toward the quarry wall.

Zee transformed.

Wolf.

Near-black fur.

Crimson-and-gold eyes.

No horns.

No scales.

Only pursuit.

He caught the fleeing man.

Dragged him down.

Killed him.

Kael stopped.

“He was running away.”

Wolf Zee shifted back.

Blood covered his mouth.

“I know.”

Kael’s face changed.

That answer frightened him.

Not because Zee did not understand.

Because he did.

And did it anyway.

Then Zee was gone again.

---

Ner did not chase him.

He freed prisoners.

Gold shattered collars.

Bloodsong calmed panicked heartbeats.

Tessa reached the injured Wolf girl and pressed both hands against her throat.

“Stay with me.”

Amara knelt beside them.

The girl grabbed her sleeve.

“I want my mother.”

“We will find her.”

“Promise?”

Amara looked toward the cages.

Then back.

“Yes.”

She lifted the child into her arms.

Kael led Darkheart soldiers through the lower cells.

“Prisoners first! Soldiers second!”

Behind them, Zee kept killing.

Rell soldiers fought.

Then Rell soldiers surrendered.

Some survived.

Some did not.

One group of eleven dropped their weapons together.

Zee entered the line.

Darkness rolled from him.

One soldier raised both empty hands.

“We surrender.”

Zee killed him.

Then the next.

Then the next.

Darkheart soldiers stopped moving.

Nobody understood what they were seeing.

This was not Southhold.

At Southhold, Zee had verified guilt and consciously decided surrender did not erase it.

Here—

he was no longer asking.

No evidence.

No distinctions.

Uniform became guilt.

Presence became guilt.

Running became guilt.

Fear became invitation.

Twenty surrendering soldiers died before anyone could reach him.

And Zee enjoyed it.

The begging.

The fleeing.

The fact that nothing in the quarry could stop him.

---

Zareth felt him from Drakonis.

Then stopped understanding him.

The Dragon Link filled with blood.

Wolf pursuit.

Vampire hunger.

Witch power.

Dragon heat.

Rage.

Joy.

But no deliberate thought.

Zareth shifted immediately.

True Dragon form tore into the sky.

**Zee.**

Nothing.

Not silence.

Worse.

Noise.

Zareth flew harder.

---

At the quarry, Zee caught another Rell soldier against the wall.

Young.

Sixteen.

Seventeen at most.

Military armor too large around the shoulders.

Sword still sheathed.

No blood on it.

One leg trapped beneath fallen stone.

Zee raised one hand.

The boy stared at him.

“Please.”

Zee’s fingers closed.

Magic gathered.

Normally, Zee would have noticed everything instantly.

Clean blade.

No blood scent.

No combat sweat.

The boy had never reached the fight.

He had been trapped when the platform collapsed.

None of that mattered inside Zee’s rage.

“Please.”

The quarry darkened beneath Crimson power.

Then a shadow passed overhead.

Zareth landed hard enough to shake the basin.

True Dragon form.

Massive wings.

Claws sinking into stone.

His voice thundered.

“ZEE!”

No response.

Zareth opened the Link completely.

Not to control.

Not to command.

To show.

Ner carrying a crying child from chains.

Tessa pressing blood-soaked cloth against the Wolf girl’s neck.

Amara holding that girl against her chest.

Kael standing among surrendering soldiers.

Darkheart guards staring at their King.

Rescued families huddling together.

Then the young Rell boy beneath Zee’s hand.

One concept crashed through everything.

**LOOK.**

Zee snarled.

“They attacked my people.”

Zareth’s answer came through both words and the Link.

**Some did.**

“They took children.”

**Some did.**

“They deserve this.”

Zareth’s enormous head lowered.

Crimson-and-gold eyes met Dragon eyes.

**SOME DO.**

Some.

The word entered where rage had erased categories.

Some.

Not all.

Zee looked down.

Finally.

The boy.

Young.

Terrified.

Clean weapon.

No blood.

No fight.

Zee’s hand remained raised.

The boy whispered:

“Please.”

Zee lowered it.

And for the first time since the child had been cut—

choice returned.

The realization nearly sickened him.

Not because he had almost killed an enemy.

Because he had almost killed someone without deciding whether he was one.

---

Oren Vael emerged from the broken platform.

Blood on one side of his face.

He saw the dead soldiers.

Saw Zee.

Then smiled.

“You monster.”

Usually the word meant nothing.

This time it landed differently.

Oren looked toward the injured Wolf girl.

“And it worked.”

Zee turned.

“What?”

“I cut one child.”

Oren laughed.

“And you became exactly what Rell needed everyone to see.”

There was the truth.

Ugly.

Zee had allowed Oren to choose where the monster pointed.

That could not stand.

He crossed the distance calmly.

No frenzy.

No feeding.

Oren backed away.

“You killed surrendering men.”

“Yes.”

“You proved me right.”

“No.”

Zee caught him by the throat.

“You proved you were willing to hurt a child because you thought her father’s debt made her yours.”

Oren struggled.

Zee’s human pupils returned.

Clear.

Present.

Choosing.

“She was never yours.”

Snap.

Oren died instantly.

Zee released the body.

Deliberate.

Quick.

Finished.

---

The quarry rescue succeeded.

Twenty-six of the twenty-seven kidnapped citizens came home.

One captive died before Tessa could reach him.

Fourteen had died on the Safe Road.

Seventy-six Rell soldiers died in the quarry.

Twenty had surrendered before Zee killed them.

The number remained twenty.

No correction.

No excuse.

No later discovery that secretly made them guilty.

Twenty surrendered.

Zee killed them anyway.

As Darkheart prepared to leave, a young guard approached.

“Majesty?”

Zee looked at him.

The guard straightened too quickly.

Fear.

Zee smelled it.

Not enemy fear.

His soldier.

His person.

Afraid of him.

Something predatory inside Zee liked the scent.

Just for a second.

That frightened him more than Oren’s accusation.

The guard swallowed.

“Orders?”

Zee looked across the quarry.

Bodies.

Freed citizens.

Kael watching him carefully.

Ner holding a child’s hand.

Zareth still in true Dragon form.

“Take everyone home.”

The guard bowed immediately.

Too immediately.

Zee watched him leave.

He had spent years making enemies fear Darkheart.

Now Darkheart had seen something it had never seen before.

A King who could lose the ability to choose where his violence stopped.

And part of the monster inside him had enjoyed being feared anyway.

---

# Chapter Ninety-Three

## What Darkheart Saw

There was no victory feast.

No songs about the quarry.

No speeches.

The official Darkheart report contained one sentence Zee refused to remove:

**Twenty Rell soldiers surrendered and were subsequently killed by King Zee Darkheart during the loss of his deliberate judgment.**

Merek stared at the wording.

“Foreign kingdoms will use this against you.”

“They should.”

“They will remove everything around it.”

“Probably.”

“They will call it prisoner slaughter.”

Zee looked at him.

“It was.”

Merek went silent.

Zee did not hide it.

That mattered.

It did not undo it.

---

Ner entered Zee’s room that evening.

Alone.

Zee sat near the window.

No crown.

No weapons.

Ner closed the door.

“You lost control.”

“Yes.”

“You killed people who surrendered.”

“Yes.”

“You nearly killed someone who had not fought.”

“Yes.”

No excuses.

Ner crossed the room.

“What did it feel like?”

Zee thought.

Then answered honestly.

“Good.”

Ner’s expression did not change.

“The killing?”

“The running.”

Zee looked toward the dark glass.

“The begging.”

Silence.

“The fear.”

His fangs descended slightly without intention.

“The fact that they could not stop me.”

Ner listened.

“When Zareth reached me, I was not tired.”

Ner said nothing.

“I was not finished.”

Zee looked at him.

“I wanted more.”

That was the part he needed said aloud.

Ner nodded once.

“And now?”

“I still like those things.”

No redemption.

No lie.

“I still like hunting people I believe deserve it.”

“Yes.”

“I still like feeding.”

“Yes.”

“Fear.”

“Yes.”

“Screams.”

Ner’s mouth tightened.

“Yes.”

Zee leaned forward.

“That is not the problem.”

“No.”

“The problem is that at the quarry, I stopped deciding who deserved what.”

There.

Correct.

Zee looked toward Ner.

“I do not need someone deciding my morality.”

“Good.”

“I need someone capable of telling me when I stop deciding at all.”

Ner understood.

“Witness.”

“Yes.”

“Not permission.”

“No.”

“Not control.”

“No.”

Ner sat opposite him.

“If I see it, I tell you.”

“Yes.”

“And if you disagree?”

Zee’s expression darkened.

“Tell me anyway.”

That was all.

---

“I almost became Mara.”

Ner shook his head immediately.

“No.”

Zee frowned.

“I killed people without distinction.”

“For minutes.”

“Mara did it for years.”

“That is not the important difference.”

Ner leaned forward.

“Mara killed people because of what they might become.”

Zee listened.

“You killed because rage destroyed your judgment.”

“That sounds better.”

“It is not better.”

Good.

Ner continued.

“It is different.”

That was why Zee trusted him.

No comforting lie.

No exaggerated condemnation.

Facts.

---

Kael came after midnight.

No bow.

No ceremony.

“You scared me.”

Zee nodded.

“I know.”

Kael shook his head.

“No. I have watched you drain people dry.”

“Yes.”

“I have watched you smile while enemies begged.”

“Yes.”

“You killed Elara’s killers.”

“Yes.”

“I have seen you enjoy all of it.”

Zee waited.

“The quarry was different.”

“Yes.”

Kael’s jaw tightened.

“He was running away.”

Zee remembered.

“I know.”

“That answer was when I got scared.”

Silence.

Kael stepped closer.

“If that happened inside Darkheart…”

Zee knew the question.

Kael asked anyway.

“Could you kill one of us?”

Zee answered carefully.

“If you were innocent?”

“Yes.”

Before the quarry, the answer would have been immediate.

Never.

Now Zee refused the lie.

“Yesterday?”

Kael waited.

“For a little while…”

Zee swallowed.

“I do not know.”

That hurt.

Kael looked away.

“So why should I trust you?”

“You do not have to.”

Kael looked back.

Zee continued.

“I want people who choose me.”

“You made me.”

“I saved you.”

“Yes.”

“That gives me no ownership over what you choose next.”

Kael stood silent for a long time.

“If I leave?”

“I will not stop you.”

“No blood oath?”

“No.”

“No command?”

“No.”

Kael stared at him.

Then sighed.

“I hate that you make leaving sound so reasonable.”

Zee almost smiled.

“Are you leaving?”

“No.”

“Why?”

Kael looked toward the city.

“Because Darkheart is still my home.”

Choice.

That mattered more now than ever.

---

The emergency rule was written the next morning.

Simple.

If Zee completely lost deliberate control again, civilians moved away first.

Nobody approached him alone.

Nobody tried casually restraining him.

Kael was not expected to fight him.

Ner was not expected to physically overpower him.

Darkheart soldiers were ordered to protect civilians, not prove loyalty by dying near their King.

And Zareth became the final intervention.

Not because Zareth controlled Zee.

Because he had the best chance of surviving long enough to reach him.

True Dragon durability.

Dragon strength.

And the Link.

When Zee read the final line, Zareth stood across from him in human form.

“If it happens again, I hit you.”

Rez, who had arrived from Vesper halfway through the meeting, answered immediately.

“Approved.”

Zee looked at him.

“No one asked you.”

“I approve harder now.”

Zareth smiled.

Zee looked back at him.

“You think hitting me will work?”

“No.”

“That is reassuring.”

“I said I would hit you.”

Zareth’s expression became serious.

“I did not say I would win.”

That was the truth.

Zee accepted it.

---

Rez waited until the council ended.

Then punched Zee across the jaw.

Hard.

Vampire strength now.

Zee’s head snapped sideways.

Everyone froze.

Rez flexed his hand.

“That was personal.”

Zee touched his jaw.

“Feel better?”

“A little.”

Ner laughed once.

Even Zareth did.

Then Rez became serious.

“Vesper publicly condemned what happened.”

Zee nodded.

“Good.”

Rez blinked.

“That easy?”

“Vesper is not Darkheart.”

“No.”

“You are not my subject.”

“No.”

“You do not owe me lies.”

Rez studied him.

“Foreign rulers are asking whether Vesper supports prisoner slaughter.”

“And?”

“I told them no.”

“Good.”

“I also told them Rell attacked Darkheart citizens and enslaved families.”

“Also good.”

Rez stared.

“You understand I may publicly disagree with you again.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“I would be disappointed if you stopped.”

Brotherhood intact.

Independence intact.

Good.

---

Zareth spoke to Zee alone that night.

Not aloud.

Through the Link.

**I need you to understand what happened.**

Zee stood on the eastern balcony.

**I do.**

**No.**

The Link opened wider.

Zee felt the quarry again through Zareth.

Not his own memory.

Zareth’s experience of him.

Blood hunger.

Wolf pursuit.

Dragon heat.

Witch power.

Rage.

Pleasure.

Violence.

All Zee.

Then—

nothing where his deliberate thought should have been.

Zee went cold.

Zareth’s mental voice was quieter.

**I felt you disappear.**

**I was there.**

**Your power was there.**

Pain moved through the Link.

**Your hunger was there.**

Heat.

**Your rage was there.**

Then the frightening truth.

**I could not find the part of you that decides.**

Zee stared into darkness.

That scared him more than monster.

More than murderer.

More than foreign condemnation.

Choice was his identity.

Victor feared prophecy.

Mara feared potential.

Oren believed ownership erased choice.

Zee had built Darkheart around the opposite idea.

Then lost his own.

For minutes.

Enough.

Zareth sent one final thought.

**Next time, I hit you sooner.**

Zee almost laughed.

**You are enjoying that part.**

**Immensely.**

Good.

Brother.

Not master.

---

Rell expected Darkheart to retaliate with armies.

Zee attacked something else.

Ownership.

Kael led raids on labor prisons.

Tessa established medical camps along the Safe Roads for escapees who arrived starved, beaten, or injured.

Amara hunted transport routes and broke prisoner convoys.

Ner used Bloodsong carefully to find separated relatives inside holding camps.

Rez froze Rell-connected accounts moving through Vesper banks.

Zareth destroyed two military bridges after civilians cleared them.

Zee personally burned three record halls.

Debt contracts.

Inherited service ledgers.

Prison labor claims.

Ownership documents.

Thousands of pages turned to ash.

A Rell official screamed:

“You cannot erase debt with fire!”

Zee watched the records burn.

“I just did.”

He did not kill the man.

The official had surrendered.

This time Zee noticed.

This time Zee chose.

Prison.

---

Rell began losing people faster than territory.

Workers disappeared overnight.

Families abandoned factory districts.

Debtors crossed rivers.

Servants left noble estates.

Mixed households traveled under Darkheart protection.

Even Rell soldiers deserted after realizing Darkheart would accept them if they came without prisoners or stolen property.

Rell demanded every person be returned.

Its formal message arrived before the full council.

Merek read the demand.

Eight pages of legal argument.

Zee wrote one word beneath it.

**No.**

Returned unopened beyond that page.

---

Within two months, two thousand three hundred and eleven former Rell subjects had entered Darkheart protection.

They needed homes.

Food.

Healers.

Roads.

Schools.

Patrols.

More administrators.

More soldiers.

Another settlement began south of the river.

Then another beside the Safe Road.

Rell had attacked Darkheart because too many people were leaving.

The attack caused thousands more to leave.

Every blade.

Again.

No one needed to quote anything.

The world was doing the work itself.

---

Zee stood above the newest settlement while construction fires burned below.

Twenty-four.

Still dark.

Still predatory.

Still willing to kill.

Still willing to feed.

Still enjoying the fear of enemies who deserved to fear him.

The quarry had not redeemed him.

It had taught him something worse.

He could not honestly promise it would never happen again.

He would not insult Ner.

Kael.

Rez.

Zareth.

Or himself with that lie.

What he could promise was awareness.

If the line disappeared again, people now knew what they were looking for.

And Zee knew too.

The monster had never been the problem.

Zee liked the monster.

He had built parts of his kingdom with its teeth.

The danger was losing the ability to choose where those teeth pointed.

Before Rell, Zee had crossed that line without knowing it was gone.

Now he knew exactly where it was.

That did not make him safer.

It made every future step across it a choice heavier than before.

# Chapter Ninety-Four

## The Man Who Killed Gods

The first warning was a corpse.

Not Human.

Not Witch.

Not Vampire.

A god.

Darkheart scouts found the body three miles beyond the northern boundary.

It had fallen from the sky.

No heartbeat.

No divine regeneration.

No return.

One wound crossed its chest.

Black.

Still burning.

Zee crouched beside it.

Ner stood behind him.

“This is not like the one you killed.”

“No.”

Zee touched the earth beside the wound.

The grass had died.

Not burned.

Denied.

Even the dead god’s residual power refused to heal around the injury.

Zee’s expression sharpened.

“Something made sure this stayed dead.”

A voice answered from the trees.

“I did.”

Zee stood.

A man walked into the clearing.

Human-shaped.

Tall.

Dark coat.

No crown.

No armor.

One black blade strapped across his back.

His heartbeat was slow.

His blood smelled Human.

Mostly.

But something underneath it made Zee’s Vampire senses recoil.

Not Demon.

Not God.

Not Witch.

Darkness with structure.

Ner’s Gold rose.

The stranger looked at it.

“Beautiful.”

Ner’s expression cooled.

“Do not.”

The man smiled.

Then looked at Zee.

“Zee Darkheart.”

“Unfortunately.”

“You drained a god.”

“Yes.”

“You survived divine blood.”

“Yes.”

“You corrupted what remained.”

Zee’s eyes narrowed.

“No.”

The man tilted his head.

“No?”

“My blood changed it.”

“That distinction matters to you?”

“Yes.”

The stranger smiled faintly.

“Good.”

Zee looked at the dead god.

“Name.”

“Cassel Rhune.”

“And what are you?”

Cassel pulled the black blade from his back.

The dead god’s remaining aura recoiled from it.

Ner whispered:

“Zee.”

He felt it too.

Cassel answered himself.

“Godslayer.”

Silence.

Zee looked at him.

Then at the dead god.

“Dramatic profession.”

Cassel laughed.

“I expected more fear.”

“You came to my border alone.”

“Yes.”

“That usually means confidence or stupidity.”

“Which am I?”

Zee’s pupils narrowed into slits.

“I have not decided.”

Cassel smiled wider.

“Then decide while fighting.”

He moved.

---

Fast.

Not Vampire fast.

Different.

Efficient.

The black blade struck Zee’s forearm.

Crimson-black scales caught it.

For half a second.

Then split.

Zee’s eyes widened.

The blade cut through scale and flesh.

Black fire entered the wound.

Zee jumped backward.

Healing began.

Stopped.

That was new.

Cassel saw his expression.

“There.”

Zee looked at his arm.

The wound remained open.

Dark Divinity burned along the edges.

His Vampire regeneration pushed.

Wolf vitality followed.

Dragon durability resisted.

Crimson biology searched for an answer.

Nothing immediate.

Cassel attacked again.

Zee smiled.

“Oh.”

Ner knew that smile.

“You are enjoying this.”

“Yes.”

“That is concerning.”

Cassel’s blade came for Zee’s throat.

Zee ducked.

Assassin movement.

Palm into elbow.

Knee.

Turn.

Cassel absorbed the strike and drove his forehead into Zee’s face.

Horn met skull.

Cassel staggered.

Zee did not.

“Human,” Zee said.

Cassel wiped blood from his forehead.

“Very.”

Then black force erupted from his free hand.

It hit Zee like a collapsing cathedral.

He flew through three trees.

Ner’s Gold struck Cassel from the side.

Cassel raised the blade.

Gold touched Dark Divinity.

Cracked.

Ner stared.

Cassel looked at him.

“I did not come for you.”

“Then stop hitting my boyfriend.”

Zee climbed from the broken trees.

Blood ran down his arm.

“I had it handled.”

Ner looked at the three destroyed trees.

“Clearly.”

Cassel watched them.

“You love each other.”

Zee’s face cooled.

Cassel continued.

“That creates weaknesses.”

“No.”

“It always does.”

Zee disappeared.

Vampire speed.

Cassel turned late.

Zee caught him by the throat and drove him into the ground.

The clearing cratered.

Cassel stabbed upward.

The blade entered Zee’s side.

Deep.

Zee snarled.

Cassel twisted.

The wound burned.

Healing died around it.

Then Zee smiled down at him.

“You think pain makes me release people?”

Cassel’s eyes changed.

First uncertainty.

Good.

Zee grabbed the blade with one hand.

Silver hurt.

Magic hurt.

This—

this hurt differently.

Black Divinity burned directly through supernatural resistance.

Zee pulled himself farther onto the blade.

Closer.

Cassel stared.

“That should stop you.”

“It did.”

Zee’s fangs descended.

“From healing.”

Then he bit Cassel.

---

The blood was wrong.

Not poisonous.

Worse.

Dark Divinity moved inside it like something with intention.

It entered Zee’s mouth.

Touched Crimson blood.

And attacked.

Zee released Cassel immediately.

Black veins spread across his jaw.

Ner moved.

“Zee!”

Zee dropped to one knee.

His body tried processing it.

Demon.

No.

Divine.

No.

Corruption.

No.

Dark Divinity refused every category.

It did not want to become part of him.

Crimson biology pushed back.

Hard.

The foreign force burned out through Zee’s mouth in black smoke.

Zee spat blood.

Cassel stood slowly.

Now genuinely interested.

“You rejected it.”

Zee wiped his mouth.

“It rejected me first.”

“No.”

Cassel stared at him.

“Most things touched by Dark Divinity either submit or rot.”

Zee stood.

His wound still open.

“I do neither.”

Cassel’s expression darkened.

“That is exactly why you are dangerous.”

Zee laughed once.

“You killed a god and came to lecture me about danger?”

“I kill gods because gods become untouchable.”

“I am not a god.”

“You consumed one.”

“And remained me.”

“For now.”

There.

Motive.

Zee understood.

Cassel did not want his blood.

Did not want hybrids.

Did not care about Darkheart.

He believed Zee might someday become divine.

And Cassel killed divinity before it became permanent.

Zee’s expression cooled.

“You came to kill what I might become.”

Cassel did not deny it.

The similarity to Mara was immediate.

Not exact.

But close enough to irritate him.

“That is a dangerous argument around me.”

Cassel lifted the blade.

“I have killed nine gods.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Then you should know better than to mistake one.”

---

They collided again.

Witchcraft shattered the ground beneath Cassel.

Dark Divinity broke the spell before it closed.

Zee shifted Wolf.

Near-black.

Four-legged.

He vanished into the trees.

Cassel turned.

Listened.

Wrong sense.

Zee came from behind.

Jaws caught Cassel’s sword arm.

Cassel drove black force through Zee’s ribs.

Wolf Zee released.

Rolled.

Changed human mid-motion.

Claws struck.

Cassel blocked two.

Third opened his chest.

Blood.

Human blood laced with darkness.

Zee smelled fear now.

Tiny.

Beautiful.

Cassel smiled despite it.

“You like that.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He cut Zee across the face.

The wound stayed.

Zee touched it.

Blood.

Then smiled.

“You do too.”

Cassel said nothing.

That answer was enough.

Two dark men.

Different rules.

Cassel killed gods because he believed unchecked divinity inevitably became tyranny.

Zee killed threats because he believed choice mattered more than blood.

Neither considered himself clean.

Good.

Clean people were exhausting.

Then Cassel raised the blade toward Darkheart.

“Your kingdom follows you like worshippers.”

Zee’s smile vanished.

“They are citizens.”

“Kings always say that before temples.”

“You know nothing about them.”

“I know they kneel.”

“Some do.”

“They obey.”

“Sometimes.”

“They fear you.”

Zee remembered the quarry.

That one landed.

Cassel saw it.

Mistake.

Zee crossed the distance.

One fist hit Cassel’s jaw.

Then another.

Dragon force.

Vampire strength.

Wolf brutality.

Assassin placement.

The third strike broke bone.

Cassel hit the ground.

Zee stepped on his sword arm.

Cassel looked up.

“You are proving—”

Zee broke the arm.

Cassel screamed.

Zee liked it.

Deliberately.

Choice intact.

“That,” Zee said quietly, “was for using my people to explain me.”

Then black force exploded.

Zee flew backward.

Cassel escaped into the forest.

Not running blindly.

Strategic retreat.

Zee started after him.

Ner caught his wrist.

Zee turned.

Ner did not tell him not to kill.

He asked one thing.

“Are you choosing?”

Zee looked toward the blood trail.

Human pupils returned.

“Yes.”

Ner released him.

“Then go.”

Zee smiled.

And hunted.

---

# Chapter Ninety-Five

## Dark Divinity

Cassel Rhune made it twelve miles.

Zee gave him six.

Then stopped chasing.

Cassel realized too late.

The Godslayer entered an abandoned mountain shrine and found Zee already sitting on the altar.

Cassel stopped.

“How?”

Zee smiled.

“Assassin.”

“I left false trails.”

“I know.”

“Three.”

“I know.”

Cassel looked toward the entrance behind him.

Then back.

“You stopped following.”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Six miles ago.”

For the first time, Cassel looked annoyed.

Zee liked that too.

“Your mistake,” Zee said, “was assuming hunting means following.”

Cassel drew his blade with his unbroken hand.

His other arm hung badly.

Dark Divinity crawled through the fracture.

Repairing it slowly.

Not healing.

Forcing function.

Interesting.

Zee stood.

The wounds Cassel gave him still had not fully closed.

Face.

Arm.

Side.

Black edges.

Pain remained.

He had not felt this damaged for years.

It made him vicious.

Not uncontrolled.

Vicious.

Different.

---

Cassel attacked first.

The shrine exploded.

Black Divinity cut through old wards.

Zee threw himself sideways.

Silent magic collapsed a pillar.

Cassel sliced through it.

Zee expected that.

The falling stone hid the knife.

Assassin blade entered Cassel’s thigh.

Cassel snarled.

Zee appeared behind him.

Claws opened his back.

Cassel spun.

Black blade through Zee’s stomach.

Both stopped.

Close.

Bleeding.

Cassel whispered:

“You cannot heal.”

“Currently.”

“You cannot adapt to Dark Divinity.”

“Yet.”

Cassel’s eyes hardened.

“That word is why I came.”

Zee grabbed his wrist.

“Then you still do not understand me.”

He slammed Cassel into the altar.

Again.

Again.

Stone broke.

The Godslayer drove black force through Zee’s chest.

Zee staggered.

Cassel pulled the blade free.

For the first time since his newborn death—

Zee’s body felt quiet.

No rapid healing.

No immediate adaptation.

No easy answer.

Cassel saw it.

“You feel mortal.”

Zee looked down at the wound.

Then laughed.

Cassel frowned.

“What is funny?”

“I was never immortal because I healed quickly.”

The shrine shook.

Crimson-and-gold eyes lifted.

“I am immortal because death already tried.”

Zee stepped forward.

“And lost.”

Cassel struck.

Zee caught the sword between both hands.

Dark Divinity burned through his palms.

Flesh split.

Smoke rose.

Zee did not release it.

# Chapter Ninety-Six

## Before the Same Sun Set

Cassel Rhune died before dawn.

Zee remained beside the ruined shrine after the Godslayer’s body went cold.

Blood covered the snow.

Most of it was his.

Black Divinity still burned through the wounds Cassel had opened.

One cut crossed Zee’s face.

Another split his shoulder.

A deeper wound remained beneath his ribs where Cassel’s blade had entered and refused to let Vampire healing close it properly.

His scales were cracked.

His hands were burned.

His heart still carried damage from the blade Cassel had driven through it.

Zee stood anyway.

Zareth watched him in human form.

“You need a healer.”

“I need breakfast.”

“You were stabbed through the heart.”

“I noticed.”

“That was not a joke.”

“It hurt like one.”

Zareth stared at him.

Through the Link came irritation wrapped around concern.

**You are barely healing.**

Zee looked down at the blackened edge of the wound in his side.

His Crimson biology had learned something during the fight.

Not how to use Dark Divinity.

Not how to absorb it.

Only how to resist being opened quite as deeply by it the next time.

Small.

Incomplete.

The burns still hurt.

The wounds still resisted healing.

Black Divinity remained dangerous.

Good.

Zee preferred dangerous things that stayed dangerous.

Ner arrived as morning light reached the mountains.

He took one look at Zee.

“No.”

Zee frowned.

“No what?”

“Whatever you are about to say.”

“I was going to say hello.”

“You were going to say you are fine.”

Zee smiled.

“I am alive.”

“That was not the question.”

Ner approached and touched the skin near Zee’s ribs without touching the wound itself.

Bloodsong reacted immediately.

Then recoiled.

His expression hardened.

“This is wrong.”

“Godslayer.”

“I know.”

“You asked.”

“I did not.”

Zareth looked between them.

“I am going back to Drakonis before this becomes domestic.”

Zee looked at him.

“You are already involved.”

“That is exactly why I am leaving.”

Through the Link came warmth.

Then Zareth shifted.

True Dragon form exploded across the mountain ridge.

Wings opened.

He launched toward Drakonis.

Ner watched him disappear.

Then looked back at Zee.

“We are going home.”

Zee opened his mouth.

Thunder answered first.

Not ordinary thunder.

The sky turned white.

Then black.

Clouds formed in seconds.

The mountain pressure changed hard enough to make stone groan.

Ner looked upward.

“That is not weather.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“No.”

A figure descended through the storm.

Bare feet never touched the ground.

Gold-white armor.

A spear made from condensed lightning.

Eyes filled with blue divine fire.

The air bent around him.

Not because of magic.

Authority.

The mountain itself seemed to recognize him.

Zee’s smile widened.

Ner sighed.

“Of course.”

The God looked at Cassel’s corpse.

Then Zee.

“So.”

Zee wiped blood from his mouth.

“So?”

“You killed the Godslayer.”

“Yes.”

The God’s gaze moved over Zee’s wounds.

“You are weaker than I expected.”

Zee looked at his own bleeding chest.

“Rude.”

The God ignored that.

“I am Kharos.”

The storm intensified.

“Lord of the Tempest Throne.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Congratulations.”

Ner covered his face briefly.

Kharos’s expression hardened.

“You have killed divine blood before.”

“Yes.”

“You consumed it.”

“Yes.”

“You survived.”

“Yes.”

“And now you have killed one who carried Dark Divinity.”

Zee’s smile disappeared.

Kharos descended another foot.

“Mortals are beginning to mistake survival for authority.”

“I am not mortal.”

“You are not divine either.”

“I know.”

“That distinction will be corrected today.”

Zee glanced toward Cassel’s corpse.

Then back at Kharos.

“You waited until after he cut me apart.”

“I observed an opportunity.”

Zee laughed.

Actually laughed.

Blood ran down his side while he did it.

Kharos frowned.

“You find this amusing?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Zee’s fangs descended.

“Because Cassel already reminded me how much I enjoy fighting things that can hurt me.”

The storm stopped moving.

For one second.

Then Kharos attacked.

---

Divine lightning struck first.

Zee moved.

Too slow.

The bolt hit his shoulder.

His entire body locked.

Crimson-black scales cracked.

The old Black Divinity wound reopened.

Zee hit the ground.

Kharos raised one hand.

Gravity changed.

Zee slammed deeper into stone.

Ner’s Gold surged.

Kharos looked toward him.

“Kneel.”

Divine authority struck.

Ner’s knees buckled.

He caught himself with one hand.

Gold shook around him.

Zee’s eyes changed.

Slits.

“Do not.”

Kharos looked back.

“Do not what?”

“Order him.”

“You command everyone around you.”

“No.”

Zee pushed against the divine pressure.

Muscles tore.

Dragon force answered.

He stood.

Slowly.

“They choose whether they stay.”

Kharos drove the spear forward.

Zee caught the shaft.

Lightning exploded through his body.

His hands burned.

Still he held it.

Kharos stared.

Zee smiled.

“You keep expecting pain to make me obedient.”

Then Witchcraft struck.

Silent.

One closed fist.

The stone beneath Kharos collapsed.

Not enough to hurt a God.

Enough to shift his footing.

Assassin lesson.

Position first.

Zee pulled.

Vampire strength.

Dragon force.

Kharos stumbled one step.

Wolf instinct saw the opening before thought finished forming.

Zee struck his knee.

Hard.

Divine bone cracked.

Kharos roared.

The storm answered.

A wall of wind threw Zee across the mountain.

He landed badly.

One rib broke.

Then another.

His healing remained slow.

Cassel’s wounds still interfered.

Kharos flew toward him.

“You should already be dead.”

Zee rolled aside as the spear hit stone.

“I hear that often.”

Kharos backhanded him.

Divine strength broke part of Zee’s jaw.

Zee spat blood.

Then laughed again.

Kharos finally looked disturbed.

Good.

---

The fight crossed the mountain.

Kharos controlled the sky.

Zee controlled nothing that easily.

So he stopped fighting the sky.

He went into the forest.

Wolf form.

Four-legged.

Near-black fur.

Crimson-and-gold eyes.

No horns.

No scales.

No Dragon features.

Only predator.

Kharos descended after him.

Mistake.

Lightning destroyed trees.

Zee was never where it landed.

Wolf instinct read pressure shifts.

Air displacement.

Static.

Movement.

Kharos raised the spear.

Wolf Zee changed direction before it moved.

Then changed back to human form behind him.

One hand lifted.

“Down.”

Witch force struck Kharos from above.

Divine authority resisted.

For half a second.

Enough.

Zee hit him.

Fist.

Elbow.

Horn.

Claw.

No wasted motion.

Cassel had wounded Zee.

Nanda Parbat had taught him what to do when power could not solve a fight.

Kharos drove lightning into Zee’s abdomen.

Zee convulsed.

The God grabbed him by the throat.

“You are nothing beside divinity.”

Zee’s eyes became very calm.

Human pupils.

Choice.

“Then why did you wait until I was wounded?”

Kharos froze.

There.

Fear did not arrive yet.

But doubt did.

Zee bit his wrist.

---

Divine blood entered Zee’s mouth.

Hot.

Storm-heavy.

Powerful.

His Crimson biology reacted immediately.

Not worship.

Not transformation.

Processing.

The divine blood tried to expand.

Zee’s body crushed it down.

No God nature.

No storm authority.

No divinity.

Only nourishment.

Pressure.

Adaptation.

Kharos screamed and ripped free.

Zee swallowed.

The old Black Divinity wounds burned violently.

For one terrible second, divine blood and anti-divine residue collided inside him.

Then Zee’s body separated them.

Not perfectly.

Enough.

The next time Kharos’s authority crashed into Zee, it still hurt.

But Zee recognized the pressure sooner.

Braced sooner.

Survived cleaner.

Small.

Not immunity.

Just Zee learning.

Kharos saw it.

“You are changing.”

“I always am.”

“That is the abomination.”

Zee wiped divine blood from his mouth.

“No.”

His eyes narrowed into slits again.

“That is the consequence.”

Then he attacked.

---

By sunset, the storm was dying.

So was Kharos.

One divine arm hung broken.

His spear was gone.

Zee had thrown it into a ravine after breaking three of his own fingers taking it.

Kharos’s regeneration kept repairing wounds.

Zee kept reopening them.

Witchcraft disrupted position.

Wolf instinct predicted retreat.

Vampire speed closed distance.

Assassin technique targeted the same damaged joints.

Crimson Demonic Dragon force endured impacts that should have shattered him.

Zee himself looked worse.

Blood everywhere.

One eye swollen.

Three black Godslayer wounds still open.

Scales broken.

Breathing heavy.

Still smiling.

Kharos backed toward the edge of the mountain.

The God finally smelled afraid.

Zee stopped.

Enjoyed it.

Fully.

Deliberately.

Kharos understood.

“You could finish this.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you waiting?”

Zee stepped closer.

“Because you came here believing you were above fear.”

Kharos’s divine fire flickered.

Zee smiled.

“I wanted you to meet it.”

Kharos raised one trembling hand.

“You cannot kill what I am.”

Zee reached him.

“I already have.”

He bit.

Kharos screamed.

Zee fed deeply.

Divine regeneration fought.

Then weakened.

Storm clouds collapsed overhead.

Kharos struck Zee.

Once.

Twice.

The third blow barely moved him.

Zee kept drinking.

The God’s heartbeat slowed.

Divine light dimmed.

Fear became panic.

Zee pulled back before the final beat.

Kharos sagged in his grip.

“Please.”

There.

A God begging.

Zee’s face remained calm.

He could have prolonged it.

Wanted to.

Instead he chose enough.

“Now you understand.”

He broke Kharos’s neck.

Then tore the remaining divine life from him through blood.

The storm stopped.

Completely.

Kharos died.

Permanently.

No escape.

No avatar.

No return.

The Godslayer lay dead before dawn.

The God lay dead before sunset.

Same day.

Zee looked toward the darkening sky.

“Long day.”

Then the river below the mountain rose upward.

---

Not flooded.

Rose.

A column of water climbed from the valley against gravity.

Ner moved beside Zee.

Gold ready.

Zee watched.

Water spiraled through the air.

Divine blood from Kharos’s corpse had reached cracks in the mountain.

Underground streams.

The water reacted violently.

Then became still.

Impossible stillness.

A woman stepped from it.

No gasp.

No struggle.

No wet stumble.

She walked through suspended water as if crossing a palace floor.

Dark hair fell down her back.

Pearl-black armor covered her shoulders and waist.

A crown of dark silver rested against her head.

Not decorative.

Royal.

Her eyes were deep blue-black.

Not glowing.

Worse.

Watching.

She looked at Kharos’s corpse.

Then Cassel’s blood still dried across Zee.

Then at Zee himself.

The wounds.

The divine blood.

The broken scales.

She showed no awe.

Only irritation.

“You killed a god.”

Zee looked at Kharos.

“Yes.”

“You killed a Godslayer this morning.”

“Yes.”

Her gaze moved toward the river still climbing behind her.

“And somehow both became my problem.”

Zee smiled.

“Long day.”

She stared at him.

For one second.

Then:

“I already dislike you.”

Zee’s smile widened.

“Good.”

The woman looked toward the water.

“You have made the ocean angry.”

Zee glanced at the dead God.

“Tell it to wait.”

Ner started laughing.

The Queen did not.

Not yet.

---

# Chapter Ninety-Seven

## The Queen Beneath the Water

Her name was Nymeris Thalryn.

She did not offer it immediately.

First she ordered Zee away from Kharos’s corpse.

Zee looked at her.

“No.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“That was not a request.”

“That is unfortunate.”

“You are standing beside a divine rupture connected to every underground current beneath this mountain.”

Zee glanced downward.

“Still sounds like a request.”

Ner stood several feet away, enjoying this far too much.

Nymeris noticed.

“You find this entertaining?”

“Extremely.”

“Why?”

Ner smiled.

“People usually need longer before ordering him around.”

Zee looked at him.

“Whose side are you on?”

“Mine.”

Fair.

Nymeris stepped closer to the dead God.

The river responded.

Water curled around her wrist.

Not Bloodsong.

Not ordinary Witchcraft.

Older.

Oceanic.

Pressure moved through it.

Zee felt something beneath the surface.

Abyss.

Depth.

The sensation of water so deep sunlight had never reached it.

Nymeris touched two fingers to Kharos’s blood.

The river convulsed.

Her expression hardened.

“You killed the holder of a Tempest Throne beside a watershed connected to the deep currents.”

Zee leaned against a broken stone because his body had finally started objecting to the day.

“And?”

“And divine authority does not simply vanish politely.”

“What did it do?”

“It fell.”

Zee frowned.

“Into what?”

“The water.”

That got his attention.

Nymeris looked toward the river.

“Kharos’s death created a pressure fracture through the current network. My eastern boundary felt it before he finished dying.”

“Your boundary?”

Now she finally looked directly at him.

“I am Queen Nymeris Thalryn.”

The water behind her rose higher.

“Reigning Queen of Nhalaris.”

Ner’s expression changed.

Zee’s did not.

He had never heard the name.

Nymeris noticed.

“Of course surface kings forgot.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“You hid underwater.”

“We survived underwater.”

“Same result.”

“No.”

The answer carried enough authority that even Zee stopped smiling for half a second.

Good.

He liked her better already.

---

Nhalaris was older than several kingdoms Zee knew.

That was all Nymeris volunteered.

Not where it stood beneath the ocean.

Not how many people lived there.

Not how its armies moved.

Only enough.

An ancient underwater civilization.

Its own laws.

Its own military.

Its own magic.

Its own throne.

Its royal bloodline had carried a relationship with the Abyss longer than surface records remembered.

Siren blood lived inside that inheritance.

Old.

Hereditary.

Royal.

Not every bearer expressed it the same way.

Nymeris did.

But not like Ner.

Her voice did not command blood.

It affected water.

Pressure.

Resonance through deep currents.

The ocean heard her differently than people did.

Zee studied her.

She caught him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“I am looking.”

“That is what staring is.”

“No.”

Ner laughed again.

Nymeris looked toward him.

Then stopped.

Something passed through the air.

Small.

Almost inaudible.

Ner’s Bloodsong answered automatically.

One low resonance beneath his heartbeat.

Nymeris’s eyes sharpened.

Ner’s smile vanished.

“There is something in your voice.”

Nymeris studied him.

“There is something impossible in yours.”

Zee looked between them.

Ner stepped closer.

Not threatened.

Curious.

“Siren?”

Nymeris’s expression changed by only a fraction.

“Partly.”

Ner’s Gold moved faintly around his fingers.

“My mother’s line.”

Nymeris watched the resonance around him.

“That is not ordinary Siren blood.”

“No.”

“What happened to you?”

Ner glanced at Zee.

Nymeris followed the look.

Then closed her eyes briefly.

“Of course.”

Zee frowned.

“What does that mean?”

“It means I have known you less than an hour and you have already become responsible for two separate problems.”

“Only two?”

Nymeris stared.

Ner laughed again.

Good.

---

Then Nymeris noticed Zee’s wounds properly.

Her humor disappeared.

“What did that?”

“Godslayer.”

“And where is he?”

“Dead.”

She looked toward the ruined shrine above them.

Then at Kharos.

“And that?”

“Also dead.”

Nymeris stared at him.

Zee waited.

Finally:

“What?”

“You killed both today?”

“Yes.”

“You killed a Godslayer before sunrise.”

“Yes.”

“Then fought a true God while those wounds were still open.”

“Yes.”

“And killed him before sunset.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked at Ner.

“Is he always like this?”

Ner considered.

“Unfortunately.”

Zee looked offended.

Nymeris looked back at the black wounds.

“Dark Divinity.”

Zee’s eyes sharpened.

“You know it.”

“I know of it.”

“Godslayers?”

“Yes.”

“How many?”

Nymeris smiled faintly.

“Surface kings really do believe nothing exists until they personally meet it.”

Zee stood straighter.

“That was unnecessarily insulting.”

“It was accurate.”

“Worse.”

Nymeris’s gaze returned to the wounds.

“You are resisting it.”

“A little.”

“You did not absorb it.”

“No.”

“Good.”

Zee frowned.

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

“Because attempting to hold Dark Divinity without being chosen by it would be an excellent way to destroy yourself.”

“I was not planning to.”

Nymeris looked at the dead God.

“No?”

“No.”

“He changes around pressure.”

Not awe.

Assessment.

“Usually.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

Most people called it terrifying.

Monster.

Impossible.

Weapon.

“What?”

“You did it again.”

Zee answered mentally.

**I noticed.**

**You smiled.**

**I smile around dangerous people.**

“Dragons do not live underwater.”

“No.”

Nymeris’s expression remained calm.

“But dead ones sink.”

Silence.

Zareth stared.

Zee looked at her.

“That was dark.”

Nymeris glanced toward him.

“You killed two immortal threats before dinner.”

“Fair.”

**I like her less now.**

Zee answered:

**Unfortunately.**

The river split.

Not physically.

Magically.

One current flowed downstream.

Another pulled backward beneath it.

Nymeris knelt beside the water.

Her face changed.

Queen now.

No irritation.

No jokes.

Responsibility.

“My eastern ward is weakening.”

Zee crouched beside her despite the pain in his ribs.

“What happens if it breaks?”

“Pressure from the Abyss enters channels not built to hold it.”

“Meaning?”

“Villages beneath the shelf collapse.”

“How many people?”

Nymeris looked at him.

“Eleven thousand under the eastern reach.”

Not because they were his.

Because he understood the look on her face.

Calculation.

Distance.

Time.

People.

A ruler trying to decide which disaster could be allowed because not all of them could be stopped.

He knew that expression.

She saw recognition in him.

Not sympathy.

Recognition.

“You understand.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked back toward the water.

“Most kings ask what happens to their trade.”

“I hate trade meetings.”

“That may be the first sensible thing you have said.”

Zee almost smiled.

Then pain tore through his side.

He hid it badly.

Nymeris noticed.

“You are injured.”

“I remain aware.”

“And you are considering helping.”

“Yes.”

“You cannot even stand properly.”

“I am standing.”

“You are leaning on a rock.”

“The rock is supportive.”

Ner turned away because he was laughing.

Nymeris stared at Zee for a long moment.

Then something changed.

Not affection.

Respect.

Small.

Earned.

“You do not know my people.”

“No.”

“You have never seen Nhalaris.”

“No.”

“You owe us nothing.”

Zee looked toward the unnatural current.

“I killed the God.”

“Yes.”

“That made the fracture.”

“Yes.”

“Then part of it is mine.”

Nymeris studied him.

That answer mattered.

Not because Zee took blame for everything.

Because he took responsibility for what was actually his.

She understood that too.

They worked through the night.

Not to repair the entire oceanic boundary.

Impossible.

Only to stop the fracture from widening.

Nymeris controlled the water.

Ner used Bloodsong resonance to identify where living currents carried the divine disturbance.

Zee used Witchcraft to break divine residue from the stone without touching Nymeris’s Abyssal magic directly.

Zareth carried collapsed boulders from the river channel in human form until he became irritated and shifted into true Dragon form to move the rest.

Nymeris stood waist-deep in the river.

Her voice changed.

Not louder.

Deeper.

The water responded like something remembering its Queen.

Ancient Siren resonance moved through the current.

Not compulsion.

Not Bloodsong.

A royal call through water itself.

The fracture closed.

Mostly.

Nymeris emerged from the river.

For the first time, she looked tired.

Zee noticed.

Did not comment.

Queens disliked obvious observations as much as kings did.

Good.

---

By morning, the rumors had already started.

Cassel Rhune.

True Godslayer.

Dead.

Kharos.

True God.

Dead.

Same day.

Killed by the same man.

Surface reports disagreed on everything else.

Some claimed Zee had stolen Dark Divinity.

False.

Some claimed he had become a god.

False.

Some claimed he had killed Kharos with Cassel’s weapon.

False.

One report called him:

**THE MAN WHO KILLED GODS.**

Zee read it and frowned.

“That is dramatic.”

Zareth looked over his shoulder.

“You say that like you are not.”

“I am tasteful.”

Ner laughed.

Nymeris looked genuinely confused.

“Do surface people always name everything?”

“Yes,” Zee said.

“No,” Ner said simultaneously.

Nymeris looked between them.

“I see.”

Zee burned the report.

---

Nymeris prepared to return to Nhalaris before noon.

The river rose around her again.

Zee stood nearby.

Still wounded.

Still bleeding slightly beneath fresh bandages.

She looked at him.

“You owe my kingdom a visit.”

Zee stared.

“I do not do underwater.”

“You will.”

“That sounded like an order.”

“It was.”

Zee smiled.

Nymeris did not.

Then almost did.

Almost.

Ner noticed.

Zareth noticed.

Zee did not care.

There was nothing romantic in it.

Something stranger had begun.

Two rulers who understood responsibility.

Two people accustomed to being obeyed.

Two kingdoms that had existed without needing each other.

Until one dead God connected them through water.

Zee folded his arms.

“What happens if I refuse?”

Nymeris stepped backward into the rising river.

“I will come back.”

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is diplomatic.”

“Surface diplomacy is better.”

“No.”

She sank without splashing.

Then stopped.

Only her face remained above the impossible water.

“Ner.”

He looked at her.

“We should speak again.”

Bloodsong hummed faintly.

Ner nodded.

“I think so.”

Then Nymeris looked at Zee one last time.

“Try not to kill another god before I repair the damage from this one.”

Zee considered.

“No promises.”

Her eyes narrowed.

“King Darkheart.”

“Queen Thalryn.”

Then she vanished beneath the water.

The river fell normally.

Silence returned.

Zareth looked at Zee.

“She is going to become a problem.”

Zee smiled.

“Probably.”

Ner stepped beside him.

“You like her.”

“As a person.”

“I know.”

Zee looked at him.

“No jealousy?”

Ner stared.

“You are gay.”

“Correct.”

“And I have eyes.”

“Also correct.”

Ner smiled.

“Besides, I like her too.”

Zareth groaned.

“Excellent. Now there are three of you.”

Zee looked toward the river.

Somewhere far beneath oceans surface kingdoms barely understood, Queen Nymeris Thalryn ruled an ancient civilization tied to the Abyss and old Siren blood.

Zee knew almost nothing about her.

She knew almost nothing about him.

That was fine.

They had time.

A reason to meet again was enough.

Behind them lay the blood of a Godslayer.

Ahead of them lay the corpse of a God.

Before the same sun had set, Zee Darkheart had killed both.

And before the next sun fully rose, another kingdom had entered his life.

Not through conquest.

Not prophecy.

Not destiny.

Through consequence.

The world had become larger again.

And darker with it.

# Chapter Ninety-Eight

## The Kingdom Beneath the Ocean

Three months passed before Zee visited Nhalaris.

Nymeris reminded him twice.

The third message contained no words.

Only a sphere of seawater floating above the Darkheart council table.

Zee stared at it.

Rez stared at Zee.

Ner smiled.

Zareth leaned back in his chair.

“She is getting impatient.”

Zee looked at him.

“You sound pleased.”

“I am.”

The sphere burst.

Water hit Zee directly in the face.

Silence.

Rez started laughing first.

Ner followed.

Zareth did not even try hiding it.

Zee wiped water from his eyes.

“I hate her.”

Ner stood.

“No, you don’t.”

“I am reconsidering.”

A folded shell rested where the sphere had been.

Zee opened it.

One sentence.

**COME BELOW, SURFACE KING.**

Zee’s eye twitched.

---

Nhalaris did not sit on the ocean floor.

It existed inside it.

That distinction became clear when Nymeris opened the passage.

Zee, Ner, and Zareth stood on a black coastal cliff while seawater climbed upward into an arch.

Not a portal.

A road.

Water held apart by pressure and ancient magic.

Nymeris waited beyond it.

Dark armor.

Silver-black crown.

Completely dry despite standing inside the sea.

“You came.”

Zee stepped through.

“I was assaulted by correspondence.”

“You ignored two requests.”

“They were very long.”

“They were six sentences.”

“Exactly.”

Ner walked behind him.

Zareth entered in human form.

Nymeris looked toward the Dragon prince.

“No true form below the inner gates.”

Zareth raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because you are enormous.”

Fair.

Zee smiled.

Zareth privately sent:

**I dislike this kingdom already.**

Zee answered:

**You dislike doors.**

**Correct.**

---

The descent took nearly an hour.

Not because they walked downward.

Because Nhalaris moved around them.

Currents shifted.

Stone opened.

Water became corridors.

Then suddenly—

the ocean disappeared.

A city stretched beneath a living dome of deep-blue pressure.

Towers of black coral.

Silver bridges.

Bioluminescent gardens.

Water channels flowing upward along walls.

Siren guards in dark armor.

Others without visible Siren traits.

Families.

Merchants.

Soldiers.

Children.

An entire civilization hidden beneath the surface kingdoms.

Zee stopped.

Nymeris noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring again.”

“This one is deserved.”

That almost made her smile.

Almost.

Ner’s Bloodsong hummed faintly.

Dozens of distant voices answered the city around him.

Not directly.

Resonance.

Ancient Siren blood everywhere.

His expression changed.

Nymeris looked toward him.

“Too much?”

“A little.”

She nodded.

No mockery.

“Do not listen to everything.”

“I am not trying.”

“That is usually when it is worst.”

Ner looked at her.

Recognition.

Not identical power.

But experience.

That mattered.

---

The Nhalaris council hated Zee immediately.

That helped.

Seven ministers.

Three military commanders.

One Abyssal priestess.

None bowed.

Good.

Zee did not ask them to.

One minister spoke first.

“You killed Kharos.”

“Yes.”

“You ruptured our eastern current.”

“Yes.”

“You entered Nhalaris armed.”

Zee looked down at himself.

“I am always armed.”

Nymeris closed her eyes.

The minister continued.

“Your presence threatens the stability of this court.”

Zee looked toward Nymeris.

“Do they always speak like this?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It is.”

The minister looked offended.

Good.

Then another woman placed a map of the eastern current across the table.

The damage remained.

The fracture they closed on the surface had prevented collapse.

It had not repaired the deeper channels.

Three villages still operated under emergency pressure wards.

Nymeris looked toward Zee.

“This is why I summoned you.”

“Ordered.”

“Yes.”

Zee smiled.

“What do you need?”

No argument now.

Work.

Nymeris pointed.

“Divine residue embedded itself into an old Abyssal boundary.”

Zee studied the map.

“And if we remove it?”

“The boundary may fail.”

“If we leave it?”

“It spreads.”

“How many people?”

“Eight thousand seven hundred within the affected reach.”

Zee’s humor disappeared.

There.

Same burden.

Different kingdom.

Nymeris noticed.

“You understand why I did not wait politely.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Zee looked toward the map.

“Then we fix it.”

One minister objected.

“He is the reason it exists.”

Zee looked at him.

“Yes.”

The man paused.

Zee continued.

“That is why I am helping.”

No defensiveness.

No excuse.

Just responsibility.

Nymeris watched him carefully.

Another small piece of trust moved into place.

---

The repair took four days.

Zee did not command Nhalaris.

That was important.

Nymeris did.

Her engineers.

Her Siren wardens.

Her military.

Her laws.

Zee listened.

Mostly.

On the second day he ignored one safety order and nearly got crushed under deep-current pressure.

Nymeris found him afterward bleeding from both ears.

“You are impossible.”

“I survived.”

“That is not the same as listening.”

“I listened.”

“You did the opposite.”

“I heard you first.”

Nymeris stared.

Ner turned away to hide a smile.

Zee looked toward him.

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“You are thinking loudly.”

“Zareth says the same thing.”

Through the Link from another chamber:

**Because you are both annoying.**

Zee smiled.

Good.

---

The final breach sat beyond Nhalaris’s eastern shelf.

Open ocean.

Dark enough that even Zee’s Vampire sight struggled.

Nymeris entered the water first.

Not swimming.

Belonging.

The ocean carried her.

Ner followed inside a Golden breathing sphere.

Zee had one too.

He hated it.

“This is humiliating.”

Nymeris’s voice reached them through water resonance.

“You cannot breathe underwater.”

“I do not need much air.”

“You need some.”

“Technicality.”

She ignored him.

Zareth remained in human form until the passage widened.

Then shifted.

True Dragon form filled the dark water.

No fire.

No flight.

But enormous strength.

The Dragon Link carried his displeasure.

**I hate swimming.**

Zee answered:

**You look majestic.**

**I will drown you.**

**I cannot permanently die.**

**Then I will drown you repeatedly.**

Nymeris looked back.

“You two are arguing.”

Zee frowned.

“How do you know?”

“You both look irritated.”

Fair.

---

The divine residue had become a knot of storm-light beneath the shelf.

Nymeris anchored the current.

Ner used resonance to locate living pressure around it.

Zareth held the collapsing rock.

Zee entered the center.

The old Black Divinity scars across his body burned.

Not because Dark Divinity was present.

Because divine pressure recognized wounds that had once denied divinity.

Useful.

Painful.

Zee smiled.

Nymeris saw.

“You enjoy pain too much.”

“Only interesting pain.”

“That sentence is deeply concerning.”

Zee raised one hand.

Witch precision.

No giant blast.

He separated divine residue thread by thread.

Nymeris held the current around it.

Their magic did not merge.

Did not need to.

They worked beside one another.

Queen.

King.

Each controlling what belonged to them.

The final divine strand broke.

The ocean surged.

Zareth roared through the water.

Ner’s Gold snapped outward.

Nymeris lifted both hands.

Her voice changed.

Deep Siren resonance moved through miles of water.

The current obeyed.

Not like compulsion.

Like inheritance.

The Abyss recognized her.

The rupture closed.

Completely.

Nhalaris survived.

---

That night, Nymeris invited them to dinner.

Not diplomacy.

Dinner.

A distinction Zee noticed immediately.

No ministers.

No guards at the table.

Only Zee.

Ner.

Zareth.

Nymeris.

Zee looked around.

“Where is everyone?”

“I dismissed them.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted one meal without hearing someone explain why your existence threatens oceanic stability.”

Zee smiled.

“Reasonable.”

Nymeris poured wine.

Ner looked toward the food.

“Is that still moving?”

“Yes.”

“No.”

Zareth picked it up and ate it.

Ner stared.

Zareth shrugged.

“Dragon.”

Zee laughed.

Nymeris finally did too.

Not almost.

Actually.

The sound changed something.

Small.

Not romance.

Ease.

By the end of the night, Nymeris no longer called Zee Surface King every time she addressed him.

Only half the time.

Progress.

---

# Chapter Ninety-Nine

## The People Behind the Crowns

Nymeris came to Darkheart six months later.

Without warning.

Zee found her in Southhold arguing with a mason.

He stopped in the street.

“Why are you here?”

Nymeris looked over.

“To see whether your kingdom actually functions.”

The mason glanced between them.

Zee frowned.

“You could have started at the castle.”

“I have seen castles.”

She gestured toward Southhold.

“I wanted this.”

Homes.

Markets.

Wolf children chasing Vampire children through muddy streets.

Witches repairing protective runes on the school.

Former Rell workers building their own shops.

Kael arguing with a guard.

Tessa yelling at three patients.

Amara carrying lumber despite not being asked.

Nymeris watched all of it.

“This is not what surface reports describe.”

“Surface reports are written by people who dislike me.”

“They describe an army of hybrids.”

“I have four.”

“Five, if you count Rez.”

“He is Vesper.”

Nymeris glanced at him.

That answer mattered.

“You could claim him.”

“He would punch me again.”

“Again?”

Zee said nothing.

Nymeris smiled.

“I need that story.”

“No.”

---

Ner found them near the school.

Nymeris greeted him before Zee.

That offended Zee unnecessarily.

“You like him more.”

Nymeris looked at Ner.

“Yes.”

Ner smiled.

Zee stared at both of them.

“This alliance is becoming hostile.”

“Good,” Nymeris said.

Ner’s Bloodsong reacted when she stepped close.

Her Siren resonance answered more clearly now.

Still different.

Ner listened.

“You carry something deeper than the surface Siren lines I have encountered.”

Nymeris’s expression sharpened.

“My House descends from the royal Abyss line.”

“Does every Thalryn inherit it?”

“No.”

“Every Queen?”

“No.”

Ner nodded.

No more questions.

Nymeris noticed.

“You stopped.”

“You would tell me if you wanted me to know.”

She looked at Zee.

“Keep him.”

Zee blinked.

“I was already planning to.”

Ner laughed.

---

Nymeris stayed three weeks.

Not as guest decoration.

She attended councils.

Argued over Safe Road expansion.

Insulted Darkheart drainage systems.

Improved them.

Visited Kael’s training yards.

Asked Tessa about hybrid medicine.

Let Amara take her hunting through the southern forest and returned covered in mud, furious, and apparently happier.

She spent one afternoon with Rez when he arrived from Vesper.

The two argued about trade law for four hours.

Zee left after twenty minutes.

Cowardice sometimes meant survival.

Zareth arrived on the fifth day.

He and Nymeris immediately disagreed about whether oceanic territory included Dragon flight paths over open sea.

Neither yielded.

Zee watched them for half an hour.

Ner stood beside him.

“This is your fault.”

“I did nothing.”

“You introduced them.”

“I did not control the result.”

“That is usually your defense.”

Fair.

---

The attack came on Nymeris’s seventeenth day.

Not against her.

Against Southhold.

Again.

A mercenary company from a western kingdom wanted refugees returned for unpaid taxes and military desertion.

Different motive.

Same ugly assumption.

That people remained owned after leaving.

This time Southhold responded before Zee did.

Bells rang.

Children entered shelters.

Witch barriers rose.

Wolf trackers moved outside the walls.

Vampire defenders took rooftops.

Kael commanded the eastern street.

Tessa moved medical teams.

Amara vanished into the trees.

Zee stood beside Nymeris on the tower.

She watched.

“You are not moving.”

“I am.”

“You are standing.”

“I am watching first.”

Old Zee would already have been in the enemy line.

Nymeris understood the change.

“Your people know what to do.”

“Yes.”

“That bothers you.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because they learned by being attacked.”

Nymeris looked toward the battlefield.

“So did mine.”

There.

Same burden again.

Then the mercenaries broke through the western barrier.

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Now.”

He moved.

Nymeris moved too.

Not because Zee asked.

Because civilians were threatened.

---

Zee hit the first line in human form.

Crimson-black scales spreading over his arms.

One-word Witchcraft breaking weapons.

Vampire speed cutting through formation.

Wolf instinct reading motion.

Controlled.

Dark.

Efficient.

Nymeris fought differently.

Water erupted from underground wells.

Not enough to flood Southhold.

Enough to tear mercenaries off their feet.

Her voice carried through it.

Abyssal resonance.

Pressure.

Direction.

One man tried reaching a child shelter.

Nymeris slammed him into stone with a column of water.

Zee looked over.

“That was excessive.”

Nymeris stared.

“You broke someone’s leg with your face ten seconds ago.”

“Horn.”

“That does not improve it.”

Good.

They fought well together.

Not perfectly.

Zee pushed.

Nymeris contained.

Nymeris controlled space.

Zee hunted openings.

Neither commanded the other.

Neither needed to.

When the mercenary commander surrendered, Zee stopped.

Immediately.

That mattered after Rell.

Nymeris noticed.

He heard the commander’s heartbeat.

Smelled fear.

Wanted blood.

Still chose prison.

Nymeris said nothing.

She did not need to.

---

Afterward, they found six dead Darkheart citizens.

Three soldiers.

Three civilians.

Not clean.

Never clean.

Zee stood over the bodies.

Nymeris beside him.

No one spoke for a while.

Then she said:

“You count them all as yours.”

“Yes.”

“Even people who arrived months ago.”

“Yes.”

“Even if they were born elsewhere.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked toward him.

“That is why they keep coming.”

Zee’s jaw tightened.

“That is why they keep dying too.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

She did not soften the answer.

“They die because other rulers still think leaving is theft.”

Zee said nothing.

Nymeris continued.

“You are responsible for what happens under your protection.”

“Yes.”

“You are not responsible for the existence of cruelty beyond it.”

Zee almost argued.

Then stopped.

Not because she had absolved him.

She had not.

She was drawing the same distinction Ner often demanded of facts.

Responsibility without delusion.

Queen thinking.

Zee understood.

That was rarer than sympathy.

---

Later that night, Zee found Nymeris sitting alone on the southern wall.

No crown.

Hair loose.

She looked less like Queen of Nhalaris.

Still unmistakably one.

He sat beside her.

For once, neither began with an insult.

Nymeris spoke first.

“When I was nineteen, a pressure collapse killed two hundred people beneath the western shelf.”

Zee looked at her.

She had never told him anything personal before.

“I ordered the evacuation too late.”

“Why?”

“I believed the wardens when they said the barrier would hold.”

Silence.

“It did not.”

Zee understood immediately.

“How long did you blame yourself?”

Nymeris laughed without humor.

“I have not stopped.”

“There.”

She looked at him.

“That is stupid.”

“Yes.”

“Was that supposed to help?”

“No.”

He leaned back.

“I blame myself for people dying where I am not.”

“That is also stupid.”

“Yes.”

They sat in silence.

Then Nymeris smiled faintly.

“Good.”

“What?”

“Now we are both stupid.”

Zee laughed.

There.

Not diplomacy.

Not alliance.

Friendship.

Something deeper than usefulness.

Chosen slowly.

Earned.

---

Nymeris remained another week.

When she finally left, Darkheart children knew her name.

Tessa had forced her to take three medical books back to Nhalaris.

Amara had given her a hunting knife.

Kael had somehow lost money to her playing cards.

Rez sent trade proposals.

Zareth claimed he still disliked her.

Nobody believed him.

Ner walked with her to the river passage.

Zee followed.

Nymeris looked between them.

“Nhalaris will send a permanent diplomatic vessel to the coastal river.”

Zee raised an eyebrow.

“That sounds suspiciously like friendship.”

“It is administration.”

“Of course.”

She looked at Ner.

“And I want you to visit.”

Ner nodded.

“I will.”

Then at Zee.

“You too.”

“I just went.”

“Six months ago.”

“Recently.”

“No.”

Zee sighed.

Nymeris stepped toward the water.

Then paused.

“Zee.”

His expression changed.

She rarely used his name without sarcasm.

“What?”

“If Darkheart is attacked beneath the coastline, send for me.”

He stared.

Nymeris continued.

“If Nhalaris is attacked near the surface, I will send for you.”

Not treaty language.

More personal.

Trust.

Zee nodded once.

“Done.”

She entered the river.

Then looked back.

“And fix your drainage.”

Zee’s face hardened.

“I knew you ruined the moment on purpose.”

Nymeris smiled.

Then vanished beneath the water.

Ner stood beside him.

“You love her.”

Zee looked at him sharply.

“Not like that.”

“I know.”

Zee looked back toward the river.

Chosen family had never needed one shape.

Aurelia had taught him that blood mattered.

Rez had taught him blood was not required.

Zareth had taught him connection could begin before language.

Ner had taught him love could survive change.

Nymeris was teaching him something else.

Two rulers could become family without either surrendering a crown.

And somewhere in the months ahead, that friendship would continue growing.

Not toward prophecy.

Not toward destiny.

Toward choices neither of them had made yet.

For now, that was enough.

# Chapter One Hundred

## The Year the Sea Came Ashore

Zee turned twenty-five while standing knee-deep in seawater that should not have existed.

Darkheart was forty miles inland.

That made the situation irritating.

Nymeris found it worse.

She stood in the flooded market of Southhold with water curling around her boots.

“This is not mine.”

Zee looked at the water.

“It came from your direction.”

“The ocean is not one enormous bucket I personally manage.”

“That sounds irresponsible.”

Nymeris stared at him.

Ner laughed behind them.

“You two have known each other too long.”

It had been more than a year since Zee killed Kharos.

Long enough that Nymeris no longer arrived at Darkheart as a foreign Queen.

She still arrived with guards.

Still carried Nhalaris authority.

Still argued with Zee before most meals.

But Southhold knew her.

Darkheart children recognized her.

Nhalaris had begun recognizing Zee too.

Not all of them liked him.

That was fine.

Zee liked very few councils himself.

---

The flood came from beneath the earth.

Tessa discovered the first body.

Not drowned.

Drained.

A Vampire woman lay beside an underground spring with every drop of blood gone.

No bite marks.

No wounds.

Kael crouched beside her.

“What does that?”

Ner touched the water.

His Bloodsong recoiled.

“Something beneath us.”

Nymeris knelt immediately.

Her expression changed.

“What?”

Zee asked.

She looked toward the flooded street.

“Abyssal current.”

“You said it was not yours.”

“It is not.”

“Convenient.”

Nymeris ignored him.

“There are currents beneath the world older than Nhalaris.”

That got Zee’s attention.

“How old?”

“Old enough that my people built around some instead of disturbing them.”

Amara arrived from the northern road.

“Tracks.”

“What kind?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing I know.”

Good.

Zee smiled.

Nymeris noticed.

“Why are you happy?”

“New monster.”

“You have terrible instincts.”

“Usually effective.”

---

The thing emerged after sunset.

It came through the flooded well.

Long.

Pale.

Almost transparent.

No eyes.

Too many joints.

Its mouth opened across its chest.

Three Darkheart soldiers attacked first.

One died before Zee reached them.

The creature touched him.

His blood left his body through unbroken skin.

Tessa shouted:

“Do not let it touch you!”

Zee was already moving.

The creature struck.

He caught one limb.

Instant mistake.

Blood pulled toward his skin.

Vampire instinct screamed.

Crimson biology resisted.

His veins darkened.

He tore free.

“Annoying.”

Nymeris raised both hands.

Water slammed the creature against stone.

It twisted inside the pressure.

Not swimming.

Using water like flesh.

Nymeris’s eyes narrowed.

“It belongs to the Deep Below.”

Zee looked at her.

“That sounds dramatic.”

“It is trying to drink your kingdom.”

“Fair.”

The creature lunged.

Zee disappeared beneath it.

Vampire speed.

Claws opened its underside.

No blood.

Only black fluid.

Amara attacked from the flank in Wolf form.

Kael bound two limbs with Witchcraft.

Ner hit the creature with Bloodsong.

Nothing.

He frowned.

“No heartbeat.”

Tessa shouted from behind a shield line:

“Then stop trying to talk to it!”

Ner glared.

“I was not talking.”

“You were singing.”

“Different.”

The creature broke Kael’s chains.

Nymeris’s water caught it again.

Zee understood.

“Hold the upper half.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“Why?”

“Because I want the lower half.”

“That sentence was horrifying.”

“Hold it.”

She did.

Zee moved.

Silent Witchcraft compressed the stone beneath the creature.

Wolf instinct tracked every joint.

Dragon force entered his arms.

He caught two limbs.

Pulled.

The creature screamed.

Not from a mouth.

From the water.

Nymeris flinched.

“There.”

Zee saw it.

A black organ beneath the translucent body.

Not heart.

Anchor.

He drove his hand through the creature.

Closed his fist.

“Break.”

The anchor ruptured.

The thing collapsed.

Water hit the street all at once.

Zee stood dripping.

Nymeris stared at him.

“You put your hand inside it.”

“Yes.”

“Without knowing what it was.”

“Yes.”

Thirty-one injured.

Two streets destroyed.

Queen.

Ruler.

Nymeris kept staring.

The enemy commander looked confused.

Her judgment.

No ceremony.

Not lover.

Not subordinate.

Family.
